meta.source: Meeting video transcripts (ASR, un-diarized); member attribution is name-based with per-position confidence.

cases.name: Local Law — Short-Term Rental Regulations

timeline.summary: Following up on the RELIP recreation-use amendment, the planning department presented a draft local law requiring a special use permit (with town-board-reviewed standards on traffic intensity by road classification, buffering, setbacks for outdoor facilities, and a discretionary catch-all) for new recreation centers across the CB, RB, GB, PLI and RELIP zoning districts. The board declared lead agency, referred the draft to the planning boards and interested agencies, and scheduled a public hearing for March 9. Councilman Berra pressed for more specificity on traffic-impact triggers, buffer/setback adequacy near residential lots (citing tennis-court noise), and possible square-footage limits, while Councilman Milim cautioned against an overly broad discretionary clause that could unduly deter desirable projects; Supervisor Schiliro noted the town's parking formula already constrains oversized facilities.

Following a brief, uncontested public hearing, the board adopted a local law amending the town's alternative veterans tax exemption levels (covering roughly 175 North Castle veterans across service, combat, and disability categories), consistent with a county-level recommendation.

The board closed the public hearing and adopted the recreation-center special use permit local law after extensive line-item drafting review with the planning director. Key changes: excluding BMX and skateboard parks entirely from the permitted-use definition (requiring a future zone text amendment rather than just a special use permit for either), keeping swimming pools in the definition despite a debate over whether a private pool could undercut the town's planned acquisition of its municipal pool, removing 'franchise sports'/limiting to seating capacity language to exclude stadium-scale spectator venues, adding instructional-class language (yoga, Pilates, etc. generically rather than by name), and rejecting a proposed 25,000-40,000 sq ft size cap in favor of relying on existing zoning constraints (parking formula, floor-area ratio, setbacks).

After closing the public hearing, the Board adopted (via SEQRA negative declaration/neg-dec and a unanimous vote) the local law permitting level 1 and level 2 electric-vehicle charging stations as an accessory use in business, office and industrial districts, continuing the more conservative, incremental approach discussed at the prior meeting. No further amendment to allow level 3 fast chargers was made at this hearing.

Public hearing on a local law amending the code to require four LPC meetings per year (matching the state minimum) instead of six, while allowing additional meetings as needed. A parallel idea discussed in executive session — increasing LPC membership beyond the current 8 of 9 seats to absorb two interested applicants — was not included in the noticed law, so Roland advised adopting this amendment now and running a separate local law on membership later. The board closed the hearing and adopted the amended local law by voice vote (no roll call).

The board received the Assessor's memo recommending a local law to update the senior-citizen and disability tax-exemption income formula: raising the qualifying threshold (roughly from the mid-$30,000s to ~$58,000, about a 40% increase) and electing not to deduct IRA distributions from income. The change is expected to roughly double eligible residents (from ~30-35 to ~60). Members favored the Assessor's recommendation; Berra also asked her to report the cost borne by other taxpayers. Item received and a public hearing set for the February 14 meeting.

Public hearing on a local law (originally titled to 'prohibit' BESS, corrected to a definitional amendment clarifying that a battery energy storage system is not a 'public utility'), aimed at closing a loophole after a Mount Kisco case argued BESS qualifies as a public utility substation. Attorney Doug Worden, for Catalyze Energy, urged the board instead to adopt a durationally reasonable moratorium and develop a BESS code, citing a June 2024 PSC order targeting 6 GW of storage statewide and ESRG (the town's own engineer) approval of technologies like the Tesla Megapack 2. The board and town attorney Roland Barone rejected the need for a moratorium (the use is already not permitted) but cited volunteer-fire-service and water-supply safety fears; extended discussion also covered not inadvertently restricting normal residential EV/battery uses. The board closed the hearing but deferred the vote to a future meeting to correct the local law, neg-dec and notice documents; a confirmatory motion received the county Planning Board, town Planning Board and Snyder & Snyder letters.

The board received the draft short-term rental (STR) local law, short environmental assessment forms, and a resident email (Tan Nguyen, Dec 18, 2025), then scheduled a public hearing for January 28, 2026. Following a Zoom meeting that day with Airbnb representatives (attended by the Planner, Town Administrator and counsel), the board opted to hold the referral to the town/county planning boards until a more finalized draft exists after a follow-up Airbnb meeting, while still setting the hearing date (which may be opened and adjourned/kept open). Rende stressed the town needs a defensible law 'with teeth' to pursue offenders. A council member pressed that a standalone (non-zoning) law still requires a mandatory referral at some point.

The board received the proposed local law amending the town code definition of 'electric vehicle charging station' (Sec. 355-4) to permit level-3 charging, plus full environmental assessment forms (parts 1-3). It referred the law to the Westchester County and town planning boards and circulated to interested/involved agencies, and scheduled a public hearing for January 28, 2026 — all on voice votes. Before the item was formally stated, a council member recused himself, explaining the item originated from a request by his employer, IBM, creating an appearance of conflict; counsel recommended the recusal.

The board held a public hearing on a proposed local law creating a regulatory framework for short-term rentals, requiring a building-department permit plus an operating permit, occupancy/vehicle limits, a 120-day annual cap, noise restrictions, and a notarized affidavit or affirmation of primary residence. Town Planner Adam Kaufman summarized the draft and Attorney Roland answered questions on enforcement (police can issue violations) and affirmation forms. After public comment, the board closed the hearing, received the Planning Board memo (dated March 10), adopted a negative declaration, and adopted the local law by voice vote. Enforcement, public education, and a license-fee schedule were flagged as follow-up items.

cases.name: Gateway Residential Development (former Marianis Gardens) — Special Use Permit Extension
cases.applicant: 45 Bedford Road LLC / NCD Acquisitions LLC (Marianne Gardens)

timeline.summary: The board denied a one-year extension of the special use permit for the 43-unit Marianne Gardens redevelopment at 45 Bedford Road, first approved in 2019. Town Attorney Roland Baroni recommended denial, citing changed circumstances since approval — COVID-era traffic pattern shifts near the schools/Route 22 intersection and vacancy trends in nearby office buildings. Applicant's counsel Corey Salomon (Zarin & Steinmetz) argued there was no material change and that the ownership dispute (Mark Marianne's interest emerging from bankruptcy) had just been resolved that day, making the applicant ready to proceed. Numerous residents opposed the extension citing historic preservation (adjacent to the Bedford Road Historic District and St. Stephen's Church) and traffic/air-quality concerns near the schools; one resident (Neil Bauman) was more ambivalent, predicting the property would sit vacant regardless of the outcome. The board adopted a resolution of denial by consensus.

The applicant presented a revised plan for the 4.1-acre downtown-zoned (RMFDA) parcel, reducing the unit count from 43 to 34 rental units (townhouse and stacked-flat buildings), reorienting buildings to front Bedford Road and Maple, and proposing a modest deed-restriction modification to open up the site's center. The existing community benefits package on the table totals $1.25 million ($250K parking, $750K sewage treatment plant, $250K water infrastructure), which the applicant offered to reallocate but not necessarily increase. Multiple Board members pushed back hard: on the shift from anticipated condo taxation to rental, on building massing and height relative to the historic district, on traffic and school-age-children impacts, and on removing the deed restriction, with one member saying she would 'like to see a much different plan' that is more subtle for what she called one of the town's historic gateways.

Following a work session, the Board referred the applicant's traffic study to the town's traffic consultant for independent review, with Councilman Berra specifically asking the consultant to consider Board members' concerns (echoed by Councilman Milim) that the study's traffic count data may not fully reflect real-world conditions on Bedford Road.

The board received three letters and heard the applicant's request, prompted by a Planning Board recommendation, to use the town right-of-way along Maple Avenue to create a shallower, better-landscaped stormwater/floodplain basin, to establish an easement (with HOA-maintained plantings), and to interpret or amend a one-acre deed restriction so rear patios and fences would be permitted. Town Planner Adam Kaufman supported the aesthetic benefit and applicant-maintenance arrangement, and attorney Roland advised the board could interpret the 'structures' language or hold a public hearing to amend it. Several residents spoke in opposition, including a St. Stephen's Church warden urging deferral to the ARB and a letter from Sharon Tombach urging the board not to schedule hearings, grant easements or weaken the deed restriction. The board declined to set a public hearing, requesting overlay renderings showing the deed-restriction line and comparative basin designs, and tabled the matter to reconvene in two weeks.

The board received a letter from Veneziano & Associates and revised plans (motion to receive carried) for the 34-townhouse Gateway project, then took up four related items flowing from Planning/Conservation/ARB review: a license to use the Maple Avenue right-of-way for expanded floodplain/stormwater storage, a license to use town land behind the annex (Cornell-Birdsall House) for 2-to-1 wetland-buffer mitigation, an amendment to the community benefit agreement adding $250,000, and a proposed amendment to the town's deed restriction to allow patios and screening fences in the deed-restricted area. Town Attorney Roland advised the deed-restriction change legally requires a public hearing (the licenses and CBA do not); the board leaned toward scheduling that hearing for May 22 and discussed whether to also let the Landmarks Preservation Committee weigh in. Extensive discussion covered future Maple Avenue widening options, density, and the historic meaning of the deed restriction; no final vote on the licenses/CBA is captured in the transcript.

The applicant asked the board to amend a deed restriction (barring 'structures') on land the town conveyed, to permit seven six-foot privacy fences and eight roughly 225 sq-ft at-grade stone/paver patios on the eastern side of the 34-townhouse Gateway project — placements driven by the planning board's request to spread the units out. Town Attorney Roland explained the 1962-63 New York City deed restriction (tied to watershed/flood-control protection since rendered obsolete by the Route 22 realignment) and that the town later conveyed to Winkler intending mainly to protect the church viewshed. Residents (Julie DeFilippo of Wampus Close HOA, Ed Woodyard, and Sharon Combach by Zoom) urged denial or continuance, arguing the restriction runs with the land and can only be modified by NYC and warning against a 'camel's nose' precedent. The transcript ends mid-hearing during Combach's statement; no final vote is captured.

Request for a one-year extension of the special use permit granted June 28, 2023; the Planning Board had just granted site plan approval two nights earlier. The board approved the extension. Milim noted he had opposed the project all along but saw no basis to deny the extension and voted in favor reluctantly.

After public comment from neighboring Wampus Lake Estates residents citing an unsecured, unfinished excavation site as a safety hazard and nuisance, and from a board member (Vataj) proposing a shorter 120-day extension conditioned on immediately filling the hole and installing a proper fence, the town attorney advised that state case law entitles the vested special use permit to a full one-year renewal absent a material change in conditions. The board adopted the fourth consecutive one-year extension 4-1 (DiGiacinto opposed), with Supervisor Rende disclosing that some project principals have contributed to his campaign but stating the approval predates his tenure and he could remain impartial. The applicant's attorney denied the permit had ever lapsed and said a new, experienced developer (RMA Development/Ralph Rossi) is now driving the project forward, expecting visible progress within about 120 days and committing to level the excavation and improve fencing in the interim.

cases.name: Street Naming & Addressing — Airport Campus, 113 King Street (E-911 Referral)

trajectory.status: amended petition received; board declared intent to act as SEQRA lead agency; referred to town/county planning boards and conservation board
hearing opened and immediately re-adjourned to May 24, 2023
public hearing continued; adjourned pending formal school district input and staff preparation of negative declaration/resolution

timeline.summary: The Board received a revised Preliminary FEIS reflecting a new development alternative in which the applicant seeks a senior zoning district for the campus, with roughly 125 townhouses and conversion of one existing office building into about 52 apartments (demolishing another). Several members voiced significant reservations — about the choice of senior zoning versus other multifamily options, condo taxation status, and a 200-year-old barn slated for removal — before voting to refer the document to town professionals for review, with the Supervisor noting the school district superintendent had previously raised concerns about the tax-revenue-to-student-impact ratio of prior alternatives.

timeline.status: amended petition received; board declared intent to act as SEQRA lead agency; referred to town/county planning boards and conservation board
timeline.summary: The applicant presented an amended petition dropping the previously proposed extended-stay hotel entirely and rezoning the full 32 acres to RMF-A for 88 fee-simple townhouses (80 market-rate, 8 affordable), age-targeted (not age-restricted) with first-floor primary suites — a change from the earlier plan of a smaller age-restricted senior building plus a hotel. Board members, led by concerns about school-district cost impact from three-bedroom, non-age-restricted units (informally relayed as a Byron Hill School District concern), asked whether the applicant would consider making some units age-restricted, and debated whether the existing ~$2 million community benefits agreement (negotiated under an earlier, denser iteration of the project) should change given the reduced density and dropped hotel. The applicant maintained the $2M community benefits figure requires the requested 88-unit density to remain economically viable and firmly opposed reducing it further. The board voted to receive the amended documents, declare its intent to act as lead agency under SEQRA, and refer the application to the town and county planning boards and conservation board, while also directing that the planning boards be given the option to evaluate the original age-restricted alternative and asking staff (planner, engineer, traffic consultant) for a comparison memo on school-district impact.

The applicant presented the rezoning of a 4.4-acre parcel to RMF-SCH (age-restricted senior housing, ~50 units) and the remaining ~34+ acres to RMF-A (125 fee-simple townhouse-style units), citing a projected $3.3M in new tax revenue (about $2.25M to the school district) versus a prior approved 500,000-sq-ft office/hotel alternative, and described plans to extend public water from Old King Street with an on-site tank as the project's principal public benefit — explicitly stating no separate "community benefit" contribution was anticipated given the scale of that water investment. Hudson Riverkeeper (Mike Do Long) and the Natural Resources Defense Council (Henry Brann) asked the board to delay action, revealing that a 2006 conservation easement with Westchester Land Trust restricting development on roughly 6 acres near the Kensico Reservoir watershed had not been accounted for in the site plan, and requested 60-90 days to negotiate a resolution with the applicant before the board adopted findings. The Town Planner relayed Planning Board recommendations on density/economics balance, water infrastructure adequacy, view screening (retaining the berm), airport noise attenuation beyond code minimums, internal walking trails, and traffic. The board adjourned the hearing to April 26 without voting on the FEIS or rezoning, pending both the applicant-Riverkeeper/NRDC negotiations and Kellard Sessions' (the town's engineering consultant) review comments.

timeline.status: hearing opened and immediately re-adjourned to May 24, 2023
timeline.summary: As previewed at the prior meeting, the board briefly reconvened this hearing only to receive four items (Kellard Sessions' FEIS review memo, the Town Planner's memo on Planning Board comments, a traffic letter from Hardesty and Hanover, and a noise-analysis completeness memo from HMMH) and immediately re-adjourn to May 24, since the applicant was still negotiating with Westchester Land Trust and with Riverkeeper/NRDC over the conservation-easement conflict raised at the prior meeting and expected any resulting site-plan changes to require FEIS revisions.

timeline.status: public hearing continued; adjourned pending formal school district input and staff preparation of negative declaration/resolution
timeline.summary: The board held a public hearing on rezoning both remaining Eagle Ridge parcels (the office-business-hotel parcel and the RMF-SCH senior parcel) entirely to RMF-A for an 88-unit, three-bedroom, fee-simple, age-targeted townhouse development, replacing the previously contemplated hotel. The applicant added a new $240,000 recreation fee (at standard per-unit rates) on top of an existing roughly $2 million community benefits/mitigation package, framing it as exceeding requirements since the site already carries an IBM-era park-dedication covenant. Board member Barbara DiGiacinto pressed for consideration of the less-dense RMF zoning classification (comparable to Whippoorwill Hills/Ridge) instead of RMF-A, challenged the applicant's density-yield math (ultimately corrected to a 130-unit maximum allowable under RMF-A, not the ~97 previously cited), and requested rainwater-harvesting/irrigation study given town water-supply strain. Extensive public comment, led by longtime resident Linda Fernberg, raised cumulative downtown traffic and on-street parking concerns spanning Eagle Ridge, the Maple Avenue "lumberyard" project (~26-28 units), and the Marianne's property (~34 units) — combining for roughly 140+ new units feeding onto Maple Avenue and Main Street, the town's only two arteries out of downtown — and asked whether a promised downtown parking study would be completed before further approvals. The hearing was adjourned without a vote pending formal written input from the Byron Hill School District superintendent and staff (Town Planner, Director of Water & Sewer) preparing a negative declaration and resolution.

As required by its August SEQRA findings and rezoning, the applicant filed a petition and map/plan/report (prepared by the town's engineer D&B) to extend Water District No. 8 by running a main up King Street over I-684 to the site, with a 300,000-gallon storage tank and pump station. Attorney Roland advised adopting the order calling a public hearing while negotiating a water-contribution agreement and referring the ~$3 million cost estimate to the Kellard firm for review. Members raised questions about inflation and cost escalation (DiGiacinto), tank sizing discrepancies and coordination with a possible future combined million-gallon tank and Water District 4 extension (Milim/Rende, with Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal). The board voted by roll call to refer the map/plan to Kellard and to adopt the order calling a public hearing for February 14, 2024 (DiGiacinto, Hussain and Supervisor Rende recorded aye).

A public hearing under Town Law was opened on a petition to extend Water District 8 to bring municipal water to the former MBIA campus (redevelopment), replacing on-site wells via a 12-inch main from New King Street over I-684 to the site, an oversized 297,000-gallon tank and pump station sized to also serve a future District 4. The applicant, building privately at 30-40% below public-bid cost, said it is not seeking action yet pending a D&B basis-of-design report (expected end of month) and a water-contribution/capital agreement. The board received the revised map, plan and report, then adjourned the hearing without a specific date, anticipating a follow-up work session.

The board received a January 13, 2025 memo from KSCJ Consulting on the assignment of new street names and addresses for the Airport Campus and referred it to the Town E-911 Coordinator. The naming committee had to revisit the plan because it had not accounted for the amenities building (senior/older housing) remaining on site. Received by voice vote.

cases.name: Ramadan Crescent Moon & Star Display at Wampus Brook Park (and Annual Display Policy)

timeline.summary: Approved a proposal from OLA Consulting Engineers for electrical engineering services on the Wampus Brook Park lighting upgrade (bid specs, bid review, construction administration), with two changes negotiated on the spot: striking a clause requiring the town to credit OLA in its publicity/signage, and flagging a 15% markup on reimbursable expenses as unusually high, to be avoided as a matter of practice in future contracts even though allowed to stand this time.

The board approved the Armonk Lions Club request to hold its annual fall folder roll at Wampus Brook Park on June 6-9, 2024, subject to receiving all required documentation. Motion, second, all in favor.

The board awarded the bid for replacement of the north bridge at Wampus Brook Park to Mega Painting and Contracting and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement. Members expressed relief that, after years of rebids at unreasonable prices, a sensible bid had finally come in. Approved by voice vote.

The August 14, 2024 bid award to Mega Painting & Contracting was rescinded because the contractor could not meet the town's stringent insurance requirements. The board debated whether to draw on the 5% bid bond or impose a penalty; the Town Attorney explained the options, and members agreed the contractor appeared to have acted in good faith and had not sought to lower requirements, so the board rescinded without penalty. The board then awarded the bid to the second-lowest bidder, JT Oranzio General Contracting, and authorized the supervisor to sign. Both actions passed by voice vote.

The board approved the Armonk Lions Club's request to hold the Fol-de-rol at Wampus Brook Park June 5-8, 2025. Councilman Milim recused himself as Lions Club president (deeming himself an interested officer under the ethics code) but, after discussion, spoke about the event in his individual capacity; the supervisor and Ethics Board chair questioned whether recusal was even required. Members praised Milim's revitalization of the club and noted the Lions' $20,000 donation to the Wampus North Bridge repair and other charitable giving. Adopted by voice vote.

The board approved a payment requisition to J.T. Oranzio for the Wampus Brook Park North Bridge replacement, with members praising the finished work. The board thanked the Lions Club, which committed $20,000 from folder-roll fundraising toward the project. Motion carried.

The board approved a resident request to install a crescent moon and star display at Wampus Brook Park to mark Ramadan (Feb 17-Mar 19, 2026), separate from the December holiday-season display of prior years. Because Ramadan shifts annually by the lunar calendar, the board established a protocol: the requester need only notify the Town Clerk in writing each year of the holiday's start and end dates by the last board meeting of the month prior, and directed Parks staff not to place this display during December. Discussion emphasized not burdening the resident with an in-person appearance each year.

cases.name: Personnel — Resignations/Retirements, Appointments, and Terminal Leave

timeline.summary: The board approved the appointment of Josephine Egan as Confidential Secretary to the Supervisor (effective January 1, 2024) and J. Carvey as Hourly Librarian (effective January 16, 2024), and accepted resignations from Susan Kramer (library, Jan 2), Kevin Mills (library, Dec 7, 2023) and Adam Woodruff (highway department, Dec 30, 2023). Members welcomed Egan warmly, with the Supervisor and colleagues expressing confidence she would be an asset to the whole board.

The board approved three personnel items by voice vote: appointing Arthur Ellis as an alternate to the Board of Ethics (5-year term to Jan 11, 2028); appointing Linda Cervich as Librarian 1 (hourly, effective Jan 29, 2024); and authorizing Finance Director Abbas to attend the 2024 NYS Government Finance Officers Association conference (April 17-19). Routine and uncontested.

Accepted the retirement resignation of Detective Sergeant Kevin Finetti (effective July 30, 2024); approved the probationary appointment of Danielle D. Thomas as Senior Office Assistant in the Building Department (effective June 13, 2024); and accepted, with regrets, the resignation of Melissa Horowitz from the Landmark Preservation Committee (effective June 23, 2024). The board noted thank-you letters are sent to departing volunteers.

The board unanimously appointed Alfonso D'Abruzio as a seasonal road maintainer in the Highway Department, effective May 19, 2025, and reappointed Adam Barnett to the Conservation Board for a two-year term expiring May 14, 2027, thanking him for his service. The consensus agenda was also approved.

The board received the resignation of Irwin Hernandez from the Water and Sewer Department (effective June 18, 2025) and of Michael Calderola from the Police Department (effective July 1, 2025), and approved court office personnel attending the 2025 NYS Association of Magistrates Court Clerks annual conference in Albany (Sept 28-Oct 1, 2025). All approved by voice vote as routine personnel items.

The board acted on four personnel items, each by motion, second, and unanimous voice vote: appointment of Jennifer Paglieli as Librarian (effective Sept. 25, 2025); acceptance 'with regret' of Mary Jacobs's resignation as hourly Library Clerk (effective Oct. 18, 2025); reappointment of Beira Bull Tata to the Architectural Review Board for a five-year term ending Sept. 30, 2030; and appointment of Eric Bell to the Library Board for a five-year term ending Dec. 31, 2030. The consensus agenda was also approved.

The board acted on several personnel matters by voice vote: accepted the retirement/resignation of Assistant Building Inspector Michael Cromwell (eff. Jan 31, 2026, with thanks for long service) and the resignation of full-time librarian Diana Wendell; made the probationary appointments of Elizabeth Esposito (part-time assistant court clerk and part-time intermediate police clerk, eff. Jan 12) and Henry Sieno (part-time fire inspector, eff. Jan 19); and approved a terminal-leave pay plan for retiring Police Chief Peter Simonson, whom Rende reported is doing well in retirement.

cases.name: Special Use Permit Extension — Additional Horses at 263 Bedford Banksville Road

timeline.summary: The applicants sought a special use permit for up to 20 horses (of 23 allowed) on a 21.62-acre parcel and asked the Board to refer the matter to the Planning Board and County Planning Board to begin site-plan review. Represented by an environmental planner and joined by neighbors (including a former town councilman) who had worked cooperatively with the applicants beforehand, the presentation emphasized pre-application neighbor outreach, screening/buffer commitments near an adjoining property, and a proposal that the special permit not automatically run with the land upon a future sale.

The Board received the County Planning Board's letter, the North Castle Planning Board's recommendation, and the Planning Board's declaration of intent to act as lead agency, continuing the referral process begun the prior meeting.

The Board received supporting materials and scheduled a September 13, 2023 public hearing on a special use permit application to keep additional horses at 263 Bedford Banksville Road, after the applicant obtained favorable recommendations from the Conservation Board, Architectural Review Board, and Zoning Board of Appeals.

The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the resolution approving a special use permit for a horse farm on the applicant's 21-acre property, after working through final conditions (building inspector safety inspections, delivery/manure-removal hours aligned with the noise ordinance, manure storage limits, and a requirement that future owners seek amendment for any operational changes). Neighbors and the applicant's team were highly complimentary of each other; multiple board members and residents praised the collaborative process and the low-impact, conservation-minded design preserving most of the property.

Counsel requested a first extension of a special permit (originally granted September 13, 2023) for additional horses as a personal accessory equestrian use, after delays obtaining Westchester County Health Department approvals. Nothing about the application had changed. The board found it straightforward and adopted the extension resolution by voice vote.

The board received a letter and adopted a resolution granting a one-year extension of a special use permit for additional horses, given ongoing construction of equestrian buildings and a new residence that will not be completed by the 9/13/2025 expiration. The applicant's attorney reported construction is proceeding smoothly with no issues. Received and extension granted to September 13, 2026 by unanimous voice vote.

cases.name: Special Permit — Troy's Nursery Garden Design LLC (Easter Event & Fall Festival)

timeline.summary: The board received a special event permit application from Troy's Nursery / Garden Design LLC for an Easter event on April 24, 2024 at 97 Bedford Banksville Road, and scheduled a public hearing for March 20, 2024 by voice vote. A council member flagged that the application stated no parking arrangements had been made, to be resolved at the hearing along with police-department requirements and insurance certificates.

The board opened and closed a public hearing on a special event permit for an Easter event on April 24, 2024, with no public opposition and no applicant representative present. The board received recommendations from police, fire district, and the building inspector, adopted a negative declaration, and approved the permit resolution unanimously.
The board received a special event permit application for an October 6, 2024 fall festival (petting zoo, face painting, pumpkin painting, music) and scheduled a public hearing for September 25, 2024.

Public hearing on a special-event permit for a fall festival (pumpkin/face painting, petting zoo, possible band) on October 6th. The board opened the hearing, read correspondence, adopted a negative declaration, and adopted the approving resolution, all by unanimous voice vote. Applicant Maria Cece asked whether repeat events could avoid the recurring permit process; the board and Town Planner Adam Kaufman explained a blanket approval covering multiple pre-dated events for the year could be possible.

A single consolidated special-event permit was sought for an Easter event (April 13, 2025) and two fall festivals (October 5 and 12, 2025), streamlining the applicant's prior year-by-year filings. The board opened the hearing, received PD/fire district/building inspector recommendations, heard the applicant and complimentary board comments, adopted the neg dec and the resolution, and closed the hearing. The board discussed possibly enacting a future local law to allow low-impact, repeat on-premises events with only building-inspector/PD/fire sign-off; special counsel noted that would require a town-code change and could not be done now.

The board received and approved a special-permit application from Troy's Nursery for an Easter event (March 29, 2026) and a fall festival (Sundays in October 2026). Under the town's new streamlined policy, such applications are pre-reviewed by staff so applicants no longer need individual public hearings, which the board praised as a customer-friendly improvement.

cases.name: Declaration of Restrictive Covenants — 12 AFFH Units, Airport Campus Development

timeline.summary: The Board reconvened its public hearing on rezoning the former MBIA office campus to multi-family senior housing districts, receiving the Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) and a letter from the North Castle Historical Society urging preservation of the historic 1820s Weber farmhouse on site. The applicant reported progress on relocating a needed water storage tank to the adjacent Greco parcel (benefiting both the project and the town's broader water district needs) and on resolving objections from NRDC and Riverkeeper. The board pressed the applicant on options and cost for relocating the historic farmhouse (roughly $200,000 based on comparable moves) rather than demolishing it, and on getting formal fire department feedback given the scale of development. The applicant hoped to close the hearing and obtain a findings statement/rezoning decision at the August meeting.

The applicant and town consultants worked through remaining FEIS completeness issues (road geometry, stormwater basin siting near unit backyards, unit bedroom-count/density tradeoffs between the RMFA and RMF zones, fire department comments, and traffic study updates related to the Cooney Hill driveway), with the town planner and traffic consultant indicating no objection to deeming the FEIS complete pending final NRDC/Riverkeeper conservation-easement resolution and Armonk Fire Department comments expected before the next meeting.

The applicant reported an agreement in principle with NRDC and Riverkeeper covering an expanded 9+ acre conservation easement, phosphorus-loading reduction (from roughly 50% to over 80% removal) to protect the Kensico Reservoir watershed, and ongoing stormwater reporting, while preserving a disagreement over whether an existing easement is legally revocable. The board debated Armonk Fire Department concerns (lack of a ladder truck, cumulative impact of several pending town projects) and whether to hold the applicant to a specific age-targeted vs. age-restricted unit-mix percentage similar to the Eagle Ridge project, ultimately treating this site as distinguishable given its dedicated 55+ apartment building and location. The board also pressed on sidewalk connectivity to the Route 120 bus stop. The FEIS was moved toward completeness, setting up a findings statement and rezoning vote.

After roughly eight years of the property sitting vacant and multiple years of public process, the Board closed the public hearing and adopted both the SEQRA findings statement and a resolution rezoning the former MBIA office campus for 50 age-restricted rental apartments and 125 age-targeted, fee-simple-taxed townhomes (including affordable units). The central negotiated issue was a covenant requiring that 50% of the market-rate (non-affordable) townhomes include a first-floor primary bedroom, reached after extended back-and-forth between the board and Toll Brothers over percentages ranging from 25% to 60%. The board also addressed airport-noise disclosure requirements in offering plans and rental/sale agreements, fire department sprinkler assurances, and declined to require site-wide sidewalks, leaving that to the Planning Board site plan process. Public comment included a resident (Bob Okan) and a longtime resident (Julie) expressing concern about the pace and scale of recent development in Armonk.

The board approved receipt of a declaration of restrictive covenants regarding the 12 Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing (AFFH) units at the Airport Campus development and authorized the supervisor to sign the agreement and county reporting forms. Staff explained this is now a standard county requirement that the local municipality co-sign. Adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Personnel Actions — Parks & Recreation Appointments, Librarian Resignation, Library Board Appointment

timeline.summary: The board approved a slate of personnel items by successive voice votes: probationary appointment of Thomas Farrington as skilled laborer in Water & Sewer (eff. March 31, 2025); salary adjustments for Library Director Kathryn Feely and Assistant Library Director Angela Cook (eff. Jan 1, 2025); terminal leave payments for William Gallagher (Water & Sewer) and Angel Morales (Police); and authorization for Patrick Ritchie to attend a NYS tax receivers/collectors training in Lake George (June 8-11, 2025). The consensus agenda was then approved.

The board approved three personnel actions by voice vote: the probationary appointment of William Etzel as Librarian 1 at the North Castle Public Library (eff. March 16, 2026), the probationary appointment of Jeffrey (Highway Department, eff. March 16, 2026), and a terminal-leave payment to Michael Cromwell of the Building Department. A consensus agenda was also approved.

The board approved a probationary appointment of Dylan Ruckstuhl to Recreation Supervisor effective May 26, 2026, after confirming in response to a member's question that the position was a previously vacant one rather than newly created. The board also accepted, with good wishes, the resignation of Parks groundskeeper Joseph Liberardi effective May 15, 2026, and reappointed Susan Gefen to the Landmark Preservation Committee for a further three-year term (the recording's stated expiration year appears to contain an ASR transcription error given the meeting date). All three items passed on motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

The board approved a series of routine personnel actions by voice vote: probationary appointment of a full-time library assistant (name rendered by ASR as Michelle Mack Dividy) effective June 1, 2026; probationary appointment of Joseph Patti as hourly library clerk effective June 11, 2026; receipt of resignation letters from Assistant Building Inspector William Seagmuller and Office Assistant Yudvan Hernandez (Building Department), both effective May 22, 2026; and appointment of Lauren Lombardi as a records digitization intern in the Town Clerk's office effective June 1, 2026, after a board member confirmed the intern had no financial relationship with the department.

The board approved the provisional appointment of a Senior Office Assistant in Recreation & Parks effective June 29, 2026 (noted as already budgeted in the 2026 budget), the probationary appointment of Ruri Corden as Parks Groundsman effective July 6, 2026, received with regret the resignation letter of lead librarian Stephanie Paul effective June 15, 2026, and appointed a new library board member to a five-year term. All items passed on individual motions, seconds, and voice votes (aye).

cases.name: Resolution Opposing NYS ADU Preemption Legislation (S.4547-A)

timeline.summary: As a late addition prompted by Governor Hochul's State of the State address, the board unanimously adopted a resolution opposing proposed state legislation (S.4547-A) that would preempt local zoning control over accessory dwelling units — barring parking requirements for ADUs within a half-mile of a bus stop, among other provisions — which board members argued would effectively eliminate single-family zoning and override home rule. The board cited North Castle's own long-standing ADU law (since 1984), middle-income housing program, and affordable-housing requirements as evidence the town already supports the state's stated housing goals responsibly, and directed that the resolution go to the Governor, Senator Harkham/Epstein, and Assemblyman Burdick, while residents were urged to write in as well.

Continuing the fight against the state ADU-preemption bill adopted as a resolution at the prior meeting, Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto reported testifying at the NYS Assembly's Westchester budget hearing (and planned to testify at the Senate hearing) about the town's long affordable-housing record, and urged the board to lobby to strip the bill's roughly $85 million in associated budget funding. Supervisor Schiliro added detail on the bill's transit-oriented-development provision — which could allow up to 25 units/acre with no parking requirement within a quarter mile of a bus stop, a major exposure for North White Plains — and called it one of the most important issues of his tenure, urging mass resident mobilization (letters to Senator Mayer, Senator-elect Harkham, and Assemblyman Burdick).

The board devoted extensive time to the ADU/transit-oriented-development (TOD) provisions embedded in the Governor's budget (S.8006, parts AA and EE), with Supervisor Schiliro and Director of Planning Adam Kaufmann presenting a map showing that a half-mile TOD radius around the North White Plains train station (25+ units/acre, no parking requirement) would reach deep into existing residential neighborhoods on an aging road network. All board members reiterated unified, strong opposition, urging thousands of resident emails to Senator Mayer, Senator-elect Harkham, and Assemblyman Burdick before an expected end-of-March budget vote, while noting a proposed exemption for towns with existing ADU laws (like North Castle) as likely short-lived given anticipated future 'look-back' pressure to conform.

Supervisor Schiliro reported the ADU/transit-oriented-development provisions were removed from the Governor's final budget, and that state Senator Pete Harkham (a co-sponsor of the ADU bill) told him he would pull back his support, at least for 2022. The board thanked residents for the volume of emails sent to Senator Mayer and Assemblyman Burdick, crediting the response with helping demonstrate opposition, while cautioning the issue could resurface in a future legislative session.

cases.name: Ethics Code Amendment — Legal Review and Public Hearing Status

timeline.summary: The Board continued working through the Ethics Board's proposed expansion of disclosure obligations, debating procedural sequencing (local law drafting, Labor Counsel review, and public hearing timing), penalty provisions for non-compliance (town officers/employees/volunteers can be censured, suspended, or removed), and whether to narrow the town's broad definition of "relative" toward Westchester County's narrower spouse/dependent-child standard. No hearing was scheduled at this meeting; the matter was referred back for further drafting.

The Ethics Board presented its revised recommendation to amend the Code of Ethics (§27-2, §27-6E) to expand who must file an annual disclosure statement and to require more detailed disclosure of real estate and business interests, including through trusts and closely-held entities. Discussion grew heated over whether attorney-drafted language incorporating a councilman's edits had become too legalistic for lay volunteers to understand, and over a disputed characterization of the Ethics Board's vote as "unanimous" when one member had abstained. The Board voted unanimously to schedule a public hearing for October 26, 2022, while several members said they still favored simpler, earlier draft language.

After further work on the definition of "interest," the disclosure statement, and disclosure exemptions, the Board closed the public hearing and formally adopted the local law amending Chapter 27 (Code of Ethics) §27-2 and §27-6E, concluding a multi-meeting process that began in October with significant board disagreement over language complexity and disclosure scope.

Raised under liaison updates, the board discussed the stalled ethics-code amendment proposed by the Ethics Board, on which special counsel had opined a portion was legally invalid/overreaching. Because a substantive change requires re-drafting and a new public hearing (with the existing hearing to be closed), the board set a deadline for members to submit comments to counsel by the August 13 meeting and agreed to take it up in executive session then. DiGiacinto objected that airing the matter under a liaison update, tied to an executive-session request not on the agenda, was 'not fair.' No vote taken; direction only.

cases.name: 901 North Broadway — Church Special Use Permit & Site Plan

timeline.summary: The Board received a revised architect's letter and Planning Board recommendation on the church's proposed house-of-worship use in an existing office building, but the Director of Planning flagged unresolved items — a needed off-street parking variance, an unauthorized use of the site by an adjacent gas station's vehicles, and a required breakdown of all uses/square footage throughout the building — that must be resolved before further action; a communication breakdown between the applicant's architect and the town was also aired.

The Board received a letter from the Director of Planning on the church's special use permit and site plan application and referred the building/lot coverage variance to the Zoning Board of Appeals and the special use permit application to the Westchester County Planning Board, since the existing building exceeds code maximums for building and lot coverage. The Board scheduled its own public hearing on the special use permit for January 25, 2023, to follow the ZBA and county reviews.

The Board reopened and then adjourned the public hearing on the church's special use permit. A nearby property owner, Zachary Goldstein, who is mid-construction on a new fine-dining restaurant with accessory brewing at an adjacent site, raised concern that the State Liquor Authority's 200-foot rule (measuring distance to a church) could block his pending liquor license if the church is approved first. The Board directed him to consult a liquor-license attorney and have that attorney correspond with the Town Attorney, noting the Board may be able to grant a waiver, and did not resolve the conflict at this meeting.

The Board closed the public hearing and approved the special use permit for the church, following a positive Planning Board recommendation. The Town Attorney confirmed via correspondence with the neighboring restaurant's liquor-license counsel that the State Liquor Authority's 200-foot rule would not be a problem because the building is multi-tenant, resolving the conflict flagged at the January 25th meeting.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge (3 North Castle Drive) — Declaration of Covenants and stormwater easement/maintenance agreement
cases.applicant: Mayfair-Don Armonk / Zarin & Steinmetz (Cory Salomon) with Meyer Jabara Hotels

timeline.summary: The applicant requested to amend the previously adopted environmental findings statement (3 stories / 115 keys / ~72,800 sq ft) to a 4-story, 124-key, ~82,000-sq-ft Home2 Suites-brand hotel, explaining the additional story reflects amenity space (meeting room, fitness center, pool) required by the hotel brand rather than a height increase — the building remains at the zoning-compliant 45-foot height, with a smaller footprint devoted to more ground-floor amenities. A member of the public strongly opposed the fourth story, arguing it would visually read as much taller given the site's elevated bluff. Supervisor Schiliro recused himself due to his employment at adjacent IBM; the Board received the materials without voting, directing staff to prepare a resolution for a future meeting.

The Board adopted an amended SEQRA findings statement allowing the proposed Eagle Ridge hotel to be built as four stories (rather than three) within the same 45-foot code height limit, after the applicant obtained a ZBA variance permitting the additional story. Councilman Berra pressed at length for language guaranteeing the building's visible ('tape measure') height would not increase, but the Town Attorney advised that could not be added without effectively amending the zoning code outside the required process; Berra ultimately did not press for a roll call and the amendment passed.

A package of documents for a school-bus easement/dedication over an IBM-owned private road (to allow Byram Hills buses into the Eagle Ridge subdivision) plus a related utility easement. The board received one letter but tabled items 2-5 (motion to table passed unanimously) because of unresolved issues: an incorrect IBM corporate name, typos, an over-broad indemnity, questions about the town plowing scope and the map's hash-marked area extending to the security gate, and Councilman Berra's lost markup. Counsel and members will circulate corrections (edits due by close of business Tuesday) before it returns to a future agenda.

The board received a November 6, 2024 letter from Zarin & Steinmetz regarding Eagle Ridge and authorized the supervisor to sign the Declaration of Covenants and Restrictions and the Stormwater Control Facility Easement and Maintenance Agreement. Councilman Berra questioned whether the easement (town right to inspect and default obligation to perform maintenance) imposed liability on the town; the Town Attorney explained roughly 30 such DEC-designed agreements exist, the town is the default performer and charges back the HOA, with no undue liability. Rende reacted with mild impatience to the questions. Receipt and signature authorization both passed by voice vote (one board member recused).

cases.name: 14 Middle Patent Road — Special Use Permit

timeline.summary: The Board received the application materials, discussed SEQRA lead-agency coordination with the Planning Board, and referred the matter to town and county planning boards and scheduled a September 13, 2023 public hearing. The 42-acre parcel already had a 2008 special permit for 10 horses (since lapsed from non-use); the applicant sought to expand to 26 non-commercial, owner-occupied show/competition horses that would not all be on-site simultaneously (many spending winters in Florida), with a new barn addition and equine management plan.

The public hearing opened but was adjourned to October 11, 2023, at the applicant's request, to allow the Conservation Board (which had not met in August or September) time to weigh in on a mitigation/bonding and license-agreement issue tied to construction work extending into a conservation easement area, similar to a separate matter (the Levine project) the applicant's team was also handling.

The Board reconvened the previously opened special use permit hearing, received a letter from Dan Hylis requesting an adjournment, and adjourned the hearing to the November 29, 2023 meeting without substantive discussion.

The Board approved a special use permit expanding an existing private, non-commercial equestrian facility to 26 horse stalls on 41.62 acres for a family competing at the Olympic/professional level, following favorable recommendations from the ARB, Conservation Board, and Planning Board and a resident open house the applicant's team described as well received. At a board member's request, the resolution's language was tightened to flatly prohibit any horse shows (rather than only 'for-profit' shows) to close a potential future loophole, and manure/delivery truck traffic was restricted to weekday daytime hours.

cases.name: Extension of Special Use Permit — St. Nersess Armenian Seminary, 486 Bedford Road

trajectory.status: lead agency declared; public hearing scheduled (January 24, 2024)

timeline.status: lead agency declared; public hearing scheduled (January 24, 2024)
timeline.summary: St. Nersis Armenian Seminary sought a special use permit and an associated 50-foot side-yard setback variance for a new house (a future dean's residence) and a two-room guest-speaker addition to its married-student housing building, which sits roughly 30-33 feet from a residential property line (backing onto homes on Tripp Lane). The Board declared itself lead agency, asked for a clearer aerial view of the distance to adjoining residential properties before the hearing, and referred the matter to the Zoning Board of Appeals for the variance, scheduling the public hearing for January 24, 2024.

The Board closed the public hearing and approved St. Nersis Armenian Seminary's special use permit for a two-room addition (guest accommodations, no kitchen) to its married-students building and a new two-bedroom single-family residence for a future dean, both roughly 280 feet from the nearest Tripp Lane residence and requiring a side-yard setback variance (30 feet actual vs. 50 feet required) to be sought separately from the ZBA. The applicant committed to shielded, dimming parking-lot lighting and screening at the front of the property in response to a neighbor's written concern, and the Planning Board had already recommended approval.

Public hearing on a special use permit to modify the 5.5-acre R-2A seminary campus with a two-room/two-story guest addition to the married-students building and a new two-bedroom single-family dean's residence. Coverage remains well under limits (7% building, 15.5% land); a 30-foot side-yard setback requires a variance, and Planning Board, ARB and neighbor screening/lighting concerns were noted for follow-up. Residents (Historical Society) spoke in strong support, praising the seminary as gracious neighbors. The board closed the hearing and adopted the negative declaration and the resolution by voice vote (5-0).

The board received a letter and adopted a resolution granting a one-year extension of a special use permit for building modifications at the St. Nersess Armenian Seminary, giving the applicant additional time to address conditions of approval. No applicant appeared (a routine extension); passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Public Comment — Tributes to Tony Futia

timeline.summary: Resident Ed Loberman detailed New York's new credit-card surcharge law (Gen. Business Law Art. 29-A §518, effective Feb 11, 2024), which allows municipalities/town attorneys to enforce penalties, and urged the town to take up enforcement locally rather than defer to the county. Rende responded that the enforcement 'onus' concerned him given the town's limited staff and suggested complaints route to the county Department of Consumer Affairs, while noting the law limits vendors to passing through their actual processing fees. Loberman pushed back that local enforcement is the law's intent. No action taken; matter to be reviewed with counsel.

Resident Tony Voutier (89) used the public comment period to describe his 25-year effort challenging the federal income tax and his correspondence with Donald Trump, unrelated to town business. The board took no action; Supervisor Rende thanked him, and Town Attorney Roland cautioned the public not to rely on tax advice given in the room without consulting a tax professional.

During public comment and community announcements, residents raised several matters. Ed Loberman urged the board to restore the public speaking time limit from three minutes to five and to allow public comment on all agenda items in person (not just via Zoom or at public hearings). Ed Woodyard updated on the 250th-anniversary documentary screenings and historic-site preservation efforts (Sands Mill, Miller Hill), prompting Rende to float purchasing a replica cannon for the Miller Hill battlefield. The town-wide cleanup (April 26, 9 a.m.–1 p.m.) was promoted by sustainability liaison Jose Berra. No formal action taken.

During public comment several residents (Mike Shaliro of 14 Orchard Drive and a longtime resident/judge) offered tributes to the late Tony Futia, a passionate civic gadfly and former water superintendent who died in April, recalling his ward-vote petition, his primary runs, and his dedication to the town despite frequent disagreements. Supervisor Rende and Councilwoman DiGiacinto responded warmly with their own recollections. No action taken.

cases.name: North Castle Community Park Turf Field — Certificate of Final Completion and Payment Requisition No. 2 (Shaw Sports Turf)
cases.applicant: Friends of North Castle Public Library

timeline.summary: The board approved the Friends of North Castle Public Library's request to use Community Park (access road and parking) for the September 28-29, 2024 Armonk Outdoor Art Show, including an alcohol permit and waivers of the alcohol and tent permit fees. Outgoing show director Nicole Blau recapped a weather-disrupted but successful 2023 show that netted $115,000 for the library and introduced incoming director Nancy Razzner.

The board authorized Parks and Recreation Superintendent Matt Trainer to go out to bid for replacement of the deteriorating wooden Wampus Brook North Bridge, after a resident/board member (Norma Hill) warned of a fall/liability risk from the worn planking. Motion to bid passed unanimously.

The board approved the Friends of the Library's request to use North Castle Community Park (including access road and parking) for the annual Armonk Outdoor Art Show on September 26-27, 2026, together with an alcohol permit and waivers of the permit fee and tent permit fee, on a voice vote.

The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a certificate of final completion for the turf field installation (completed May 1) and approved payment requisition No. 2 to the contractor, with a contractual retainage and one-year bond still held by the contractor. Board members praised the finished field and the cooperative-purchasing approach used to select the contractor, noting the same contractor and process would likely be used for the pickleball courts.

cases.name: Reappointment — George Tropeau to the Conservation Board (term to March 11, 2028)

timeline.summary: The board reappointed Vincent Giordano to the Conservation Board for a two-year term expiring October 9, 2026, with members commending his service. Approved by voice vote.
The board reappointed Diane Borgia to the Library Board for a five-year term expiring December 31, 2029. Motion made and seconded, adopted by voice vote.

The board reappointed Craig Benedict to the Conservation Board for a two-year term ending April 23, 2027. Members described him as an experienced and important member of the board. Adopted on a voice vote.
The board reappointed George Tropeau to the Conservation Board for a two-year term expiring March 11, 2028. The motion was made 'with appreciation and thanks,' seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Resolution — Receipt of Voluntary Animal Shelter Contributions (Agriculture & Markets Law §109)

timeline.summary: The board adopted a resolution authorizing the Town Court to apply for a Justice Court Assistance Program grant in the 2024-2025 cycle for up to $30,000, primarily to scan and preserve criminal case files the court is required by law to retain (some dating to the 1800s). Rende praised the court staff for identifying the opportunity and asked the administrator to have the town's grant writer keep pursuing similar grants. Adopted by voice vote.

The board adopted a resolution requesting North Castle be officially included in the federal Highlands boundary (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service) to qualify for Highlands Conservation Act grant funding and technical assistance. Members raised concerns about whether joining could bind the town to federal environmental regulations, but Attorney Roland and materials from Kerry Kasak clarified that merely joining imposes no obligation and only enables the town to apply for grants (with any accepted grant to be reviewed closely for conditions). Adopted by voice vote.

The board adopted a resolution authorizing a New York State Archives Local Government Records Management Improvement Fund grant application for the conservation of historical records in an amount not to exceed $75,000, and authorized the supervisor to sign the application. Moved, seconded, all in favor.

The board adopted a resolution regarding receipt of voluntary animal shelter contributions pursuant to New York State Agriculture and Markets Law Section 109. One member called it 'a great idea'; the item passed on motion, second, and voice vote (aye) without further discussion.

cases.name: Receipt of Ferrari Companies Petition to Rezone 333 Main Street for Residential Use

timeline.summary: Supervisor Rende gave a lengthy explanation of exploring the purchase of 333 Main Street (the 'Boys/Du Bois Schiller' building) to consolidate town hall, police, court and staff under one roof, citing 2007 strategic-plan findings, ADA/code and egress deficiencies, sewage backups in the police locker room, and 30-year 'temporary' water/sewer trailers; the building owner proposed a 'friendly eminent domain' process, an appraisal and bond counsel are engaged. The board voted to authorize the supervisor to sign an Arconnex agreement for a test-fit/feasibility study, which staff said mainly pays for work already done. Town Historian Sharon Tombach objected the property sits in Landmarks Preservation District No. 1 and the two-page agreement read like an open-ended 'blank check'; the board pointed to its stated scope and hourly rates. It passed 4-1 by roll call (Milim, Berra, Hussain, Rende aye; DiGiacinto no, calling it premature). The board also adopted a companion bond-counsel resolution allowing all professional fees from that date forward to be captured into any future financing.

The board received a SEQR short-form EAF Part 1 and the appraisal (BS F&F LLC / Mike Ferrari, dated Nov. 18, 2024) and adopted an order calling a public hearing on February 12, 2025 for the friendly eminent-domain acquisition of 333 Main Street to house all town offices, the police department, and the water/sewer staff currently in 30-year-old trailers. Supervisor Rende laid out the deficiencies (cited since a 2007 study) — flooding police locker rooms, inadequate holding cells, ADA non-compliance, an unsafe farmhouse annex — and urged an outright referendum from the start rather than the minimum permissive referendum. Members broadly supported pursuing the opportunity but urged cost scrutiny, at least two public hearings, a parallel study of the existing town-hall campus, and aggressive public outreach. Special counsel Bob Spolzino explained why condemnation benefits the town (it brackets/forces the negotiation and forecloses competing buyers).

The 333 Main Street property (the Boyes law-firm building, owned in part by presenter Michael Ferrari) had been targeted a year earlier by the town for possible eminent-domain acquisition as a new town hall, drawing opposition; Ferrari included it in his RFEI concept as a conversion to ~40 residential units and disclosed he is separately filing a rezoning petition (to be completed the next day) to change it from commercial to residential, independent of any town-hall decision. Board members clarified this is a separate matter a future town board would decide, and that a private rezoning is not protected by permissive referendum — the board can grant or deny it. Whippoorwill Hills residents (a 150-home HOA adjacent via Log Cabin Way) voiced concern about traffic, construction disruption, and sightlines. No action was taken; the petition was not yet before the board.

The board voted only to RECEIVE (not consider or refer) a petition from Ferrari Companies to rezone 333 Main Street to permit residential use, after special counsel Bob Spolzino distinguished the ministerial act of receiving from the discretionary act of considering. The receipt passed on a roll call (DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Rende aye; Berra abstained). Milim, who is leaving the board, opined that the rezoning does not fit the comprehensive plan given already-approved units (Airport Campus 175, Mariani 34, Lumberyard 20, Summit Club). Berra's abstention triggered a sharp exchange with Rende over whether a member may abstain without stating a reason under Robert's Rules.

cases.name: Resignation — Judy Kitt from Open Space Committee

timeline.summary: The board accepted the resignation of Mitzy Weissman from the Beautification Committee, effective January 13. Councilwoman DiGiacinto praised her contributions as a master gardener and environmentalist and her family's long town history. Accepted by voice vote with appreciation for her service.

The board received the resignation of Planning Board member Jim Jensen, effective March 27, 2025, after 11 years of service. DiGiacinto read Jensen's stated reason — that the town bypassed site-plan review for the IBM community park (turf-field) project, which he viewed as an ethical issue — triggering a heated exchange over whether the project was handled properly. Rende and Milim defended the process (engineer and DEC review, no shortcuts) and argued the Planning Board review was not required, while DiGiacinto maintained a public hearing/planning review should have occurred; Berra, the Planning/Conservation liaison, had not objected to skipping review. The board voted to accept the resignation with thanks. Motion carried.

The board accepted a letter of resignation from Austin Farkas of the building maintenance department, effective April 11, 2025. Members praised him as an exceptional employee in the newly formed maintenance department who left for the private sector, and noted resumes for a replacement are already coming in. Adopted on a voice vote.
The board accepted, with regret, Judy Kitt's letter of resignation from the Open Space Committee effective July 22, 2025, noting she had been a good member. Motion carried.

cases.name: New Street Address Assignment — 100 Business Park Drive Condominium Units

timeline.summary: The Board received the Planning Board's declaration of intent to act as lead agency for SEQRA review of a proposed 146,650-square-foot self-storage warehouse building, with no objection — members agreed the Planning Board was well suited to handle it.

Received the KSCJ Consulting recommendation to establish a new wetland mitigation bond followed by a five-year monitoring/maintenance bond, and (per a June 5, 2024 letter) authorized the Supervisor to sign the wetland mitigation planting, maintenance and monitoring bond agreement with WMG Armonk Warehouse Owner LLC. Approved routinely.

The board received a KSCJ Consulting memo on assigning new street addresses to base-space commercial condominium units, changing 100 Business Park Drive to 100, 112, 114 and 116 Business Park Drive, and referred the matter to the town E-911 coordinator by unanimous voice vote.

cases.name: Summit Club at Armonk (former Brynwood) — SPDES Permit and Paper Sewer District
cases.address: Summit Club at Armonk (formerly Bonnie Briar/Brynwood)

timeline.summary: The Board received materials on amendments to the temporary special use permit for the golf course (including a proposed maintenance building and continued public access during residential construction) and a request to consider a new permanent special use permit for the club, including public (non-member) access. The Board referred the conservation easement to the Open Space Committee and referred the new SUP application to the Planning Board and County Planning Board, while noting the temporary permit would not lapse because an extension had been timely requested.

With its prior temporary special use permit having lapsed at year-end, the applicant requested and received a six-month extension (to June 30, 2023) to keep offering golf to members this season, while the Board scheduled a combined March 22 public hearing on three related items: converting to a permanent special use permit (including a relocated maintenance/storage building), a local law temporarily allowing paid public (non-member) golf access during construction of the 73 residential units, and a waiver/reduction of parkland recreation fees for market-rate units (down to $1,000 for affordable units) based on the club's extensive on-site recreation amenities, consistent with prior SEQRA findings language. The applicant also submitted the required conservation easement restricting the golf course lot to open-space/golf use if the club ever ceases operating.

The board received (by voice vote) Summit Club's draft SPDES discharge permit, permit fact sheet, and NYSDEC notice of complete application for a resized wastewater treatment plant Summit will operate. The Town Attorney explained that a transportation-corporation 'paper' sewer district petition (for ~73 homes) will come next meeting and sit dormant unless the private operator defaults, in which case the town would step in with an operating district funded by those residents. Treated as a formality/notification.

cases.name: Map Clarification — New Town Roadways and Names, Airport Campus Subdivision
cases.address: Airport Campus Subdivision (Weber Farm / Fieldstone Knoll / Cove View), North Castle
cases.applicant: Airport Campus developer (in contract with Toll Brothers; represented by Tony Beniziano)

timeline.summary: The applicant presented a reworked concept for the 38.8-acre Airport Campus site: 125 fee-simple, age-targeted (not age-restricted) townhouses on RMFA-zoned land plus roughly 50 age-restricted apartment units in the existing office building rezoned RMFSCH, replacing an earlier all-age-restricted-apartment plan that the school district had flagged as creating a school-tax shortfall. The Board gave generally favorable informal feedback on the concept — citing improved projected school tax revenue (~$2.2M vs. ~$1.4M previously) — but wants written feedback from the school superintendent before proceeding, and Board members raised concerns about controlling future unit-size growth and the net fiscal impact on schools.

The board approved the Road Naming Committee's recommendations for new roads in the Toll Brothers airport campus subdivision (Weber Farm Road, Cove View Way, and Fieldstone Knoll), with notification to the E911 coordinator, because tax lot numbers must be assigned before the plat can be filed. Members objected to the committee attaching conditions/stipulations (preserving historic field stones and requesting a WWII commemorative plaque), agreeing that naming a road is a town responsibility that cannot be bartered; those requests will be passed to the developer only as non-binding suggestions. The board also directed staff (via Kevin/Adam) to build developer notification into the future road-naming process. Approved by voice vote.

The board adopted a corrected configuration of new roadways in the airport campus subdivision. The road names recommended by the Road Naming Committee were unchanged; only the road configuration was clarified so the entrance road to the 50-unit senior housing has a proper address consistent with 911/emergency addressing, verified with the builder and police department. On the Town Attorney's advice the board voted to adopt the sketch map.

cases.name: Summit Club (formerly Brimwood) — Golf Course Conservation Easement & Recreation Fee
cases.applicationType: conservation easement / declaration of restrictive covenants
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners, LLC (represented by Mark Weingarten, DelBello Donnellan Weingarten Wise & Wiederkehr LLP)
cases.lastStatus: approved (public hearing closed; conservation easement and restrictive covenants adopted with four amendments)

trajectory.status: local law and temporary special use permit adopted (golf course public use); conservation easement / recreation fee hearing adjourned, unresolved
approved (public hearing closed; conservation easement and restrictive covenants adopted with four amendments)

timeline.status: local law and temporary special use permit adopted (golf course public use); conservation easement / recreation fee hearing adjourned, unresolved
timeline.summary: In this, the first public hearing on these items, the applicant (11.5 years into the overall approval process) sought urgent relief: a local law and temporary special use permit to let the 130-acre golf course reopen to public play for the season after its prior temporary permit lapsed December 31, pending completion of the residential site plan. The board approved both. The board did not resolve two linked, contested issues: (1) the affordable-housing recreation fee, where the applicant sought a full waiver (citing extensive on-site amenities — an 18-hole course, pool/fitness clubhouse, 6 tennis and 2 pickleball courts) while board members pushed back, floating a compromise of roughly $1,700/unit payable at closing instead of the standard $3,500-$10,000/unit; and (2) whether an independent third-party land trust must hold the golf-course conservation easement, which the applicant resisted on cost grounds. The board adjourned the conservation-easement hearing for further negotiation, including a planned meeting with the town's Open Space Committee.

As a final step before returning to the Planning Board to complete site plan approval for its residential component, the applicant asked the board to resolve two outstanding conditions from the original special permit findings: (1) a per-unit affordable-housing recreation fee, which the applicant argued should be reduced to zero given the development's open space/recreational amenities but ultimately offered to accept at $1,000 for all ~65 market-rate units; and (2) the structure of the required conservation easement over the ~130-acre golf course, where the applicant resisted paying for an independent third-party land trust (citing high endowment/stewardship costs, roughly $40,000 baseline plus $100,000 stewardship) and instead proposed relying on town/open-space-committee approval requirements, a covenant merging the golf course and residential lots, and reimbursing the town directly for its own monitoring costs. The applicant also noted the project carries an unusual $1.05 million community benefits agreement (paid per unit) of which about $190,000 has already been spent on a Windmill Farm-area wall, with roughly $860,000 remaining, and offered that money as a possible funding source for easement costs if the board required it. No resolution was reached; the board adjourned the hearing to May 24 while continuing to negotiate the easement-holder and fee questions.

timeline.status: approved (public hearing closed; conservation easement and restrictive covenants adopted with four amendments)
timeline.summary: After months of negotiation over whether an independent third-party land trust must hold the golf-course conservation easement, the board settled on pursuing Westchester County as a no-cost "second holder" (the county owns six golf courses and has relevant expertise), with a fallback option to revisit the North American Land Trust for a lower-cost hybrid arrangement if the county option fails. The board closed the public hearing and unanimously approved the conservation easement and declaration of restrictive covenants with four amendments: (1) annual inspections begin one year after the easement is recorded rather than one year after the final certificate of occupancy; (2) future modifications to the easement require only a simple majority of the town board rather than unanimous consent; (3) deletion of the last sentence of paragraph 3(H); and (4) a fertilizer/pesticide/herbicide restriction limited to those approved in an integrated turf grass and pest management plan, as requested by the Open Space Committee.

cases.name: Purchase of Two Storage Container Units for IBM Community Park (Connex West)
cases.address: IBM Community Park (near the turf fields)

timeline.summary: Following a townwide parks survey (600+ household responses) and over a year of Parks & Recreation Advisory Board study, town youth sports organizations (baseball/softball, soccer, football, lacrosse) unanimously recommended converting IBM Community Park fields 1 and 2 to artificial turf at an estimated $2.7 million — cheaper and higher-capacity than a $3.7 million Lombardi Park grass-and-drainage alternative. Advocates cited chronic field closures from poor drainage, more than doubled practice/game capacity from cross-field layouts, and turf's greater durability under heavy, year-round youth-sports use. The Board received the memo and directed staff to bring back a construction manager/bid-specification proposal (via Kellard Sessions) for a future vote rather than acting that night.

The board received the Westchester County DPW and NYS DEC lead-agency circulation responses, adopted a negative declaration, and approved the roughly $4.1 million agreement (via Sourcewell cooperative purchasing with Derosa Sports Construction) for artificial turf fields at IBM 1 and 2, plus a Hydro Environmental Solutions proposal for soil-fill testing. Councilman Milim championed the project with survey and park-and-rec data showing turf as the top-requested capital project; the supervisor and Councilman Hussain strongly supported paying from the ~$25M fund balance rather than bonding. Councilwoman DiGiacinto urged bonding instead and raised concerns about not doing soil testing first given possible contamination and about future capital needs (town hall, pool, water lines). Numerous residents spoke in strong support, and all items were adopted by voice vote.

The board considered a request to purchase two new green storage container units for equipment near the IBM Park turf fields, to be paid from fund balance, replacing rotted existing containers. Vataj strongly objected that metal containers cheapen a multimillion-dollar turf investment (his "Ferrari with used tires" analogy) and pushed for a prefab garage-style structure, while DiGiacinto defended the containers as utilitarian, secure, and cost-conscious but asked for full all-in cost comparisons of any alternative. With no motion made, the item was tabled to the next meeting for staff to bring back options.

cases.name: Lombardi Park — Public Water Supply Extension vs. Well Rehabilitation
cases.lastStatus: in progress; engineering proposal to advance at next meeting

trajectory.status: administrative resolutions adopted; hearing opened, pending 45-day permissive referendum period
in progress; engineering proposal to advance at next meeting
