timeline.summary: The Board continued debating whether to extend Water District #4 piping to Lombardi Park (roughly $461,000 per an initial Keller & Sessions estimate) or rehabilitate the park's existing well (potentially over $300,000 once duplicate treatment infrastructure like chlorination and UV disinfection is included), given ongoing PFAS concerns and the park's heavy use by children. The town confirmed bid documents for the water-district extension had already gone out, with cost comparisons expected at the next meeting; one board member questioned whether the eventual scope (effectively a water fountain and three bathrooms) justified the six-figure cost.

timeline.status: administrative resolutions adopted; hearing opened, pending 45-day permissive referendum period
timeline.summary: The Board opened a hearing and adopted the required administrative resolutions to formally propose extending Water District #4 into Lombardi Park (piped option, competitively bid after a non-competitive emergency estimate of about $461,000), triggering a mandatory 45-day permissive-referendum waiting period before a final vote in January; the Board can still choose the alternative of rehabilitating the park's existing well (about $373,000, roughly a third of which is for expanding the parks garage to house treatment equipment) or abandon the process if a cheaper option is found. Board members debated the true cost driver of the well option and future operating-cost implications of a self-run treatment system, with general agreement to keep exploring the well cost further before deciding.

timeline.status: in progress; engineering proposal to advance at next meeting
timeline.summary: The Board held a work session and coalesced around a substantially upgraded plan: instead of a narrow, single-purpose water service line into the park, run a full 8-inch public water main up School Street to the park, roughly 1,000 feet shorter than the originally proposed route through school-easement land, extending Water District #4's boundary along the way. The upgrade is expected to be substantially funded by the town's approximately $1.2 million in remaining, use-it-or-lose-it ARPA (federal COVID relief) funds, and would add three new fire hydrants and design provisions (valves/tees) for future, resident-initiated extensions to neighboring streets (Cox Avenue, Anthony Court, Byron Ridge Road) at no cost to the town unless residents opt to connect. The Board directed staff to bring back a formal engineering proposal and district-extension paperwork (map/plan/report, EAF, notice to affected property owners, and a subsequent public hearing) for approval at the next meeting, with construction not expected to be delayed by the parallel legal process.

cases.name: North Castle Pool and Tennis Club — Pool Deck Renovation Bid Award
cases.address: North Castle Pool and Tennis Club

timeline.summary: The Board approved a package of engineering proposals for a comprehensive evaluation of the pool and tennis club's plumbing, deck, and domestic water treatment (required by the Health Department, separate from an already-approved item), reasoning that fixing only isolated leaks or the deck without addressing underlying infrastructure risks having to reopen or demolish the deck again later; the study will also assess whether some existing deck areas are worth retaining as the facility is reimagined, with board members acknowledging the town may need to accept losing a future season to do the work properly.

The board approved, as a group, engineering proposals for comprehensive conceptual improvements to the town pool facility (pool, deck, plumbing, building, tennis/basketball), separate from the already-approved domestic-water treatment needed to open this season. The goal is a full facility evaluation to avoid piecemeal work — potentially reducing unused deck area, using pervious pavers, and upgrading the building — accepting that a future season might be lost to do it properly. Members stressed opening on time this year. Adopted by voice vote.

The board awarded the pool deck renovation contract to (Tony) Casali/Casal Inc., approving both add-on items recommended by the town engineer: a roughly $29,700 sub-base protection allowance (to avoid uncapped change-order exposure if subsurface conditions are poor) and a roughly $49,000 upgrade to a longer-lasting 'diamond bright' pool finish, which also offers darker color options that help retain water warmth. The base bid came in well under the $5 million bond originally authorized (roughly $3.2 million), prompting discussion (unresolved) of using leftover bond capacity for bathroom/locker-room improvements or the adjacent parking lot rather than reducing the bond outright. Work is slated to begin around September 8, with 180 days to complete, targeting a Memorial Day reopening.

cases.name: Terminal Leave Payment — Lisa Larson, Parks & Recreation Department

timeline.summary: The board approved a terminal leave payment for Liz Duffy, senior recreation leader in the Senior Citizens Recreation Department, by voice vote. A council member noted she has been working part time remotely and will continue in a part-time in-person role starting in April, calling it a good solution for everyone.
The board approved the terminal leave payment for retiring Police Department member Kevin Finateri, with members wishing him well. Approved by voice vote.
The board approved a terminal leave payment to Lisa Larson of the Parks and Recreation Department. Routine personnel item, moved and seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Agreement with Arc Westchester — Main Street Armonk Maintenance 2026

timeline.summary: After roughly ten months of negotiation, Bank of America consented to a temporary construction easement and permanent easement on its former branch property to allow completion of the town's downtown Armonk parking improvement project on the former Verizon lot. The board authorized the supervisor to sign the agreement; Councilwoman DiGiacinto recused herself because relatives with an interest in a neighboring Main Street commercial property could arguably benefit.

Following a recommendation from the Landmark Preservation Committee, the board opened and held a public hearing to landmark the roughly 100-year-old Armonk Barber Pole (a Made-in-Chicago Koch No. 909), which the property-owning family enthusiastically supported. Board members discussed only the pole (not the building) and debated adding a future designation plaque, to be placed on the building with owner permission. The hearing was closed and the board unanimously adopted the landmark designation by voice vote.
The board authorized the supervisor to sign a 2026 agreement with Arc Westchester for maintenance of Main Street, Armonk. Passed unanimously by voice vote.

cases.name: Probationary Appointments — Water & Sewer and Parks & Recreation

timeline.summary: The board approved, by individual motions and votes, the probationary appointments of Anthony Stevens (effective June 3, 2024), Joseph D. Santesis, and Andrew Sigenga as skilled laborers filling open positions in the Water & Sewer Department. Town Administrator Kevin said he was impressed with the candidates interviewed and glad to fill the openings under superintendent 'Sal.' All appointments adopted unanimously.

The board made two probationary appointments effective December 11, 2025: William Segmuller as Assistant Building Inspector and Yvonne Henriquez as Office Assistant (Automated System). Both passed unanimously by voice vote.

The board approved a series of probationary appointments by voice vote: Brian Kidoff as skilled laborer in Water & Sewer (effective April 13), Leroy Crawley as skilled labor in Water & Sewer (effective April 27), Nicholas Champagne as skilled labor in Water & Sewer (effective April 27), and Jorge Hodaro as groundskeeper in Parks & Recreation (effective April 13). Each passed on a motion, second, and aye vote.

cases.name: Receipt of Resignation — Brendan Malloy, Parks & Recreation Advisory Board

timeline.summary: The board accepted, with regret and thanks, the resignation of Allison Miller from the Sustainability Committee effective April 27, 2024. The Supervisor noted the town clerk's office sends a formal thank-you letter to departing volunteers on behalf of the board.
The board received the resignation of Jane Rothschild from the North Castle Public Library, effective January 16, 2025, and wished her well. Accepted by voice vote.
The board received the letter of resignation from Brendan Malloy from the Parks and Recreation advisory board, effective February 14, 2026, and thanked him for his service. Accepted by voice vote.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — 23 Bedford Banksville Road (wood/metal manufacturing)
cases.applicant: Greenwich Realty Group, LLC (counsel Tony Veneziano)

timeline.summary: Received county and town Planning Department letters on a proposed zoning text amendment to permit light industrial use (woodworking and iron/aluminum assemblage) by special use permit in the GB General Business district; the Planning Board gave a positive recommendation. The board scheduled the public hearing for June 26. Members flagged that the drafted use language is broad and asked to tour the site before the hearing, citing an observed active/disturbing operation and environmentally sensitive wetlands to the rear. Barbara DiGiacinto recused herself (her husband owns 25% of Band Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property).

A noticed public hearing on 23 Bedford Banksville Road was opened and immediately adjourned to a date uncertain because the applicant felt they were not fully ready. DiGiacinto recused herself due to a family financial interest — her husband John DiGisono owns 25% of Ban Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property. The board opened and adjourned by voice votes.

Following a rezoning to CBB at the prior meeting, the board held a public hearing on a special-use permit to legalize existing specialized wood-product and metal-assemblage manufacturing, with conditions limiting occupancy to 20, keeping storage inside, and requiring proper handling/ventilation of chemicals and fumes. A resident (Jen) questioned why a permit would be granted before the building inspector confirmed safety; counsel and the board explained the operating/building permit review follows the use approval. The board adopted the neg dec and resolution and closed the hearing. A late redline of the conditions circulated the day of the meeting prompted a board member's objection to '11th hour' document changes.

cases.name: AI Engineers Proposal — Water District No. 9 Quarry Heights Water Main Extension Distribution System

timeline.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign an agreement with Westchester Joint Water Works (WJWW) to begin extending public water to the long-troubled Quarry Heights neighborhood, where wells have dried and been contaminated. WJWW, under a DOJ/DEC consent order, earmarked ~$1.1 million in lieu of penalties to extend mains and make roughly 14 connections; the agreement commits the town to later form a water district (in reverse of the usual order) to absorb those and remaining properties, buy water from WJWW, and resell it. Sal Misisti explained plans to install three master-meter interconnection points and later extend districtwide, pursuing grants given the high rock-excavation cost. Residents Diana Kandrea and Nico Marino pressed for equitable connection of all homes and possible cost recovery from the contaminator; the board committed to a special public informational meeting. Approved by voice vote.

The board held a public hearing on extending Water District No. 9 to the Quarry Heights area under Article 12A of Town Law, addressing chronic well-water/PFAS problems among roughly 48 homes. Town Attorney Roland explained that two preliminary resolutions would let the town apply to the State Comptroller and better position the project for grant funding, with a worst-case per-home cost around $46,700 over the life of the bond. Residents spoke strongly in favor (a signed petition and letter were submitted into the record), and the board adopted a 21-day open comment period before both preliminary resolutions passed 5-0 by roll call (Berra, Vataj, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Rende all aye). Board members voiced unanimous, emphatic support and commitment to pursue grants.

Under agreements, the board approved receipt of a proposal from AI Engineers for the Water District No. 9 Quarry Heights water main extension distribution system (design work supplementing the map/plan/report). Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Tony Castell Inc. — Kent Place Parking Lot (Former Verizon Property) Final Payment
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (bid documents by Kellard)

timeline.summary: The board approved authorizing a bid for improvements to the Kent Place parking lot, a new downtown parking addition, with an 18-month completion date. Bid documents prepared by Kellard were ready to release. Approved by unanimous voice vote of the members present.

The board approved payment requisition No. 4 to Tony Casale Inc. for the completed Kent Place parking-lot improvements, already cleared by the town's engineer. Members praised the finished lot (now open and in use) and discussed remaining holdback, extra fence work, and fall overseeding, plus plans to encourage Main Street business owners/employees to use the new lot and to advance a future parking-district effort.

The board accepted the contractor's affidavit of release of liens and a one-year guarantee bond and approved final payment requisition number five to Tony Castell Inc. for the Kent Place parking lot improvements. Councilwoman DiGiacinto recused herself because her family owns commercial property on the west side of Main Street. Motion made and all in favor.

cases.name: Interim MS4 Stormwater Reports (period ending January 2, 2026)

timeline.summary: The board accepted the interim MS4 stormwater reports for the period ending September 1, 2024, prepared by town engineer KSCJ Consulting, detailing routine compliance activities such as catch-basin cleaning, street sweeping, and education/training. Approved by voice vote as a standard annual filing.

The board accepted the interim MS4 stormwater reports for the period ending January 2, 2025, prepared by town engineers KSCJ, and authorized the supervisor to sign. Described as annual housekeeping to promote stormwater safety practices and reduce pollution. Councilwoman DiGiacinto moved it; adopted by voice vote.

The board accepted the interim MS4 stormwater reports for the period ending January 2, 2026 from the town engineer and authorized the supervisor to sign the reports. Routine compliance item, moved and seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Public Hearing — Acquisition of 333 Main Street via Eminent Domain

timeline.summary: Continued public hearing on whether to acquire 333 Main Street via eminent domain procedure law to relocate town hall, police and court from the deficient 15 Bedford Road campus. About two dozen residents spoke, nearly all opposed or urging a pause: they objected to an open-ended 'blank check,' warned the ~$7M appraisal would balloon in court (owner's counsel already disputes it), demanded a full cost comparison with renovating/expanding 15 Bedford Road, and voiced fears the historic 10-acre town hall site would be sold for development. The board received a batch of letters/emails into the record and Supervisor Rende announced an ad hoc concept study committee and a commitment to a public referendum. No vote to close was taken; the hearing was adjourned and continued to the March 12 meeting.

The board reconvened the continued public hearing on acquiring 333 Main Street by eminent domain procedure law to relocate Town Hall, citing deteriorated, non-ADA-compliant, and unsafe conditions in the current facilities (police basement flooding, mold, undersized space per a 2007 study). Dozens of residents spoke or submitted letters; a clear majority opposed or expressed concern about eminent domain, traffic, historic-district loss, potential development of the current town parcel, and lack of cost information, while some developers argued the purchase is financially sound. The board repeatedly stressed no decision would be made without full cost studies of multiple options and a town-wide referendum, and committed to an FAQ, a process one-pager, and possible mailings. The board received several resident letters into the record and voted to recess/adjourn the hearing to April 23, 2025 (with the option to postpone further by public notice). No acquisition decision was taken.

The board reconvened the public hearing to consider acquiring 333 Main Street under the Eminent Domain Procedure Law. As noticed, the hearing was opened and immediately adjourned to an undetermined future date because the board is still gathering information. Resident Andrew Lester spoke against the acquisition, calling the property undesirable and urging a holistic, process-driven review before proceeding.

cases.name: IMA with Westchester County — Grasslands Firing Range Training

timeline.summary: Approval of an intermunicipal agreement with Westchester County (via a NYSERDA/Con Ed incentive program) to install EV charging stations at no cost to the town, with authorization for the Supervisor to sign. Construction is slated for Hergenhan and Community Park, then Town Hall and Clove Road. Members discussed pricing/time-limit enforcement to avoid overcrowding and logistical timing around other park work. Approved on a voice vote.

Approval of an intermunicipal agreement for the STOP-DWI patrol project (reimbursement up to $8,400/year for overtime checkpoint work), with authorization for the Supervisor to sign. DiGiacinto voiced concerns about the reimbursement cap, overtime rates by rank, and the many procedural steps required to be reimbursed, but supported the long-running program. Approved on a voice vote.

Approval of an intermunicipal agreement with the Westchester County Department of Public Safety Services for police training at the Grasslands Reservation firing range, with authorization for the Supervisor to sign. A recurring year-end renewal; approved on a voice vote.

cases.name: Public Hearing and Adoption of Preliminary Resolutions Establishing Armonk Parking District No. 2
cases.address: West side of Main Street, Armonk
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Town Planner Adam Kaufman; Town Attorney; Town Administrator; Comptroller)

timeline.summary: The board considered receipt of the Armonk Parking District map, plan and report and Environmental Assessment Form for the west side of Main Street, and whether to direct the town attorney to prepare an order calling for a public hearing. Adam Kaufman explained the district would improve and manage parking, adding a net 65 spaces (including the Verizon lot), with the town paying roughly one-third of the cost based on assessed value including the library. Councilman Berra raised substantive concerns that the town's share was really closer to 60% (counting the 49 Verizon-lot spaces) and questioned which properties were included. The board voted to receive the map plan/report (aye) and separately voted to have the attorney prepare for the public hearing (aye), with the explicit understanding the terms could still be modified; a public hearing was targeted for the first meeting in June.

The board voted to adopt an order calling for a public hearing on June 10, 2026 regarding formation of the Armonk Parking District. Discussion revisited the town's history of funding the Verizon-lot library parking, with Supervisor Rende arguing the town's prior investment and developer-funded community benefit agreements justify moving forward. Councilman Berra raised sharpened financial and equity concerns, calculating the town's effective cost share as high as roughly 49-66% (versus the ~33% previously cited) once the existing Verizon-lot investment is counted, questioned the 'hopscotch' inclusion of some parcels (including 12 Maple Avenue) and exclusion of others (like the Citibank parcel), and warned of possible overcrowding if off-street parking requirements are relaxed for participating properties. Councilman Vataj asked about adding the Citibank parcel and the process/cost of later modifying district membership. The board ultimately voted unanimously to set the June 10 hearing, with at least one member noting she still had serious concerns but would support the hearing notice itself since the terms remain modifiable afterward.

The board held the public hearing on establishing Armonk Parking District No. 2 to fund, manage, and regulate the public parking area behind the west side of Main Street, with the district members' assessed-value-based share supplemented by the town's contribution (tied to the library's parking demand). Public comment was extensive and mixed: the library board president (personal capacity) supported it but asked for traffic calming; a North White Plains resident opposed it as an inequitable taxpayer subsidy of Armonk businesses; a restaurant investor at 12 Maple Avenue criticized decades of delay and a community-benefits-agreement (CBA) obligation now in limbo after his site plan approval lapsed; an attorney for the DiGiacinto family properties and the 12 Maple Avenue owner spoke in support; and another resident said misinformation emails had caused confusion. After a lengthy, at times heated exchange between Supervisor Rende and Councilman Berra over the town's true cost share and an email Rende called "misinformation," the board closed the hearing and adopted, by 3-1 roll-call votes (Vataj, Hussain, and Rende in favor; Berra opposed; DiGiacinto recused), a SEQRA negative declaration, a resolution making certain determinations, and a preliminary resolution approving establishment of the district. The matter now proceeds to the state comptroller for final approval, expected to take several months.

cases.name: 23 Banks Road (Banksville) — Contractor's Yard Special Use Permit & Masonry Retail Zoning Text Amendment
cases.applicationType: special use permit / zoning text amendment

timeline.summary: The board received notice that the planning board intended to act as SEQRA lead agency on a roughly 10-acre Banksville property near the Mianus River, where the applicant needs a site plan and an eventual town board special use permit to legalize a long-standing, unpermitted contractors' yard operating within about 15 feet of a wetland. After extended debate about whether the town board should instead assert lead agency — given the wetland sensitivity, unresolved building-code violations, and the board's ultimate special-permit authority — the board declined to contest lead agency and let it default to the planning board, over Supervisor Schiliro's reservations. Councilman Berra recused himself from the entire item due to a personal/family conflict (the property is owned by the family of a former town figure, John Deacon Sr.).

Returning to the contractor's-yard legalization issue flagged in January, the incoming tenant's attorney requested a special use permit (proffering an 18-month sunset with no new aggregate material brought in, only removal) to legalize a decades-old, roughly 2.5-acre unpermitted contractor's yard near a DEC-regulated wetland, plus a new zoning text amendment and companion special use permit to allow a smaller (~0.8-acre) masonry/stone retail business to replace it, consolidated closer to the front of the site with roughly 1.5 acres restored as wetland buffer. Resident Jen strongly criticized the site as a long-standing eyesore and safety hazard (large trucks maneuvering on a narrow road) but supported cleanup, while also flagging that neighboring non-conforming businesses in Banksville may need similar scrutiny. The board, at Councilman Berra's urging, added a direct referral to the Conservation Board for input before the public hearing (rather than only via the planning board's later site-plan review) and scheduled three related public hearings for April 27.

cases.name: Proposal — Asbestos Remediation Bid/Spec & Management Services, Old Recreation Building, 85 Cox Avenue

timeline.summary: Parks liaison Councilman Milim presented two options for the deteriorating former recreation building at Lombardi Park, whose basement houses the park's water system: (1) demolish and rebuild a similarly sized structure, or (2) demolish and instead relocate/upgrade the water system into a two-story addition on the adjacent parks garage, freeing the old building's footprint for parking and a small concession window. Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto, after touring the building, argued strongly for outright demolition without replacement as fiscally responsible given the building's disrepair (mold, failing furnace, crumbling ceiling) and the garage's already-improved condition. The board declined to authorize the proposed engineering/architecture agreements (~$6,120 plus related costs) immediately, instead agreeing to schedule a board site visit (inviting the Parks & Rec Advisory Board) followed by a public agenda item to weigh options — including possible food-scrap-composting use — before committing funds, while flagging the aging furnace as a near-term risk requiring contingency planning (temporary heaters) if it fails before the issue is resolved.

The board approved a proposal from Quality Environmental Solutions and Technologies Inc. to provide bids, specifications, and management services for asbestos remediation at the old recreation building. A member questioned whether the open-ended management-services scope was needed given licensed remediators, asking staff to keep a close eye on cost; the board concluded that professional oversight/air monitoring is money well spent for accountability, especially in light of a separate project just tabled over disputed prior management. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: IT Network Support Contract — Logically (2022)

timeline.summary: Councilman Berra flagged several contract terms in the proposed 2022 IT network-support agreement with Logically (successor to the town's prior vendor, Sullivan): an unexplained new-client 'onboarding fee' despite an ongoing vendor relationship, a 1.5%/month late-payment interest charge plus attorney's-fee/collection-cost language, a confidentiality clause needing a Freedom of Information Law carve-out, and — most significantly — an early-termination fee formula combined with an annual CPI-or-greater price-escalation clause that could raise costs regardless of actual inflation. The board agreed to table the contract pending clarification from the vendor and Town Attorney Baroni on these points.

The board approved the police department portion of the Logically network support contract (with the onboarding fee and payment-term issues from the prior meeting already corrected, saving roughly $7,000-8,000). The town hall/administrative portion remained tabled after Councilman Hussain flagged that the contract's flat 'four hours per month' technology-task-force support allotment (non-cumulative if unused) poorly matched the task force's actual uneven workload; the board asked staff to renegotiate toward an hourly not-to-exceed structure with a designated point person instead.

cases.name: Cohen Law Group Legal Bill — Wireless Communications Law Billing Detail Dispute

timeline.summary: For the second consecutive meeting, Councilman Berra withheld support for paying a roughly $3,900 special-counsel invoice from the Cohen Law Group (wireless communications law work) over block-billed time entries he felt were disproportionate to the work described, requesting the attorney self-audit and confirm the billed hours were accurate. Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto and Supervisor Schiliro pushed back sharply, arguing the detail already provided was typical of attorney billing and that further line-item scrutiny risked questioning the attorney's integrity after he had voluntarily under-billed in the past; the exchange grew testy before the board split the item from the warrant, approved the rest of the warrant, and agreed to send a general request for confirmation back to the attorney pending the next meeting.

The disputed roughly $3,900 Cohen Law Group invoice returned to the warrant a third time; Councilman Berra maintained he had no basis to conclude the charges were unjustified but was not comfortable voting to approve, and this time voted no on a roll call (rather than abstaining as in a prior meeting) after town attorney Roland Baroni clarified the item had to be pulled from the consent warrant and voted on separately if any member wanted to vote against it. The rest of the board voted aye and the payment was approved.

cases.name: RM-FD-SCH Senior Citizen Housing District — Floating Zone to Mapped District Conversion

timeline.summary: The board advanced a local law converting the RM-FSCH (senior citizen housing) floating zone to a mapped zoning district, on the town attorney's recommendation, to give the board more flexibility: unlike a floating zone, a mapped-district rezoning petition the board finds without merit can simply be declined rather than processed to conclusion (and risk litigation over a denial). Councilman Berra asked clarifying questions about scope and whether a parallel approach might apply elsewhere in the code but did not object. The board declared lead agency, referred to the planning board, and scheduled an April 27 public hearing.

Town-initiated local law converting the residential multifamily senior citizen housing (RM-FD-SCH) zoning classification from a floating zone to a traditional mapped district, restoring language giving the Town Board discretion to decline to even process a rezoning petition it finds inappropriate (rather than being obligated to act on any application). Prompted in part by lessons from a past senior-housing project (referenced by a resident, Christine Angelton, as an unfinished, poorly-maintained development on her block) where the board felt it lacked the ability to simply decline an application. Adopted unanimously with a negative declaration after a public hearing with one resident speaker.

cases.name: Armonk Lions Club Request to Hold the Fol de Rol at Wampus Brook Park

timeline.summary: Councilman Hussain, as Parks & Rec Advisory Board liaison, asked the Beautification Committee and Parks & Rec board to reopen dialogue on where to place several donated items (ADA-compliant picnic tables and small 'mushroom' children's tables) previously approved for Wampus Brook Park, citing concerns from Historical Society members and other residents that the location/items may not be appropriate. Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto, as Beautification liaison, defended the process as deliberated (November/December 2021 meetings) and suggested waiting to see the actual installed items before judging them. Resident Jen, a Parks & Rec Advisory Board member who voted yes originally, publicly said she now wants to reconsider given she only learned afterward that the tables would be permanently cemented in place rather than movable, calling the original vote rushed by a year-end spending deadline.

The board considered the Lions Club's annual request to hold the Fol de Rol at Wampus Brook Park. Supervisor Rende, a Lions Club member, weighed whether he should recuse but concluded there was no conflict since the club receives no town funds and pays none to the town. He also flagged, as he had the prior year, that some individuals had improperly and without authorization collected parking fees at town-owned lots (Wampus South and behind the firehouse) used for the event, stating firmly that no parking charges are permitted at any town park for any festival. The board approved the request, noting town staff support the event for cleanup and liability reasons.

cases.name: NYS Uniform Fire Prevention & Building Code — Mandatory Local Law Update
cases.lastStatus: work session concluded; ready to schedule public hearing

trajectory.status: work session concluded; ready to schedule public hearing

timeline.summary: New York State mandates town-wide adoption of a roughly 30-page revised uniform building/fire code by year end. The Town Planner and Building Inspector had highlighted five or six sections where the board retains discretion (e.g., raising the building-permit threshold from 64 to 144 sq ft, food-truck inspection/permitting requirements). The board debated whether to schedule this as the very next work session (April 6) or push it a week to accommodate the Ethics Board, ultimately prioritizing it given the hard year-end adoption deadline and multiple required public hearings.

timeline.status: work session concluded; ready to schedule public hearing
timeline.summary: Continuing the work session series, the board worked through the remaining discretionary sections of the code update with the Building Inspector and Town Planner: (1) kept the existing 64-square-foot (rather than the state's 144-square-foot) threshold for when a shed/accessory structure requires a building permit, after extended debate about setback/zoning implications on small lots, with Matt Milim dissenting in favor of a larger or lot-size-tiered threshold to reduce resident burden; (2) affirmed keeping the town's existing exemptions for playground equipment, swings, low garden walls, small treehouses (capped at 144 sq ft), and shallow above-ground pools, which staff confirmed the state had approved; (3) kept the existing 12-month/2-year building permit validity window rather than the state's shorter recommendation, while separately directing that escalating renewal fees (via the master fee schedule, not the code itself) be used to discourage indefinitely stalled "zombie" construction projects, a concern Jose Berra raised; and (4) kept operating permits administratively separate from certificates of occupancy per the Building Inspector's preference. The board concluded the code update was ready for a public hearing.

cases.name: Food Truck Permitting & Special-Event Law Amendment

timeline.summary: The board discussed amending town code to require a (fee-optional) permit for food trucks at special events, closing a gap where town-sponsored events were exempt from permitting entirely — an issue that surfaced after a food-truck problem at a recent "Frosty" event and a request for Opening Day. Members agreed the fix was uncontroversial and quick, and directed staff to draft language and move straight to an agenda item/public hearing rather than a further work session.

Building on the March discussion, the board and Building Inspector Rob Malelo dug further into the new state mandate requiring each municipality to individually inspect and permit food trucks (fire suppression, gas lines, equipment mounting, etc.), which the Building Inspector called impractical given inconsistent standards town-to-town, the added cost/burden on food truck operators, and the lack of any advance industry consultation by the state. The board discussed writing to the Governor's office and coordinating with neighboring towns (Mount Kisco, Bedford) on a joint advocacy push, and floated alternatives like centralizing inspections at the county level (as is already done for food-truck health inspections), while acknowledging time pressure given the state's year-end adoption deadline.

cases.name: Shaw Sports Turf Change Order No. 3 — Community Park Artificial Turf Field

timeline.summary: Staff recommended re-bidding the smaller North Bridge at Community Park separately from the South Bridge (previously bid together at ~$220,000 combined, with the North Bridge portion around $95,000) in hopes a firm specializing in smaller work would offer a better price; the existing decking is rotting and slippery. The board agreed to place the rebid authorization on an upcoming agenda and asked staff to also look at longer-lasting slip-resistant surfacing.

The board considered a memo from KSCJ Consulting and Change Order No. 3 (about $75,000) for additional electrical power and data improvements on the community park artificial turf field project, authorizing the Supervisor to sign. DiGiacinto objected to the letter's 'as requested by the town' wording and pressed for detailed justification, learning much of the cost stemmed from rerouting buried electrical lines and adding access boxes discovered during excavation. Vataj and Berra questioned pricing reasonableness and asked to be notified of change orders in advance; staff confirmed the same approved unit rates applied. The board approved the change order.

cases.name: IND-A Zoning District Warehouse Use — Zone Text Amendment
cases.address: New King Street / Airport Industrial District
cases.lastStatus: public hearing adjourned at applicant-adjacent counsel's request

trajectory.status: public hearing adjourned at applicant-adjacent counsel's request

timeline.summary: A town-initiated local law clarifying that warehouse uses are a permitted principal use throughout the IND-A zoning district (not just at the airport itself), correcting what staff viewed as a drafting error, without expanding the district's boundaries. The board received comment letters from the County Planning Board and NYC DEP and scheduled a public hearing for May 11, 2022.

timeline.status: public hearing adjourned at applicant-adjacent counsel's request
timeline.summary: The public hearing to adopt the town-initiated local law clarifying that warehouse uses are permitted throughout the IND-A district was opened but immediately adjourned to a later date at the request of attorney Dan Hollis, who represents a party involved in the matter; no substantive discussion occurred.

cases.name: Special-Counsel Retainer — Greenwich American Center / King Street Development (Tishman Speyer)
cases.address: King Street (Greenwich American Center, Greenwich CT)

timeline.summary: A large residential development is being proposed on a King Street parcel that is technically within the Town of Greenwich, CT but whose traffic, density, and shopping impacts would fall mostly on North Castle. The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a letter to the Greenwich Planning & Zoning Commission ahead of the developer's pre-application meeting, flagging density, traffic, and retail/shopping-pattern impacts for study; Adam Kaufman (Town Planner) will monitor via Zoom and further comment letters are expected as the project develops.

As an add-on item, the board considered a retainer agreement with Connecticut special counsel (subject to Barone's final review) to follow the Tishman Speyer / Greenwich American Center development on King Street in Greenwich, now proposing 198 townhouse units, to protect North Castle's interests and possibly negotiate community-benefit funding for downtown Armonk impacts. Both the motion to add the item to the agenda and the motion to approve the retainer passed 3-1, with Councilwoman DiGiacinto opposed on both, saying she was not confident the town has standing or that she understood the value well enough to commit funds. Councilman Berra championed the item and Rende joined a conference call with the proposed counsel.

cases.name: Final Payment (Requisition #8) — North White Plains Community Center Renovation

timeline.summary: Authorized the Supervisor to sign a grant disbursement agreement releasing $125,000 in state funding (secured with the help of Assemblyman David Buchwald's office) for the North White Plains Community Center project, following an extended administrative process with the state.

The board considered final payment (requisition #8) and release of the guarantee bond to AFL General Construction for the North White Plains Community Center renovation. Councilman Berra objected that library-board concerns (a shower door lacking a proper sweep and a kitchen-cabinet ADA layout) were never resolved, and Supervisor Rende raised a broader concern that the architect (Sullivan Architecture) failed to properly oversee the work. Administrator Kevin said both the architect's and engineer's punch lists were fully completed. The board agreed to defer the payment to the next meeting to reconcile the punch list and check back with the library board.

cases.name: Mother's Green Nursery — 11 Bedford Banksville Road Special Use Permits
cases.applicant: Brothers Green Corp (Richard and Ted Greene)

trajectory.status: referred to town and county planning boards

timeline.status: referred to town and county planning boards
timeline.summary: Brothers Green Corp, operating a contractor's yard/storage use on the 3.7-acre property (partly in wetlands/wetland buffer) since 1984 and owning it since 2007, sought a special permit to legalize the long-standing use after being told during an unrelated 2019 home-renovation permit review that no site plan approval of record existed for the property. The applicant argued the use predates modern wetlands regulation and requested the permit maintain the status quo (using existing concrete-block boundary markers placed in the 1990s) without any expansion. The board referred the application to the town and county planning boards, discussed inviting the conservation board given the wetland buffer, and agreed to schedule a joint site walk; a Planning Board site-plan application was filed in parallel.

The Board held reconvened public hearings on two special use permits for a nursery operation dating back over a century, predominantly located within a wetland and wetland buffer: one legalizing the existing nursery use (triggered when the owner sought a building permit for house renovations and had no underlying site plan approval) and one for an associated contractor's yard. Extensive debate arose over the town attorney's inclusion of an unprecedented term limit/sunset clause in the draft resolution given the property's wetland sensitivity and the possibility that environmental standards could tighten over time; several members initially favored a limit of 20-30 years, but after further discussion the entire Board reversed position and voted unanimously to adopt both special use permits with no term limit, while several members said the town should separately study a broader, prospective policy on term-limiting special permits in sensitive areas.

cases.name: Local Law Updating Administration & Enforcement of NYS Uniform Fire Prevention, Building & Energy Conservation Construction Codes

timeline.summary: The Board received a local law developed over several months with the town planner and building inspector to update code administration and enforcement, including shed and tree-house permit thresholds (an inconsistency between the existing 64-square-foot shed threshold and a 144-square-foot tree-house threshold was flagged by a resident and referred to the public hearing for further consideration). The Board voted to receive the local law and scheduled the public hearing for July 13, 2022.

With no members of the public signed up to speak, the Board closed the public hearing and adopted the local law as amended, setting a uniform 64-square-foot permit threshold to resolve the earlier shed-versus-tree-house inconsistency (rather than the tree house's original 144-square-foot allowance).

cases.name: Video Conferencing Policy for Public Participation and Board Member Remote Attendance

timeline.summary: Continuing from the May 24 local law adoption, the Board debated at length what the state's 'extraordinary circumstances' standard for board members appearing remotely in a non-public location should mean in the town's implementing policy, with Councilman Berra repeatedly pressing town attorney Roland on statutory-construction and legislative-history questions and proposing the policy explicitly track the state's non-exhaustive 'including but not limited to' language. The Board adopted the policy largely as drafted (mirroring the state amendment) so that a policy would be in effect before the next meeting, with the understanding it could be amended later after members consulted their state legislators.

The Board further amended and re-adopted its video-conferencing policy, striking a provision allowing remote public participants to submit comments via Zoom chat (agreeing it was not required by the state statute and could be reconsidered later if needed) and confirming board members may still attend executive sessions remotely under the policy.

cases.name: Local Law Removing Sheds, Fences & Generators from RPRC Review (Town Code 12-22)

timeline.summary: The Board received Director of Planning Adam Kaufman's proposed local law streamlining permitting for sheds, fences, and generators by removing them from Residential Project Review Committee review in favor of a direct building-permit process, with debate over clarifying that the shed size threshold applies to unfinished-interior storage sheds and over whether the building inspector should retain discretion to refer generator or fence applications back to the RPRC if a potential problem is spotted. The Board voted to receive the proposal with the unfinished-interior clarification and scheduled the public hearing for July 13, 2022.

The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the local law removing sheds, fences, and generators from Residential Project Review Committee review in favor of a streamlined building-permit process.

cases.name: Local Law Restricting Parking Vehicles on Lawns (Town Code 355-21)

timeline.summary: The Board received a proposed local law adding restrictions on parking vehicles on residential lawns, motivated both by aesthetic/property-value complaints (concentrated in North White Plains) and as a code-enforcement tool to help identify suspected illegal apartments where a building inspector otherwise cannot act without probable cause. After discussion of edge cases (temporary event parking, gravel/driveway-expansion permits, curb damage, and enforcement mechanics), the Board declared intent to act as lead agency, referred the law to town and county planning boards, and scheduled the public hearing for July 27, 2022.

After a public hearing, the Board declined to vote on the lawn-parking restriction, closing the hearing without adoption. Members were split: Councilman Berra said he was not convinced the law would move forward as drafted and preferred more resident input, while Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto (who had fielded most resident feedback) and others favored keeping the option open for a revised version at a future meeting.

cases.name: Local Law Adding Stop Sign at Cox Avenue / School Street (Armonk)
cases.address: Cox Avenue at School Street, Armonk
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Peter Simonson)

timeline.summary: The Board received a letter from Police Chief Peter Simonson proposing a local law amending the Vehicle and Traffic chapter to add a stop sign at Cox Avenue's intersection with School Street in Armonk, and scheduled a public hearing for July 27, 2022.
With no opposition raised, the Board closed the public hearing and adopted the local law adding a stop sign at the Cox Avenue/School Street intersection in Armonk.

cases.name: Brothers Green Nursery, 11 Bedford Road — Amended Special Use Permit (Nursery + Contractor's Yard)

timeline.summary: Applicant's counsel (Zarin & Steinmetz) and engineer presented an amended application reorganizing the site to keep nursery uses (CBB district) in front and contractor's-yard-type equipment (e.g., a topsoil screener) in the rear GB-zoned portion under a separate special permit, plus added stormwater measures (crushed-stone storage area, grass berm) to protect nearby wetlands. Board members pressed for pesticide/fertilizer-use limitations, no-idling/off-site-repair conditions, and conservation board input before the hearing; the Board received the letter and scheduled the public hearing for August 10, 2022 (with a possible adjournment to September given the August timing).

The Board opened concurrent hearings on the nursery-use legalization and the newly-split contractor's-yard special permit for the rear GB-zoned portion of the property. The applicant confirmed the conservation board had given a favorable recommendation and the planning board had adopted a negative declaration but not yet transmitted its formal recommendation. Councilman Berra pressed the applicant's attorney on what would prevent future expansion or a change in use if the property were sold, and was told the confined yard footprint and wetland buffer areas functionally cap the equipment/vehicle scale. Both hearings were left open, to be adjourned into September pending the planning board's recommendation, consistent with the town's practice of not finalizing land-use hearings in August.

cases.name: Flood Damage Prevention Local Law Update (Ch. 177)

timeline.summary: The Board began the process of updating Chapter 177 (Flood Damage Prevention) to comply with FEMA/National Flood Insurance Program requirements after a New York State DEC directive, receiving the Director of Planning's letter, EAF, and draft local law and scheduling the public hearing for October 12th (later adopted at that meeting) to meet an October 14th FEMA compliance deadline.

Following a New York State DEC directive to update Chapter 177 (Flood Damage Prevention) to comply with current National Flood Insurance Program regulations (44 CFR 60.3), the Board held a brief, uncontroversial public hearing and adopted both a SEQRA negative declaration and the local law itself, essentially adopting the state's model language into town code.

cases.name: Pollinator Garden / Property Maintenance Local Law Amendment

timeline.summary: The Board reviewed a draft local law creating an exemption from the property-maintenance code for pollinator gardens (with a 10-foot structure setback and a front-yard area cap), incorporating language changes suggested by a councilman and a proposal from a Conservation Board member/nursery owner to exclude New York State-prohibited and invasive plant species. Members debated whether to also restrict pollinator gardens in side/rear yards near property lines, with one member calling further rear-yard restriction unnecessary government overreach, before voting to schedule a public hearing and to circulate the draft to the Conservation Board, Mianus River Gorge Preserve, and Beautification Committee beforehand.

After further review with the Director of Planning and Building Inspector, the Board concluded the proposed amendment would actually be more restrictive than existing law (capping pollinator gardens at 25% of a yard where no cap currently exists) and that the Building Inspector already treats pollinator gardens as exempt "cultivated gardens" under the current code. The Board closed the public hearing and took no action, leaving the property-maintenance code unchanged.

cases.name: 2023 Preliminary Town & Special District Budget

timeline.summary: The Board formally received the 2023 tentative town and special-district budgets from the Director of Finance, as required under New York State law before opening public hearings, and scheduled the preliminary-budget public hearing for November 16, 2022. The Supervisor previewed that the budget carries no town-tax increase and is structurally balanced.

The Director of Finance and Town Administrator presented the $37 million 2023 preliminary budget, a roughly 3% decrease from 2022 driven mainly by completion of the paving program, with a zero property-tax-rate increase for the second consecutive year and the levy well under the state tax cap. The Board praised the process and department heads for trimming costs; the Supervisor noted a roughly $700,000 fund-balance surplus was being rolled back in rather than drawn down. The public hearing was kept open until the December meeting for further resident comment.

cases.name: 731 North Broadway — Bedrock Plaza Corp Special Use Permit

timeline.summary: The Board received the application materials (short-form EAF, planning board recommendation) for Bedrock Plaza Corp's request for a special use permit to allow more than one residential use in a building within the Central Business zoning district, and scheduled the public hearing for January 11, 2023 at the applicant representative's request (citing vacant offices since August and a scheduling conflict later in January).

The Board closed the public hearing and unanimously approved Bedrock Plaza Corp's special use permit converting vacant second-floor office space into three additional apartment units, finding the conversion reduces required parking and improves an underused North Broadway property. The Town Planner and multiple Board members framed the project as evidence the town's existing zoning already accommodates the kind of housing the Governor's proposed statewide housing mandate was meant to force, and objected to that mandate.

cases.name: 162 Bedford Road (former Lombardi property) — AFFH Completion Deadline Extension

timeline.summary: The Board considered a request to amend Town Code §355-28 to extend the deadline for affordable housing (AFFH) units at the former Lombardi property to receive a certificate of occupancy from December 31, 2022 to December 31, 2024 (the applicant asked for 2025), citing delay in obtaining Westchester County Department of Health approval. The Board directed the Planning Director to prepare the amended local law and short-form EAF, referred it to the town and county planning boards, and scheduled a public hearing for January 11, 2023, without committing to a specific new deadline.

The Board opened and then adjourned the public hearing on extending the deadline for the affordable-housing (AFFH) units at 162 Bedford Road to reach 75% completion, pending a Planning Board recommendation. The applicant reported the long-delayed Westchester County Department of Health sign-off was imminent and the building permit could issue within days. The Board leaned toward a date-certain extension to December 31, 2024 (rather than an 18-months-from-permit-issuance alternative), while Councilman Berra reiterated that he personally wanted stronger assurance the affordable-unit reduction from 20% to 10% would actually translate into a completed project, given he had opposed the original reduction.

cases.name: Cross Road Town Parcel — Proposed Sale to Marinovic
cases.address: Cross Road (connecting Pine Ridge Road to Old Hickory Way)

timeline.summary: The Board discussed a request to sell a town-owned strip of land on Cross Road to adjoining landowners the Marinovics. After debate over sequencing, the Board directed the Town Attorney to first solicit an offer from the Marinovics and then obtain an appraisal (expanded in scope to also value the incremental benefit to the purchasing property) rather than ordering the appraisal first.

The Board received the real estate appraisal from RDN Valuations for the town-owned Cross Road parcel. The Town Attorney reported he had reached out to the Marinovics' counsel for a purchase offer but had not yet received a reply, and confirmed a second neighboring party had also expressed interest; the Board asked him to follow up and solicit a written bid from whichever party remained interested.

cases.name: 62-64 Cox Avenue — Breezemont Day Camp Zoning Legalization

timeline.summary: The Board received the applicant's proposed local law to make day camps a permitted or special-permit use in residential districts, which would legalize longtime day camp operator Breezemont's non-conforming status and let it make facility improvements. The Board declared itself lead agency and referred the proposal to the town and county planning boards, while flagging density (60 campers/acre, 1,000-camper cap), a resident's complaint about the camp's PA system, staffing levels, and the precedent of prior legalizations (citing gas station legalizations) as issues to work through before a hearing.

With a positive Planning Board recommendation that eliminated special events and required a formal parking/shuttle plan (Breezemont reported reaching an off-site parking agreement with Hillside Church), the Board scheduled the public hearing on the zoning text amendment and expressed strong, unanimous support, several members calling Breezemont a beloved, longstanding community asset.

cases.name: Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) — Catalyze Energy, 10 New King Street (ESRG Peer Review)
cases.applicant: Catalyze Energy (represented by Doug Ward, Snyder & Snyder)

timeline.summary: Catalyze Energy petitioned the Board to adopt a battery energy storage system (BESS) local law, based on a NYSERDA model code, that would permit BESS facilities in the IND-AA industrial zoning district, and presented its own proposed 5-megawatt/20-megawatt-hour project for the district near the New York City reservoir watershed. The Board found the proposal directionally attractive (grid resilience, resident bill credits) but, led by Councilwoman DiGiacinto, raised serious fire-safety and watershed-contamination concerns after she attended a fire commissioners' meeting on the topic, and pushed to engage independent fire/hazmat experts and DEP input before scheduling a public hearing. The Board declared itself lead agency and referred the matter for planning board input rather than setting a hearing date, calling that premature.

The board received ESRG's code-compliance peer review and additional-considerations memo on Catalyze Energy's proposed battery energy storage system at 10 New King Street (the town's only IND-AA district, ~900 ft from Kensico Reservoir). Members voiced strong opposition, citing extensive fire-training burdens on volunteer departments, potential month-long thermal-runaway fires and noxious fumes, reservoir/pollution risk, and little local benefit for a for-profit developer. North White Plains and Armonk fire departments were reported as not supporting it. The board voted only to receive the report; Roland noted the applicant understands it will not be placed on another agenda, though members invited any 'particularly compelling' new mitigation information.

cases.name: Senior & Disability Property Tax Exemption Sliding-Scale Local Law

timeline.summary: The Board scheduled a February 8, 2023 public hearing on adopting new RP-459-C (persons with disabilities and limited income) and RP-467 (senior) sliding-scale property tax exemption levels, following the Town Assessor's recommendation, but declined the Assessor's suggestion to also allow deduction of unreimbursed Medicare expenses from income, citing the inability to verify eligibility and unbudgeted fiscal exposure (an estimated jump from 29 to as many as 100 eligible households). One member raised a concern that state/county guidance language does not clearly guard against applicants artificially lowering reported income via business or capital losses, and asked staff to research whether additional safeguard language was legally permissible.

The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the local law amending Chapter 288 (Article II Senior Citizens Tax Exemption and Article III Exemptions for Persons with Disabilities), conforming to the county's new expanded income sliding scale — the first increase to these thresholds in about a decade. A member flagged that the scale jumps from a 50% exemption at $50,000 income down to 5% at roughly $58,000, and raised concern that the exemption has no asset test, meaning someone with significant liquid wealth but low reported taxable income could still qualify; the Board agreed to have the Assessor track participation and report back annually so the law can be revisited if needed.

cases.name: 360 Main Street (Sunoco) — Outdoor Display & Sales Special Use Permit
cases.applicant: Ziden Realty Corp (represented by Corey Salomon, Zarin & Steinmetz)

timeline.summary: The Board received Ziden Realty Corp's special use permit application to allow outdoor display and sales (firewood, wiper fluid, salt, propane, etc.) in front of the Sunoco gas station/convenience store at 360 Main Street, and referred it to the town and county planning boards. A Board member raised a sidewalk-clearance question (minimum walkway width for pedestrians) that the Town Attorney and applicant's counsel disagreed about applying to this location, and another asked what would happen to the special permit if the building were later demolished or substantially altered (staff confirmed it would require a new amended site plan/special permit).

With a positive Planning Board recommendation in hand and the applicant confirming the outdoor display area would maintain the required four-foot-wide pedestrian sidewalk clearance, the Board scheduled the public hearing for April 12, 2023.

cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue — Mixed-Use Residential Development ("The Gardens", 45 Bedford Road LLC)
cases.applicationType: special use permit (site plan review to follow at Planning Board)
cases.lastStatus: referred to Town and County Planning Boards; special use permit public hearing set for June 14, 2023

trajectory.status: informal design review, no vote taken
referred to Town and County Planning Boards; special use permit public hearing set for June 14, 2023

timeline.status: informal design review, no vote taken
timeline.summary: In an early design-review session, the applicant presented a substantially revised concept for the three Bedford Road-facing buildings — rotated to present gutter lines to the street (matching the rest of the block), lowered to two stories (about 10 feet shorter than the three-story buildings elsewhere on site), pulled out of the deed-restricted setback area, and set close to the sidewalk with traditional clapboard/shutter detailing, cobblestone accents, and street trees intended to evoke a historic Armonk streetscape. The board received the Bedford Road revisions very favorably as a major visual improvement, while flagging that the Maple Avenue-facing (taller, three-story) buildings had not yet been fully rendered and that density/taxation-form tradeoffs remained an open concern for at least one board member.

timeline.status: referred to Town and County Planning Boards; special use permit public hearing set for June 14, 2023
timeline.summary: The applicant presented updated renderings showing the Maple Avenue-facing buildings lowered by four feet (to 26 feet at mid-roof, still three stories) and a mix of enclosed and exposed garages responding to prior board feedback, framing the plan as a substantially improved iteration after roughly a year of revisions. Board discussion centered on density (units and overall square footage relative to the site's actual buildable acreage), the visual impact of exposed/uncovered garages, wetland-buffer encroachment by some units, and — most contentiously — whether the town's key "gateway" view of St. Stephen's Church driving down Maple Avenue would be preserved; one member pushed hard for a costly (~$20,000) fully rendered video simulation before further board sign-off, which a majority felt was premature ahead of Planning Board input and instead agreed to request three additional static rendered views (from Route 22, and both directions along Maple Avenue) once Planning Board comments are incorporated. The board voted to refer the application to the Town and County Planning Boards and set a public hearing on the special use permit for June 14, with one member abstaining from the referral vote rather than voting no.

cases.name: Fourth Two-Year Extension of Special Use Permit — Park Place Long-Term Parking Structure
cases.applicant: Park Place ownership (represented by counsel; project referenced in connection with Bill and Chris Fisher)

timeline.summary: The board approved a third two-year extension of the special use permit for a long-term parking structure near the county airport, whose current site plan approval was set to expire in August. Counsel cited ongoing delays tied to a Westchester County water-availability issue (the subject of the New King Street water-main IMA elsewhere on this agenda) rather than litigation, which had previously been resolved. The board asked about project economics given interest-rate changes but did not condition the extension on further review.

The board received a letter and adopted a resolution granting a fourth two-year extension (to July 2027) of the special use permit for a mechanized long-term parking structure. The applicant explained the delay was due to water-service issues with Westchester County that are now largely resolved, with the county bringing public water along New King Street. Counsel noted public water (not a well) is required partly because nearby wells were contaminated and for fire prevention. Motion passed on a voice vote.

cases.name: Catalyze Energy Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) — New King Street
cases.lastStatus: under review; local law/special permit framework to be drafted

trajectory.status: under review; local law/special permit framework to be drafted

timeline.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to execute an intermunicipal agreement with Westchester County for construction of a water main on New King Street within Water District No. 8, which board members noted would help resolve water-availability constraints affecting the Park Place parking structure and, pending a separate district-extension petition, could eventually serve the Eagle Ridge/airport campus site.

timeline.status: under review; local law/special permit framework to be drafted
timeline.summary: ESRG presented its board-commissioned peer review of Catalyze Energy's proposed grid-connected battery energy storage system on New King Street (in the town's only IND-AA district), finding the initial application lacked sufficient detail against New York State fire code requirements for BESS, and offering additional recommendations given how new the technology is. The Town Planner recommended the Board decide whether to permit BESS use in that district at all and, if so, adopt a special-permit local law based on the NYSERDA model ordinance incorporating ESRG's recommendations, with fire department and NYC DEP input given the site's proximity (about 900 feet) to the Jessica (Kensico) Reservoir system; the applicant confirmed the site would be effectively exclusive on that electrical line due to grid capacity limits.

cases.name: Live Televising of Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) Meetings

timeline.summary: A work session examined whether to televise ZBA meetings live, as is already done for Town Board and Planning Board meetings. ZBA Chairman Joe Monacelli said the board was not ready to start, citing an upcoming loss of a longtime member and difficulty maintaining a quorum, and suggested waiting until 2024. Resident advocate Ed Lowerman argued strongly for immediate live televising, citing transparency, precedent-setting variance decisions, and that most residents (especially seniors) will not seek out recorded meetings online. No vote was taken; the board indicated it would continue to explore the issue.

Following the prior work session, the Board voted to require live NCTV broadcast of ZBA meetings (approximately $325/meeting, with archived on-demand viewing at no extra charge), moving forward faster than the ZBA chairman's earlier suggestion of waiting until 2024. Implementation was contingent on availability of the town's videographer, targeted for the ZBA's next meeting.

cases.name: Special Use Permit Extension — Gateway Residential Redevelopment (former Mariani Gardens)
cases.applicant: The Gateway / Toll Brothers (JD Sumer representing applicant)

timeline.summary: After extensive negotiation, the Board closed the public hearing and adopted (by roll call vote) a resolution granting the special use permit for the townhouse redevelopment of the former Mariani Gardens/nursery site, incorporating Planning Board recommendations on reduced building height, corrected room labeling (den/office rooms without unauthorized closets), and building-coverage relief. A major point of debate was pedestrian connectivity: rather than commit to an uncertain sidewalk/walkway easement across a reluctant private landowner's property into Armonk Square, the board and applicant agreed to a hybrid approach — the applicant commits to building a sidewalk to the Maple Avenue bus stop, with a $250,000 community-benefit payment in lieu of the Armonk Square walkway if the necessary easement cannot be secured. The board also directed that community-benefits-agreement (CBA) provisions be tightened to ensure future ownership transfers (beyond outright sale) trigger CBA acceleration.

The applicant requested a second one-year extension of the special use permit for the Gateway multi-family redevelopment at the former Mariani Gardens site. Instead of a full year, the board granted only a short extension to July 23, 2025, conditioned on the applicant paying delinquent taxes (a $49,016.82 payment including penalties was made the day of the meeting) and bringing the eyesore vacant property into compliance with the town's property-maintenance code (Chapter 241) — including removing stored rock/equipment, filling the excavation, and mowing. Supervisor Rende disclosed campaign donations from LLC members but affirmed impartiality. The motion, framed by special counsel Spolzino and moved by DiGiacinto, passed 4-1 on a roll-call vote with Councilman Berra opposed.

cases.name: Proposed Local Law — Short-Term Rental Regulations (Chapter 355)

timeline.summary: The Board reviewed a draft local law (originating from an earlier proposal by Volta) permitting EV charging stations as an accessory use in business, office and industrial zoning districts, limited to level 1 and level 2 (slower) chargers and capped at 20% of off-street parking, while prohibiting level 3 DC fast chargers and highway-destination advertising. Board members disagreed on whether excluding fast chargers unduly limited the benefit to residents versus protecting the town from becoming a highway-adjacent charging destination. The board declared itself SEQRA lead agency and referred the proposal to the county planning board, police and fire departments, with a public hearing to be scheduled around July 26.

The board continued its public hearing on a proposed local law regulating short-term rentals of homes, incorporating prior board and town-attorney comments. No residents spoke. The board agreed to add a sworn affirmation (class E felony if false) that the dwelling is the owner's primary residence at both permit-application points, but rejected DiGiacinto's proposals to limit short-term rentals to lots of one acre or greater and to require owner presence. Because the law amends the zoning chapter, the board could not adopt it without the pending Planning Board referral, so the hearing was adjourned to the March 11 meeting.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Recreation Center (Pickleball) at 100 Business Park Drive

timeline.summary: The Board received application materials for a special use permit to legalize an existing ~1,740 sq ft private employee gym and approve a new ~26,460 sq ft recreation area (11 indoor pickleball courts plus small retail/party space) inside a proposed mixed-use self-storage warehouse building, and referred the matter to planning boards with a September 13, 2023 hearing scheduled. A board member raised concerns about parking assumptions, whether use would be genuinely limited to town residents versus outside pickleball-league traffic, and — more broadly — the scale and setback reductions of recent warehouse development along Business Park Drive.

The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the SEQRA negative declaration approving the special use permit for the employee gym legalization and new 11-court indoor pickleball facility. A board member noted mixed feelings about the scale of recent warehouse development on Business Park Drive generally but supported the pickleball use itself as a good community amenity.

cases.name: Mittman Subdivision — 13-Acre Open Space Donation, 655 Bedford Road

timeline.summary: The applicant proposed subdividing roughly 20 acres adjacent to his estate into four lots (revised down from an original six-lot plan) — including a lot to be transferred to his daughter — while offering to donate two non-buildable lots totaling about five acres to the town, with permanent deed restrictions against building. The Board referred the donation to the Open Space Committee and referred the broader subdivision/addressing matter to the town's E-911 coordinator; the applicant noted Westchester Land Trust had declined the conservation-easement approach, leading to the direct-donation structure instead.

The Board accepted a roughly 13-acre open-space parcel donation adjacent to an existing town park, connected to the Mittman subdivision, following a favorable recommendation from the Open Space Committee; approval was conditioned on the town obtaining title insurance acceptable to the town attorney, and board members noted the donation expands contiguous town open space to nearly 24 acres and protects wetlands.

cases.name: Crescent and Star Lighting Ceremony for Ramadan

timeline.summary: The Board revisited a years-old, previously stalled idea to name the Wampus Park gazebo in memory of former Councilwoman and longtime Deputy Supervisor Becky Kitridge (served 1979-2011), favoring a tasteful plaque rather than prominent signage; because the Lions Club originally built and funded the gazebo and the Landmarks Preservation Committee has jurisdiction, the Board referred the matter to the LPC and the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board and asked Councilman Milim to raise it with the Lions Club before returning with a recommendation.
The board approved a request from Assad Giuliani for a crescent and star lighting ceremony in observation of Ramadan at Wampus Park on February 17. Approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Car Washes as Principal Permitted Use in P.O.I. District — 125 Business Park Drive (Basis Acquisitions)
cases.lastStatus: public hearing continued; adjourned without a set date

trajectory.status: public hearing continued; adjourned without a set date

timeline.summary: The Board reconvened a hearing on a petition from Basis Industrial Acquisitions LLC to amend the zoning code to allow car washes as a principal permitted use in the P.O.I. (planned light industrial) district at 125 Business Park Drive, and adjourned the hearing without discussion to the October 25, 2023 meeting.

timeline.status: public hearing continued; adjourned without a set date
timeline.summary: Basis Industrial Acquisitions presented a detailed proposal for a single-bay, full-service car wash with 21 parking spaces, a 39-foot front-setback variance, PFAS-free chemicals with 90%+ water recycling, and low projected volume (roughly 5-10 cars/hour); the Board spent extensive time on stacking/queue capacity, PFAS well-water testing conditions, noise, and whether a car wash counts as a 'personal service' consistent with the comprehensive plan. Neighboring Business Park Drive tenants (Arrow Hardware/Al Mayolo and Joe Gellard, a former owner of the parcel who recounted a contentious eminent-domain history tied to the town's search for a water source for the Eagle Ridge project) objected, citing queue-length spillover onto the street, incompatibility with the comprehensive plan, and unresolved neighborhood flooding they attribute to nearby development. The Board agreed it needed more information and a fuller response to the Planning and County Planning Board memos before proceeding, and adjourned the hearing without setting a return date.

cases.name: Refuse, Recyclables Collection/Transfer/Disposal Services — Bid Award (2024-2029)

timeline.summary: The Board authorized the town to go out to bid for collection, transfer, and disposal of refuse and recyclables for residential and commercial properties townwide, following an executive session the prior week to finalize added/alternate bid items.

After a lengthy debate — including a 330-response resident survey (roughly 40% wanting the status quo, 50% wanting weekly single-stream pickup at about $80,000/year more, 10% wanting twice-weekly pickup) and Sustainability Committee testimony that single-stream recycling causes about 30% contamination and would effectively cost more than trash disposal by devaluing recovered mixed paper — the Board awarded the new multi-year refuse and recycling contract while keeping the existing dual-stream, alternate-week recycling system rather than switching to weekly single-stream, citing cost (roughly a half-percent tax-rate equivalent) and environmental contamination concerns. The Board also secured a side-letter commitment from the contractor to credit the town for its new food-scrap composting program, and directed the Sustainability Committee to spend the next year researching the tradeoffs (including surveying residents jointly with the town) before revisiting the single- vs. dual-stream decision, which the contractor confirmed can be changed annually.

cases.name: IBM Community Park Artificial Turf Field — DEC Letter & Soil Fill Characterization

timeline.summary: The Board approved a roughly $125,000 proposal from Keller & Sessions Engineering (part of an estimated $2.7 million total project) to prepare bid documents, soil testing, and a stormwater pollution prevention plan for converting IBM Community Park fields 1 and 2 to artificial turf, framed as addressing overuse of existing grass fields (cited in a 600-household survey) by roughly seven-fold increasing playable capacity. A resident (Larry) questioned whether the pre-bid spend was justified and whether IBM's fields actually have drainage problems (as opposed to Lombardi Park, which does); board members disputed the drainage claim for IBM but agreed on the need for engineering work before any construction decision.

The board received a May 2, 2025 letter from the NYS DEC and a May 12, 2025 preliminary soil fill materials characterization from Hydro Environmental Solutions for the IBM Community Park artificial turf field improvements. The Supervisor noted the excavated material was confirmed clean and stable and can be reused at other town sites (Clove Field, Quarry Heights park), saving carting and fill costs by using town staff and equipment.

cases.name: Core Sports Physical Therapy — Recreational Training Center Special Use Permit, 130 Business Park Drive
cases.applicant: Core Performance of Westchester LLC (Core Sports Physical Therapy)

timeline.summary: A 10-year tenant physical therapy practice sought a special use permit to formally delineate roughly 4,000 square feet of its space as a distinct youth/adult sports-development recreational training use (separate from its medical physical-therapy operation, for insurance-liability reasons), largely restoring pre-COVID group training programming. The Board received the application materials, discussed whether the use is closer to 'medical' than 'recreational' for parking-calculation purposes, and referred it to the Town and Planning Boards with a public hearing scheduled for November 29, 2023.

Following a favorable Planning Board recommendation and no anticipated negative impacts, the Board closed the public hearing and adopted a resolution approving the special use permit formalizing Core Sports's recreational training space as distinct from its medical physical-therapy use.

cases.name: Board of Ethics Code of Ethics Amendments (Staggered Terms, Recusal, Disclosure)
