cases.applicant: Town of North Castle Board of Ethics

timeline.summary: The Board of Ethics formally requested a public hearing on three code amendments: staggered terms for alternate ethics board members, expanding the recusal/abstention requirement to cover interests held within the prior six months, and revised annual real-estate-interest disclosure requirements. Town board members disagreed sharply over process — whether a joint work session with the Ethics Board should precede drafting the local law, or whether the board could proceed directly to a public hearing since the recommended language was already final and uncontroversial — with the disagreement echoing a similar process dispute from the prior meeting. The Board ultimately voted to schedule the public hearing directly for December 13, 2023, skipping a work session.

The Board held the public hearing and unanimously approved all three Board of Ethics-recommended code amendments: closing a resign-and-return loophole around recusal, staggering the terms of the two alternate ethics board members (requiring the current alternates to be reappointed to staggered five- and one-year terms), and expanding the annual real-estate disclosure statement to cover investment properties held by the officeholder/spouse and, more broadly, an enumerated list of relatives. The Board declined to fold a proposed 'advance notice of disclosure requirements at interview' practice into the formal code itself, agreeing instead it should be handled administratively (e.g., as part of the volunteer application process), and flagged a separate concern about possible campaign-contribution 'structuring' around the code's $500 recusal threshold for the incoming board to examine next year.

cases.name: Clove Road Ballfield Renovations, North White Plains
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (requested by Valhalla baseball league via Superintendent of Recreation & Parks Matt Trainor)
cases.lastStatus: approved; referred to Parks & Recreation Advisory Board

trajectory.status: approved; referred to Parks & Recreation Advisory Board

timeline.summary: Superintendent of Recreation & Parks Matt Trainor requested authorization to have Keller & Sessions prepare a no-cost renovation proposal for the Clove Road field's outfield/infield grading and a longstanding clay 'lip' problem, following a request from Valhalla baseball league (Bob Candria) and echoing a roughly decade-old, repeatedly-deferred community request. Board members raised process concerns about moving forward without first vetting the scope through the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board and consulting other groups that use the field (as had been done for the IBM Community Park turf project), but agreed to authorize seeking a proposal while looping in the advisory board.

timeline.status: approved; referred to Parks & Recreation Advisory Board
timeline.summary: The Board approved a Keller & Sessions survey and consulting-services proposal to assess whether a capital drainage/grading project is actually needed at the Clove Road field, after the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board itself was split on whether the issue required capital spending versus maintenance, and referred the matter back to that advisory board given a decade-long resident request (via Little League volunteer Bob Candria) for improvement.

cases.name: 2024 Town and Special Districts Preliminary Budget

trajectory.status: public hearing opened (first of two hearings)

timeline.status: public hearing opened (first of two hearings)
timeline.summary: Director of Finance Abbas Surah presented the $39.2 million 2024 preliminary budget (up 5.3% year over year, driven by inflation, new labor contracts, and higher pension contributions), funded 60% by property taxes and 40% by other revenue (PILOT agreements with IBM and Eagle/Berman, sales tax, interest income, and strong building-department revenue). The total tax levy is $23.3 million, roughly $2 million under the state's 2% tax cap, and the town-portion tax rate is projected flat versus 2023 for the median $1.2 million home. The Board opened the first of two required budget hearings, with the second scheduled for the sole December meeting.

The Board closed the second and final public hearing and adopted the 2024 town budget with a 0% increase in the town tax rate, which the Director of Finance described as structurally balanced; a minor adjustment was made using fund balance after department budget requests changed slightly (notably an unbudgeted increase in insurance rates) between the initial presentation and adoption.

cases.name: Armonk Close (Lumberyard) — Reduce AFFH Units from Four to Two

timeline.summary: Developer Mike Ferrari asked (bifurcating off a separate future request to relocate units to 470 Main Street) that the board amend the zoning code so his 20-unit condo project could immediately reduce its affordable requirement from four units (20%) to two (10%), rather than waiting for the code's existing incentive that automatically drops it to two upon obtaining COs/75% completion by June 30, 2025. His stated need was to finalize a condo offering plan now (his attorney said the unit-count uncertainty prevents filing). The board debated whether the uncertainty truly blocks marketing; Berra opposed advancing it (fearing it as leverage for the later relocation request), Hussain said he would hold at 20%, and Milim viewed it as only a marketing-convenience with no real delay. Ferrari, frustrated, withdrew the request after concluding the votes were not there; no action taken.

Developer sought confirmation that, having reached over 80% completion (verified by the building inspector), the affordable (AFFH) requirement drops from 20% (four units) to 10% (two units), so its offering plan can be filed with the Attorney General. Hussain and Berra objected that the justification rested on the applicant's own attorney's letter rather than a direct AG statement, and that the letter's '0?' reference was confusing; Hussain wanted a commitment this was the last AFFH request. DiGiacinto and Milim held the reduction was clearly earned and appropriate. Adopted 3-2 by roll call (Milim aye, DiGiacinto aye, Hussain no, Berra no, Rende yes), with an added recital that the developer is well beyond 80% complete.

cases.name: Public Water System Easement Agreement (Summit Club)
cases.applicant: Del Bello Donnellan Weingarten Wise & Wiederkehr (Mark Weingarten) for the Summit Club

timeline.summary: The applicant seeks to convert the temporary special use permit for the golf club into a permanent one, covering operational parameters (up to 500 members, a 100-child summer camp, events, and 10 guest cottages) plus a related parking variance and the maintenance-facility site plan. After lengthy discussion, the board voted to refer the matter to the local and county planning boards (leaving the ZBA parking-variance referral to come through the planning board) and to schedule a public hearing for May 22, 2024. Town Planner Adam Kaufman framed the item and Attorney Roland advised on procedure; both referral and hearing motions carried on voice votes. Members pressed for a single consolidated submission and for tighter limits on events, cottages, social membership, and the duration of public golf access.
The board approved a public water system easement agreement for the Summit Club project and authorized the supervisor to sign it.

cases.name: Proclamation — Adoption of the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism

timeline.summary: Supervisor Rende read a proclamation declaring May 2024 Jewish American Heritage Month in the Town of North Castle, developed together with Councilman Matt Milim. The board moved to authorize the Supervisor to sign and date it effective May 8, 2024. Adopted unanimously by voice vote.

The board read and adopted a proclamation recognizing the growing problem of antisemitism and adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition, including its 11 contemporary examples, and directing town agencies (including the police department) to make it available as an educational resource. A council member gave an impassioned statement citing FBI hate-crime and ADL statistics and a recent neo-Nazi rally in nearby Greenwich. Adopted unanimously by voice vote effective May 8, 2024.

cases.name: Residential Contract of Sale to Oliver and Samantha Baranovic (0.334 acres)
cases.address: Town-owned parcel contiguous to 101 Old Hickory Way, Bedford (Crossroad)

timeline.summary: The board received a request from the Bonistalls to acquire a vacant town-owned lot the town obtained through an in rem tax foreclosure (roughly $12,000 in tax arrears accumulated over ~10 years) that the owner wishes to merge into his residence under a covenant against further subdivision. Town Attorney Roland explained the history and noted the assessor should value the parcel with and without the restriction and that any sale cannot be a gift of town funds. The board referred the matter to the town attorney, the assessor, and the Planning Board (highway foreman deemed unnecessary) by motion and vote.

The board approved a residential contract of sale of a 0.334-acre town-owned parcel contiguous to 101 Old Hickory Way for a private, non-gated driveway, authorizing the Supervisor to sign. The buyers had spent since 2022 obtaining RPRC, Conservation Board, wetland, and culvert-mitigation approvals, and the contract includes a covenant surviving closing that keeps the passageway open for town emergency-vehicle access. The price was reviewed by the assessor and is stated in the contract. The board first received a related letter from an interested neighbor into the file, then approved the sale, which is subject to permissive referendum by statute. Passed by voice vote.

cases.name: The Enclave (Toll Brothers, formerly Airport Campus/MBIA site) — Water District Improvements Acceptance
cases.applicant: Airport Campus developer (counsel Chris Carthy team) / KSCJ Consulting

timeline.summary: Second read of the water district contribution and capital expenditure agreement following the prior extension of Water District 8 to include the airport campus. The board received the KSCJ Consulting cost memo (June 5, 2024) and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement, which uses privately financed development to build out public water (Westchester Joint Waterworks) and lays groundwork to interconnect with Water District 4. Counsel projected closing/construction around 2025 subject to DOT and DEP approvals.

The board adopted a resolution accepting and dedicating water district improvements (pump station, water tank, mains) built as part of the Enclave's 125-townhome redevelopment of the former MBIA/airport campus site, including a temporary-power provisioning plan pending permanent ConEd service, so the developer can obtain certificates of occupancy for units already under contract (first phase of 19 townhomes closing in August). Board members noted the project's community benefit of bringing new municipal water capacity to the area and that the development will be fully taxed rather than under a PILOT arrangement.

cases.name: Breezemont Day Camp (HZBR LLC) — Special Use Permit (Schedule Public Hearing)

timeline.summary: Received the LPC recommendation to landmark the historic Armonk barber pole and scheduled a public hearing for July 10, 2024. Members confirmed the business owner is enthusiastic and asked that owner consent/maintenance documentation be delivered to the Town Attorney before the hearing; the designation is understood to cover the pole itself.

Received the special use permit application and short-form EAF (Part 1) for operation of a summer day camp, now permitted after the town recently legalized day camps. The board scheduled the public hearing, coordinating with the Planning Board (July 8) and setting the town board hearing for July 10, 2024; not time-sensitive since operation would begin next summer.

cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue (Wren of the Woods) — Community Benefits Agreement Amendment Request
cases.applicant: Remix / 12 Maple Owner LLC (counsel Tony Veneziano; Stefan Martinovich)
cases.lastStatus: received; referred to town attorneys for review, no decision

trajectory.status: received; referred to town attorneys for review, no decision

timeline.summary: Authorization for the Supervisor to sign a Community Benefits Agreement providing $100,000 (over seven years) plus parking mitigations for a ~3,600 sq ft restaurant, after the ZBA waived 33 of 48 required spaces and the Planning Board conditioned site plan approval on a CBA. Berra objected that Section 2F's transfer language guts the acceleration provision and pressed to personally review the private parking leases; DiGiacinto objected to the seven-year (front-loaded gap) schedule, the $100,000 amount, and valet-parking impacts on Armonk Square, and also wanted the leases. Applicant argued total mitigation value (~$2.1M) far exceeds comparable CBAs. Adopted 3-1 by roll call (Milim aye, Berra aye, DiGiacinto no, Rende yes; Hussain had dropped off Zoom), conditioned on board members viewing the leases by June 18, moving the payment schedule up one year, and adding an anti-precedent sentence.

timeline.status: received; referred to town attorneys for review, no decision
timeline.summary: The applicant's principal argued at length that, since the Main Street parking district is now moving forward and 12 Maple Avenue would pay into it, the project's separate $100,000 Community Benefits Agreement parking-mitigation payment should be waived to avoid 'double-dipping' on the same parking-mitigation objective, citing planning department memos and a zoning board precedent. The board received the request and the applicant's July 6 litigation-hold letter, directed him to submit full written comments to the clerk, and referred the matter to the town attorneys for review; no vote was taken. Board members were sympathetic in principle but noted the CBA was negotiated with uncertainty about whether the parking district would ever materialize.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Little Sparrows Nursery School Expansion (Hillside Church of Christian Ministry Alliance)
cases.applicant: Hillside Church of the Christian Missionary Alliance (attorney Stephen Veneruso)

timeline.summary: The board received the application to modify an existing special use permit to legalize the Little Sparrows nursery school operating six classrooms when the permit only allowed two — discovered during interior renovation permitting. The school (~60 children) also needs one likely variance for outdoor-recreation-space square footage (code requires 200 sq ft per child). The board scheduled a public hearing for July 24 and referred the application to the town and county planning boards, coordinating timing with the ZBA (meeting July 11) so the applicant can resolve everything before the September school year.

Public hearing on a special use permit to legalize enlargement of the Little Sparrows Nursery School from two to six classrooms, which the school had been operating for years under an old two-classroom permit. Attorney Veneruso explained a needed outdoor-recreation-space variance (code requires 200 sq ft/child; ~800 sq ft available for a typical max of 11-12 children) would still be sought from the ZBA. The board adopted a negative declaration and then a resolution granting a one-year special use permit conditioned on the ZBA variance, building-department sign-off and fire approval, and closed the hearing. Members praised the school as a good neighbor; Berra flagged a deteriorating retaining wall at the parking lot as a safety housekeeping item.

cases.name: Two-Way Radio Communications Satellite Receiver System — Metrocom Wireless Proposal
cases.applicant: Metrocom Wireless Incorporated (via Town Administrator Kevin)

timeline.summary: The board approved and authorized the Supervisor to sign a Metrocom Wireless proposal (off state bid, meeting procurement policy) to replace the town's 20-year-old analog police radios with an encrypted digital system, funded from general-fund balance. The system brings the Highway Department onto the same network so police and highway can communicate directly during storms and emergencies, and eliminates dead spots where cell service fails. Approved by voice vote.

At the police chief's request, the board approved funding a two-way radio communications satellite receiver system and a Metrocom Wireless Inc. proposal of roughly $14,000 to replace older equipment and eliminate communication dead spots. The expandable system will also serve highway, water and sewer and enable cross-department coordination in emergencies. Adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Discussion — Allocation of Funds for Capital Projects / Capital Reserve Funds

timeline.summary: Prompted by the new Road Naming Committee liaison appointment, DiGiacinto asked the board to clarify what a liaison position entails, noting members are neither chair nor committee member but a bridge to the town board. Rather than a formal work session, the board reached consensus to have staff (Eliana, via Administrator Hay) draft guidelines, with members submitting their own input, referencing Barone's recollection that liaisons historically served as an information bridge.

At DiGiacinto's request the item was discussed in public session. Town Administrator Kevin Hay explained the two types of state capital reserve funds (specific vs. type, each with capital-improvement and equipment subcategories), the resolutions and permissive-referendum rules to establish or expend them, and the state comptroller's guidance that the town's healthy fund balance should be designated to specific projects (roughly no more than 15% of tax revenue undesignated). The board reached consensus to have the administrator and finance office refine project cost estimates (salt dome, turf fields, radio system, North Bridge, town-building maintenance) and then hold a work session before adopting establishing resolutions. DiGiacinto asked that library/town-building maintenance needs be folded in.

cases.name: 45 Hurlingham LLC — Wetland Mitigation Planting Bond Extension and 5-Year Maintenance/Monitoring Bond Extension

timeline.summary: On the town engineer's (KSCJ/Kellard) recommendation, the board approved extension of a wetland mitigation planting bond and a five-year extension of the maintenance and monitoring bond. The applicant said most work is complete and did not object to the town continuing to hold security. Added to the agenda late; approved by voice vote.

On the town engineer KSCJ's recommendation, the board approved a one-year extension of the wetland mitigation planting bond plus a corresponding five-year maintenance and monitoring bond extension. KSCJ had not yet verified all plantings were complete; attorney Jerry Tortorella explained plantings were done but a contractor changeover delayed the as-built certification, after which a town inspection would start the five-year monitoring clock. Members confirmed the bonds are de minimis cash amounts. Approved.

cases.name: Summit Club Sewage Works Corporation and Standby Sewer District Formation
cases.address: Summit Club (formerly Brentwood/Whippoorwill) residential golf course community

trajectory.status: referred / public hearing to be scheduled (October 2024)

timeline.status: referred / public hearing to be scheduled (October 2024)
timeline.summary: Attorney Mark Winegarten presented the petition to form a privately-owned Summit Club Sewage Works Corporation (required by state law since the town declined to operate the plant itself) and an accompanying standby town sewer district that would only activate if the private operator defaults, plus stock-escrow, O&M, and easement agreements. The board received and referred all documents to the town attorney and authorized preparation of an order for an October public hearing. Water/sewer director Sal and Town Attorney Roland debated at length whether a provision letting the town inspect the plant on odor/resident complaints could create a de facto town obligation; the applicant's counsel maintained it created a right, not an obligation, and the board left the language as drafted pending the hearing.

Continuing from the September 11 meeting, the board approved the stock escrow agreement and the sewage works operation/maintenance agreement and license for the Summit Club Sewage Works Corporation. Water/sewer director Sal and Town Attorney Roland debated at length whether the operation-and-maintenance agreement's inspection clause improperly obligated the town to proactively monitor the plant; the board ultimately approved (rescinding and re-voting one item) with Sal's proposed amendment tying any town inspection right to a prior regulatory-agency non-compliance determination, to be run past the developer's counsel.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Gavi Restaurant Mixed-Use Building

timeline.summary: The board considered receipt of a special-use-permit application to add a 5,000 sq ft mixed-use building with first-floor retail plus two one-bedroom first-floor apartments and two two-bedroom second-floor apartments (four units total). The written application erroneously described the apartments as being only on the second floor; the applicant clarified the layout orally and will submit an amendment letter. The board referred the revised submission to the town and county planning boards and scheduled a public hearing for November 20, 2024 (moved one week from the originally noticed November 13 to allow adequate county/planning-board review time).

Public hearing on a special use permit for a new 5,000 sq ft mixed-use building with two ground-floor retail spaces and four apartments (two 1-bedroom on the first floor, two 2-bedroom on the second), with basement garages for tenants. County and Planning Board correspondence and the SEQRA short form were received; Town Planner Adam Kaufman confirmed no unusual county comments and that site-plan details return to the Planning Board. No residents spoke. The board closed the hearing, adopted a negative declaration, and adopted the resolution granting the permit (all by voice vote). Board members suggested (non-binding) bike racks and more permeable parking surfaces.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Chapter 60 — Residency Exemption for Building/Fire Inspector Titles

timeline.summary: The board considered receipt of a proposed local law amending Chapter 60 to change the residency requirement for the assistant building inspector (and fire inspector) from residing within the town to residing in New York State, matching the existing standard for the building inspector. Town Administrator Kevin explained Westchester County Human Resources requires this change in connection with a recent appointment. The board received the local law and scheduled a public hearing for October 23, 2024.

The board held a public hearing (no public comment) and adopted a local law using the home-rule exemption to relieve resident building inspector and fire inspector titles from the state's town-residency oath requirement, so long as they still live in New York State.

cases.name: Probationary Appointment — Jose Sala, Highway Department Mechanic

timeline.summary: The board approved the probationary appointment of Paul Taft as assistant building inspector, effective October 10, 2024, contingent on setting the Chapter 60 residency public hearing per Westchester County HR requirements. The position was budgeted and is part of a transition ahead of an expected retirement in the building department. Approved by voice vote with best wishes to Taft.
The board approved the probationary appointment of Jose Sala as a mechanic in the Highway Department, effective January 9, 2025, by voice vote.

cases.name: Conference Attendance — Kevin Neely, Assistant Assessment Clerk (NYS Assessors Cornell Conference)

timeline.summary: The board approved a request from Highway General Foreman Jamie Norris to attend the League of Municipalities Conference in Atlantic City, November 14-17, 2024, with lead mechanic Matthew Hirsch, using a town vehicle. The Supervisor encouraged board members and staff to treat such conferences (including the upcoming Association of Towns convention) as continuing education. Approved by voice vote.

The board approved Assistant Assessment Clerk Kevin Neely's attendance at the New York State Assessors Association Cornell Conference on July 14 and 15, 2025. Rende highlighted that Neely received a scholarship of up to $1,200, making the roughly $700 conference cost effectively no cost to the town, and noted its focus on artificial intelligence. Approved by voice vote with congratulations.

cases.name: AI Engineering Proposal — Quarry Heights Water District #9 Extension (Map, Plan & Report)
cases.applicant: Resident (Rob Kanana) / Westchester Joint Water Works

timeline.summary: During public comment, resident Rob Kanana (69 James Street) said the town board had not responded to his email about the Quarry Heights water-line project and voiced community anxiety over contamination, drought, temporary above-ground hookups freezing, and whether homes will be connected before the $1.1 million (DOJ consent-order-funded, Westchester Joint Water Works) money runs out in the rocky terrain. Supervisor Rende explained the process is unusually 'backwards' (no map-plan-report because the work is capped by available funds), apologized for missing his email, said the town knows little more than residents, and committed to a community meeting once next steps and cost-sharing are known. No vote; discussion only.

The board approved AI Engineering's proposal for the required map, plan and report to extend Water District No. 9 (Quarry Heights), the first legal step toward bringing water service to remaining area residents. The firm, already familiar with the terrain from prior feasibility and sewer work, will follow with a separate design/construction-management proposal; the town is also researching grant funding. A member confirmed any out-of-scope work would require board approval before payment. Motion carried.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit Application — Armonk Outdoor Art Show Closing Reception

timeline.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit application from Michelle Falkenstein for an opening reception for an art exhibit at the North Castle Public Library on December 7, 2024. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

The board approved an alcohol permit application for the Armonk Outdoor Art Show 'Armonk Has a Heart' closing reception at the North Castle Public Library on October 9, 2025. Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Work Session: Dedicated Pickleball Courts at Lombardi Park
cases.address: Lombardi Park (near Anthony Court), North Castle

timeline.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a proposal with Aquest to conduct a pre-demolition inspection of the old recreation building at Lombardi Park. Motion made and seconded, adopted by voice vote with no discussion.

Recreation Superintendent Matt Traynor and Town Engineer Joe Tramelli (Kellard Sessions) presented concept plans, developed from a 2023 ballfield-improvement study, to add four dedicated pickleball courts, a small maintenance building with ADA-compliant bathrooms, and additional parking at Lombardi Park, at a rough estimated cost of $300,000 for courts alone (or up to $1.4 million if ~70 new parking spaces were added) and roughly $800,000 for the maintenance building. The board and many residents debated alternative sites (Winkler Park, Wampus Park South/Mompus, IBM's paddle courts), noise impacts on Anthony Court and Winkler-area homes, whether to build in phases, and whether to fund the project from the town's recreation trust fund (roughly $582,000-$600,000, generated by developer fees, not tax dollars). No vote was taken; the board directed staff to develop firmer cost estimates and consider alternative locations for the displaced storage containers, with a future work session or meeting agenda item to follow.

cases.name: Zoning Text Amendment / Local Law — 23 Bedford Banksville Road light-industrial special use (CB-B)
cases.applicant: Greenwich Realty Group LLC (attorney Tony/Anthony Veneziano; owner Mark Masiello)

timeline.summary: Attorney for Greenwich Realty asked the board to reset a public hearing to legalize two interior industrial uses (wood processing and iron/aluminum assemblage) at a split-zoned CBB/GB property. Councilman Milim strongly objected that rezoning the whole parcel to GB (as originally proposed) would expand the potential for a warehouse/self-storage use that neighbors had opposed. After a brief executive session for counsel's advice, the board directed that instead the entire parcel be zoned CBB with the two uses added by special-use permit, and voted to schedule the public hearing for February 12, 2025, pending a re-referral to the county. DiGiacinto recused herself (her husband owns 25% of Band Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property).

A local law/zoning text amendment to create a narrowly-tailored light-industrial special use (wood processing and pre-cut metal/aluminum assemblage) applicable essentially only to this one 10.8-acre, 15,500 sq ft pre-1990 building, legalizing existing tenant operations while dropping a previously proposed self-storage use. Framed by the board as a compromise (worked out with planner Adam Kaufman and in executive session) to protect the Banksville hamlet from larger uses. The board opened and closed the public hearing, adopted a SEQRA negative declaration, and adopted the local law. Councilman Berra secured amendments requiring indoor storage, ventilation of fumes/odors, a 'not subsequently expanded' building limit, and town-board review/approval of the operation plan; a formal special-permit application will follow at a later meeting. DiGiacinto recused herself.

cases.name: North Castle Public Library Hourly Staff Salary Increases (effective Jan 1, 2026)

timeline.summary: The board approved hourly staff salary increases for library employees Diana Cunningham (hourly librarian), Karen Prophet (hourly librarian), Susan Medico (hourly clerk), and Nicholas Shallcross (hourly clerk), effective January 10, 2025. Passed by voice vote.

The board approved salary increases for the North Castle Public Library's hourly staff, effective January 1, 2026, consistent with the library director's memo and the budget. Adopted by voice vote after brief confirmation that the figures were budgeted.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit — Katona Classic Stage (Whippoorwill Hall)
cases.address: Whippoorwill Hall, North Castle Public Library, Armonk
cases.applicant: North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee

timeline.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit application from the North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee for a reception at Whippoorwill Hall on April 4, 2025 (7 PM), with a waiver of the permit fee. Members thanked committee members, including Ed Woodyard, for their work. Adopted by voice vote.
The board approved an alcohol permit application from Katona Classic Stage for theatrical performances at Whippoorwill Hall, April 24 to May 4, 2025. Routine motion carried.

cases.name: Public Hearing — 2026 Town and Special Districts Preliminary Budgets

timeline.summary: Public hearing on Board of Ethics-recommended amendments: barring a town board member/candidate from voting on matters involving anyone who contributed over $500 in the aggregate (effective no earlier than Jan 1, 2026), an apportionment rule for committee contributions, a failure-to-file-disclosure violation, applicant disclosure for real-property applications (27.6F), a bar on land-use committee members representing third parties (27.10), and a prohibition on electeds/department heads serving as political party officers (27.22-C). Supervisor Rende voiced strong opposition to the party-officer ban and mandatory contribution-based recusal as a First Amendment overreach, while other members largely supported the package with reservations. After extensive debate the board adjourned the public hearing (no adoption) and, by roll-call vote, referred both the Board of Ethics recommendations and Councilman Berra's redline changes to legal counsel for a written opinion, targeting reopening by roughly June 11.

Comptroller Abbas Sura presented the $43.7 million 2026 preliminary budget (about 3% appropriations increase), which produces a 4.81% property-tax-rate increase, uses about $3.2 million of fund balance, and overrides the state tax cap by roughly $600,000. Numerous residents objected to exceeding the tax cap and to reliance on reserves, arguing for deeper spending cuts; the board defended the plan as a fiscally responsible pivot away from years of over-hoarded reserves and deferred maintenance (citing one-off 2025 costs for roofs, salt domes, police radios, and lawsuits). No vote was taken; the board adjourned the public hearing to December 10 and agreed to hold additional public budget work sessions to look for cuts.

cases.name: Final Payment Requisition No. 1 — Southern Industries Corp. (Water District No. 4 / School Street Extension)

timeline.summary: The board awarded the construction bid for the Water District No. 4 School Street extension to Southern Industries Corp., following evaluation of 11 bids and a recommendation from the engineer's office. Members emphasized holding a pre-construction meeting as was successfully done on the prior (Casale) project. Motion carried.

The board considered the final payment requisition (~$33,900, including ~$11,600 miscellaneous additional-work allowance and a mobilization charge) to Southern Industries for the Water District No. 4 (School Street) extension, plus receipt of a general release. Councilman Berra questioned paying a mobilization charge to a contractor the town released for underperformance when a replacement contractor also had to be paid to mobilize. Supervisor Rende and Attorney Roland explained the release was a negotiated arrangement to separate quickly before winter and avoid a surety dispute. The requisition was approved by voice vote.

cases.name: Purchase of F-350 Pickup Truck for Parks Department

timeline.summary: The board approved purchasing a new Ford F-150 and F-250 for the water and sewer department through the Sourcewell cooperative contract, paid from the 2025 operating budget. The Supervisor confirmed with Sal that the vehicles were budgeted, came in under budget by over $2,000, and replace vehicles due for replacement. Adopted on a voice vote.

The board approved purchasing a Ford F-350 for the parks department from the National Auto Fleet Group through the Sourcewell contract, funded by the 2025 operating budget, at roughly a 3.5% discount. The Administrator confirmed it replaces a vehicle coming out of service. Adopted on a voice vote.

cases.name: Local Law amending Chapter 325 (Vehicles & Traffic), Section 325-55, Schedule 13 — No Parking Anytime on Old Mount Kisco Road
cases.address: Old Mount Kisco Road, Armonk (near Main Street / Wago Avenue)

timeline.summary: The board received a memo from Police Chief Simonson recommending an amendment to Chapter 325 (Vehicles and Traffic), Section 325-55, Schedule 13, to establish no-parking-anytime restrictions on portions of Old Mount Kisco Road, and scheduled a public hearing on the local law for June 11, 2025.

Amends the town code to prohibit parking on portions of Old Mount Kisco Road (east side from Main Street north to Crossroad; west side from Main Street to Wago Avenue) in response to years of resident complaints about hazardous parking by commercial employees on a narrow, curving residential road with heavy pedestrian use. Lt. McCormick presented photos and a safety analysis, noting NYSDOT had also agreed to add a stop sign at the Main Street intersection. A public hearing was opened, several residents spoke, and it was closed; the board adopted the local law (motion by Jose Berra, seconded by Barbara DiGiacinto), to be filed with the Secretary of State. Board members flagged a possible 'whack-a-mole' displacement of parked cars to be revisited if it arises.

cases.name: Payment Application No. 5 — Papatito Construction (Water District No. 4 New Well)

timeline.summary: The board awarded the bid to Papatito Construction Co. Incorporated for the Water District No. 4 new well site work and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement, by unanimous voice vote (water/sewer superintendent 'Sal' present and satisfied).

The board approved payment application number five to Papatito Construction for site work on the Water District No. 4 new well project. Town Administrator Kevin Hay reported strong progress, with the tank backfilled and the building expected early February. Motion made and all in favor.

cases.name: Receipt of Long Pond Dam 2025 Dam Safety Inspection Report

timeline.summary: The board approved a WSP USA proposal for engineering services for the Long Pond dam safety inspection, an obligation because DEC requires Class B dams to be inspected every four years. Supervisor Rende recused himself (a person had once consulted him about the matter in his capacity as a lawyer). Approved.
The board voted to receive the Long Pond Dam 2025 dam safety inspection report. Supervisor Rende recused himself as he has in the past. Received.

cases.name: Personnel Appointments — Librarian, Library Clerk, and Recreation Supervisor

timeline.summary: The board approved the probationary/provisional appointment of Irwin Hernandez as a Water and Sewer maintenance worker and the appointment of Luke Wynn Land as a seasonal road maintainer in the Highway Department, both effective June 16, 2025. Members welcomed the additions while noting the water/sewer department still needs more staff.

The board adopted three personnel actions effective November 10, 2025: the probationary/promotional appointment of Diana Wendell to full-time Librarian; the provisional promotional appointment of Michelle McDavid to full-time Library Clerk; and the provisional appointment of Kimberly Williams to Recreation Supervisor (Senior Citizens). Rende wished Williams luck and acknowledged the work of the outgoing Liz Duffy (staying on part-time). The librarian and clerk positions were noted as budgeted for 2025. All passed by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Mianus River Gorge — Special Use Permit for Scientific Research Center

timeline.summary: The board received a request from Mianus River Gorge Inc. for a special use permit for a scientific research center in a residential zone and scheduled the public hearing for August 13, 2025 (moved up from a proposed September 10). Executive Director Rod Christie explained the preserve has operated at the site since the 1950s and only recently learned a special use permit was needed in connection with a building project; it has already been through zoning and planning with no objections. Approved by voice vote to set the hearing.

The board opened and closed a public hearing on a special-use permit letting Mianus River Gorge, in operation since 1953, formalize/expand its scientific research center on ~960-1,200 protected acres in a residential zone. No neighbors spoke in favor or opposition. The board adopted a negative SEQRA declaration and the resolution granting the permit; site-plan approval to follow at the Planning Board. Motions carried unanimously by voice vote.

cases.name: KSCJ Consulting Memo — New Street Names/Addresses for Eagle Ridge; Referral to E911 Coordinator

timeline.summary: The board approved the road naming committee's recommendation to name the new Eagle Ridge subdivision roads 'Kesper Crossing' and 'Parkview Road,' with notification to the town's E-911 coordinator. Councilman Hussain recused himself because he works for IBM, which is adjacent to the property, then returned. Passed by voice vote as a routine item.

The board received a KSCJ Consulting memo (dated Jan. 13, 2025) assigning new street names and addresses for the Eagle Ridge development and referred it to the town E911 coordinator. Councilman Berra recused himself, citing his association with IBM and consistency with prior Eagle Ridge recusals. Passed with Berra recused.

cases.name: Ethics Code Amendments — Work Session

timeline.summary: The Ethics Board chair asked, during public comment, to resume the ethics-code public hearing (commenced April 9) on September 24. The board discussed that special counsel Bob Spolzino delivered his opinion May 28 but no board member has yet submitted written comments to counsel; the Supervisor and members set August 27 as the deadline for member comments. Counsel (Roland) advised that if substantive changes are made the existing hearing must be closed and a new hearing re-noticed and republished. No formal vote; targeted for the September 24 meeting.

Continuation of a multi-year effort to revise the town Ethics Code, held as a work session on a rewritten draft prepared by special counsel Bob Spolzino with Board of Ethics input. Key debates: adding a sentence so a campaign loan (even if repaid) is treated as a contribution; broadening the 'interest' definition to cover an applicant's relative, partner, or business associate (with concern that 'business associate' is undefined and legally vague); the effective date of a new $500 contribution-triggered recusal rule; and Section 5, which would force land-use applicants to disclose campaign contributions to board members. The board reached rough consensus to keep the loan/business-associate language, adopt a rule-of-necessity/abstention fix (moving the recusal cross-reference), and rework Section 5 so F1 disclosure applies only to Town Board applications while F2 (interest-based) applies to all boards. No vote taken; counsel will redraft and the item will be placed on a future agenda to schedule a public hearing.

cases.name: Trust for Public Land — Conservation Finance Feasibility Study (work session)
cases.applicant: Trust for Public Land / Open Space Committee

timeline.summary: The board approved three related actions with the Trust for Public Land: authorizing a letter requesting technical advice on funding sources for land conservation and open space, receiving TPL's conservation finance feasibility proposal (dated Aug 5, 2025) with referral to the town attorneys, and authorizing the Supervisor to sign the TPL professional services agreement subject to attorney approval. Each carried by voice vote. Praise was given to Planner Adam Kaufman and Carey Kazak / the Open Space Committee for their work.

TPL presented a draft feasibility study on funding options to establish a dedicated conservation/land-preservation fund: a real estate transfer tax under the Hudson Valley Community Preservation Act, a property-tax-funded special reserve, or general obligation bonds. No action was required as it was a work session. The board's clear consensus was to advance the real estate transfer tax option for voter polling, with several members opposing any property-tax increase. Next steps are a voter poll (which the board will review) aiming toward a possible November 2026 ballot referendum.

cases.name: Call for Public Hearing — Extension of Water District No. 9 (Quarry Heights, North White Plains)

timeline.summary: The board voted to receive the AI Engineers map, plan and report for a proposed extension of Water District #9 to serve the Quarry Heights area of North White Plains. Supervisor Rende explained this is the first formal step to bring safe public water to roughly 44 of 55 homes whose private wells have suffered drought-related dry-ups and high PFAS levels; the work is costly due to heavy rock, and the town will pursue grants (enlisting the visiting Governor's office representative). A well-attended, generally positive informational meeting was held the prior evening, and a landing page with Sal's presentation was created. Passed by voice vote (all in favor).

The board adopted, by roll-call vote, the order calling a public hearing on the long-awaited extension of Water District No. 9 to serve the Quarry Heights section of North White Plains, where residents have faced dry wells and high PFAS levels; water will be supplied by Westchester Joint Water. Members discussed notifying the roughly 44 additional (plus 11 original = ~55) affected property owners, who will share the bond/debt service; the board directed the Town Clerk to mail notice (regular/certified, not registered) with an affidavit of mailing, per counsel, and to post the order on the project landing page. Counsel outlined next steps (design, Health Department submittals, bidding, grants, and state comptroller approval after the hearing). Roll call recorded ayes from Vataj, DiGiacinto, Hussain and Supervisor Rende.

cases.name: Pool Structural Engineering (Macri Consulting) and Authorization to Bid

timeline.summary: A late-added bond resolution authorized up to $5M (15-year) in financing for town pool improvements so that design/engineering costs could be rolled into the bond rather than paid from fund balance. It provoked extended debate led by Berra over Section 5's broad delegation of the town board's powers (bond terms, form, credit enhancements) to the supervisor; Milim and special counsel Spolzino argued the terms are largely market-driven and the board retains authority over expenditures. It passed 4-1 on a roll call (Milim, Hussain, DiGiacinto, Rende aye; Berra no) and is subject to permissive referendum.

The board hired Macri Consulting for structural engineering of the pool deck (~$26,300) and authorized the town to go out to bid for the construction work, subject to Macri's specifications, to keep the project on schedule (bids by mid-February) to reopen the pool by early June. Members debated confusing agenda wording and whether they should review the bid specs before publication; staff explained professional services aren't bid and specs are published (Jan 6) before board review. The Macri hiring (5A) passed by voice vote; the authorization to bid (4E) passed on a roll call, with Berra voting yes despite wanting to see the plans.

cases.name: Authorization to Execute Consent Judgment — Towns Center LLC v. Town of North Castle

timeline.summary: The board authorized the town attorneys to execute consent judgments in the tax-certiorari matters of Armac 80 Associates, LLC (Index No. 63577-21) and 84 Business Park Associates (Index No. 63574-21). Approved by voice vote with no discussion.

The board authorized the town attorney to execute a consent judgment resolving Towns Center LLC v. Town of North Castle (index number 65584/21), approved by voice vote without discussion on the record.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Live Bow Corporation Cigar Bar and Social/Life Members Club

timeline.summary: The applicant's attorney presented an early-stage special use permit application for a members-only cigar lounge and social club in two vacant former retail units (previously an Oriental market) in the Sir John's shopping plaza at 911 North Broadway. The proposed low-intensity, self-contained lounge would offer lounge/table seating, cigar and accessory sales to members and guests only (not the general public), light food and beverage, a conference room, and no live entertainment, exterior alterations, or amplified sound; membership would be tiered and priced later, with occupancy capped by fire code and required parking (one space per three members plus one per seat). Board members asked about vacant-store history, projected membership size, parking calculations, alcohol/membership structures, and state tobacco licensing requirements, with no objections raised. The board voted to receive the application, refer it to the town and county planning boards, and schedule a public hearing for May 27, 2026.

The board held a continued public hearing on a special use permit for a members-only cigar bar and social club in a former bakery space (18 on-site parking spaces, 50-person occupancy). Extensive debate centered on whether to cap total club membership: the applicant's attorney argued strongly against any numeric membership cap as an overreach and inconsistent with how other membership clubs (gyms, country clubs) are regulated, while board members favored a cap to preserve control over intensity of use. After a closed-door recess, the board settled on a 150-member cap (with the ability for the applicant to return and request an increase), added a condition specifically permitting cigar/cigarette smoking while excluding hookah and marijuana use (per the applicant's own proposal), and closed the hearing before adopting the special use permit resolution as amended.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Town Code Chapter 325 (Vehicle & Traffic) — One-Way Streets, No-Parking, and Off-Street Parking on William Street, McClure Street, and Old Orchard Street, North White Plains
cases.address: William Street, McClure Street, and Old Orchard Street, North White Plains (Corey/Quarry Heights)
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Reagan Huffnagle) and Highway Department

timeline.summary: The board received a memo from Police Chief Reagan Huffnagle proposing amendments to Town Code Chapter 325 (Vehicle and Traffic): changing the direction of travel on a one-way street, adding 'no parking any time' restrictions on portions of William Street, McClure Street and Old Orchard Street, and amending an off-street parking area, all in North White Plains. The board voted to receive the memo and separately voted to schedule a public hearing on the proposals for May 27, 2026. One member cautioned that not everyone in the affected area may support the changes and urged that the hearing be well publicized; another noted some of the proposals originated from area residents themselves rather than only the police and highway departments.

Following renovation of the Corey (Quarry) Heights park (including a new basketball court), the police chief and highway foreman recommended making William Street one-way southbound from James Street to Old Orchard Street and prohibiting parking on William and McClure Streets, citing dangerously narrow (13-14 foot) roadway widths that block emergency vehicle access. Several Quarry Heights residents objected strongly, tying the proposal to broader frustration over the town's handling of the park project and an unresolved multi-year PFAS well-water contamination crisis in the neighborhood; other residents supported the safety rationale, citing a documented ambulance-access delay. The board adopted the local law by voice vote, while directing police/highway staff to reconsider the proposed no-parking restriction on the single block of Old Orchard Street as potentially counterproductive.

cases.name: Proposed Crosswalk Evaluation and Design (Old Route 22, near DEC lot/Beehive)
cases.applicant: NYC Department of Environmental Protection (permit); North Castle Police Department

timeline.summary: The board approved a five-year confirmation and renewal of NYC Department of Environmental Protection land-use permit conditions for the DEP-owned parking lot on Old Route 22. Councilman Jose Berra raised a long-standing need for a marked crosswalk near the lot (across from Beehive), noting the permit affirmatively allows the town to make safety modifications, that he had discussed it with Police Chief Reagan Huffnagle (who was supportive) and previously with former Chief Simonson, and that Town Planner Adam Kaufman had already researched the issue and had a pending grant request to the county. The board discussed the likely modest cost of a required traffic-engineering siting study plus curb/ADA-ramp and paint work, and directed staff to obtain a cost estimate so the board could decide whether to proceed immediately or wait on the grant. The DEP permit renewal itself passed on motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

The board considered a roughly $9,500 two-phase proposal (about $3,000 for a traffic study, $6,500 for design) to evaluate and design a pedestrian crosswalk across old Route 22 near a leased DEC parking lot and a restaurant, citing a handful of past traffic incidents in the vicinity. Several board members argued the expense was unnecessary for a straightforward crosswalk on a demapped town road and that town staff (highway foreman, police lieutenant, town planner) could assess and implement it directly. The board tabled the proposal so staff could evaluate it in-house first, with the understanding that an outside engineering study would still be pursued if staff determined it necessary.

cases.name: Zoning Text Amendment — Recreation Centers Permitted in RELAB District
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (prompted by a boutique cycling-studio proposal)

timeline.summary: The board received the planning board's positive recommendation and comment letters from the county planning board and NYC DEP on a proposed zoning text amendment to add recreation centers as a permitted principal use in the RELAB district. The change was prompted by a proposed 17-bike boutique cycling studio on Business Park Drive, whose principals presented their concept. Board members were broadly supportive but wanted to evaluate area-wide traffic and parking capacity before final action, and scheduled a public hearing for the January 26 meeting.

cases.name: Outdoor Dining / Temporary Tent Regulations Extension

timeline.summary: The board extended North Castle's COVID-era temporary outdoor-dining and tent regulations for the three hamlets from a May 31 expiration to October 1, 2022, after Supervisor Schiliro relayed that restaurants needed a longer commitment window before investing in tents given supply-chain costs. Discussion covered New York State's six-month/calendar-year cap on temporary tents (which the town cannot locally preempt) and a plan to have Building Inspector Rob Melillo draft a town letter supporting individual businesses' state variance applications for longer tent placement. The board reported zero parking complaints under the program to date and adopted the extension unanimously.

cases.name: 2022 Labor Counsel Retainer — Keane & Beane

timeline.summary: As part of the organizational agenda, the board debated renewing the town's labor-counsel retainer with Keane & Beane for 2022. Councilman Berra questioned whether a shorter engagement or a competitive process made more sense than committing a full year sight-unseen; Town Attorney Baroni explained the agreement is terminable on 30 days' notice but that reserving the firm's calendar has value to the professional. The agreement passed on a roll call vote with Berra dissenting/withholding support.

cases.name: Deputy Supervisor Annual Stipend — Barbara DiGiacinto

timeline.summary: Supervisor Schiliro proposed a $4,500 annual stipend for newly appointed Deputy Supervisor Barbara DiGiacinto, matching the rate historically paid to prior deputy supervisors. Councilman Berra and a second member objected, questioning whether the role — largely presiding at meetings in the supervisor's absence — merited a separate stipend given rising administrative-staff costs (town administrator, assistant, confidential secretary). The motion failed on a roll call vote, and DiGiacinto said she would continue serving as deputy supervisor without additional pay.

cases.name: Zoning Text Amendment — Recreation Centers Permitted in RELAB District
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (on its own motion, after the triggering applicant withdrew)

timeline.summary: The board closed the public hearing and adopted, on its own motion, a zoning text amendment adding recreation centers as a permitted principal use in the town's narrow RELIP (light industrial) district, matching the use already allowed in other industrial districts. The original applicant — a boutique cycling studio — had already lost its Library Court space and withdrew, but the board proceeded anyway so the use would be available going forward, citing a comprehensive-plan precedent (the former bowling alley/gym conversion) and planning staff's view that there was no significant conflict with the comprehensive plan. Councilman Berra (participating remotely) raised concern about the lack of any size cap that could let an unexpectedly large facility be built as-of-right, floating a square-footage trigger for a special use permit, but the board opted to adopt the amendment without a cap now and revisit size limits at a future meeting, noting that site plan review and traffic-study requirements would still apply.

cases.name: Water District 2 Wastewater Treatment Plant — NYSDEC Water Quality Improvement Grant

timeline.summary: The board received notice of a $2,968,000 NYSDEC Water Quality Improvement Grant award for the Water District 2 wastewater treatment plant enhancement project and authorized the supervisor to sign the grant agreement. The water/sewer superintendent explained the town will now negotiate a formal DEC work plan and timeline, with funds dispersed as the project progresses; the earlier public hearing on a bond resolution for the project was cited as part of what made the town competitive for the award.

cases.name: Film Permit — ABC Studios "Fleishman Is in Trouble" (33 Bayberry Road)

timeline.summary: The board approved a two-day, $6,000 filming permit for ABC's "Fleishman Is in Trouble" at 33 Bayberry Road (7am-midnight), during which resident Jen argued the town's notification process is backwards — neighbors learn of street closures only after board approval, unlike the advance-notice requirement for something as minor as a home addition — and questioned whether filming fees were too low relative to what homeowners are paid. Town Clerk Allison explained current process (with police involvement to manage traffic/parking) and noted it had been substantially revised roughly 15 years ago after disruptive filming incidents; board members agreed the notification-timing point was reasonable and worth revisiting, while cautioning against adding process that would slow the town down. The permit was approved as submitted.

cases.name: 23 Whippoorwill Road East — Verizon Parcel Purchase (Municipal Parking Expansion)

timeline.summary: The board re-adopted its May 2021 resolution authorizing the supervisor to purchase a vacant Verizon-owned parcel at 23 Whippoorwill Road East for $50,000, adding the required permissive-referendum language. Supervisor Schiliro called it a long-sought opportunity, secured at well below earlier asking prices, to expand municipal parking behind the west side of Main Street.

cases.name: Playground Equipment Purchase — Winkler, Lombardi, Clove Road & IBM Community Parks

timeline.summary: The board authorized the supervisor to sign purchase agreements with GameTime/MRC Recreation for new playground equipment (including poured-in-place surfacing) at Winkler Park, Lombardi Park, Clove Road Community Park and IBM Community Park, capping a roughly nine-month public-input process led by Parks & Rec. Installation costs and timing remain subject to supply-chain delays and will be finalized closer to delivery.

cases.name: Technology Task Force — Initial Member Appointments

timeline.summary: The board formally appointed the first members of the new Technology Task Force (Brian Singer, Claire Lovell, Gladys Vera, Jared Nussbaum, Mike Acavan, and Noy Sukhavira), with Councilman Hussain (initiative lead) and Town Clerk Allison Simon as ex officio staff, to examine town technology operations, resident communications, data security, and misinformation handling, with a first progress report expected at the April meeting.

cases.name: Police Department Promotions — Lieutenant Huffnagle & Sergeant Aaronberg
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (North Castle Police Department)

timeline.summary: On Chief Peter Simonson's recommendation, the board approved the probationary promotion of Sergeant Reagan Huffnagle to Police Lieutenant and Police Officer Donald Aaronberg to Police Sergeant, filling vacancies created by Lieutenant Brant Salmon's retirement, effective February 26, 2022.

cases.name: Board of Ethics Annual Report & Proposed Ethics-Education Work Session
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle Board of Ethics

timeline.summary: Board of Ethics chair Brett Summers gave the annual report, highlighting Westchester County's new mandatory ethics-education requirement and a Mount Kisco Village planning-board ethics violation (an improperly executed recusal) as cautionary examples, and recommended a joint work session with the town board to consider adding a mandatory ethics-training requirement and expanding annual disclosure filings to planning board/ZBA members. The town board agreed to schedule a work session on ethics education, while distinguishing it from broader employee-policy training (raised by Councilman Hussain) that would need to account for collective-bargaining constraints.

cases.name: Zoning Text Amendment — Warehouses Permitted in IMD-AA District (7 New King Street)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (on its own motion, at the property owner's request)

timeline.summary: Planning staff identified that the code only expressly permits warehouses at the airport, leaving an existing (and proposed-to-be-expanded) warehouse at 7 New King Street technically non-conforming; the applicant's attorney asked the town board to initiate a text amendment on its own motion (bypassing the usual 50%-of-district-owners petition threshold) to clarify that warehouses (excluding truck terminals) are permitted in the IMD-AA district, limited to New King Street and the North Castle portion of the airport. After debate about the precedent of the board initiating zoning changes for a private applicant, the board declared intent to act as lead agency and referred the draft to planning boards and interested agencies (including the Town of Greenwich, given nearby Connecticut residences), but declined to schedule the public hearing yet, opting to first review agency feedback.

cases.name: SCADA System Service Agreement — Water & Sewer Operations

timeline.summary: The board authorized a five-year SCADA (water/sewer monitoring) service and software-license agreement with Westchester Water Works, which water/sewer superintendent Sal presented as saving roughly $20,000 over five years versus annual renewal. Councilman Berra questioned whether the vendor's right to terminate for convenience undermined the value of locking in five-year pricing, but ultimately supported the agreement given the vendor's long track record and reputation.

cases.name: North White Plains — Illegal Multi-Family Conversion Enforcement
cases.applicationType: code enforcement (public comment, no board action)

timeline.summary: Resident Tony raised long-standing frustration (complaints dating to 1974) over unenforced illegal three-family home conversions in North White Plains, describing visible construction activity, deliveries, and online rental listings for what he alleged were illegal units, and proposed requiring homeowner/insurer registration with the building department at purchase as an enforcement tool. Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto responded with two recent building-department enforcement examples (one cleared as a legal renovation, one halted after a Zillow listing tipped off the department), acknowledging real legal limitations (e.g., inspectors cannot look in windows without a warrant) constrain enforcement.

cases.name: Police Department Facility Improvements — Assessment & Schematic Study
cases.address: 15 Bedford Road, Armonk (Town Hall / Police Department)
cases.applicationType: resolution / professional services contract (municipal building study)

timeline.summary: Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto raised alarm after touring the police department with the chief that a proposed $20,000 Sullivan Architecture study/schematic-design contract for renovating the locker rooms, evidence room, and front desk could be the first step toward a multi-million-dollar project the board had not actually agreed to pursue, especially amid volatile construction material costs. After debate — including a creative suggestion (from Councilman Berra) to explore relocating the historic Marianni office building to free up space for an expanded police facility — the board approved a scaled-back version of the contract, limited to the initial assessment and one work-session review step, capped at $10,000, before authorizing any further design work.

cases.name: 63-Acre Byron Lake Road Conservation Parcel — Westchester Land Trust Deed Acceptance
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle / Westchester Land Trust

timeline.summary: The board authorized the supervisor to execute the assignment and assumption of a conservation easement and accept a deed from the Westchester Land Trust for a roughly 63-acre tract on Byron Lake Road, donated by the O'Day family (Eric and Robyn O'Day) over an aquifer, preserving it from residential development; Councilman Berra caught a grantor/grantee transposition error in the draft documents that was corrected before signing.

cases.name: Wholesale Nursery/Farm — Special Use Permit Amendment & Site Plan Revision (Joint Conservation Board Review)
cases.address: Bedford Road area, Armonk (exact address unclear from recording)
cases.applicationType: special use permit amendment / site plan
cases.applicant: Existing nursery/landscaping business (property owner and operator; name not clearly resolvable from audio)

timeline.summary: The applicant, represented by land-use counsel and a civil engineer, sought to amend a circa-1980 special use permit to restore a residence destroyed by a past fire, add limited seasonal retail (produce, eggs, honey, plants) as an adjunct to its existing wholesale nursery/landscaping operation, add horse paddocks, beehives, and new storage/office structures, and resolve outstanding building-code violations tied to a pending Justice Court matter. Discussion centered on reconciling the current site plan with a decades-old approved plan, wetland-buffer disturbance from both historic and newly proposed plant-storage areas near a stone wall bordering the wetland, and screening for paddocks. Conservation Board members pressed for a wetland characterization study and clearer differentiation between areas that would and would not see continued buffer disturbance before recommending action; the applicant's attorney proposed capping the retail display area (roughly 5% of the site) and codifying operational restrictions in the special use permit language to prevent future expansion without a new town board review.

cases.name: Fisher Lane Park Commuter Parking Lot — Westchester County License Renewal & Annual Permit Cycle
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle / Westchester County

timeline.summary: The board renewed its annual license agreement with Westchester County for the Fisher Lane Park commuter parking lot (April 2022-March 2023), confirming the town roughly doubles its cost back in permit revenue, and separately noted the town clerk's office had just switched resident parking permits from a six-month to an annual renewal cycle, saving an estimated six weeks of cumulative staff processing time per year.

cases.name: Temporary Sign Code Amendment / Possible Sign Moratorium

timeline.summary: The Town Planner flagged that the current sign code creates compliance and uniformity problems (the town cannot legally allow one type of sign while disallowing a similar one) and floated a possible short-term moratorium on new signage while the code is rewritten, prompted by a specific pending application staff found concerning. The board leaned toward scheduling a work session soon rather than adopting a moratorium outright, wanting to understand implications (e.g., for real-estate signs) first.

cases.name: Accessory Apartment (ADU) Sunset Provision — Public Hearing Reconvene

timeline.summary: The board discussed reconvening a public hearing (adjourned since November) on removing the code's "sunset provision," which currently forces homeowners with a legal accessory apartment to reapply for a permit every time the property changes ownership. The Building Inspector wants it resolved this year so he isn't forced to compile a re-application list. The board also aired frustration over the near-impossibility of enforcing against illegal (unpermitted) accessory apartments given limited inspection authority.

cases.name: Town-Wide EV Charging Station Installation (Livingston Energy)
cases.address: Town Hall / Community Park / North White Plains Community Center

timeline.summary: The Town Administrator reported the town is close to finalizing a proposal with Livingston Energy to install EV charging stations at Town Hall, Community Park, and the North White Plains Community Center, with the town's contribution estimated around 20% of cost (roughly $30,000) after grants, plus a per-unit annual maintenance fee, while users pay a per-charge fee the town sets to recoup electricity costs. The board broadened the discussion into a policy conversation about how the town should proactively site charging infrastructure to support Hamlet businesses rather than cede the market to private highway-corridor chargers.

cases.name: Highway Department Bid Awards — Catch Basins, Guiderails, Pavement Markings & Millings Disposal

timeline.summary: Resolution accepting bids solicited by the Highway Superintendent for catch basins, highway materials, guiderails, pavement markings, and paving-related items including options for storing vs. removing/disposing of road millings. The board amended the resolution's language from Highway Superintendent "awarding" bids to "soliciting" them (since only the board can award), and added a condition that no new (non-replacement) guiderails be installed until a dedicated work session on discretionary guiderail policy, while directing staff to bring back a clearer breakdown of the millings storage-vs-removal decision with better documentation.

cases.name: North Castle Pool — Breezeway & Exterior Painting/Repair

timeline.summary: Approved roughly $25,000-$30,000 (funded from fund balance) to repaint the pool building exterior and breezeway interior and repair falling stucco/concrete, ahead of the summer season and membership sales; the board also confirmed a walk-through of the facility would be scheduled once the pool is drained and refilled.

cases.name: Kellard Sessions Consulting — MS4 Stormwater Management Engineering Services

timeline.summary: Approved an engineering services agreement with Kellard Sessions Consulting for compliance work under the NYSDEC Phase II stormwater management (MS4) program, authorizing the Supervisor to sign.

cases.name: Playground Equipment Installation — Pat Corsetti Inc. (Winkler Park, Lombardi, Clove Road, North Castle/IBM Community Park)
cases.address: Winkler Park; Lombardi; Clove Road; North Castle (IBM) Community Park

timeline.summary: Approved an agreement with Pat Corsetti Inc. for furnishing and installing playground equipment at four town parks, funded by recreation subdivision fees, subject to the contractor accepting Town Attorney-negotiated changes: reducing a 50% deposit requirement, resolving unclear dump-site/security-during-curing provisions (given the town is self-performing excavation), extending the payment-default cure period from 5 to 45 days, and striking a prevailing-party attorney's-fees clause.

cases.name: Board of Ethics — Education & Financial Disclosure Requirements Expansion
cases.lastStatus: work session discussion; public hearing to be determined

trajectory.status: work session discussion; public hearing to be determined

timeline.status: work session discussion; public hearing to be determined
timeline.summary: The Board of Ethics recommended: (1) a mandatory three-minute educational video plus Q&A for department heads, elected officials, and members of the Planning Board, ZBA, ARB, and Assessment Review Board, to be shown at existing department-head and committee meetings and voluntarily offered to other boards; (2) expanding annual disclosure-form obligations for that same group to cover non-primary-residence real estate interests and business interests that do business with the town (dropping a broader county-style "all business interests" disclosure as too burdensome); and (3) codifying that alternates automatically hold over until replaced and giving alternates a defined term. The Town Board directed staff to move forward on producing the video and to have the Town Attorney confirm whether a public hearing is legally required to expand who must file disclosure forms; the meeting ended without a final resolution on whether Labor Counsel/Town Attorney sign-off is needed before the revised disclosure form is distributed.

cases.name: Whippoorwill Hills HOA — Tree Replacement Mitigation & Maintenance Bond Agreement

timeline.summary: Following litigation over a neighbor's unauthorized removal of nine mature regulated trees in the HOA's buffer zone, the Planning Board's November 2021 resolution required the HOA to post a bond/security and submit a two-year tree maintenance and monitoring plan. The HOA asked the Town Board to reject the Town Engineer's (Kellard Sessions) recommendation for a second, separate ~$1,628 maintenance bond on top of the ~$11,945 planting bond, arguing it was superfluous since the full planting-bond amount would already be held for the entire two-year maintenance period. The board agreed, and approved the legal agreement as revised to explicitly state the existing bond also covers maintenance/monitoring, waiving the second bond.

cases.name: Birchgrove Drive — Con Edison Underground Electrical Failures & House Fire

timeline.summary: Multiple Birchgrove Drive residents described repeated dangerous power surges over recent months, including one that caused a house fire at 20 Birchgrove Drive four weeks earlier that displaced a family, plus flickering lights and a temporary emergency disconnection at another home. Con Edison had begun a duct-replacement project expected to remedy roughly eight homes plus a broader "power quality test" to identify further issues, but residents reported poor internal Con Ed communication (conflicting statements about which lines were checked) and a claim that Con Ed believed the town wouldn't allow pavement to be dug up on the recently repaved street. The board pledged to keep pressuring Con Ed, confirmed it has no objection to road excavation/repaving if needed to fix the underground lines, and discussed drafting a written communication to Con Edison and designating a single town point of contact (Town Administrator Kevin) for residents.

cases.name: Hotel Occupancy Tax — Home Rule Request Renewal

timeline.summary: Routine renewal of a home-rule request resolution asking the NY State Senate and Assembly to extend the town's hotel occupancy tax legislation, which generates modest revenue currently (roughly $10,000-15,000/year from IBM's learning center non-employee rentals) with potential to grow to $100,000+ if area hotel occupancy increases. Adopted without discussion.

cases.name: Remote Board Participation & Public Zoom Access — Open Meetings Law Update
cases.lastStatus: work session discussion; public hearing to be considered

trajectory.status: work session discussion; public hearing to be considered

timeline.status: work session discussion; public hearing to be considered
timeline.summary: With the COVID executive order authorizing remote public meetings expiring, the board discussed two separate questions: whether to adopt New York's new Open Meetings Law amendment allowing board members to participate remotely under narrowly-defined "extraordinary circumstances" (illness, disability, caregiving, or other significant/unexpected events) without the public having to be present at the member's remote location (while still requiring an in-person quorum), versus relying on the pre-existing default law (remote participation allowed from a noticed public place, open to the public, with no extraordinary-circumstance test) which the town has never used; and separately, whether to continue allowing the public to watch/participate in town board meetings via Zoom going forward, which the board concluded does not require a local law, just a board decision/agenda item. The board directed staff to get a definitive answer from the Town Attorney on whether adopting the new law forecloses the old default option, and agreed to place both a public-Zoom-access decision and a possible public hearing on adopting the new remote-participation local law on the next meeting's agenda, while keeping all options open.

cases.name: Summit Club (formerly Brynwood) — Amended & Restated Water District #2B Contribution Agreement
cases.lastStatus: deferred; vote postponed to next meeting

trajectory.status: deferred; vote postponed to next meeting

timeline.status: deferred; vote postponed to next meeting
timeline.summary: After a nearly two-hour work session, the board considered authorizing the Supervisor to sign an amended and restated water district contribution agreement splitting the existing Water District #2 (Windmill) into subsidiary districts 2A and 2B, following the developer's inability to develop a satisfactory new well supply at the original well field as contemplated years earlier (per state comptroller guidance, since dissolving/reforming the district risked triggering bond acceleration). Jose Berra raised detailed legal questions — disputing the recital language that the developer made "best efforts" to find water, probing bond-acceleration risk from reallocating debt service among the ~365 remaining district users, and questioning the town's liability exposure under a contractual "authority and enforceability" representation (Section 10B) — all of which the Town Attorney addressed without identifying material risk. The board ultimately declined to vote, with Matt Milim and Barbara DiGiacinto arguing residents needed more time to review and comment (citing a still-unresolved indemnification question raised by a resident, Ed [surname unclear], at the work session) and noting a companion bifurcation resolution still needed to be finalized with the Town Engineer.

cases.name: Local Law Authorizing Video Conferencing for Public Bodies (Public Officers Law 103-a)

timeline.summary: The Board held a public hearing on a local law implementing the state's new open-meetings amendment allowing individual board/committee members to appear remotely under extraordinary circumstances, with a majority still required to be physically present. After debate over a typo (correcting "members of" to "authorizes members of all") and a lengthy separate debate about whether to also allow general Zoom viewing/participation by residents, the Board closed the hearing and adopted the local law as amended. A related verbal resolution allowing one-time resident Zoom participation at the next (June 8) meeting failed on a process objection from Councilman Berra, but a second motion to agendize a permanent resident-Zoom-participation policy for the next meeting passed unanimously.

cases.name: 7 McDonald Avenue — Happy Cat Hotel & Spa Zoning Text Amendment
cases.applicationType: zoning text amendment / SEQRA lead agency
cases.applicant: Christina Marazza (Happy Cat Hotel & Spa franchise)
