timeline.summary: The board approved an alcoholic-beverage permit for an Atlantic Westchester company picnic at the Lombardy Park pavilion on May 30, 2026, by voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Resolution on Proposed SEQRA Amendments in the 2026 State of the State / Executive Budget
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (at request of Assemblyman Chris Burdick)

timeline.summary: A late-added resolution urged the Governor to pursue proposed State Environmental Quality Review Act (SEQRA) reforms — including housing exemptions and a two-year EIS timeline — as a standalone bill open to municipal input rather than embedding them in the executive budget, to protect home rule. Town Planner Adam Kaufman explained the request originated with Assemblyman Chris Burdick. Councilwoman DiGiacinto and Councilman Berra pushed for softer, less-restrictive language (e.g., 'supports streamlining' and broader tolling wording), while Supervisor Rende and Councilman Hussain argued the resolution's sole purpose was to keep the reform out of the budget and that detailed language edits were premature. On a roll-call vote the resolution was adopted 4-0 with Councilman Berra abstaining (citing insufficient time to discuss).

cases.name: Resolution — TAP Grant Application for North Broadway Pedestrian Improvements
cases.address: North Broadway, North White Plains (Reservoir to Sir John's Plaza)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Town Planner Adam Kaufman / grant writer)

timeline.summary: A late-added resolution supported a Transportation Alternatives Program (TAP) grant application to NYSDOT for up to $8,620,000 and authorized the Supervisor and Town Attorney to sign, with the package due the next day. The ~$8.5M project (an 80/20 grant, ~$1.7M town match) would build new sidewalks, curbs, street trees, bus shelters, pedestrian lighting on both sides of North Broadway plus a signalized crosswalk at the Nethermont path. The board discussed how it would fund the match (fund balance vs. bonds) and confirmed the scope cannot be reduced arbitrarily once awarded. Adopted by voice vote.

cases.name: Indemnity Agreement — Sustainability Committee Table on Cleanup Day

timeline.summary: A late-added item authorized the Supervisor to sign a standard indemnity agreement (with DeCicco's/Chico's) allowing the Sustainability Committee to set up a table on town-wide cleanup day to sell food-scrap composting kits and distribute cleanup supplies. The agreement had not been posted to the agenda; Attorney Roland's two language concerns (including removal of the word 'sole') were resolved. Because the committee's event falls on a date before the next meeting, the board approved it by voice vote.

cases.name: Contract Award — Land Christen Co. for Water District No. 2 Rehabilitation of Wells 3 and 4

timeline.summary: The board awarded a contract to the Land Christen company for rehabilitation of Water District No. 2 wells 3 and 4 and authorized the Supervisor to sign, funded from Water District No. 2's fund balance. Water superintendent 'Sal' explained the spec includes priced worst-case alternatives (e.g., extra surging hours) to avoid later change orders, described declining production in the wells, and noted well 3 had a failed pump requiring investigation. Approved by voice vote; work must start within two weeks of award.

cases.name: Promotion of Sergeant Joel Thomas to Police Lieutenant

timeline.summary: The police chief presented Sergeant Joel Thomas (NCPD since 2005, senior sergeant, accreditation program lead and de facto IT officer) for promotion to administrative lieutenant to fill a vacancy created by the chief's own recent promotion, effective March 26, 2026. The board unanimously adopted the promotion (all in favor) and the supervisor administered the oath of office with Thomas's family present. Celebratory, no dissent.

cases.name: 250th History Moment — North Castle's Revolutionary War Women (Women's History Month)

timeline.summary: As part of the town's 250th-anniversary commemoration, sixth-grader Zelda June Topolski of H.C. Crittenden Middle School delivered a Women's History Month 'history moment' on the roles and sacrifices of North Castle women during the Revolutionary War, including Widow Ann Miller and the Miller House (Washington's headquarters). No action was taken; the supervisor also announced a new high-school civics spotlight program featuring student Paloma Hussain. Purely ceremonial and community-focused.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Virgin Mary & St. Damian Coptic Orthodox Church
cases.applicant: Virgin Mary & St. Damian Coptic Orthodox Church (Father Paul)

timeline.summary: The board opened and held a public hearing on a special use permit for a church operating since 1913 that had never received one; the permit is a prerequisite for the planning board to approve a site plan allowing construction of a handicap-access sidewalk to the church basement for elderly parishioners. Town Planner Adam Kaufman explained the procedural background and the clerk read the notices, including a well-received historical memorandum from resident Nora Emanueli. Father Paul confirmed no exterior/structural changes beyond accessibility. The board received the planning board recommendation, closed the hearing, and adopted the resolution granting the special use permit (all in favor).

cases.name: Authorization of Funds — North Castle 250th Art Contest Committee Opening Reception (not to exceed $1,000)
cases.applicant: North Castle 250th Celebration Arts Committee (Marianne Hamilton, chair)

timeline.summary: Committee chair Marianne Hamilton requested up to $1,000 to fund the April 9, 2026 opening reception of a 250th-anniversary art contest exhibit at the library (33 submissions, 13 from students), covering prizes/gift certificates, framing/hanging materials, PR, and reception costs. Councilman Hussain probed the proportionality of spending (e.g., prizes shouldn't crowd out other categories) and asked that Town Administrator Kevin be given discretion to align reimbursements with the stated categories. The board unanimously authorized the funds (all in favor), with reimbursement via submitted receipts.

cases.name: Audit Engagement / Consensus Letter (Agreements A & Consensus B) — Tabled

timeline.summary: The supervisor announced that the audit engagement item (Agreements A) and the related consensus letter (B) would be tabled for further consideration. Councilman Berra flagged that the engagement letter identified 'management override of controls' as a significant risk of material misstatement and was inconsistent with the 2024 agreement with the same firm. The supervisor and counsel agreed it was inappropriate to debate a tabled item, but confirmed Berra's concerns were valid, had been communicated to Town Administrator Kevin, and would be addressed at a meeting the next day.

cases.name: Payment Application No. 7 — Papadino Construction (Water District No. 4 New Well Project)

timeline.summary: The board approved Payment Application No. 7 to Papadino Construction Company Inc. for site work performed at the Water District No. 4 new well project. Routine consent-style approval, moved and seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: KSCJ Consulting Recommendation — Younger Star Residence Wetland Bonds (14 Tall Woods Road)

timeline.summary: On the town engineer's recommendation, the board voted to release the wetland mitigation bond and extend the five-year monitoring and maintenance bond through August 2029 for the Younger Star Residence project. Routine approval, moved and seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Street Address Assessment — Madonna Subdivision (130 Mount Kisco Road), E911 Referral

timeline.summary: The board received a March 5, 2026 memo from KSCJ Consulting regarding assessment of new street addresses for the Madonna subdivision at 130 Mount Kisco Road and referred it to the town E911 coordinator. Routine, moved and seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Hospital for Special Surgery — Use of Town Roads for Bike HSS Community Event (Sept 19)

timeline.summary: The board approved a request from Hospital for Special Surgery to use town roads for the Bike HSS bike-and-walk/run community event on Saturday, September 19, with the motion amended to refer the request to professional staff. The supervisor voiced strong personal support, crediting HSS with a successful ACL surgery. Clarified the date as September 19th, not the 9th.

cases.name: Employment Agreement — Chief of Police Reagan Hufnagle (effective Jan 1, 2026)

timeline.summary: The board authorized the supervisor to sign the employment agreement with Chief of Police Reagan Hufnagle, effective January 1, 2026. Moved, seconded, all in favor with no discussion.

cases.name: Annual Stipend — Jamie Norris, Highway General Foreman (effective Jan 1)

timeline.summary: The board considered an annual stipend for Highway General Foreman Jamie Norris, effective January 1, prompted by the discovery that compensation for his additional duties had been unilaterally removed by a prior supervisor and never restored. Councilman Berra praised Norris but objected to setting compensation mid-year rather than during budget sessions and abstained ('stood'). On a roll call the measure passed 3-0 (DiGiacinto aye, Hussain aye, Rende yes; Berra abstained; Vataj absent). A lengthy exchange followed between Rende and Berra on the meaning and propriety of abstention, with counsel explaining an abstention is a non-vote that still effectively counts against passage since a majority of the full board is required.

cases.name: Town Clerk Allison Simon — 2026 NYS Town Clerks Association Conference (Albany, Apr 19-22)

timeline.summary: The board approved Town Clerk Allison Simon's attendance at the 2026 New York State Town Clerks Association Conference in Albany, April 19-22, 2026. Moved, seconded, all in favor. The supervisor expressed interest in a scheduled NYS Department of Health session.

cases.name: Library Staff — American Library Association Conference (Chicago, Jun 25-28)

timeline.summary: The board approved attendance by Library Assistant Director Angela Cook and librarian Roxanne Guzman at the American Library Association conference in Chicago, June 25-28, 2026. Moved, seconded, all in favor.

cases.name: Capital Projects & Parks Update — Liaison/Supervisor Report

timeline.summary: The supervisor and administrator reported on several projects: the School Street water-line extension is complete, restoring potable water and reopening the bathrooms at Lombardi Park after several years; Quarry Heights park improvements are planned using in-house staff and saved topsoil; the turf-field project (delayed by snow) expects turf delivery in mid-April with completion and a ribbon-cutting by late May; and Clove Road work resumes soon, with repaving planned at Lombardi and North White Plains community park lots. Also reported: NC Vine Cutters cleanup by The Eagle, recreation hiring for camps/pools (lifeguards, staff over 16), and an emergency-managers/EOC meeting covering the county's expiring five-year hazard-mitigation plan and potential FEMA funding. Berra asked whether FEMA funds could help dredge Byron Brook to alleviate School Street flooding.

cases.name: Armonk Lions Club $15,000 Donation to North Castle Police Department
cases.applicant: Armonk Lions Club (Matt Milim, private citizen / former council member; Mike Roseman, treasurer)

timeline.summary: The Armonk Lions Club, represented by former council member Matt Milim (now a private citizen) and treasurer Mike Roseman, presented a $15,000 check to the North Castle Police Department to help fund a replacement trailer, tied to the Lions Club's 50th Fol-de-Rol. Supervisor Rende suggested he and Councilwoman DiGiacinto (both Lions members) might need to recuse, but Town Attorney Roland advised there was no conflict in merely accepting a check and that the three-member exception applied. The board voted to accept the donation by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Resolution Authorizing Hiring of Joel R. Ditchner (Ditchner Law LLC) as Special Counsel — Con Edison Rate Settlement Monitoring
cases.applicant: Ditchner Law LLC (Joel R. Ditchner) / Westchester municipal consortium

timeline.summary: The board considered a resolution to hire Joel R. Ditchner of Ditchner Law LLC as special counsel to represent North Castle, alongside other Westchester municipalities, in monitoring the Con Edison rate settlement over its three-year agreement. North Castle would be municipality 38 of an expected 40 in the consortium, at the same cost as the prior engagement. After brief questions about the added cost being for ongoing monitoring ('holding their feet to the fire'), the board approved it by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Filming Permit Application — Sweet Spot (web promotional video)

timeline.summary: The board considered a filming permit application from Sweet Spot for a web promotional video on April 14, 2026 at 428 Main Street in Armonk. The motion included referring the application to staff, and it was confirmed staff had already reviewed it. Approved by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Step Increase — Employee 003949, Librarian 1 Step 3 to Step 5

timeline.summary: The board considered a step increase for employee 003949 from Librarian 1 Step 3 to Librarian 1 Step 5, effective April 1, 2026. After an initial voice vote, Councilman Berra sought a roll-call vote and the board moved to rescind and re-vote so he could abstain. On the roll call it passed 4-0 with Berra abstaining (DiGiacinto aye, Vataj aye, Hussain aye, Rende aye, Berra abstain). Berra said the employee was excellent but that he opposes mid-year compensation changes absent extraordinary circumstances; Supervisor Rende argued at length that speaking against an item and then abstaining is a misuse of the abstention.

cases.name: Police Department Promotion and Appointment — Sergeant Stephen Vitello; Officer John Gagan
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Regan Huff-Nagle)

timeline.summary: Chief Regan Huff-Nagle recommended promoting Detective Stephen Vitello to the budgeted, vacant position of police sergeant effective April 23, 2026, citing his tenure since 2015, service as a school resource officer, and promotion to detective in 2024. The Chief separately recommended appointing John Gagan, a Mount Vernon police officer and former Westchester County seasonal park ranger, to police officer effective April 25, 2026, following a full background investigation and panel interview. The board approved both by voice vote and Supervisor Rende administered oaths of office to each, with family members present for photos.

cases.name: Parks & Recreation Advisory Board Memo Supporting Development of Dedicated Pickleball Courts
cases.applicant: Parks & Recreation Advisory Board (Matt Trainor, Superintendent of Recreation and Parks; resident Peter Gold)

timeline.summary: Matt Trainor presented a Parks & Recreation Advisory Board memo, backed by resident Peter Gold's research on regional pickleball trends, in support of exploring dedicated pickleball courts, with Winkler Park's aging tennis/basketball courts suggested as a pilot site since they need replacement regardless. Board members broadly supported the concept but diverged on siting and trade-offs: several favored converting or sharing existing tennis courts (Winkler, Community Park's platform-tennis courts, the pool-area tennis court) over building on new/passive parkland, with concerns raised about Wampus Brook Park South's proximity to the historic district, potential loss of tennis capacity, planning/conservation board review for any new site, and possible added parking near the Winkler Park senior center. No vote was taken; the board indicated it wants Trainor's site recommendation brought back for discussion at a future work session.

cases.name: Additional Funding Request — North Castle Revolutionary War 250th Steering Committee ($9,500)
cases.applicant: North Castle Revolutionary War 250th Steering Committee

timeline.summary: The 250th Steering Committee, which has worked with confidential secretary Josephine Egan and the town administrator's office, requested an additional $9,500 (roughly $1,000 above already-incurred costs) to cover July 4th celebration expenses and printing/postage for a private-fundraising outreach effort, describing the added amount as a buffer for contingencies. Supervisor Rende noted the celebration has been registered with national/state semiquincentennial programs and pledged a personal $500 donation toward it. The board approved the request unanimously.

cases.name: R&A Ice Cream — Town Pool Concession Services Agreement (2026 Season)

timeline.summary: The board approved an agreement with R&A Ice Cream to operate concession services at the town pool for the 2026 season and authorized the Supervisor to sign it, with Matt Trainor confirming there were no outstanding questions.

cases.name: North Castle Historical Society — Reimbursement Request for Whippoorwill Hall Event Costs ($202)
cases.applicant: North Castle Historical Society (Sharon Tomback, co-historian)

timeline.summary: The board considered a $202 reimbursement request from the Historical Society for the sound/lighting technician's fee at an April 12, 2026 event ('the Andre/Arnold conspiracy' presentation) at Whippoorwill Hall. Councilman Berra said he supported the payment but wanted advance notice in the future that the town, rather than the Historical Society, would be covering that cost; Town Clerk Allison Simon and Supervisor Rende clarified the town customarily waives its own hall-use and beverage-license fees for the Society but this technician fee is a separate, outside cost, noting a similar cost was covered for a prior Society event about two years earlier. The board approved the reimbursement.

cases.name: Payment Application No. 8 — Pappa Tillo Construction, Water District No. 4 Well Project

timeline.summary: The board approved payment application number eight to Pappa Tillo Construction Company for site work on the Water District No. 4 well project. Supervisor Rende asked about the remaining/final billing status; Town Administrator Kevin confirmed roughly $21,000 remained, covered by the water district, with the work not yet complete.

cases.name: Funding Approval — Laserfiche Cloud Software Upgrade

timeline.summary: The board approved funding to upgrade the town's Laserfiche cloud records software, a benefit-all-departments upgrade offered at a discount outside the normal budget cycle. Councilwoman DiGiacinto initially questioned why it wasn't budgeted for 2026, but after Town Clerk Allison Simon explained the vendor's off-cycle discount rationale, DiGiacinto made the motion to approve, and Councilman Berra confirmed it should aid productivity.

cases.name: Creation of a Building Maintenance Department; Transfer of Anthony Ruvo

timeline.summary: The board formally created a Building Maintenance Department to codify a function (a lead maintenance mechanic and two maintenance mechanics reporting directly to the Town Administrator) that had already been operating successfully outside the Parks & Recreation Department. Town Administrator Kevin confirmed the change does not alter employee duties, which remain governed by civil-service titles and job descriptions, though the crew continues to assist with snow/storm response as part of its facilities-maintenance duties. The board separately approved the retroactive transfer of Anthony Ruvo, lead maintenance mechanic, into the new department effective January 24, 2025.

cases.name: Engineering Agreements — Cider Mill Sewer Maintenance/Replacement (KSCJ Consulting; Carlin Simpson Associates)
cases.applicant: KSCJ Consulting; Carlin Simpson Associates LLC

timeline.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign agreements with KSCJ Consulting for civil engineering services and Carlin Simpson Associates LLC for geotechnical/environmental engineering and subsurface soil and foundation investigation, both tied to the proposed removal and replacement of a sanitary sewer main near Cider Mill. Supervisor Rende noted he had confirmed with Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal that the work is necessary and covered by the sewer district.

cases.name: License Agreement with Westchester County — Fisher Lane Commuter Parking

timeline.summary: The board approved a license agreement with Westchester County for Fisher Lane commuter parking covering April 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027, and authorized the Supervisor to sign it. Approved by voice vote without discussion.

cases.name: Consulting Agreement — Bonadio and Company LLP (GASB 87/96 Services for 2025 Audit)

timeline.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign an agreement with Bonadio and Company LLP for 2025 GASB 87 and GASB 96 professional consulting services related to the town's annual audit, approved by voice vote without discussion.

cases.name: Agreement to Host the Westchester Municipal Officials Association Dinner at Whippoorwill Club

timeline.summary: The board considered authorizing the Supervisor to sign an agreement to host the Westchester Municipal Officials Association dinner on May 14, 2026 at the Whippoorwill Club, a hosting duty that rotates among member municipalities roughly every five to six years and last fell to North Castle in 2019. Councilman Berra objected that the roughly $120-per-person cost (once gratuity and service fees are added to a $90-95 base) was extravagant for elected officials to approve amid recent tax increases, prompting Supervisor Rende to explain that comparable neighboring towns (Rye Brook, Pound Ridge, Port Chester) had hosted at similarly priced country clubs or restaurants because the town lacks an in-house venue large enough for the roughly 70-80 attendees. The item passed 3-1 on a roll call vote, with Berra dissenting.

cases.name: Parks & Recreation Appointments, Committee Reappointment, and Conference Travel Authorization
cases.applicant: Recreation and Parks Department; Receiver of Taxes; Landmarks Preservation Committee

timeline.summary: The board approved a series of personnel and committee items by voice vote: promotion/appointment of Alexander Hayder to groundskeeper in Recreation and Parks effective May 6, 2026; appointment of Casey Ennis as gym attendant in Recreation and Parks effective April 12, 2026; appointment of Natalie Broden as an intern in Recreation and Parks from April 20 to June 20, 2026; the seasonal appointment of Joshua Feldman as junior clerk in Justice Court effective April 23, 2026; reappointment of Martin Rube to the Landmarks Preservation Committee for a two-year term expiring April 22, 2028; and authorization for Receiver of Taxes Patrick Ricky to attend a NYS Association of Tax Receivers and Collectors training seminar June 7-10, 2026, including reimbursement of a roughly $200 registration fee, meals, and gas/tolls, plus use of a town-owned vehicle.

cases.name: Community Preservation Survey / Open Space Funding Mechanism (Public Comment)

timeline.summary: Resident Andrew Lester spoke against a mailed survey (paid for by a conservation-affiliated organization, not the town) gauging support for a special assessment or real estate transfer tax of roughly 1.25%-1.5% to fund future open-space purchases, calling the survey's wording one-sided and warning the tax would be uncapped, non-transparent, and would depress home values and complicate sales. Councilman Jose Berra questioned Lester and confirmed he supported open space in principle but preferred a bond-financed approach tied to specific projects, as used historically (e.g., the former Erika Property, now the John Fava Preserve). Supervisor Rende clarified the survey was designed and funded by the Conservation Committee and a land-trust-affiliated firm, not the town board, that the board never saw the questions in advance, and that it cost the town nothing; other unidentified board members said they personally opposed a dedicated open-space fund that could let future boards buy land without the scrutiny a bond vote requires, while noting the town's strong balance sheet gives ample borrowing capacity if a genuine opportunity arose. No vote was taken; the matter remains at the survey/discussion stage.

cases.name: Resolution Authorizing Supervisor to Sign Westchester County DOH Certificate — 2026 Summer Camp Applications
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Parks & Recreation summer camp program)

timeline.summary: The board adopted a resolution authorizing the Supervisor to sign the Westchester County Department of Health certificate required for the town's 2026 summer camp program applications. The item passed without discussion on a motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Approval to Issue RFP for Auditing Services

timeline.summary: The board approved issuing a request for proposals (RFP) for the town's auditing services. Supervisor Rende asked for a brief explanation, and it was clarified the RFP was a routine competitive check ('sharpening the pencils') to gauge market interest and confirm the town is getting the best price, not a sign of dissatisfaction with the incumbent auditor. Approved by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: KSCJ Consulting Recommendations — Shapiro Residence Wetland Bond, Aqua Works Final Payment, and Round Hill Realty Bond Reduction
cases.applicant: KSCJ Consulting (town engineering consultant); Aqua Works Incorporated; 111 Round Hill Realty LLC

timeline.summary: On KSCJ Consulting's recommendation, the board approved three unrelated capital/land-use bond matters by separate voice votes without discussion: (1) establishing a five-year wetland mitigation monitoring and maintenance bond for the Shapiro Residence project (exact address unclear in the recording); (2) final payment (Application No. 2) to Aqua Works Incorporated for the School Street watermain extension, together with receipt of a general release and a one-year guarantee bond; and (3) a reduction of the construction performance bond for the common driveway serving the 111 Round Hill Realty LLC Rolling Hill subdivision at 10 and 20 Round Hill Road. All three passed on motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Fee Schedule Amendment — Special Event Application Fee Reduced from $250 to $50

timeline.summary: The board approved a modification to the Master Fee Schedule reducing the special event application fee from $250 to $50. Supervisor Rende thanked Town Clerk Allison Simon for bringing the change forward, calling it 'a wise choice.' Approved on motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Special Event Road-Use Permits — Wall Street Rides FAR (Autism Research) and Jewish Board of Family and Children's Services Cycling Events
cases.applicant: Wall Street Rides FAR; Jewish Board of Family and Children's Services

timeline.summary: The board approved two separate requests for the use of town roads for charity cycling events: one from 'Wall Street Rides FAR' benefiting autism research, scheduled for Saturday, October 3, 2026, and one from the Jewish Board of Family and Children's Services for a cycling/support event on Sunday, October 18, 2026. Town Clerk Allison Simon confirmed both applications had already been sent to staff for review. Both passed by motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Highway Department Materials & Services Contracts (Highway General Foreman Jamie Norris)

timeline.summary: At the request of Highway General Foreman Jamie Norris, the board awarded a set of contracts covering highway maintenance materials and services — including paving materials, milling and disposal, catch basin materials, concrete, winter highway materials, aggregate stone, guardrails, pavement markings, and street light maintenance — and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreements. Approved by motion, second, and voice vote (aye) without discussion.

cases.name: Agreement — Preparation of Evaluation Criteria for the Town Community Conservation Plan
cases.applicant: Outside environmental/planning consultant (firm name not clearly captured by ASR)

timeline.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign an agreement with an outside consulting firm (name garbled in the recording) to prepare evaluation criteria for the town's Community Conservation Plan. This item followed the earlier public-comment discussion of the conservation survey and potential open-space funding mechanism, though it is a separate scope-of-work contract rather than a funding decision. It passed on motion, second, and voice vote (aye) without further discussion.

cases.name: Receipt of 2025 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and Auditor's Letter (Bonadio Group)

timeline.summary: Michael Connolly of the Bonadio Group presented the town's fiscal year 2025 financial statement audit, reporting an unmodified (clean) opinion consistent with the prior year and noting no significant new accounting standards this cycle. The board thanked Comptroller Abbas, Town Administrator Kevin, and department heads, and highlighted that the town again received a GFOA Certificate of Achievement for Excellence in Financial Reporting. The board voted to accept both the audit report and the required year-end communication letter.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge Subdivision — Performance Bond and Inspection Fee (Reed/Rede North Castle Drive, Armonk)
cases.address: Reed North Castle Drive, Armonk (Eagle Ridge subdivision)
cases.applicant: Eagle Ridge (developer); recommendation from Town Engineer (KSCE/Kellard Sessions)

timeline.summary: The board approved a town engineer's recommendation to establish the subdivision performance bond and subdivision inspection fee for the Eagle Ridge development. One board member recused, citing employment with IBM given the property's past association with IBM interests; the item passed by voice vote with no substantive discussion.

cases.name: Water Service Connection Bid Specifications — William and James Streets (Quarry/Corey Heights)
cases.address: William Street and James Street, North White Plains (Corey/Quarry Heights)
cases.applicant: AI Engineers (proposal); Town Water & Sewer Department

timeline.summary: The board approved hiring AI Engineers (fee negotiated down from roughly $200,000 to $90,000) to prepare bid specifications for extending municipal water service from an existing main to eight Quarry Heights homes affected by long-standing well contamination, with homeowners responsible for interior plumbing hookup costs. Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal detailed a multi-year fight with the state DEC and Westchester Joint Water Works over funding, describing DEC's refusal to fund hookups (unlike a prior, fully DEC-funded extension on Wampus Avenue) pending determination of a PFAS contamination source, and the town's use of subpoenas and court intervention (alongside the town attorney) to press the issue. Residents pressed for a future meeting with DEC/investigation officials to get direct answers.

cases.name: Proclamation Honoring the Armonk Lions Club's 50th Anniversary of the Fol-de-Rol

timeline.summary: Supervisor Rende read a proclamation honoring the Armonk Lions Club's 50 years of running the Fol-de-Rol, recognizing former council member (now private citizen) Matt Milim and Mike Roseman for their volunteer leadership. Multiple board members offered laudatory remarks about the Lions Club's community giving (funding fire, police, art, and library programs) and thanked the Police, Parks, and Highway Departments for supporting the event; individual board voices beyond the presiding Supervisor were not clearly identifiable in the ASR transcript.

cases.name: Proclamation Honoring Doug Minicelli and the Armonk Vine Cutters

timeline.summary: Supervisor Rende read a proclamation recognizing Doug Minicelli, founder of the Armonk Vine Cutters, for his volunteer work removing invasive vines that damage trees on town open space, noting his recent recognition by Westchester County. Board members praised Minicelli's dedication and encouraged residents to volunteer with the group; individual board voices beyond the presiding Supervisor were not clearly identifiable in the ASR transcript.

cases.name: Appointment of Mark Schuback to the Board of Ethics (Five-Year Term)

timeline.summary: The board considered appointing Mark Schuback to a five-year term on the Board of Ethics, expiring June 10, 2031. No second was immediately offered; Councilwoman DiGiacinto asked to speak first, stating Schuback was well-qualified but voicing concern that the board's recent failure to reconfirm a prior appointee (Brett Summers) to a board or committee position could create a public perception of intimidation or retribution against volunteer board/committee members for exercising independent judgment. She said she was nonetheless glad to support Schuback's appointment. The recording jumps forward immediately after her remarks, so the final vote tally is not captured on tape, but the appointment appears to have proceeded to adoption based on the discussion.

cases.name: Board & Committee Reappointments — Landmarks Preservation Committee and Conservation Board

timeline.summary: The board approved the reappointment of Linda Fernberg to the Landmarks Preservation Committee for a three-year term expiring June 10, 2029, a second reappointment to the Landmarks Preservation Committee for the same three-year term (the appointee's name was not clearly captured by the ASR), and the reappointment of Jane Black to the Conservation Board, where board members noted an apparent discrepancy between the agenda's listed two-year term (expiring 2028) and the three-year terms used for the other appointments; the board let the resolution stand as written rather than correct it on the spot. All three passed on motions, seconds, and voice votes (aye).

cases.name: Wetland Mitigation Monitoring & Maintenance Bond — 4 Vincent Lane (Swort Residence)

timeline.summary: The board approved the town engineer's (KSCJ Consulting) recommendation regarding Tom and Sarah Swort's residential project at 4 Vincent Lane, Armonk, establishing a five-year wetland mitigation monitoring and maintenance bond. Adopted on a motion, second, and voice vote (aye) without discussion.

cases.name: Payment Application No. 9 — Papetil Construction, Water District No. 4 New Well Project

timeline.summary: The board approved payment application number nine to Papetil Construction Incorporated for site work performed on the Water District No. 4 new well project, on a motion, second, and voice vote (aye), without discussion.

cases.name: Alcohol Permit — Private Birthday Party, Community Park Pavilion

timeline.summary: The board approved an alcohol permit for a private birthday party at the Community Park Pavilion on July 26, 2026, on a motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Summer Camp Facility Use & Bus Lease Agreements with Byram Hills Central School District
cases.address: H.C. Crittenden Middle School and Wampus Elementary School, Armonk

timeline.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a summer-camp facility-use agreement with the Byram Hills Central School District for use of H.C. Crittenden Middle School and Wampus Elementary School from June 29 through August 7, 2026, and a companion bus lease agreement covering the same dates. Both passed on motion, second, and voice vote (aye) without discussion.

cases.name: Mold Remediation Contract — Servpro of Northern Westchester County (Highway Garage)

timeline.summary: The board approved a contract with Servpro of Northern Westchester County for mold remediation at the highway garage and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement. An unidentified board member questioned how the pricing was obtained and why the process had taken roughly six months; staff explained an earlier contractor found the job too large and re-testing was needed before Servpro, which had the capacity, was engaged. Supervisor Rende used the item to illustrate a broader point (echoing his parking-district remarks) that deferring the garage roof repair for years due to cost had ultimately led to a costlier mold problem, estimated at roughly $38,000 in remediation on top of a $197,000 roof replacement. Approved on a voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Town Hall Campus Advisory Task Force — Master Plan Presentation and Public Forum
cases.address: Town Hall municipal campus, Bedford Road, Armonk (approx. 10.5-acre site including current Town Hall/Village Hall, Highway Department, and the Birdsall House)
cases.applicant: Town Hall Campus Advisory Task Force (Alan Blum, chair; Rich Rosen, architect; Susan Geffen, designer; Diana Barra; George DePue; Adam Kaufman, Town Planner)

timeline.summary: The all-volunteer Town Hall Campus Advisory Task Force presented the results of a roughly three-month needs assessment of every town department, including site visits to comparable facilities in Westchester and Rockland counties, and unveiled conceptual space-relationship diagrams (not building designs) totaling about 80,000 gross square feet — roughly 46,000 sq ft for Village Hall functions and 15,000+ sq ft for the Highway Department plus new vehicle storage. The committee estimated an approximately $85 million rough-order-of-magnitude cost driven partly by New York's Wicks Law construction-bidding requirements, corrected several inaccurate figures circulating from an earlier presentation (school contribution, town budget, and reserve fund amounts), and proposed a phased build-out that keeps existing buildings operating throughout construction before demolishing the deteriorated Birdsall House. No town board vote or resolution occurred; the board's role going forward is to decide on financing (a municipal bond subject to public referendum), phasing, and hiring a professional engineer, architect, and construction manager. Supervisor Rende closed the meeting endorsing the urgency of the project and citing PESH (public-sector OSHA) violations — lack of decontamination/shower and rest facilities for highway and parks crews — as an additional driver.

cases.name: Probationary Appointment of Police Officers Thomas Rich and Preston Williams

timeline.summary: Chief Nagel recommended Thomas Rich and Preston Williams, both drawn from the Westchester County Civil Service list, for appointment as North Castle police officers after complete background investigations and interviews. The board voted to approve both probationary appointments effective June 26/27, 2026, and Supervisor Rende administered the oath of office to each in a ceremony with their families present; both will begin training at the Westchester County Police Academy on July 6.

cases.name: Public Comment: Pickleball Court Status and Parks Communication Process
cases.address: Lombardi Park; Winkler Park; Town Pool

timeline.summary: Resident Peter Gold, describing himself as a point of contact for roughly 100 pickleball players, asked for a status update on pickleball courts and criticized the town's communication process, noting that specific written questions sent to Rec & Parks staff (Matt Traynor) went unanswered. Supervisor Rende and Councilwoman DiGiacinto explained that the board is still assessing feasibility at Lombardi Park and prioritizing repairs to existing facilities in poor condition, particularly the Winkler Park tennis courts, with the rec advisory board slated to take up prioritization (including pickleball) at its July meeting. Town Administrator Kevin Hay added that the town pool renovation, already bonded, is the immediate funding priority, and that pickleball court funding would depend on how those pool bids come in by the end of June; Gold asked only that the town commit to brief, periodic status updates rather than silence.

cases.name: Ethics Board Annual Report Presentation
cases.applicant: Ethics Board (Chair Sue Schonberg, ASR rendered variously as 'Schimer'/'Schonner')

timeline.summary: Ethics Board Chair Sue Schonberg gave a brief verbal annual report, noting the board received no complaints and conducted no investigations this past year, but fielded a growing number of informal advisory-opinion requests from board and committee members seeking guidance on the ethics code, which she encouraged. She disclosed she recently found a discrepancy in the code that does not currently affect anyone but creates confusion, and said she would raise it with the ethics board before reaching out to the town attorney or special counsel Spolzino to discuss possible code improvements. A board member thanked the ethics board for its work and noted frustration that a prior ethics-code proposal had been delayed in coming to a town board vote.

cases.name: Receipt of Letter — Bosey's Water Main Transfer / Quarry Heights (Old Orchard Road) Water Service
cases.address: Old Orchard Road, Quarry Heights, North Castle

timeline.summary: The board considered receipt of a letter from Quarry Heights resident Joe Bradley regarding the status of a Westchester Joint Water Works main built around 2008 specifically to serve the Bosey's property, which runs along Old Orchard Road past roughly four other homes that lack public water and, per Sal (Water/Sewer superintendent), have reported water-quality issues. Sal explained the main is privately dedicated to Bosey's and not a North Castle municipal main, so connecting the other residents would require the town to form a new water district and take over the line from Westchester Joint Water Works; officials noted this would likely happen once a nearby property (referred to as the Jenny Clarkson/St. Christopher's site) is redeveloped and needs its own water extension. Councilwoman DiGiacinto pushed to accelerate relief for the affected residents rather than wait on speculative redevelopment, while Councilman Berra's attempt to raise a previously proposed 200-unit 'Vue' development and a 5,000-seat soccer stadium on the adjacent site was ruled out of order by Supervisor Rende as outside the scope of the letter. The board voted only to receive the letter; no district-formation action was taken.

cases.name: Tax Certiorari Consent Judgments — Rice v. Town of North Castle; Armonk Close Condominium (154 Bedford Road)

timeline.summary: The board authorized the town attorney to execute consent judgments settling two tax certiorari proceedings: Rice v. Town of North Castle and a matter involving the Armonk Close Condominium at 154 Bedford Road. cases.name: New Town Hall — Architectural and Planning Services RFP

timeline.summary: Following public comment from the town's 're-imagination committee' chair urging more detailed site/engineering information in the RFP (and a related public comment urging the board not to renew the nearby Marianis special use permit until new town hall site planning is complete), the board authorized Director of Planning Adam Kaufman to issue RFPs for architectural and planning services for the 2026 town hall project. Board members debated whether to direct the RFP toward solar/green-energy features or revised square-footage targets before hiring the architect, ultimately agreeing those decisions should follow the architect's own analysis rather than being dictated upfront.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Town Board's first meeting of 2022 combined the annual organizational agenda (routine authorizations, contracts, and liaison assignments) with a substantive regular meeting. New councilman Matt Milim was seated in place of outgoing Barry Ryder, and Barbara DiGiacinto was named Deputy Supervisor, though her proposed stipend later failed on a roll call vote. The board denied a one-year special use permit extension for the Marianne Gardens redevelopment at 45 Bedford Road, extended outdoor-dining/tent regulations through October 1, opened the door to a recreation-use zoning text amendment tied to a new fitness studio proposal, and declined to contest planning-board lead agency on a Banksville contractor-yard legalization (23 Banks Road).
meetings.durationNote: Full complement present: Supervisor Michael Schiliro and councilmembers Jose Berra, Saleem Hussain, Barbara DiGiacinto, and newly seated Matt Milim (replacing outgoing Barry Ryder). Berra recused himself from the Long Pond Park District agreement (organizational agenda item 25) and from the entire 23 Banks Road discussion due to a family/property conflict.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road — Marianne Gardens Special Use Permit Extension
cases.applicant: 45 Bedford Road LLC / NCD Acquisitions LLC (Marianne Gardens)
cases.summary: The board denied a one-year extension of the special use permit for the 43-unit Marianne Gardens redevelopment at 45 Bedford Road, first approved in 2019. Town Attorney Roland Baroni recommended denial, citing changed circumstances since approval — COVID-era traffic pattern shifts near the schools/Route 22 intersection and vacancy trends in nearby office buildings. Applicant's counsel Corey Salomon (Zarin & Steinmetz) argued there was no material change and that the ownership dispute (Mark Marianne's interest emerging from bankruptcy) had just been resolved that day, making the applicant ready to proceed. Numerous residents opposed the extension citing historic preservation (adjacent to the Bedford Road Historic District and St. Stephen's Church) and traffic/air-quality concerns near the schools; one resident (Neil Bauman) was more ambivalent, predicting the property would sit vacant regardless of the outcome. The board adopted a resolution of denial by consensus.
cases.publicComment: Multiple residents (via a letter from Judge Sue Shimer, plus Sharon, Ed, Kate Parker) urged denial citing historic preservation of the Bedford Road/landmarks districts and traffic/pollution concerns near the schools on Route 22. Neil Bauman, a longtime resident who had opposed prior proposals for the site, said the arguments were largely hypothetical but that he expected the property to remain undeveloped for years regardless of the board's decision.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted he was the only sitting member who had voted for the original zoning and one of only two who approved the special use permit, but agreed COVID-era changes — especially worsened traffic near the school/Route 22 intersection — justified denying the extension.

Argued that traffic near the school intersection had materially worsened since 2019 due to remote work and reduced school-bus ridership, making the 'change in circumstances' case for denying the extension.
Said the consistency of resident opposition was significant and that broader patterns of space use, not just traffic, had changed enough to warrant a fresh look at the project.

Said circumstances had changed and the board needed to evaluate traffic and downtown parking impacts, especially with more residential proposals expected before the board; preferred to hold off on extending the permit.

The change was prompted by a proposed 17-bike boutique cycling studio on Business Park Drive, whose principals presented their concept. Board members were broadly supportive but wanted to evaluate area-wide traffic and parking capacity before final action, and scheduled a public hearing for the January 26 meeting.

Called it a great location and idea, noting proximity to town makes it easier for residents to follow through on working out.
Said the board has considered embracing recreational uses in that district over time and scheduled a hearing to hear from the public and neighboring business owners before a final decision.

cases.name: Outdoor Dining / Temporary Tent Regulations Extension
cases.summary: The board extended North Castle's COVID-era temporary outdoor-dining and tent regulations for the three hamlets from a May 31 expiration to October 1, 2022, after Supervisor Schiliro relayed that restaurants needed a longer commitment window before investing in tents given supply-chain costs. Discussion covered New York State's six-month/calendar-year cap on temporary tents (which the town cannot locally preempt) and a plan to have Building Inspector Rob Melillo draft a town letter supporting individual businesses' state variance applications for longer tent placement. The board reported zero parking complaints under the program to date and adopted the extension unanimously.

memberPositions.evidence: Proposed extending outdoor-dining/tent rules to October 1 so restaurants could commit to tent investments, citing zero parking complaints under the program to date.

Supported extending outdoor dining through the fall while flagging the state's six-month tent limit and recommending the town send a supporting letter for businesses seeking a state variance for longer tent placement.

After extended debate about whether the town board should instead assert lead agency — given the wetland sensitivity, unresolved building-code violations, and the board's ultimate special-permit authority — the board declined to contest lead agency and let it default to the planning board, over Supervisor Schiliro's reservations. Councilman Berra recused himself from the entire item due to a personal/family conflict (the property is owned by the family of a former town figure, John Deacon Sr.).

memberPositions.evidence: Recused himself from the entire 23 Banks Road item, stating the property is owned by the family of a former colleague (John Deacon Sr.) and he had no ownership interest but wanted to avoid any appearance of conflict.

meetings.meetingSummary: With Supervisor Schiliro recovering from oral surgery and largely ceding the floor to Deputy Supervisor Barbara DiGiacinto, the board closed out the RELIP recreation-center zoning text amendment on its own motion after the triggering applicant withdrew, approved a $2.97 million NYSDEC water-quality grant for the Water District 2 wastewater treatment plant, adopted a strongly worded resolution opposing state ADU-preemption legislation (S.4547-A), approved an ABC Studios filming permit that sparked debate over resident-notification timing, and re-adopted the town's purchase of a Verizon-owned parcel on Whippoorwill Road East for municipal parking expansion.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present; Councilman Jose Berra participated remotely via Zoom for the public-hearing portion of the meeting. Supervisor Michael Schiliro, recovering from recent oral surgery, ceded most of the meeting-running duties to Deputy Supervisor Barbara DiGiacinto.

cases.name: Zoning Text Amendment — Recreation Centers Permitted in RELAB District
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (on its own motion, after the triggering applicant withdrew)
cases.summary: The board closed the public hearing and adopted, on its own motion, a zoning text amendment adding recreation centers as a permitted principal use in the town's narrow RELIP (light industrial) district, matching the use already allowed in other industrial districts. The original applicant — a boutique cycling studio — had already lost its Library Court space and withdrew, but the board proceeded anyway so the use would be available going forward, citing a comprehensive-plan precedent (the former bowling alley/gym conversion) and planning staff's view that there was no significant conflict with the comprehensive plan. Councilman Berra (participating remotely) raised concern about the lack of any size cap that could let an unexpectedly large facility be built as-of-right, floating a square-footage trigger for a special use permit, but the board opted to adopt the amendment without a cap now and revisit size limits at a future meeting, noting that site plan review and traffic-study requirements would still apply.
cases.publicComment: Resident Jen raised a general concern (echoed later re: the film permit item) that recreation-related street/traffic impacts near the two schools on Old Route 22 were not being adequately considered, though she was not speaking specifically against the applicant.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued for a square-footage cap or special-use-permit trigger so an unexpectedly large recreational facility couldn't be built as-of-right, but ultimately did not block adoption, agreeing to revisit sizing separately.
Argued against picking an arbitrary square-footage limit tonight, preferring to approve the amendment now and have the planning department come back promptly with any additional size/permit criteria.
Agreed with DiGiacinto that setting a size limit without more information would be premature and supported moving forward with the amendment as drafted.

The water/sewer superintendent explained the town will now negotiate a formal DEC work plan and timeline, with funds dispersed as the project progresses; the earlier public hearing on a bond resolution for the project was cited as part of what made the town competitive for the award.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked staff for the grant, noting it takes a large chunk out of the cost of the project for the district.

cases.name: Resolution Opposing NYS ADU Preemption Legislation (S.4547-A)
cases.summary: As a late addition prompted by Governor Hochul's State of the State address, the board unanimously adopted a resolution opposing proposed state legislation (S.4547-A) that would preempt local zoning control over accessory dwelling units — barring parking requirements for ADUs within a half-mile of a bus stop, among other provisions — which board members argued would effectively eliminate single-family zoning and override home rule. The board cited North Castle's own long-standing ADU law (since 1984), middle-income housing program, and affordable-housing requirements as evidence the town already supports the state's stated housing goals responsibly, and directed that the resolution go to the Governor, Senator Harkham/Epstein, and Assemblyman Burdick, while residents were urged to write in as well.

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill
memberPositions.evidence: Called the ADU bill one of the worst pieces of legislation he had seen since joining the town board, warning it would effectively eliminate single-family zoning and strip local control over parking, sewer, septic and setback requirements.

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill
memberPositions.evidence: Said the bill would fundamentally and irreparably change towns like North Castle for the worse and that the board should do everything it can to speak up against it.

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill
memberPositions.evidence: Highlighted that the bill would let garages be converted to apartments near bus stops with no parking requirement, worsening North White Plains' existing parking problems.
Supported the resolution, citing real water, sewer, septic and well-capacity constraints as the reason local zoning control over ADUs and density must be preserved.

cases.name: Film Permit — ABC Studios "Fleishman Is in Trouble" (33 Bayberry Road)
cases.summary: The board approved a two-day, $6,000 filming permit for ABC's "Fleishman Is in Trouble" at 33 Bayberry Road (7am-midnight), during which resident Jen argued the town's notification process is backwards — neighbors learn of street closures only after board approval, unlike the advance-notice requirement for something as minor as a home addition — and questioned whether filming fees were too low relative to what homeowners are paid. Town Clerk Allison explained current process (with police involvement to manage traffic/parking) and noted it had been substantially revised roughly 15 years ago after disruptive filming incidents; board members agreed the notification-timing point was reasonable and worth revisiting, while cautioning against adding process that would slow the town down. The permit was approved as submitted.
cases.publicComment: Resident Jen argued residents should be notified before, not after, board approval of filming permits that can close their streets for a full day, drawing a contrast with mandatory advance notice for minor home construction, and questioned whether the town's filming fees were too low; she had a heated exchange with Town Clerk Allison over the characterization of her comments as complaints.

memberPositions.evidence: Agreed that residents' general lack of awareness of relevant agenda items is a broader, important problem the board should work to fix through better communication.

Floated requiring advance mailed notice to affected residents before filming permits are decided, while cautioning that added process shouldn't slow down the town given separate complaints about town responsiveness.
Noted the filming-permit process had been substantially revamped roughly 15 years ago after disruptive shoots and said the board could look at tightening notification timing again.

cases.name: 23 Whippoorwill Road East — Verizon Parcel Purchase (Municipal Parking Expansion)
cases.summary: The board re-adopted its May 2021 resolution authorizing the supervisor to purchase a vacant Verizon-owned parcel at 23 Whippoorwill Road East for $50,000, adding the required permissive-referendum language. Supervisor Schiliro called it a long-sought opportunity, secured at well below earlier asking prices, to expand municipal parking behind the west side of Main Street.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the purchase a long-sought opportunity to expand parking behind the west side of Main Street, secured at a price well below what the town had faced in the past.

cases.name: Resolution Opposing NYS ADU Preemption Legislation (S.4547-A)
cases.summary: Continuing the fight against the state ADU-preemption bill adopted as a resolution at the prior meeting, Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto reported testifying at the NYS Assembly's Westchester budget hearing (and planned to testify at the Senate hearing) about the town's long affordable-housing record, and urged the board to lobby to strip the bill's roughly $85 million in associated budget funding. Supervisor Schiliro added detail on the bill's transit-oriented-development provision — which could allow up to 25 units/acre with no parking requirement within a quarter mile of a bus stop, a major exposure for North White Plains — and called it one of the most important issues of his tenure, urging mass resident mobilization (letters to Senator Mayer, Senator-elect Harkham, and Assemblyman Burdick).

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill
memberPositions.evidence: Reported testifying at the NYS Assembly budget hearing on the town's affordable-housing record and urged stripping the roughly $85 million in state budget funding tied to the ADU bill.

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill
memberPositions.evidence: Detailed the bill's transit-oriented-development provision allowing up to 25 units/acre with no parking requirement near bus stops, calling it especially dangerous for North White Plains and one of the most important issues of his time on the board.
Fully endorsed DiGiacinto's statement, noting the town is not perfect but is actively improving its own housing rules and shouldn't be overridden by one-size-fits-all state legislation.

cases.name: Local Law — Special Use Permit Requirement for Recreation Centers
cases.summary: Following up on the RELIP recreation-use amendment, the planning department presented a draft local law requiring a special use permit (with town-board-reviewed standards on traffic intensity by road classification, buffering, setbacks for outdoor facilities, and a discretionary catch-all) for new recreation centers across the CB, RB, GB, PLI and RELIP zoning districts. The board declared lead agency, referred the draft to the planning boards and interested agencies, and scheduled a public hearing for March 9. Councilman Berra pressed for more specificity on traffic-impact triggers, buffer/setback adequacy near residential lots (citing tennis-court noise), and possible square-footage limits, while Councilman Milim cautioned against an overly broad discretionary clause that could unduly deter desirable projects; Supervisor Schiliro noted the town's parking formula already constrains oversized facilities.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the draft a good approach but pressed for clarity on traffic-impact triggers relative to major/collector roads, adequacy of buffer/setback distances near residential lots (citing tennis-court noise as an example), and whether a square-footage cap should still be considered.
Called the draft a great start giving appropriate oversight, but flagged the catch-all provision (section six) as a risk of discouraging desirable projects the town would actually want.
Reminded the board that the existing parking formula already limits how large a recreation facility can practically be built, reducing the need for an additional hard size cap.
Said he supported recreational uses generally, especially given more people working from home and staying active, while wanting enough scrutiny to protect quality of life.

cases.name: Playground Equipment Purchase — Winkler, Lombardi, Clove Road & IBM Community Parks
cases.summary: The board authorized the supervisor to sign purchase agreements with GameTime/MRC Recreation for new playground equipment (including poured-in-place surfacing) at Winkler Park, Lombardi Park, Clove Road Community Park and IBM Community Park, capping a roughly nine-month public-input process led by Parks & Rec. Installation costs and timing remain subject to supply-chain delays and will be finalized closer to delivery.

memberPositions.evidence: Praised the roughly nine-month turnaround from initial concept to signed equipment orders as a model of the town moving quickly despite public perceptions that government is slow.

cases.name: 85 Cox Avenue (Lombardi Park) — Old Recreation Building / Water System Relocation
cases.summary: Parks liaison Councilman Milim presented two options for the deteriorating former recreation building at Lombardi Park, whose basement houses the park's water system: (1) demolish and rebuild a similarly sized structure, or (2) demolish and instead relocate/upgrade the water system into a two-story addition on the adjacent parks garage, freeing the old building's footprint for parking and a small concession window. Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto, after touring the building, argued strongly for outright demolition without replacement as fiscally responsible given the building's disrepair (mold, failing furnace, crumbling ceiling) and the garage's already-improved condition. The board declined to authorize the proposed engineering/architecture agreements (~$6,120 plus related costs) immediately, instead agreeing to schedule a board site visit (inviting the Parks & Rec Advisory Board) followed by a public agenda item to weigh options — including possible food-scrap-composting use — before committing funds, while flagging the aging furnace as a near-term risk requiring contingency planning (temporary heaters) if it fails before the issue is resolved.

memberPositions.evidence: After touring the building, argued it would be fiscally irresponsible to rebuild given its disrepair (mold, crumbling ceiling, failing furnace), and urged the rest of the board to see it firsthand before committing to any construction plan.

memberPositions.stance: cautious, wants more process before committing funds
memberPositions.evidence: Cited past missteps on town building projects (IBM Park, North White Plains Community Center) as reason to slow down, and proposed a board site visit plus a public work session/agenda item before signing any engineering agreement.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of moving the project forward carefully
memberPositions.evidence: Laid out both the rebuild and garage-relocation options, emphasized the aging water-system furnace as the urgent underlying problem, and agreed to a site visit plus agenda item before any funding commitment.

Raised the concern that relocating the park's water supply could trigger Department of Health/Board of Health review that might slow or complicate the project, recommending the town consult its water superintendent first.

cases.name: Technology Task Force — Initial Member Appointments
cases.summary: The board formally appointed the first members of the new Technology Task Force (Brian Singer, Claire Lovell, Gladys Vera, Jared Nussbaum, Mike Acavan, and Noy Sukhavira), with Councilman Hussain (initiative lead) and Town Clerk Allison Simon as ex officio staff, to examine town technology operations, resident communications, data security, and misinformation handling, with a first progress report expected at the April meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Explained the task force's purpose (technology lens on town operations, resident communications, data security, misinformation) and thanked the unusually large, highly qualified pool of applicants.
Thanked Hussain and the Town Clerk for the many hours spent selecting from an oversubscribed, highly talented applicant pool.
Called the caliber of applicants mind-blowing and credited the process as evidence of the community's high level of education and civic engagement.

cases.name: Police Department Promotions — Lieutenant Huffnagle & Sergeant Aaronberg
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (North Castle Police Department)
cases.summary: On Chief Peter Simonson's recommendation, the board approved the probationary promotion of Sergeant Reagan Huffnagle to Police Lieutenant and Police Officer Donald Aaronberg to Police Sergeant, filling vacancies created by Lieutenant Brant Salmon's retirement, effective February 26, 2022.

cases.name: Board of Ethics Annual Report & Proposed Ethics-Education Work Session
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle Board of Ethics
cases.summary: Board of Ethics chair Brett Summers gave the annual report, highlighting Westchester County's new mandatory ethics-education requirement and a Mount Kisco Village planning-board ethics violation (an improperly executed recusal) as cautionary examples, and recommended a joint work session with the town board to consider adding a mandatory ethics-training requirement and expanding annual disclosure filings to planning board/ZBA members. The town board agreed to schedule a work session on ethics education, while distinguishing it from broader employee-policy training (raised by Councilman Hussain) that would need to account for collective-bargaining constraints.

memberPositions.evidence: Agreed to add ethics education to the list of upcoming work session topics and to have Councilman Berra, as ethics-board liaison, help shape a joint session.

As ethics-board liaison, endorsed a work session, framing ethics education as protecting well-intentioned people from inadvertent violations as much as deterring bad actors, citing the Mount Kisco example.

cases.name: Local Law — Alternative Veterans Tax Exemption Levels
cases.summary: Following a brief, uncontested public hearing, the board adopted a local law amending the town's alternative veterans tax exemption levels (covering roughly 175 North Castle veterans across service, combat, and disability categories), consistent with a county-level recommendation.

memberPositions.evidence: Explained the three exemption categories and called the measure a wonderful way to honor and thank the town's roughly 175 veterans.

cases.name: Resolution Opposing NYS ADU Preemption Legislation (S.4547-A)
cases.summary: The board devoted extensive time to the ADU/transit-oriented-development (TOD) provisions embedded in the Governor's budget (S.8006, parts AA and EE), with Supervisor Schiliro and Director of Planning Adam Kaufmann presenting a map showing that a half-mile TOD radius around the North White Plains train station (25+ units/acre, no parking requirement) would reach deep into existing residential neighborhoods on an aging road network. All board members reiterated unified, strong opposition, urging thousands of resident emails to Senator Mayer, Senator-elect Harkham, and Assemblyman Burdick before an expected end-of-March budget vote, while noting a proposed exemption for towns with existing ADU laws (like North Castle) as likely short-lived given anticipated future 'look-back' pressure to conform.

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill
memberPositions.evidence: Presented a map of the North White Plains TOD radius and called this the biggest issue facing the town in his 14 years on the board, warning the proposed exemption for towns with existing ADU laws would likely be short-lived.

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill
memberPositions.evidence: Reiterated that the legislation could fundamentally and irreparably change the town and called for continued collective and individual action.

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill

Urged residents to write to representatives even without deep technical knowledge, framing civic engagement on the issue as a basic responsibility of citizenship.

memberPositions.stance: strongly opposed to the state bill
memberPositions.evidence: Called the legislation 'an atomic bomb...dropped on New York State municipalities' that should be wholly rejected rather than negotiated, and urged residents to inform coworkers outside North Castle to multiply pressure on legislators.

cases.name: Zoning Text Amendment — Warehouses Permitted in IMD-AA District (7 New King Street)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (on its own motion, at the property owner's request)
cases.summary: Planning staff identified that the code only expressly permits warehouses at the airport, leaving an existing (and proposed-to-be-expanded) warehouse at 7 New King Street technically non-conforming; the applicant's attorney asked the town board to initiate a text amendment on its own motion (bypassing the usual 50%-of-district-owners petition threshold) to clarify that warehouses (excluding truck terminals) are permitted in the IMD-AA district, limited to New King Street and the North Castle portion of the airport. After debate about the precedent of the board initiating zoning changes for a private applicant, the board declared intent to act as lead agency and referred the draft to planning boards and interested agencies (including the Town of Greenwich, given nearby Connecticut residences), but declined to schedule the public hearing yet, opting to first review agency feedback.

memberPositions.stance: cautious about precedent, ultimately supportive of the process
memberPositions.evidence: Raised concern about the town board initiating a zoning change on a private applicant's behalf setting an informal precedent for future requests, while agreeing the path is legally available and choosing to proceed carefully.
Confirmed with the town attorney that the board's own-motion action would carry no legal precedent risk and supported moving forward with the referral.
Flagged that nearby Connecticut (Greenwich) residents near the district boundary should be properly notified and given a chance to weigh in through the intermunicipal referral process.

cases.name: SCADA System Service Agreement — Water & Sewer Operations
cases.summary: The board authorized a five-year SCADA (water/sewer monitoring) service and software-license agreement with Westchester Water Works, which water/sewer superintendent Sal presented as saving roughly $20,000 over five years versus annual renewal. Councilman Berra questioned whether the vendor's right to terminate for convenience undermined the value of locking in five-year pricing, but ultimately supported the agreement given the vendor's long track record and reputation.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted the vendor's mutual termination-for-convenience clause means the five-year pricing isn't truly locked in, though he ultimately did not oppose the agreement given the vendor's reputation and history.
Vouched for the vendor's reputation as a major player in the regional water-works community and expressed confidence the termination clause posed minimal practical risk.

cases.name: IT Network Support Contract — Logically (2022)
cases.summary: Councilman Berra flagged several contract terms in the proposed 2022 IT network-support agreement with Logically (successor to the town's prior vendor, Sullivan): an unexplained new-client 'onboarding fee' despite an ongoing vendor relationship, a 1.5%/month late-payment interest charge plus attorney's-fee/collection-cost language, a confidentiality clause needing a Freedom of Information Law carve-out, and — most significantly — an early-termination fee formula combined with an annual CPI-or-greater price-escalation clause that could raise costs regardless of actual inflation. The board agreed to table the contract pending clarification from the vendor and Town Attorney Baroni on these points.

memberPositions.evidence: Identified an unexplained onboarding fee, an above-market late-payment interest rate, an open-ended collection-cost clause, and a CPI-or-greater annual escalator combined with an early-termination penalty as terms warranting clarification before signing.
Agreed the onboarding fee and other terms deserved more background before approval and supported tabling the item.

cases.name: Cohen Law Group Legal Bill — Wireless Communications Law Billing Detail Dispute
cases.summary: For the second consecutive meeting, Councilman Berra withheld support for paying a roughly $3,900 special-counsel invoice from the Cohen Law Group (wireless communications law work) over block-billed time entries he felt were disproportionate to the work described, requesting the attorney self-audit and confirm the billed hours were accurate. Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto and Supervisor Schiliro pushed back sharply, arguing the detail already provided was typical of attorney billing and that further line-item scrutiny risked questioning the attorney's integrity after he had voluntarily under-billed in the past; the exchange grew testy before the board split the item from the warrant, approved the rest of the warrant, and agreed to send a general request for confirmation back to the attorney pending the next meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Compared the disputed invoice's hours to earlier, lower-billed periods for similar work and asked that counsel confirm his time entries were accurate before the town pays, while explicitly saying he did not intend to impugn the attorney's integrity.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to further scrutiny, wants to pay
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the invoice detail was standard for attorney billing and pushed back forcefully on requests for finer-grained justification (e.g., how long a single email took to draft), calling it unreasonable.
Proposed the compromise of asking the attorney to self-certify that billed hours matched work performed, rather than itemizing individual tasks in greater depth, to resolve the impasse.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of paying, agreed a response was owed
memberPositions.evidence: Said he personally had no problem with the bill but agreed the attorney owed the board a response to Berra's outstanding question before final payment.

cases.name: RM-FSCH Senior Housing District — Floating Zone to Mapped District Conversion
cases.summary: The board advanced a local law converting the RM-FSCH (senior citizen housing) floating zone to a mapped zoning district, on the town attorney's recommendation, to give the board more flexibility: unlike a floating zone, a mapped-district rezoning petition the board finds without merit can simply be declined rather than processed to conclusion (and risk litigation over a denial). Councilman Berra asked clarifying questions about scope and whether a parallel approach might apply elsewhere in the code but did not object. The board declared lead agency, referred to the planning board, and scheduled an April 27 public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he had been interested in this conversion for some time after discussing it with the town attorney and planning director.
Asked the town attorney to explain how the floating-zone-to-map conversion would work and whether a similar approach should be considered for other special-use-permit provisions in the code.

cases.name: North White Plains — Illegal Multi-Family Conversion Enforcement
cases.applicationType: code enforcement (public comment, no board action)
cases.summary: Resident Tony raised long-standing frustration (complaints dating to 1974) over unenforced illegal three-family home conversions in North White Plains, describing visible construction activity, deliveries, and online rental listings for what he alleged were illegal units, and proposed requiring homeowner/insurer registration with the building department at purchase as an enforcement tool. Deputy Supervisor DiGiacinto responded with two recent building-department enforcement examples (one cleared as a legal renovation, one halted after a Zillow listing tipped off the department), acknowledging real legal limitations (e.g., inspectors cannot look in windows without a warrant) constrain enforcement.
cases.publicComment: Resident Tony described a pattern of newly purchased homes in North White Plains being converted to illegal three-family units without permits, straining police/fire resources, and proposed the town require owner/insurer registration at purchase as a deterrent tool.

memberPositions.stance: acknowledges the problem, defends enforcement record
memberPositions.evidence: Described two recent building-department enforcement actions in North White Plains and acknowledged legal limits (no window-peering without cause) on what inspectors can proactively investigate.

cases.name: 23 Banks Road (Banksville) — Contractor's Yard Special Use Permit & Masonry Retail Zoning Text Amendment
cases.applicationType: special use permit / zoning text amendment
cases.applicant: 23 Banks Design Group LLC (Tony Beniziano, applicant's attorney; incoming tenant/contract vendee)

The board, at Councilman Berra's urging, added a direct referral to the Conservation Board for input before the public hearing (rather than only via the planning board's later site-plan review) and scheduled three related public hearings for April 27.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued the board needed at least a preliminary assessment to have an informed work-session discussion, and helped negotiate the phased, capped-cost compromise that was ultimately approved.
Reported detail from his own site tour with the chief and architect about the crawl-space expansion option and its likely cost drivers, informing the board's scoping discussion.
