cases.name: Local Law — Special Use Permit Requirement for Recreation Centers
cases.summary: The board closed the public hearing and adopted the recreation-center special use permit local law after extensive line-item drafting review with the planning director. Key changes: excluding BMX and skateboard parks entirely from the permitted-use definition (requiring a future zone text amendment rather than just a special use permit for either), keeping swimming pools in the definition despite a debate over whether a private pool could undercut the town's planned acquisition of its municipal pool, removing 'franchise sports'/limiting to seating capacity language to exclude stadium-scale spectator venues, adding instructional-class language (yoga, Pilates, etc. generically rather than by name), and rejecting a proposed 25,000-40,000 sq ft size cap in favor of relying on existing zoning constraints (parking formula, floor-area ratio, setbacks).
cases.publicComment: Resident Jen urged the board not to add BMX and skateboarding as a combined extra barrier to entry, arguing skateboarding (already happening informally in town, low environmental impact) is meaningfully different from BMX (dirt-track, higher land impact) and that excluding both risked losing a desirable skate park proposal to a neighboring town.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to BMX/skateboard inclusion on environmental grounds
memberPositions.evidence: Argued from an environmental point of view against permitting BMX facilities as-of-right, noting such tracks strip all vegetation, and successfully pushed to exclude both BMX and skateboard parks from the as-of-right list pending a future zone text amendment if a specific proposal arose.

memberPositions.stance: wanted a size cap; opposed to allowing pools as-of-right
memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly pushed for a 25,000-40,000 sq ft cap on recreation centers as a precaution against unforeseen large-scale proposals, and separately argued the town should not permit a private competing swimming pool as-of-right given planned public investment in the town's own pool, though he ultimately did not block either provision when outvoted.

memberPositions.stance: opposed size cap; supportive of allowing private pools
memberPositions.evidence: Argued against both a hard-coded square-footage limit (preferring case-by-case special-use review) and against excluding pools from the definition just to protect a future public asset from competition, framing the town's goal as maximizing resident access to recreation regardless of provider.

memberPositions.stance: aligned with Berra on protecting the future public pool
memberPositions.evidence: Agreed with Berra that a private pool could undermine the economic viability of the town's planned public pool by splitting membership, favoring limiting private competition at least for now.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the November/December 2021 Beautification Committee process was deliberate and had majority Parks & Rec board support, and proposed waiting to see the installed items before deciding whether to move them.

meetings.durationNote: Full Town Board present (Supervisor Michael Schiliro presiding, plus Jose Berra, Barbara DiGiacinto, Saleem Hussain, Matt Milim); Board of Ethics Chair Brett Summers presented in person with Secretary Kerry, member Ed Loberman, and a member referred to as "Judge" participating remotely; Town Clerk Allison and Town Administrator Kevin also participated. Town Attorney Rowan/Roland was expected but had left before the meeting concluded, leaving the public-hearing question for the disclosure-form changes unresolved pending his advice.

cases.name: Board of Ethics — Education & Financial Disclosure Requirements Expansion
cases.status: work session discussion; public hearing to be determined
cases.summary: The Board of Ethics recommended: (1) a mandatory three-minute educational video plus Q&A for department heads, elected officials, and members of the Planning Board, ZBA, ARB, and Assessment Review Board, to be shown at existing department-head and committee meetings and voluntarily offered to other boards; (2) expanding annual disclosure-form obligations for that same group to cover non-primary-residence real estate interests and business interests that do business with the town (dropping a broader county-style "all business interests" disclosure as too burdensome); and (3) codifying that alternates automatically hold over until replaced and giving alternates a defined term. The Town Board directed staff to move forward on producing the video and to have the Town Attorney confirm whether a public hearing is legally required to expand who must file disclosure forms; the meeting ended without a final resolution on whether Labor Counsel/Town Attorney sign-off is needed before the revised disclosure form is distributed.

memberPositions.evidence: As Supervisor, said it was "crucially important" to beef up the ethics disclosure function given examples of problems in other municipalities and pushed to move forward quickly rather than let review process delay implementation to next year, while also voicing sympathy for not wanting overly broad disclosure requirements to discourage volunteers.

Said she would "hate to either lose a planning board member... or not have a new volunteer because they're just a little taken aback by having to upfront give a little too much personal information," and pressed for the revised disclosure form to be reviewed "completely from every angle" before being sent out.

Argued for both speed and transparency, saying volunteers who would hesitate to serve because they don't want to disclose real estate/business interests "we may actually want to reconsider their volunteerism," since residents need visibility into policymakers' potential conflicts.

themes.note: Entire work session devoted to Board of Ethics recommendations.

staffInput.summary: Presented the full slate of recommendations (education video, expanded disclosure scope, alternate-term housekeeping fixes), explained the legal basis for disclosure definitions (Chapter 27 code of ethics), and fielded extensive Q&A from the board.
Helped keep the discussion on time and asked the town board to weigh in on logistics for showing the educational video to volunteer committees.

Strongly advocated that the revised disclosure form and process go through Labor Counsel review before finalization, citing a past multi-year delay caused by skipping that step, and pushed back on Town Board members who called that a "red herring."

Clarified that the group intentionally scoped the education/disclosure requirement to exclude unionized labor staff, and that the disclosure-form expansion likely requires a public hearing while the education component likely does not, pending Town Attorney confirmation.

Raised the recommendation that Labor Counsel review the revised disclosure form given past back-and-forth revisions, and that logistics (collection, tracking) would run through the Clerk's office in coordination with the Board of Ethics.

meetings.meetingSummary: A long regular Town Board meeting (roughly three hours) covering a public hearing to convert the senior citizen housing (RM-FD-SCH) floating zone to a mapped zoning district, a homeowners-association dispute over a duplicate maintenance bond tied to a court-mandated tree-replacement planting at Whippoorwill Hills, an extended and emotional public-comment session from Birchgrove Drive residents about recurring Con Edison electrical failures including a house fire, a routine home-rule resolution renewing the hotel occupancy tax request to Albany, and a large consent agenda of contracts, bid authorizations, and grant/award receipts.

cases.name: RM-FD-SCH Senior Citizen Housing District — Floating Zone to Mapped District Conversion
cases.summary: Town-initiated local law converting the residential multifamily senior citizen housing (RM-FD-SCH) zoning classification from a floating zone to a traditional mapped district, restoring language giving the Town Board discretion to decline to even process a rezoning petition it finds inappropriate (rather than being obligated to act on any application). Prompted in part by lessons from a past senior-housing project (referenced by a resident, Christine Angelton, as an unfinished, poorly-maintained development on her block) where the board felt it lacked the ability to simply decline an application. Adopted unanimously with a negative declaration after a public hearing with one resident speaker.
cases.publicComment: Resident Christine Angelton, whose block hosts an existing senior-housing floating-zone project, questioned why the zone still "floats" under the new law and described ongoing unfinished-infrastructure problems (no CO, incomplete sewer hookups, poor road/landscaping conditions) from that earlier project as context for supporting more board discretion going forward.

memberPositions.evidence: Credited with leading the effort to bring this amendment forward, explaining her motivation was that the town has little large land remaining and wanted a future board to be able to simply decline an inappropriate application without being sued.

Said he's "always wary when things give the board more power, not less," but concluded this change reduces risk to the town without being exploitable by a future board, calling it "a very clear yes," while probing whether the change would have altered the outcome of the earlier problematic project.

cases.name: Whippoorwill Hills HOA — Tree Replacement Mitigation & Maintenance Bond Agreement
cases.summary: Following litigation over a neighbor's unauthorized removal of nine mature regulated trees in the HOA's buffer zone, the Planning Board's November 2021 resolution required the HOA to post a bond/security and submit a two-year tree maintenance and monitoring plan. The HOA asked the Town Board to reject the Town Engineer's (Kellard Sessions) recommendation for a second, separate ~$1,628 maintenance bond on top of the ~$11,945 planting bond, arguing it was superfluous since the full planting-bond amount would already be held for the entire two-year maintenance period. The board agreed, and approved the legal agreement as revised to explicitly state the existing bond also covers maintenance/monitoring, waiving the second bond.

memberPositions.evidence: Walked through the bond math with the HOA president to confirm the existing $11,945 bond, held for the full two years, already covered the maintenance period, agreeing the second bond was superfluous in this specific case (though standard practice elsewhere).

Questioned why the town would hold the full ~$12,000 for two years rather than reducing it after the planting was complete, but deferred to the Planning Board's prior decision and agreed not adding a second bond layer was reasonable given the HOA's own strong incentive to keep the trees alive.

cases.name: Birchgrove Drive — Con Edison Underground Electrical Failures & House Fire
cases.summary: Multiple Birchgrove Drive residents described repeated dangerous power surges over recent months, including one that caused a house fire at 20 Birchgrove Drive four weeks earlier that displaced a family, plus flickering lights and a temporary emergency disconnection at another home. Con Edison had begun a duct-replacement project expected to remedy roughly eight homes plus a broader "power quality test" to identify further issues, but residents reported poor internal Con Ed communication (conflicting statements about which lines were checked) and a claim that Con Ed believed the town wouldn't allow pavement to be dug up on the recently repaved street. The board pledged to keep pressuring Con Ed, confirmed it has no objection to road excavation/repaving if needed to fix the underground lines, and discussed drafting a written communication to Con Edison and designating a single town point of contact (Town Administrator Kevin) for residents.
cases.publicComment: Extended public comment from multiple Birchgrove Drive residents (Mark Smith and his wife Marnie, whose home caught fire; neighbors Piper/Zach at #5 and others at #8, #12, #18, #19) describing five houses with serious power-surge damage, poor Con Ed communication, and requests that the town press Con Ed to fully replace deteriorated 1960s-era underground aluminum wiring rather than a partial fix.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the town's role is to advocate and apply pressure at a level Con Edison takes seriously, stated the goal is to make the electrical situation "a non-issue" for the street permanently, and confirmed the town has no preference against digging up recently paved road if that's what's needed.

Pressed for specifics on which homes the Con Ed duct-replacement project would actually fix and flagged that Con Ed's internal and resident-facing communication seemed to be a core problem, asking residents directly what they would need to see from Con Ed for confidence going forward.

Adopted without discussion.

meetings.meetingSummary: A Town Board work session devoted entirely to how the town should handle board-member remote participation and public Zoom access once the COVID-era executive order authorizing teleconferenced meetings expires and New York's amended Open Meetings Law (new Public Officers Law 103-a) takes effect June 8, 2022. With Town Attorney Rowan/Roland dialing in for part of the session, the board worked through whether adopting the new law's "extraordinary circumstances" remote-participation option would replace or coexist with the pre-COVID default law (which allows remote participation from a noticed public place without an extraordinary-circumstance requirement, but which the town has never actually used), and debated how broadly to define "extraordinary circumstances" if it adopts the new local law. The board agreed to add two items to the next meeting's agenda: (1) allowing continued public Zoom access to town board meetings under the existing framework, and (2) considering scheduling a public hearing to adopt a local law under the new remote-participation option, while reserving final judgment on both.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present but with technical/attendance complications: Councilman Jose Berra had intermittent connectivity issues joining remotely; Councilman Matt Milim participated remotely due to recent COVID recovery/quarantine; Councilwoman Barbara DiGiacinto arrived late, explaining she was taking extra care after visiting someone in hospice. Town Attorney Rowan/Roland and Town Clerk Allison participated for portions of the discussion.

cases.name: Remote Board Participation & Public Zoom Access — Open Meetings Law Update
cases.status: work session discussion; public hearing to be considered
cases.summary: With the COVID executive order authorizing remote public meetings expiring, the board discussed two separate questions: whether to adopt New York's new Open Meetings Law amendment allowing board members to participate remotely under narrowly-defined "extraordinary circumstances" (illness, disability, caregiving, or other significant/unexpected events) without the public having to be present at the member's remote location (while still requiring an in-person quorum), versus relying on the pre-existing default law (remote participation allowed from a noticed public place, open to the public, with no extraordinary-circumstance test) which the town has never used; and separately, whether to continue allowing the public to watch/participate in town board meetings via Zoom going forward, which the board concluded does not require a local law, just a board decision/agenda item. The board directed staff to get a definitive answer from the Town Attorney on whether adopting the new law forecloses the old default option, and agreed to place both a public-Zoom-access decision and a possible public hearing on adopting the new remote-participation local law on the next meeting's agenda, while keeping all options open.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued strongly that residents need the ability to "look them in the eye" and address board members face-to-face, said in his 15 years' experience that matters a great deal, and cautioned against giving board members an "easy way out" to attend by screen rather than in person, while acknowledging pandemic experience has normalized Zoom.

Pressed repeatedly on how broadly "extraordinary circumstances" could be interpreted (e.g., whether a routine family vacation could qualify via a caregiving angle) and argued the town should define the standard as specifically as possible via something like a list, to avoid disputes over whether a member's stated reason truly qualifies.

Argued physical presence is becoming less determinative over time and that better A/V setup could let the town engage far more of its ~12,000 residents virtually, while agreeing the town should take incremental steps rather than a "giant leap" and start any changes with the town board itself before extending to other boards.

Participating remotely himself while recovering from COVID, argued the new law's flexibility would help in situations like his own (well enough to attend but not wanting to expose others), and pushed back on the idea that only a public room like a conference room could substitute, since that would just relocate exposure risk.

Said she likes the old default law because it "encourages people to plan ahead" and be physically present, arriving to the meeting itself late after taking extra COVID precautions from a hospice visit, illustrating the tension she was describing.

themes.note: Entire work session devoted to this single procedural/legal topic.

staffInput.summary: Explained the mechanics of the new Open Meetings Law amendment (quorum requirements, ADA/transcript obligations, the two-year sunset), cautioned that whether the new law forecloses the pre-COVID default remote option was legally unclear, and left before the discussion concluded, leaving the question to be resolved before the next meeting.
Confirmed current practice (in-person-only public participation since returning to the meeting room) and that other board secretaries would need direction if remote public access were formalized.

Raised the practical burden on meeting facilitators/applicants of running hybrid meetings and floated the idea of a dedicated technical support role, and discussed how to gather input from other boards and committees before extending any new remote policy beyond the town board.

meetings.attributionNote: This work session had unusually clear speaker attribution because participants were repeatedly addressed by name in a live back-and-forth legal discussion (Jose, Matt, Selene/Saleem, Roland, Allison), and the Supervisor's presiding role and self-referential comments ("my 15th year") made Michael Schiliro's statements straightforward to identify.

cases.name: Brothers Green Corp — Contractor's Yard/Nursery Special Permit (11 Bedford Banksville Road)
cases.applicant: Brothers Green Corp (Richard and Ted Greene)
cases.status: referred to town and county planning boards
cases.summary: Brothers Green Corp, operating a contractor's yard/storage use on the 3.7-acre property (partly in wetlands/wetland buffer) since 1984 and owning it since 2007, sought a special permit to legalize the long-standing use after being told during an unrelated 2019 home-renovation permit review that no site plan approval of record existed for the property. The applicant argued the use predates modern wetlands regulation and requested the permit maintain the status quo (using existing concrete-block boundary markers placed in the 1990s) without any expansion. The board referred the application to the town and county planning boards, discussed inviting the conservation board given the wetland buffer, and agreed to schedule a joint site walk; a Planning Board site-plan application was filed in parallel.

cases.name: Summit Club (formerly Brynwood) — Amended & Restated Water District #2B Contribution Agreement
cases.status: deferred; vote postponed to next meeting
cases.summary: After a nearly two-hour work session, the board considered authorizing the Supervisor to sign an amended and restated water district contribution agreement splitting the existing Water District #2 (Windmill) into subsidiary districts 2A and 2B, following the developer's inability to develop a satisfactory new well supply at the original well field as contemplated years earlier (per state comptroller guidance, since dissolving/reforming the district risked triggering bond acceleration). Jose Berra raised detailed legal questions — disputing the recital language that the developer made "best efforts" to find water, probing bond-acceleration risk from reallocating debt service among the ~365 remaining district users, and questioning the town's liability exposure under a contractual "authority and enforceability" representation (Section 10B) — all of which the Town Attorney addressed without identifying material risk. The board ultimately declined to vote, with Matt Milim and Barbara DiGiacinto arguing residents needed more time to review and comment (citing a still-unresolved indemnification question raised by a resident, Ed [surname unclear], at the work session) and noting a companion bifurcation resolution still needed to be finalized with the Town Engineer.
cases.publicComment: A resident referred to as Ed raised concerns about indemnification provisions at the preceding work session; the board felt that discussion, and broader resident feedback, was cut short by time constraints and warranted more time before a vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he wasn't comfortable voting that night because not all public comment had been heard (citing a resident's cut-off indemnification question) and noted a perception among some residents that the original Summit Club approval process felt rushed at the end, arguing a 13-day delay to the next meeting cost little.

Pushed back firmly on the "rushed process" characterization, noting the original approvals took "months and months" with substantial public input, while ultimately agreeing to postpone the vote once the Town Attorney flagged that a companion bifurcation resolution still needed to be prepared.

Extensively questioned the "best efforts" recital language, asked whether reallocating the ~14 Summit Club units' debt-service share among remaining district users could trigger bond acceleration, and asked whether Section 10B's authority/enforceability representation could expose the town to legal liability if any underlying assumption proved incorrect.

Said his sense from residents was that people wanted the water supplies kept clearly separate (not wanting "golf course water") and was surprised more residents hadn't spoken up given the complexity, concluding more time for residents to digest the agreement was warranted.

themes.note: The Summit Club water district contribution agreement, discussed for roughly 2.5 hours across a work session and the regular meeting, dominated this meeting.

staffInput.summary: Explained the state comptroller-guided approach to restructuring Water District #2 into subsidiary districts, addressed Jose Berra's legal risk questions on bond acceleration and Section 10B liability, and flagged that a companion bifurcation resolution still needed to be drafted with the Town Engineer before the agreement could be signed.

Presented the special permit application, argued the decades-long contractor's-yard use should be legalized largely on grandfathering/fairness grounds, and stated the applicant believed it met all special permit criteria.
Presented the reinstated Conservation Board annual report and raised a question about how the Brothers Green wetland use, predating modern wetlands law, should be weighed in a permit recommendation.

meetings.meetingSummary: A continuation work session (Supervisor Michael Schiliro joining remotely while recovering from COVID) walking through the remaining discretionary sections of the mandatory NYS Uniform Code update with Building Inspector Rob Malelo and Town Planner Adam Kaufman: the shed/accessory-structure building-permit size threshold, the list of code-exempt minor structures, building-permit validity periods, stalled/"zombie" construction projects, and operating-permit administration. The board also spent significant time on the separate but related new state mandate requiring individual towns to inspect and permit food trucks, which the Building Inspector and board agreed is impractical and poorly conceived, and discussed intermunicipal advocacy (a joint letter or coordinated lobbying with neighboring towns like Mount Kisco and Bedford) to push back on it. The board concluded it was ready to schedule a public hearing on the code update.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Michael Schiliro participated remotely via Zoom after testing positive for COVID; three other board members were present in person along with at least one additional member participating remotely; Building Inspector Rob Malelo and Town Planner Adam Kaufman led the technical walkthrough.

cases.name: NYS Uniform Fire Prevention & Building Code — Mandatory Local Law Update
cases.status: work session concluded; ready to schedule public hearing
cases.summary: Continuing the work session series, the board worked through the remaining discretionary sections of the code update with the Building Inspector and Town Planner: (1) kept the existing 64-square-foot (rather than the state's 144-square-foot) threshold for when a shed/accessory structure requires a building permit, after extended debate about setback/zoning implications on small lots, with Matt Milim dissenting in favor of a larger or lot-size-tiered threshold to reduce resident burden; (2) affirmed keeping the town's existing exemptions for playground equipment, swings, low garden walls, small treehouses (capped at 144 sq ft), and shallow above-ground pools, which staff confirmed the state had approved; (3) kept the existing 12-month/2-year building permit validity window rather than the state's shorter recommendation, while separately directing that escalating renewal fees (via the master fee schedule, not the code itself) be used to discourage indefinitely stalled "zombie" construction projects, a concern Jose Berra raised; and (4) kept operating permits administratively separate from certificates of occupancy per the Building Inspector's preference. The board concluded the code update was ready for a public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued for raising the shed-permit threshold to 144 sq ft (or a lot-size-tiered approach) to spare roughly 80 residents/year the RPRC and building-permit process for low-risk structures, framing it as an efficiency issue, though he ultimately conceded to keep 64 sq ft given colleagues' setback/neighbor-complaint concerns.

Raised concern that a larger permit-exempt shed size could result in an oversized structure sitting at a zero setback on small lots since exempt structures don't trigger zoning setback review, calling that potentially "intrusive" and a likely complaint driver.

Raised concern about projects that get approved and then drag on for years without completion, proposing escalating renewal fees as an incentive to finish, while acknowledging unforeseen circumstances (economic downturns) should be accommodated.

Probed the rationale for various exemptions (asking about swimming pool depth thresholds, generator RPRC exemptions) and suggested permanently exempting low-risk categories like generators and fences rather than relying on a one-time-per-property exemption form.

cases.name: Food Truck Permitting & Special-Event Law Amendment
cases.summary: Building on the March discussion, the board and Building Inspector Rob Malelo dug further into the new state mandate requiring each municipality to individually inspect and permit food trucks (fire suppression, gas lines, equipment mounting, etc.), which the Building Inspector called impractical given inconsistent standards town-to-town, the added cost/burden on food truck operators, and the lack of any advance industry consultation by the state. The board discussed writing to the Governor's office and coordinating with neighboring towns (Mount Kisco, Bedford) on a joint advocacy push, and floated alternatives like centralizing inspections at the county level (as is already done for food-truck health inspections), while acknowledging time pressure given the state's year-end adoption deadline.

memberPositions.evidence: Proposed writing a letter to the Governor's office specifically on the food truck mandate, calling it an unfair unintended consequence of the broader code update and worth coordinating with other towns like Mount Kisco already organizing a similar response.

Agreed something needed to be done "one way or another" through letters and/or the state Association of Towns, calling the requirement's practical effect "absolutely ridiculous" and harmful to small food truck businesses and commerce.

Asked whether the state was solving an actual documented food-truck-fire problem or acting without evidence, and argued that if a real problem exists, the fix belongs at a county/regional level rather than being pushed onto individual towns.

staffInput.summary: Walked the board through every discretionary code provision (shed thresholds, exemptions, permit durations, operating permits) with practical enforcement context, and gave a detailed, critical assessment of the food truck inspection mandate's impracticality.
Provided zoning-code context for how the shed-permit threshold interacts with setback requirements and structure definitions.

Was the only member to float a compromise (a short two-to-three-month extension to explore options) given the club's community service role, but acknowledged the rest of the board did not want to go that route and did not press it to a vote.

cases.name: Mother's Green Nursery — 11 Bedford Banksville Road Special Use Permits
cases.summary: The Board held reconvened public hearings on two special use permits for a nursery operation dating back over a century, predominantly located within a wetland and wetland buffer: one legalizing the existing nursery use (triggered when the owner sought a building permit for house renovations and had no underlying site plan approval) and one for an associated contractor's yard. Extensive debate arose over the town attorney's inclusion of an unprecedented term limit/sunset clause in the draft resolution given the property's wetland sensitivity and the possibility that environmental standards could tighten over time; several members initially favored a limit of 20-30 years, but after further discussion the entire Board reversed position and voted unanimously to adopt both special use permits with no term limit, while several members said the town should separately study a broader, prospective policy on term-limiting special permits in sensitive areas.
cases.publicComment: A resident wrote in supporting the project; a former nursery neighbor (unclear name) also spoke favorably during the hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Opposed any term limit on the permits from the outset as unfair to a longtime business owner who had invested in the property, arguing the town had never before term-limited a special use permit and that adequate protection already existed through code-compliance enforcement.

Initially pushed for a term limit (suggesting 20-30 years) given the property's near-total location within wetlands/wetland buffer and the likelihood that environmental protections would tighten over decades, but ultimately withdrew that position and voted to approve both permits without any limit.

Agreed some term limit might be reasonable (proposing longer than 10 years) but changed his mind by the close of the hearing, saying it was too late in a two-year process to add an unprecedented condition and that doing so would be unfair.

Was skeptical of a term limit throughout, worried it would impede the owner's ability to finance and operate the business, floated eminent domain as a theoretical alternative if the land ever became critical to protect, and ultimately concurred with colleagues to approve without a limit.
Also changed his position to support approval without a term limit, while backing a separate, broader policy review of term limits on special permits generally.

Board members raised concerns about the size and aesthetics of the displays, the precedent of allowing advertising-based charging stations, whether the town could hold the applicant to a no-audio/no-video restriction if their business model changed, and whether nearby residents/shoppers not using the charger were unfairly subjected to ads; a member reported informal neighborhood feedback was unfavorable on the advertising aspect.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed the Town Attorney on whether January 3rd was a hard outer limit or whether the extension could run longer, wanting to ensure restaurants had adequate certainty.
Said residents' main complaint was fear of losing outdoor dining, not having too much of it, and pushed to keep options flexible while the town moves toward permanent regulations.

cases.name: Pollinator Garden / Property Maintenance Local Law Amendment
cases.summary: The Board reviewed a draft local law creating an exemption from the property-maintenance code for pollinator gardens (with a 10-foot structure setback and a front-yard area cap), incorporating language changes suggested by a councilman and a proposal from a Conservation Board member/nursery owner to exclude New York State-prohibited and invasive plant species. Members debated whether to also restrict pollinator gardens in side/rear yards near property lines, with one member calling further rear-yard restriction unnecessary government overreach, before voting to schedule a public hearing and to circulate the draft to the Conservation Board, Mianus River Gorge Preserve, and Beautification Committee beforehand.

memberPositions.evidence: Supported the pollinator-garden concept but raised concern about restricting what residents can do in side and rear yards, calling additional rear-yard setbacks "a little bit of government overreach," and asked that interested community groups be notified ahead of the hearing.

Worked with the Director of Planning on wording changes so the weeds exemption also explicitly covers "other plant growth," and asked that invasive species be addressed more broadly than just New York State's prohibited list.

cases.name: 263 Bedford Banksville Road — Horse Farm Special Use Permit
cases.summary: The applicants sought a special use permit for up to 20 horses (of 23 allowed) on a 21.62-acre parcel and asked the Board to refer the matter to the Planning Board and County Planning Board to begin site-plan review. Represented by an environmental planner and joined by neighbors (including a former town councilman) who had worked cooperatively with the applicants beforehand, the presentation emphasized pre-application neighbor outreach, screening/buffer commitments near an adjoining property, and a proposal that the special permit not automatically run with the land upon a future sale.
cases.publicComment: Neighbors including former councilman Jerry Geister spoke in support, noting the applicants had proactively engaged them and agreed to additional screening near the shared property line.

memberPositions.evidence: Commended the applicant's neighbor-outreach process as a model for future applications, calling the pre-filing collaboration "a really good lesson" other applicants should follow.

cases.name: Quarry Heights / Old Orchard Street Water District Extension Study
cases.summary: The Board authorized the Water & Sewer Director to pursue a preliminary engineering study for extending public water (purchased via a Westchester Joint Water Works master connection) to roughly 43 properties in the Quarry Heights/Old Orchard Street/Starkey area currently on temporary or private water service, as a first step toward a possible new water district and to position the project for state grant funding, which typically requires projects to be "shovel ready."

memberPositions.evidence: Called the engineering study an important first step and noted the project could be positioned for state grant funding if the town can show it is close to shovel-ready.

The Board also received a revised Preliminary FEIS for the 113 King Street (former MBIA) campus redevelopment — now proposing a senior zoning district with 125 townhouses plus a 52-unit apartment conversion — and referred it to town professionals, and received a Planning Board lead-agency declaration for a large self-storage warehouse at 100 Business Park Drive.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Michael Schiliro presided with Barbara DiGiacinto, Saleem Hussain, Jose Berra and Matt Milim participating; Ethics Board chair Brett and Ethics Board member Ed both addressed the board on the disclosure-code item.

cases.name: Flood Damage Prevention Local Law Update (Ch. 177)
cases.summary: Following a New York State DEC directive to update Chapter 177 (Flood Damage Prevention) to comply with current National Flood Insurance Program regulations (44 CFR 60.3), the Board held a brief, uncontroversial public hearing and adopted both a SEQRA negative declaration and the local law itself, essentially adopting the state's model language into town code.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the change was clearly necessary and important for public safety around floodplains and building.

cases.name: Ethics Code Amendment — Expanded Financial Disclosure (Ch. 27)
cases.summary: The Ethics Board presented its revised recommendation to amend the Code of Ethics (§27-2, §27-6E) to expand who must file an annual disclosure statement and to require more detailed disclosure of real estate and business interests, including through trusts and closely-held entities. Discussion grew heated over whether attorney-drafted language incorporating a councilman's edits had become too legalistic for lay volunteers to understand, and over a disputed characterization of the Ethics Board's vote as "unanimous" when one member had abstained. The Board voted unanimously to schedule a public hearing for October 26, 2022, while several members said they still favored simpler, earlier draft language.
cases.publicComment: Ethics Board chair Brett defended the revised language as legally precise; Ethics Board member Ed, who had abstained on the underlying Ethics Board vote, argued the disclosure form should be simple and self-explanatory for lay volunteers and objected to characterizing the vote as unanimous.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly said the revised disclosure language was too wordy and "written for a lawyer," preferred reverting to the Ethics Board's earlier, simpler public-corporation language, and said he personally had concerns about the scope of private information volunteers would have to disclose — but as presiding officer moved to schedule the hearing since a majority wanted to proceed.

Argued against creating two different disclosure standards for existing versus new volunteers and reiterated an earlier-expressed concern that the more invasive disclosure requirements could discourage people from volunteering for town boards.

Quoted from an earlier work session as saying he was "100% confident" in the expanded disclosure requirements and that volunteers unwilling to be transparent about potential conflicts might not be right for these boards.

Was the councilman whose earlier edits to the interest/relative definitions were folded into the Ethics Board's revised draft; pressed the Ethics Board chair on process and precedent regarding the disclosure language during the meeting.

Sought clarification on whether the underlying legal definition of "relative" had changed or only its application via the new disclosure form, to make sure he was aligned with the rest of the board before the hearing.

cases.name: 113 King Street (Former MBIA Campus) Redevelopment
cases.summary: The Board received a revised Preliminary FEIS reflecting a new development alternative in which the applicant seeks a senior zoning district for the campus, with roughly 125 townhouses and conversion of one existing office building into about 52 apartments (demolishing another). Several members voiced significant reservations — about the choice of senior zoning versus other multifamily options, condo taxation status, and a 200-year-old barn slated for removal — before voting to refer the document to town professionals for review, with the Supervisor noting the school district superintendent had previously raised concerns about the tax-revenue-to-student-impact ratio of prior alternatives.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he had "really big initial concerns," was not convinced senior zoning (versus RMF, R10, or R5) was the right fit for the site, and questioned the plan being structured as condo taxation and the planned removal of a 200-year-old barn.

Said he wants to retain seniors in town as much as anyone but is "not sure this is the right plan," and noted the school superintendent's letter about tax-revenue-versus-student-impact had informed the board's earlier informal steer toward a senior zone.

memberPositions.evidence: Ultimately moved the process to adoption after weeks of raising concerns about legalistic drafting, working through remaining procedural questions on how the resolution language should reference the local law number.

cases.name: Pollinator Garden / Property Maintenance Local Law Amendment
cases.summary: After further review with the Director of Planning and Building Inspector, the Board concluded the proposed amendment would actually be more restrictive than existing law (capping pollinator gardens at 25% of a yard where no cap currently exists) and that the Building Inspector already treats pollinator gardens as exempt "cultivated gardens" under the current code. The Board closed the public hearing and took no action, leaving the property-maintenance code unchanged.
cases.publicComment: Resident Leith Colton, who had personally planted a pollinator garden, spoke in support of pollinator gardens' environmental value and urged the Board not to add restrictive language.

memberPositions.evidence: As the member who originally requested the code review to encourage pollinator gardens, said she'd now "prefer not to change the wording" after concluding the draft amendment was becoming counterproductively restrictive.

Had earlier pushed for restrictions so pollinator gardens couldn't take over an entire yard, but at this hearing agreed no code change was needed given the Building Inspector's existing enforcement discretion.

Called the draft amendment "a solution in search of a problem," noting the underlying language was never actually prohibiting anything and preferred pursuing pollinator-garden education instead through committees rather than a code change.

cases.name: Praise Church — 901 North Broadway Special Use Permit
cases.summary: The Board received a revised architect's letter and Planning Board recommendation on the church's proposed house-of-worship use in an existing office building, but the Director of Planning flagged unresolved items — a needed off-street parking variance, an unauthorized use of the site by an adjacent gas station's vehicles, and a required breakdown of all uses/square footage throughout the building — that must be resolved before further action; a communication breakdown between the applicant's architect and the town was also aired.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he was comfortable receiving the materials and saw no inherent issue with the church use once the outstanding parking and variance questions were worked out.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge Hotel — 3 North Castle Drive

A member of the public strongly opposed the fourth story, arguing it would visually read as much taller given the site's elevated bluff. Supervisor Schiliro recused himself due to his employment at adjacent IBM; the Board received the materials without voting, directing staff to prepare a resolution for a future meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked detailed questions about the square-footage math between three and four stories and requested to see the submitted floor plans and renderings before further discussion.

The Supervisor previewed that the budget carries no town-tax increase and is structurally balanced.

memberPositions.evidence: As presiding Supervisor, previewed that the budget process was thorough with good board input and results in no town tax increase, calling it structurally balanced.

cases.name: PFAS Water Treatment & Public Notification (Water Districts 2 & 4)
cases.summary: The Board approved an amendment to the Town's existing WSP engineering agreement to move Water District 4's School Street well into design for PFAS/PFOA treatment (likely ion exchange), after the county health department approved WSP's action plan; a parallel Langan Engineering proposal for Water District 2 (Whippoorwill/Coleman Hill area) was still pending. The bulk of the meeting was consumed by a heated public exchange in which resident Jen Clark challenged the Water & Sewer Director and board over why the public school (on Water District 2, which had a PFAS detect at/near the 10 ppt threshold) was not receiving bottled water like some private-well households near the old landfill, calling the Town's website-only messaging inadequate.
cases.publicComment: Resident Jen Clark strongly criticized the Town's PFAS communication as confusing and inconsistent — noting some private wells near the former Labriola landfill received state-supplied bottled water and filtration while Coleman Hill (on municipal Water District 2, also affected) and the public school did not — and pressed for the promised public expert panel to happen soon; she called the Town's practice of pointing to website postings for detailed information an inadequate answer.

memberPositions.evidence: Acknowledged the state's PFAS threshold rollout happened "without a plan" and shares residents' urgency, but pushed back that the Town's website and mandated notice language already provide full transparency, noting Water District 2's main well is actually below the PFAS limit and only marginally over on the smaller wells.
When asked directly by a resident whether he'd let his own kids drink the Water District 2 water, said he did not have a strong feeling against it personally.
Referenced state contacts he had shared with residents for private-well PFAS testing and said he had met with the Water & Sewer Director to get up to speed on district-specific PFAS status.
Referenced coordinating with the Water & Sewer Director on convening a public expert panel to answer resident PFAS questions, saying an outline would go to the board.

cases.name: Town Brokerage Account for Treasury Investments

Supported the plan but asked that purchases be limited to treasuries maturing in one year or less given economic uncertainty.

cases.name: 2023 Preliminary Town & Special District Budget

The Board praised the process and department heads for trimming costs; the Supervisor noted a roughly $700,000 fund-balance surplus was being rolled back in rather than drawn down. The public hearing was kept open until the December meeting for further resident comment.

Thanked the Director of Finance, Town Administrator, department heads and board for "a really, really productive process and a really great outcome."

cases.publicComment: Retired Highway Superintendent Mike Giaccio read Jamie Norris's written safety justification for the guide rail on behalf of the current foreman, who was unavailable; no residents were present to comment.

cases.name: Old Mount Kisco Road Water & Sewer Infrastructure Dedication
cases.summary: Applicant's counsel (Cory Salomon, Zarin & Steinmetz) asked the Board to accept dedication of new water main (Water District 4) and sanitary sewer main (Sewer District 2) infrastructure built by the developer of the senior housing project on Old Mount Kisco Road, via receipt and approval of the bills of sale; a separate request to reduce the developer's performance bonds was withdrawn for this meeting pending resolution of road-restoration work, to be coordinated with the Highway Superintendent once paving is scheduled. Asked whether the parcel's wetlands would affect its usable value and generally engaged constructively on how to structure the appraisal.

cases.name: Summit Club at Armonk — Golf Course Special Use Permit Amendments
cases.summary: The Board received materials on amendments to the temporary special use permit for the golf course (including a proposed maintenance building and continued public access during residential construction) and a request to consider a new permanent special use permit for the club, including public (non-member) access. The Board referred the conservation easement to the Open Space Committee and referred the new SUP application to the Planning Board and County Planning Board, while noting the temporary permit would not lapse because an extension had been timely requested.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he was 'fine with furthering' the referrals since the Board wasn't committing to anything substantive yet, just helping move the applicant's timeline along.

Noted the public-access element (allowing non-members to use the course) was new and significant, and confirmed with the Town Attorney that referring the item did not bind the Board's ultimate decision.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge Hotel — Findings Statement Amendment (Third to Fourth Story)
cases.applicant: Eagle Ridge (represented by Corey Salomon, Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.summary: The Board adopted an amended SEQRA findings statement allowing the proposed Eagle Ridge hotel to be built as four stories (rather than three) within the same 45-foot code height limit, after the applicant obtained a ZBA variance permitting the additional story. Councilman Berra pressed at length for language guaranteeing the building's visible ('tape measure') height would not increase, but the Town Attorney advised that could not be added without effectively amending the zoning code outside the required process; Berra ultimately did not press for a roll call and the amendment passed.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly pushed for findings-statement language assuring the visible height of the four-story building would not exceed what a three-story version would have looked like, calling it 'a reasonable consideration'; relented once told doing so would require amending the code outside process.
Walked through the code's height-measurement mechanics with the applicant's counsel and concluded the applicant was staying within the code, moving the item to a vote.

cases.publicComment: Corey Salomon of Zarin & Steinmetz, counsel for the applicant, confirmed the design remains compliant with the 45-foot code height limit and would not exceed it.

cases.name: Airport Campus — Reworked Townhouse/Age-Restricted Apartment Alternative
cases.applicant: Airport Campus developer (in contract with Toll Brothers; represented by Tony Beniziano)
cases.summary: The applicant presented a reworked concept for the 38.8-acre Airport Campus site: 125 fee-simple, age-targeted (not age-restricted) townhouses on RMFA-zoned land plus roughly 50 age-restricted apartment units in the existing office building rezoned RMFSCH, replacing an earlier all-age-restricted-apartment plan that the school district had flagged as creating a school-tax shortfall. The Board gave generally favorable informal feedback on the concept — citing improved projected school tax revenue (~$2.2M vs. ~$1.4M previously) — but wants written feedback from the school superintendent before proceeding, and Board members raised concerns about controlling future unit-size growth and the net fiscal impact on schools.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the reworked 125-fee-simple-townhouse concept 'substantially improved' and a reasonable compromise addressing both taxation and aging-in-place concerns, while agreeing the school's feedback is still needed.

Said his own analysis of school-age-children ratios and school levy per child suggested the project would not be fiscally 'dilutive' to the district even under conservative assumptions, and pushed for a cap preventing unit sizes from growing dramatically.

Pressed hard on the risk that an influx of elementary-age children could force the school district to hire more teachers and raise school taxes, saying she wanted certainty that her own school taxes would not rise because of the project's uncertainties.
Indicated he was 'not opposing' the reworked concept during the roundtable feedback.
Told the applicant he appreciated the rework and had 'nothing against' the plan, calling himself positive on it.

themes.note: Dominant subject of the meeting across six separate development items.
Board closed the public hearing and adopted the 2023 preliminary budget with a zero percent tax increase for the second consecutive year.
Airport Campus and 162 Bedford Road items both concerned affordable/age-targeted housing policy.

staffInput.summary: Advised on the Lombardi extension mechanics, the golf club permit's non-expiration given a timely-filed extension request, and told the Board it could not add height-related findings language for Eagle Ridge without effectively amending the zoning code outside the required process.

Walked the Board through the process and next steps for the 901 North Broadway church application, provided the letter on Airport Campus development alternatives, and fielded zoning-density questions for the Airport Campus site.

meetings.meetingSummary: This double meeting (organizational plus regular session) opened the Board's 2023 year, then closed the public hearing and approved Bedrock Plaza Corp's special use permit for 731 North Broadway, reopened and adjourned the hearing on the affordable-housing completion deadline extension for the former Lombardi property at 162 Bedford Road pending a Planning Board recommendation, and took up several new matters: a proposed local law legalizing Breezemont Day Camp's non-conforming use at 62-64 Cox Avenue, a first look at a proposed local law and site-specific application to allow a battery energy storage system (BESS) at 10 New King Street, and scheduling a public hearing on adopting new senior/disabled property tax exemption sliding scales. The Board also acted on numerous minutes, contracts, and personnel items.
meetings.durationNote: Present: Supervisor Michael Schiliro, Councilman Jose Berra, Councilman Saleem Hussain, Councilwoman Barbara DiGiacinto, Councilman Matt Milim (participating remotely from out of state per COVID-era remote-participation rules referenced at the Jan 25 meeting). Councilman Milim recused himself twice for matters involving properties in which he had a personal/family interest (a Verizon-property parking item and an earlier item).

cases.name: 731 North Broadway — Bedrock Plaza Corp Special Use Permit
cases.summary: The Board closed the public hearing and unanimously approved Bedrock Plaza Corp's special use permit converting vacant second-floor office space into three additional apartment units, finding the conversion reduces required parking and improves an underused North Broadway property. The Town Planner and multiple Board members framed the project as evidence the town's existing zoning already accommodates the kind of housing the Governor's proposed statewide housing mandate was meant to force, and objected to that mandate.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'a very good idea' that helps make North Broadway nicer and thanked the applicant for investing in the town.
Said the project 'seems like a good use' given weak office demand and was 'very much in favor,' while inviting public comment.

Argued the town's own zoning already permits exactly the kind of housing density the Governor's speech called for, said she was 'very offended' by the suggestion that towns like North Castle block housing, and 'fully supported' the application.
Said he had lived nearby and believed the area 'has so much potential' and that Bedrock Plaza 'does a good job of providing a lot of value to the community.'

cases.name: 162 Bedford Road (former Lombardi property) — AFFH Completion Deadline Extension
cases.summary: The Board opened and then adjourned the public hearing on extending the deadline for the affordable-housing (AFFH) units at 162 Bedford Road to reach 75% completion, pending a Planning Board recommendation. The applicant reported the long-delayed Westchester County Department of Health sign-off was imminent and the building permit could issue within days. The Board leaned toward a date-certain extension to December 31, 2024 (rather than an 18-months-from-permit-issuance alternative), while Councilman Berra reiterated that he personally wanted stronger assurance the affordable-unit reduction from 20% to 10% would actually translate into a completed project, given he had opposed the original reduction.

memberPositions.evidence: Said 'I think you probably know that I was opposed to reducing this' and that he 'personally would want more assurance' before supporting the extension, floating (and then not pressing) the idea of an added financial or zoning-based incentive to guarantee completion.

Expressed confidence the project would now get built given the county sign-off was imminent, and favored the date-certain 75%-by-December-2024 language as cleaner than an open-ended building-permit-linked alternative.

cases.name: 62-64 Cox Avenue — Breezemont Day Camp Zoning Legalization
cases.summary: The Board received the applicant's proposed local law to make day camps a permitted or special-permit use in residential districts, which would legalize longtime day camp operator Breezemont's non-conforming status and let it make facility improvements. The Board declared itself lead agency and referred the proposal to the town and county planning boards, while flagging density (60 campers/acre, 1,000-camper cap), a resident's complaint about the camp's PA system, staffing levels, and the precedent of prior legalizations (citing gas station legalizations) as issues to work through before a hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Said she lives about half a mile away, sees 'a lot of benefit to legalizing it,' but raised PA-system noise complaints from neighbors and cited the town's experience legalizing gas stations as a cautionary example of unintended consequences from legalization.
Called Breezemont 'a great place' with 'a lot of benefit to legalizing it' and moved the referral forward.

cases.name: 10 New King Street — Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Local Law & Project
cases.applicationType: local law amendment (zoning) / special use permit (pre-application)
cases.applicant: Catalyze Energy (represented by Doug Ward, Snyder & Snyder)
cases.summary: Catalyze Energy petitioned the Board to adopt a battery energy storage system (BESS) local law, based on a NYSERDA model code, that would permit BESS facilities in the IND-AA industrial zoning district, and presented its own proposed 5-megawatt/20-megawatt-hour project for the district near the New York City reservoir watershed. The Board found the proposal directionally attractive (grid resilience, resident bill credits) but, led by Councilwoman DiGiacinto, raised serious fire-safety and watershed-contamination concerns after she attended a fire commissioners' meeting on the topic, and pushed to engage independent fire/hazmat experts and DEP input before scheduling a public hearing. The Board declared itself lead agency and referred the matter for planning board input rather than setting a hearing date, calling that premature.

memberPositions.evidence: Described attending the North White Plains Fire Commissioners' meeting, cited a Tesla battery fire requiring 20,000+ gallons of water to extinguish, raised the site's proximity to the NYC reservoir watershed, and said before any public hearing the Board should retain a hazmat/fire expert and get DEP input, saying 'I'm certainly not opposed to the concept, but I don't want to move forward until I really understand.'

Said he 'loves the idea' conceptually for its grid and environmental benefits but asked detailed questions about fire department burden, toxic runoff risk, visual size/screening, and end-of-life decommissioning.
Managed the SEQRA/lead-agency procedural questions and agreed it was premature to set a public hearing date before referring the matter to the planning boards.

cases.name: Senior & Disability Property Tax Exemption Sliding-Scale Local Law
cases.summary: The Board scheduled a February 8, 2023 public hearing on adopting new RP-459-C (persons with disabilities and limited income) and RP-467 (senior) sliding-scale property tax exemption levels, following the Town Assessor's recommendation, but declined the Assessor's suggestion to also allow deduction of unreimbursed Medicare expenses from income, citing the inability to verify eligibility and unbudgeted fiscal exposure (an estimated jump from 29 to as many as 100 eligible households). One member raised a concern that state/county guidance language does not clearly guard against applicants artificially lowering reported income via business or capital losses, and asked staff to research whether additional safeguard language was legally permissible.

memberPositions.evidence: Relayed the Assessor's recommendation to adopt the sliding scale but hold off on the Medicare-expense deduction, noting the statewide assessors' association had taken the same cautious position, and moved to schedule the hearing.

themes.note: Bedrock Plaza approval, Lombardi extension, and Breezemont Day Camp zoning legalization dominated the land-use agenda.
Board framed the Bedrock Plaza approval as proof local zoning already supports the kind of housing the state's proposed housing mandate targets.
Battery storage fire-risk concerns were the most contentious topic of the night.
Senior tax exemption sliding scale and several routine financial/actuarial service contracts were approved.

staffInput.summary: Presented the Breezemont Day Camp legalization issues (density, parking, special events) and fielded zoning questions on the battery storage site plan/special-use-permit process.
Advised on SEQRA lead-agency mechanics for the battery storage referral and on legal limits around modifying state-derived senior tax exemption income-calculation language.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Board reopened and adjourned the public hearing on the 901 North Broadway church special use permit, now complicated by a nearby restaurant owner's concern that the church's presence could trigger the State Liquor Authority's 200-foot rule and block his pending liquor license. The bulk of the meeting was a lengthy, often critical work-session-style review of a revised 45 Bedford Road LLC downtown residential redevelopment (34 rental units, reduced from 43, with a proposed deed-restriction modification and an existing $1.25M community benefits package for parking, sewer, and water infrastructure), where multiple Board members pushed back on density, massing, historic-district compatibility, and the shift from condo to rental taxation. The Board also extended its temporary outdoor dining/parking regulations for restaurants to October 31, 2023, while beginning to plan a permanent outdoor-dining and parking-requirement framework.
meetings.durationNote: Present: Supervisor Michael Schiliro, Councilman Jose Berra, Councilman Saleem Hussain, Councilwoman Barbara DiGiacinto, Councilman Matt Milim (participating remotely from out of state, permitted under COVID-era remote participation rules). Councilman Milim recused himself from a Herrenhand Community Center naming item due to a family relationship with the donor.

cases.name: 901 North Broadway — Church Special Use Permit & Site Plan
cases.summary: The Board reopened and then adjourned the public hearing on the church's special use permit. A nearby property owner, Zachary Goldstein, who is mid-construction on a new fine-dining restaurant with accessory brewing at an adjacent site, raised concern that the State Liquor Authority's 200-foot rule (measuring distance to a church) could block his pending liquor license if the church is approved first. The Board directed him to consult a liquor-license attorney and have that attorney correspond with the Town Attorney, noting the Board may be able to grant a waiver, and did not resolve the conflict at this meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Facilitated a path forward by directing the restaurant owner to legal counsel and the Town Attorney to try to resolve the 200-foot rule conflict without delaying either applicant.

cases.publicComment: Zachary Goldstein, owner of a restaurant under construction near 901 North Broadway, testified that the church's approval could trigger the state's 200-foot liquor-license rule and jeopardize his pending liquor license, asking the Board to help find a solution.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road — Downtown Residential Redevelopment & Community Benefits Agreement
cases.applicationType: special use permit / site plan (RMFDA zoning)
cases.applicant: 45 Bedford Road LLC (Kings Capital; represented by attorney Tony and architect Ron Hoy)
cases.summary: The applicant presented a revised plan for the 4.1-acre downtown-zoned (RMFDA) parcel, reducing the unit count from 43 to 34 rental units (townhouse and stacked-flat buildings), reorienting buildings to front Bedford Road and Maple, and proposing a modest deed-restriction modification to open up the site's center. The existing community benefits package on the table totals $1.25 million ($250K parking, $750K sewage treatment plant, $250K water infrastructure), which the applicant offered to reallocate but not necessarily increase. Multiple Board members pushed back hard: on the shift from anticipated condo taxation to rental, on building massing and height relative to the historic district, on traffic and school-age-children impacts, and on removing the deed restriction, with one member saying she would 'like to see a much different plan' that is more subtle for what she called one of the town's historic gateways.
cases.publicComment: None recorded during this portion; comments were from Board members reacting to the applicant's presentation.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed on removing the deed restriction, questioned the shift to rental taxation versus the previously discussed condo-tax approach, asked pointed questions about total bedroom count and school-age-child impact, and pushed the applicant on what the $1.25M community benefits money would actually fund.

Said he was concerned the project had shifted from condo to rental without clear notice, that he generally 'struggles with condo taxation' in townhouse-style developments, and reiterated concerns about density, visual impact near the historic district, and traffic.

Said she 'really does not care for the three stories' or the garage under the first floor, called the design incompatible with the adjacent historic district and one of the town's gateways, and said she would 'like to see a much, much different plan,' while acknowledging the applicant was legally entitled to build under the existing zoning.

Noted his traffic concerns were 'slightly less' than colleagues' given the extensive traffic analysis done for the prior approved plan, but agreed the architecture needed to be more harmonious with the historic district, citing 20 Bedford Road as a model of successful historic-sympathetic renovation, and said he wanted the applicant to find common ground with the Board's concerns.

cases.name: Temporary Outdoor Dining & Restaurant Parking Regulations — Extension
cases.summary: The Board adopted a resolution extending its temporary COVID-era outdoor dining permit regulations (which allow restaurants to use parking-lot space for tents/patios) to October 31, 2023, after hearing that several restaurant owners still wanted the accommodation. The Board directed staff to use the extension period to develop a permanent framework, including possibly reducing off-street parking requirements for restaurants that build permanent outdoor dining structures, and asked for data on which restaurants are using tents and how much parking capacity is affected.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he was 'totally fine' extending the accommodation, noting the town has been 'very accommodating to restaurants' during COVID and was appalled at other communities that worked against restaurants during the pandemic.

Said he was 'not opposed' but wanted the Board to weigh the visual impact and lost parking capacity against the benefit, contrasting a well-screened tent at one restaurant with a highly visible one at another that consumes a large portion of a parking lot.

Supported extending through October 31st, noting many residents remain cautious about indoor dining and rely on outdoor options, and asked that any permanent framework include aesthetic standards for structures.

themes.note: 45 Bedford Road redevelopment and 901 North Broadway church were the dominant land-use items.
$1.25M community benefits package for 45 Bedford Road (parking, sewer, water) was discussed but not finalized or increased.
Strong Board concern that the 45 Bedford Road design does not fit the adjacent historic district / town gateway.
Outdoor dining's parking-lot impact was weighed as the Board planned a permanent framework.

staffInput.summary: Advised the restaurant owner near 901 North Broadway to seek his own liquor-license counsel and correspond with the town on a potential 200-foot-rule waiver.
Discussed the site plan revisions and deed-restriction impact for 45 Bedford Road with the Board.
Framed the choice facing the Board between continuing temporary outdoor dining measures versus formalizing a permanent outdoor dining/reduced-parking framework for restaurants.

meetings.attributionNote: Several extended exchanges during the 45 Bedford Road discussion (roughly the 40-50 minute mark) lack clear name cues in the ASR and were attributed to Jose Berra and Barbara DiGiacinto based on topical and stylistic consistency with their clearly-attributed statements elsewhere in this and other meetings in the batch; those attributions are marked medium confidence rather than high.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Board closed the public hearing and approved the special use permit for the church at 901 North Broadway, resolving the neighboring restaurant owner's liquor-license concern in the process (the applicant's attorney confirmed the 200-foot rule was not a problem for a multi-tenant building). The Board also closed the hearing on and adopted the senior citizen/persons-with-disabilities property tax exemption local law with an expanded income sliding scale, received a real estate appraisal for the town-owned Cross Road parcel adjoining the Marinovic property, and received/referred Ziden Realty Corp's special use permit application for outdoor product display at the Sunoco gas station at 360 Main Street.

cases.name: 901 North Broadway — Church Special Use Permit & Site Plan
cases.summary: The Board closed the public hearing and approved the special use permit for the church, following a positive Planning Board recommendation. The Town Attorney confirmed via correspondence with the neighboring restaurant's liquor-license counsel that the State Liquor Authority's 200-foot rule would not be a problem because the building is multi-tenant, resolving the conflict flagged at the January 25th meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'a pretty straightforward application' involving a relatively small part of an existing building with adequate parking arrangements, welcomed the applicant to the community, and confirmed the liquor-license issue was resolved.
Noted the applicant had obtained its needed ZBA variance, said 'everything's in order,' and told the applicant it would be 'a great addition to the hamlet.'

cases.name: Senior & Disability Property Tax Exemption Sliding-Scale Local Law
cases.summary: The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the local law amending Chapter 288 (Article II Senior Citizens Tax Exemption and Article III Exemptions for Persons with Disabilities), conforming to the county's new expanded income sliding scale — the first increase to these thresholds in about a decade. A member flagged that the scale jumps from a 50% exemption at $50,000 income down to 5% at roughly $58,000, and raised concern that the exemption has no asset test, meaning someone with significant liquid wealth but low reported taxable income could still qualify; the Board agreed to have the Assessor track participation and report back annually so the law can be revisited if needed.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he supported the law but wanted to make sure the town wasn't 'abused unnecessarily,' noting the lack of an asset test could let someone with substantial wealth but low reported income qualify, and asked for an annual review process with the Assessor.
Confirmed with the Town Attorney that the law could be revised or rescinded later if it wasn't working as intended, and moved the item toward adoption.

cases.name: Cross Road Town Parcel — Proposed Sale to Marinovic

The Town Attorney reported he had reached out to the Marinovics' counsel for a purchase offer but had not yet received a reply, and confirmed a second neighboring party had also expressed interest; the Board asked him to follow up and solicit a written bid from whichever party remained interested.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed the Board's prior direction was to get an offer before finalizing a sale price, and asked for a status update on outreach to both interested parties.

cases.name: 360 Main Street (Sunoco) — Outdoor Display & Sales Special Use Permit
cases.applicant: Ziden Realty Corp (represented by Corey Salomon, Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.summary: The Board received Ziden Realty Corp's special use permit application to allow outdoor display and sales (firewood, wiper fluid, salt, propane, etc.) in front of the Sunoco gas station/convenience store at 360 Main Street, and referred it to the town and county planning boards. A Board member raised a sidewalk-clearance question (minimum walkway width for pedestrians) that the Town Attorney and applicant's counsel disagreed about applying to this location, and another asked what would happen to the special permit if the building were later demolished or substantially altered (staff confirmed it would require a new amended site plan/special permit).

memberPositions.evidence: Asked for the sidewalk's dimensions to confirm adequate pedestrian clearance from the curb, prompting a disagreement between the Town Attorney and applicant's counsel over whether the code's clearance requirement applies to this exact spot.

themes.note: Church SUP approval and Sunoco outdoor-display referral were the main land-use items.
Senior/disability tax exemption sliding scale adopted with a request for ongoing fiscal monitoring.
Cross Road parcel sale process continued with an appraisal in hand but no offer yet.

staffInput.summary: Confirmed resolution of the 901 North Broadway liquor-license conflict, advised on the senior tax exemption law's revisability, and weighed in on the Sunoco sidewalk-clearance code question.
Provided the four-foot sidewalk clearance standard applied to a comparable prior gas station redevelopment for the Sunoco outdoor-display item.

The Board also received and referred Airport Campus's amended rezoning petition and preliminary FEIS (splitting the site into RMFSCH and RMFA zones for age-restricted apartments and fee-simple townhouses), with continued Board discussion of the historic 1820s house on-site, a possible extension of public water service, and lingering density concerns.

cases.name: Summit Club at Armonk — Golf Course Special Use Permit Amendments
cases.address: Summit Club at Armonk (formerly Bonnie Briar/Brynwood)
cases.applicationType: special use permit / local law / conservation easement
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners LLC (represented by Mark Weingarten, DelBello Donnellan)
cases.summary: With its prior temporary special use permit having lapsed at year-end, the applicant requested and received a six-month extension (to June 30, 2023) to keep offering golf to members this season, while the Board scheduled a combined March 22 public hearing on three related items: converting to a permanent special use permit (including a relocated maintenance/storage building), a local law temporarily allowing paid public (non-member) golf access during construction of the 73 residential units, and a waiver/reduction of parkland recreation fees for market-rate units (down to $1,000 for affordable units) based on the club's extensive on-site recreation amenities, consistent with prior SEQRA findings language. The applicant also submitted the required conservation easement restricting the golf course lot to open-space/golf use if the club ever ceases operating.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved the six-month temporary extension forward without objection and worked with the applicant to set a March 22nd date allowing time to prepare for the combined public hearings.

Pressed the applicant on whether the temporary public-golf-access proposal needed a numeric cap to reassure residents about traffic, ultimately accepting the applicant's self-regulating pricing argument ('for me, I don't need a restriction on the count'), and questioned whether the recreation-fee waiver legally required the golf amenities to serve the 'broader community' rather than only club members.

cases.name: Airport Campus — Reworked Townhouse/Age-Restricted Apartment Alternative
cases.address: Airport Campus / 113 King Street and associated properties
cases.applicant: Airport Campus developer (in contract with Toll Brothers; represented by Tony Beniziano)
cases.summary: The Board received the applicant's amended zoning petition splitting the property into a 4.5-acre RMFSCH parcel (age-restricted apartments, with a negotiated FAR cap above 0.4 tied to converting office to residential use) and a 34-acre RMFA parcel (fee-simple townhouses), plus the preliminary FEIS, and referred both to the town and county planning boards and town consultants. Discussion covered a proposed larger water storage tank (170,000+ gallons) that could let the town extend public water service toward the hamlet, the fate of a historic 1820s house on the property (the applicant is discussing relocating rather than demolishing it, with the town historical society expected to weigh in), and a still-unresolved dispute over whether a conservation easement restricts use of part of the site ("Cooney Hill") as a standalone development parcel.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed back on the applicant's claim that a conservation easement covering part of the site had 'fallen away,' asking whether the applicant had confirmed that with Riverkeeper or the land trust holding it, and stated plainly, 'I still do have concerns over the density.'
Thanked the applicant for being responsive on the historic house and zoning/taxation concessions, and urged referring the rezoning petition forward promptly so the process can keep moving.
