Golf course public-access and recreation-fee waiver were central to the Summit Club discussion.
Board and historical society engaged constructively with Airport Campus on preserving the 1820s house.

Coordinated the FAR-control zoning text language for the Airport Campus RMFSCH rezoning and fielded questions on both major applications.

meetings.meetingSummary: State Assemblyman Chris Burdick and State Senator Shelley Mayer joined the Board (in person and remotely) for an extended discussion of Governor Hochul's proposed statewide Housing Compact and Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) mandate, during which Town Planner Adam Kaufman presented data showing the TOD zone could theoretically add roughly 2,600 units around the North White Plains train station and that the accessory dwelling unit (ADU) provisions would strip the town's ability to require off-street parking near transit, worsening an already documented parking shortage; the Board and legislators agreed to keep pressing to remove the TOD provision entirely. The Board also scheduled public hearings for the Ziden Realty/Sunoco outdoor display permit (April 12) and the Breezemont Day Camp zoning text amendment (both now with positive Planning Board recommendations), and referred 45 Bedford Road LLC's traffic study to the town's traffic consultant after Board members questioned whether its data fully reflected actual conditions. The Board also swore in a new probationary police officer.
meetings.durationNote: Present: Supervisor Michael Schiliro, Councilman Jose Berra, Councilman Saleem Hussain, Councilwoman Barbara DiGiacinto, Councilman Matt Milim. State Assemblyman Chris Burdick and State Senator Shelley Mayer participated as guests (partly in person, partly remote) for the housing compact discussion.

cases.name: NY State Housing Compact / Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) Mandate — Town Opposition
cases.summary: The Town Board hosted State Assemblyman Chris Burdick and State Senator Shelley Mayer to discuss Governor Hochul's proposed Housing Compact, focusing on the TOD provision that would mandate minimum 25-units-per-acre zoning within a half mile of the North White Plains train station (an estimated ~2,600 potential new units) and an ADU mandate that would bar municipalities from requiring off-street parking for ADUs near transit, exacerbating North White Plains' documented on-street parking shortage. Town Planner Adam Kaufman presented a slide deck (praised by both legislators) documenting the town's existing record of approved multi-family and affordable housing to counter the narrative that suburbs like North Castle block housing. Both legislators committed to fighting to strip the TOD provision entirely from their chambers' one-house budget responses and asked residents to keep emailing as negotiations continued through late March.
cases.publicComment: Residents and Board members were encouraged by the legislators to continue emailing their opposition to the TOD provision through the end of March as budget negotiations continued.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the TOD mandate a 'crazy idea' that would 'devastate the Hamlet and the town,' warned it would incentivize demolishing existing affordable multi-family housing near the train station for 'luxury condominiums,' and pressed the legislators on how the one-house budget process would play out and whether more resident emails would help.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road — Downtown Residential Redevelopment & Community Benefits Agreement
cases.applicationType: special use permit / site plan (RMFDA zoning)
cases.summary: Following a work session, the Board referred the applicant's traffic study to the town's traffic consultant for independent review, with Councilman Berra specifically asking the consultant to consider Board members' concerns (echoed by Councilman Milim) that the study's traffic count data may not fully reflect real-world conditions on Bedford Road.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked that the traffic consultant's review explicitly consider Board members' concern that 'there's a lot more volume there than perhaps at times just being reflected in the traffic study,' wanting 'a very realistic picture.'

cases.name: 360 Main Street (Sunoco) — Outdoor Display & Sales Special Use Permit

Board member Barbara DiGiacinto pressed for consideration of the less-dense RMF zoning classification (comparable to Whippoorwill Hills/Ridge) instead of RMF-A, challenged the applicant's density-yield math (ultimately corrected to a 130-unit maximum allowable under RMF-A, not the ~97 previously cited), and requested rainwater-harvesting/irrigation study given town water-supply strain. Extensive public comment, led by longtime resident Linda Fernberg, raised cumulative downtown traffic and on-street parking concerns spanning Eagle Ridge, the Maple Avenue "lumberyard" project (~26-28 units), and the Marianne's property (~34 units) — combining for roughly 140+ new units feeding onto Maple Avenue and Main Street, the town's only two arteries out of downtown — and asked whether a promised downtown parking study would be completed before further approvals. The hearing was adjourned without a vote pending formal written input from the Byron Hill School District superintendent and staff (Town Planner, Director of Water & Sewer) preparing a negative declaration and resolution.
cases.publicComment: Longtime Wampus Avenue resident Linda Fernberg gave extended testimony on cumulative downtown traffic/parking strain from Eagle Ridge, the Maple Avenue lumberyard project, and Marianne's combined (~140+ units), citing a decade of unaddressed complaints and questioning whether traffic studies reflect reality; another resident (Ed) did density-math analysis showing the bedroom count is roughly unchanged from the original hotel-plus-condo plan (~264 bedrooms) despite the unit-type shift and urged a smaller unit count.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical of density, wants lower-density alternative studied
memberPositions.evidence: Proposed studying rezoning the full property to the less-dense RMF classification (like Whippoorwill Hills/Ridge) rather than RMF-A, corrected the applicant's stated maximum density calculation, and pushed for a rainwater-harvesting/irrigation plan given documented strain on the town's water supply.

memberPositions.stance: supportive on fiscal grounds, acknowledges traffic tradeoff
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the town's assessable tax base is flat-to-declining as corporate campuses vacate, framing full fee-simple development (mitigated where possible, e.g. this site being across Route 22 from downtown proper, and with community benefits money earmarked for parking) as necessary to avoid future service cuts or tax increases, while acknowledging traffic concerns raised by the public are valid.
Recused himself from this item due to his employment at IBM, whose former campus is the subject property.

themes.note: Dominant public-comment theme, spanning Eagle Ridge, the Maple Avenue lumberyard project, and Marianne's cumulatively.
Recurring announcements-section topic, not a formal case this meeting.

staffInput.summary: Guided the Summit Club easement amendment process and vote sequencing, and fielded procedural questions on the Eagle Ridge rezoning's relationship to SEQRA findings.
Tasked with preparing the negative declaration and resolution on the Eagle Ridge local law, incorporating board comments and awaiting formal school district input.

Reported the Eagle Ridge site's sewer allocation is within the IBM-era 35,000-gallon capacity and discussed capital projects to expand water/sewer capacity for pending downtown-area projects; asked to review the EAF's water/sewer sections for accuracy.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR transcript. High-confidence attributions rely on direct address, self-identification, and recusal statements. O'Connell and Associates, and a Westchester County water-main IMA for New King Street/Water District 8. Councilman Saleem Hussain recused himself from both the Eagle Ridge hearing (IBM employment conflict) and a later IBM-related alcohol permit item, and arrived after the meeting's opening for a family obligation.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge (former IBM/MBIA Campus) — Rezoning to Multi-Family Senior Housing
cases.address: Adjacent to the former IBM property (MBIA campus), North Castle
cases.applicationType: local law / rezoning (site adjacent to Westchester County Airport)
cases.applicant: Toll Brothers (represented by Corey Salomon, Zarin & Steinmetz; Josh Weissman)
cases.status: public hearing continued/adjourned to June 14 and later June 28, 2023
cases.summary: The board continued a public hearing on a local law to reclassify the former IBM/MBIA office campus from Office Business (OB-H) to a multi-family senior-housing zoning district (RMF-A/RMF-SCH), a conceptual ~88-unit project. Applicant's counsel asked the board's informal blessing to present a conceptual site plan to the Planning Board ahead of formal rezoning approval, which the board did not object to. The bulk of the meeting was a detailed discussion of airport noise: Planning Board member and Airport Advisory Board liaison Michael Pollock presented flight-frequency and noise-complaint data for the adjacent runway, prompting board debate over whether potential future-resident noise complaints should factor into the zoning decision versus being treated as a market/disclosure issue, with several members favoring a simple buyer-notification mechanism (offering plan language, construction sound-mitigation standards) rather than treating airport proximity as a reason to reconsider the zoning.
cases.publicComment: No outside public speakers on this item beyond applicant's counsel (Corey Salomon) and Michael Pollock's informational (non-applicant) testimony as a Planning Board/Airport Advisory Board representative.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of proceeding, skeptical noise data should drive the zoning decision
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the project's marketability ("this is the market we'll bear") should resolve pricing/noise tradeoffs, and said he was "not comfortable using... potential complaints... on a zoning decision on this particular case," while acknowledging the airport data was useful information.

Pushed back on relying entirely on market forces, saying "these are going to be our neighbors and residents" and that she "wouldn't be as quick to disregard" the noise concern as some colleagues; favored ensuring future buyers are clearly notified.

Pressed Michael Pollock with detailed follow-up questions on flight volume/distribution and argued that transparency of information is essential for market forces to work properly, favoring a requirement that the seller clearly disclose airport proximity to buyers.
Recused himself from this hearing because of his employment at IBM, whose former campus is the subject property; the board reordered the agenda to accommodate his late arrival and recusal.

cases.name: Park Place (11 New King Street) — Long-Term Parking Structure Special Permit Extension
cases.applicant: Park Place ownership (represented by counsel; project referenced in connection with Bill and Chris Fisher)
cases.summary: The board approved a third two-year extension of the special use permit for a long-term parking structure near the county airport, whose current site plan approval was set to expire in August. Counsel cited ongoing delays tied to a Westchester County water-availability issue (the subject of the New King Street water-main IMA elsewhere on this agenda) rather than litigation, which had previously been resolved. The board asked about project economics given interest-rate changes but did not condition the extension on further review.

memberPositions.evidence: Led the questioning on project timing and economics and moved the discussion toward approval without raising objections to the extension itself.

cases.name: Grant-Writing Services Contract — J. O'Connell and Associates
cases.status: approved, conditioned on Town Administrator confirming scope includes structured input from town advisory boards/committees
cases.summary: The board approved a two-year, ~$3,900/month contract with J. O'Connell and Associates (grant-writing consultants who have worked with Somers, Pleasantville, and Yorktown) to pursue infrastructure and other grant funding, after discussing the firm's downstate track record and the value of the engagement (framed as likely to return multiples of its cost). The board debated how broadly to solicit project ideas for the consultant to pursue — a narrower department-head-only process versus also soliciting ideas from town advisory boards, committees, and community groups (e.g., Historical Society cemetery restoration, bicentennial signage) — and approved the contract on condition that Town Administrator Kevin Hay confirm with the firm that broader community input can be incorporated without materially expanding cost or timeline.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the contract "relatively a no-brainer" once downstate-track-record concerns were addressed, and pushed to keep the process from stretching out over a year of interviews.

Argued that transparency and inclusiveness in the idea-gathering process matters and proposed the contract be approved conditioned on including input from advisory boards and committees, floating a North Castle community foundation as a related long-standing idea of his.
Helped broker a middle path — approve now with Town Administrator Kevin Hay managing which groups get consulted — so the contract wouldn't be delayed while scope questions were resolved.

Cited the Historical Society's bicentennial marker project and cemetery-restoration needs (e.g., the old Quaker cemetery) as examples of community-driven grant opportunities that broader outreach could surface.

cases.name: New King Street Water Main IMA — Westchester County (Water District No. 8)
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to execute an intermunicipal agreement with Westchester County for construction of a water main on New King Street within Water District No. 8, which board members noted would help resolve water-availability constraints affecting the Park Place parking structure and, pending a separate district-extension petition, could eventually serve the Eagle Ridge/airport campus site.

themes.note: Eagle Ridge rezoning and noise-disclosure debate dominated the meeting.
Turf-field options for Lombardi/IBM Community Park fields discussed at length as informational item, no case-level action.

staffInput.role: Planning Board member / Airport Advisory Board liaison (volunteer, not town staff)
staffInput.summary: Presented detailed flight-frequency, noise-complaint, and runway-usage data relevant to the Eagle Ridge site and answered extensive board questions on it.
Provided background on the grant-writing contract vetting process and was tasked with managing the advisory-board input process for it.
Provided legal framing on the Eagle Ridge conceptual-plan sequencing question and on disclosure obligations for airport proximity in condo offering plans.
Confirmed by phone that the FAA was not on the SEQRA circulation list as an interested/involved agency for Eagle Ridge and agreed to double-check.
Presented turf-field conversion options and cost/scheduling tradeoffs for Lombardi Park and IBM Community Park fields as an informational item; no board action taken.

meetings.meetingSummary: This transcript covers a Town Board work session (not the regular meeting that followed it) devoted to a presentation from the newly re-formed Recycling Committee, proposing to rename itself the North Castle Sustainability Committee and to launch a municipal food-scrap composting drop-off program modeled on Scarsdale's. The board was broadly supportive but spent most of the session debating scope: how many drop-off locations to start with, staffing, and budget (roughly $10-15K in initial signage/bins/pickup costs). No formal votes were taken since it was a work session; the board directed the committee to return with a refined single-location proposal.
meetings.durationNote: Work session only (regular meeting followed but is not included in this transcript). Presiding: Supervisor Michael Schiliro. Councilman Saleem Hussain and Councilman Jose Berra participated; Councilwoman Barbara DiGiacinto participated. cases.name: Sustainability Committee Rename & Municipal Food-Scrap Composting Program
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Recycling Committee, presented by co-chairs Neil Singer and Olivia Bremer)
cases.status: discussed, no vote (work session) — board directed committee to refine and return with a location/staffing recommendation
cases.summary: The Recycling Committee, seeking to rebrand as the North Castle Sustainability Committee, presented a proposal for a municipal food-scrap composting drop-off program modeled closely on Scarsdale's program, citing a potential 40% (or higher) reduction in household waste. The committee sought board guidance on number of drop-off locations (one central site vs. simultaneous sites in Armonk and North White Plains), staffing/hours, and initial budget for bins, signage, and pickup (roughly $10,000-$15,000 range depending on scope). The board was supportive of moving forward quickly but was split on whether to launch with one location first to prove the model or launch two locations simultaneously; the board also discussed a related e-waste drop-off effort and cost concerns, and asked that the committee coordinate closely with Town Administrator Kevin Hay on budget and execution.
cases.publicComment: Committee co-chairs Neil Singer and Olivia Bremer, plus committee volunteers (Alisa Bremer, Jackie Walker), presented the proposal; Scarsdale's sustainability program was cited as the model. No outside public comment beyond the committee presentation.

memberPositions.evidence: As presiding Supervisor (addressed directly as "Mike"), pushed to move quickly rather than over-plan: "I wouldn't slow yourselves down by trying to check off more boxes... just get what you can done as quickly as you can," while directing the committee to work through Town Administrator Kevin Hay on budget and execution.

As the board's liaison to the committee, engaged in detailed logistics discussion about single vs. multiple drop-off locations and e-waste cost/staffing concerns, generally favoring a methodical, incremental rollout starting with one location.

Raised the practical point that the program's pace depends on having enough trained volunteers to staff it ("as Barbara pointed out, we need volunteers"), cautioning the committee not to overcommit before it can staff the effort.

Argued for starting with a single, centralized location to prove out the model and control costs/logistics before expanding to a second site in North White Plains, in contrast to colleagues who favored launching two locations at once.

themes.note: Dominant topic of the session.
Cost of bins, pickups, signage, staffing.

staffInput.summary: Identified by the board as the coordination point for the committee's budget requests and execution logistics; not directly quoted at length in this transcript.

meetings.meetingSummary: This date combined a 6:30-7:30pm work session on whether to televise Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA/CBA) meetings live, followed by a regular Town Board meeting. The regular meeting continued a lengthy public hearing on the Airport Campus/former MBIA HQ (113 King Street) senior-housing rezoning, closed the public hearing and adopted a resolution for The Gateway (former Mariani Gardens) special use permit at 45 Bedford Road after extensive negotiation over sidewalk/walkway commitments and community-benefit funding, renamed the Recycling Committee to the Sustainability Committee with a new mission statement and budget, and advanced a proposed local law permitting electric-vehicle charging stations as an accessory use in business/office/industrial districts.

cases.name: Live Televising of Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) Meetings
cases.summary: A work session examined whether to televise ZBA meetings live, as is already done for Town Board and Planning Board meetings. ZBA Chairman Joe Monacelli said the board was not ready to start, citing an upcoming loss of a longtime member and difficulty maintaining a quorum, and suggested waiting until 2024. Resident advocate Ed Lowerman argued strongly for immediate live televising, citing transparency, precedent-setting variance decisions, and that most residents (especially seniors) will not seek out recorded meetings online. No vote was taken; the board indicated it would continue to explore the issue.
cases.publicComment: Resident Ed Lowerman spoke at length in favor of immediate live televising of ZBA meetings, disputing the ZBA chairman's reasons for delay and emphasizing transparency and senior-citizen access.

memberPositions.evidence: As presiding supervisor, opened the work session, framed the importance of the ZBA's variance-granting authority, and pressed the ZBA chair on the actual difference between Zoom availability and live TV broadcast.
Said he appreciated the ZBA's work and, while brief given the late hour, indicated general agreement with bringing more transparency to the board's proceedings.

Pushed back on the ZBA's framing that residents don't have a right to be concerned about matters outside their immediate area, arguing transparency and live broadcast should not be conflated with the separate problem of ZBA volunteer recruitment.

cases.name: Airport Campus / Former MBIA HQ (113 King Street) — Rezoning to Senior Housing & FEIS Review
cases.summary: The Board reconvened its public hearing on rezoning the former MBIA office campus to multi-family senior housing districts, receiving the Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) and a letter from the North Castle Historical Society urging preservation of the historic 1820s Weber farmhouse on site. The applicant reported progress on relocating a needed water storage tank to the adjacent Greco parcel (benefiting both the project and the town's broader water district needs) and on resolving objections from NRDC and Riverkeeper. The board pressed the applicant on options and cost for relocating the historic farmhouse (roughly $200,000 based on comparable moves) rather than demolishing it, and on getting formal fire department feedback given the scale of development. The applicant hoped to close the hearing and obtain a findings statement/rezoning decision at the August meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Led the hearing, welcomed the news that the town's water tank could be co-located on the applicant's adjacent parcel, and pushed to keep the process moving toward an August decision.
Raised concern about committing town resources to relocate the 1820s farmhouse without first having it evaluated for structural soundness and cost, warning it could become a 'money pit' for the town.

cases.name: The Gateway (former Mariani Gardens), 45 Bedford Road — Special Use Permit & CBA Resolution
cases.applicant: The Gateway / Toll Brothers (JD Sumer representing applicant)
cases.summary: After extensive negotiation, the Board closed the public hearing and adopted (by roll call vote) a resolution granting the special use permit for the townhouse redevelopment of the former Mariani Gardens/nursery site, incorporating Planning Board recommendations on reduced building height, corrected room labeling (den/office rooms without unauthorized closets), and building-coverage relief. A major point of debate was pedestrian connectivity: rather than commit to an uncertain sidewalk/walkway easement across a reluctant private landowner's property into Armonk Square, the board and applicant agreed to a hybrid approach — the applicant commits to building a sidewalk to the Maple Avenue bus stop, with a $250,000 community-benefit payment in lieu of the Armonk Square walkway if the necessary easement cannot be secured. The board also directed that community-benefits-agreement (CBA) provisions be tightened to ensure future ownership transfers (beyond outright sale) trigger CBA acceleration.

memberPositions.evidence: Negotiated directly with the applicant to secure a $250,000 community-benefit payment as a fallback if the walkway easement fails, and pressed for firmer CBA transfer/acceleration language before voting to approve.

Repeatedly pushed for a firmer, less open-ended commitment to pedestrian connectivity into Armonk Square, worried the town would end up with 'a whole lot of nothing' if the easement negotiation failed, though ultimately voted to approve.

Praised the applicant's responsiveness on architectural improvements to match the historic district look and raised the sight-line/screening question along Maple Avenue near the church for Planning Board follow-up.

Reflected on the length and thoroughness of the public process, noting that opposition, while passionate from a few residents, was not numerically large, and credited the applicant for addressing prior concerns.

cases.name: Recycling Committee Renamed to Sustainability Committee — Mission Statement & Budget
cases.summary: The Board approved renaming the Recycling Committee to the Sustainability Committee, adopted a new mission statement (revised to present tense and to reference a town board liaison generically rather than naming Councilman Berra specifically), and approved a committee structure requiring 6/12/18-month phased plans, with an annual budget of 'up to $10,000' rather than a flat figure, to allow the town flexibility.

memberPositions.evidence: Proposed structuring the budget as 'up to $10,000 annually' rather than a fixed amount, citing past tight town budgets, and praised the committee's frugal, effective work on the townwide cleanup day.

cases.name: Proposed Local Law — Electric Vehicle Charging Stations as Accessory Use
cases.summary: The Board reviewed a draft local law (originating from an earlier proposal by Volta) permitting EV charging stations as an accessory use in business, office and industrial zoning districts, limited to level 1 and level 2 (slower) chargers and capped at 20% of off-street parking, while prohibiting level 3 DC fast chargers and highway-destination advertising. Board members disagreed on whether excluding fast chargers unduly limited the benefit to residents versus protecting the town from becoming a highway-adjacent charging destination. The board declared itself SEQRA lead agency and referred the proposal to the county planning board, police and fire departments, with a public hearing to be scheduled around July 26.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued for allowing faster (level 3) charging to provide more meaningful benefit to residents and shoppers, questioning what level 1/2-only chargers would actually accomplish.
Favored moving forward slowly and cautiously with only level 1/2 chargers initially, wary of turning the town into a highway-adjacent fast-charging destination.
Suggested gathering more data on the difference in traffic draw between level 2 and level 3 charging before deciding, rather than acting on assumptions.

themes.note: Airport Campus rezoning and The Gateway special use permit dominated the meeting.
Extensive negotiation over CBA terms, transfer/acceleration provisions, and the $250,000 community-benefit fallback payment.
ZBA live-televising work session.
Sustainability Committee rename/mission and EV charging local law.
Fate of the 1820s Weber farmhouse on the Airport Campus site.

staffInput.summary: Advised on CBA transfer/acceleration language, remote-participation legal requirements for the ZBA work session, and easement/agreement mechanics for both the Gateway and Airport Campus matters.

Advised on FEIS/completeness review status for Airport Campus, SEQRA process for the EV charging local law, and the practical difficulty of the town self-funding infrastructure like sidewalks versus having a developer build it.
Provided updates on road paving, irrigation, and coordinated site walkthroughs and outreach to a historic-building-moving company for the Airport Campus farmhouse.

Future Supervisor Joseph Rende spoke during this meeting as a private resident (25 Smith Farm Road) in public comment, not as a board member — he had not yet joined the board at this time.

cases.name: Live Televising of Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) Meetings
cases.summary: Following the prior work session, the Board voted to require live NCTV broadcast of ZBA meetings (approximately $325/meeting, with archived on-demand viewing at no extra charge), moving forward faster than the ZBA chairman's earlier suggestion of waiting until 2024. Implementation was contingent on availability of the town's videographer, targeted for the ZBA's next meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved the requirement forward, noting there would be no extra cost and pushing to implement as soon as logistically feasible rather than waiting.

cases.name: Airport Campus / Former MBIA HQ (113 King Street) — Rezoning to Senior Housing & FEIS Review
cases.summary: The applicant and town consultants worked through remaining FEIS completeness issues (road geometry, stormwater basin siting near unit backyards, unit bedroom-count/density tradeoffs between the RMFA and RMF zones, fire department comments, and traffic study updates related to the Cooney Hill driveway), with the town planner and traffic consultant indicating no objection to deeming the FEIS complete pending final NRDC/Riverkeeper conservation-easement resolution and Armonk Fire Department comments expected before the next meeting.

cases.name: Request to Relocate AFFH Affordable Units Off-Site — The Byram (585 Main Street) & Summit Club
cases.applicant: Frank Madonna Sr. (The Byram) and Summit Club
cases.summary: Developer Frank Madonna Sr. requested the Board allow relocating two AFFH affordable units from The Byram (585 Main Street) to a different site (paralleling a similar off-site relocation the Summit Club had previously been granted), citing high common-charge/carrying costs and COVID-era construction cost overruns, and separately argued the town's 80%-of-market-unit-size rule was unfair for multifamily buildings. The Board declined to take any vote on the letter, with several members (led by Matt Milim) arguing it would be improper to grant a one-off exception to the code's stated 'strong preference' for on-site AFFH units without a broader public code-change process, especially given other pending projects (Eagle Ridge, Gateway, the Lumberyard) were watching for precedent. The Board agreed to schedule a future work session on AFFH policy generally rather than act on the individual request.
cases.publicComment: Resident Joe Rende (25 Smith Farm Road, later elected Supervisor) spoke in favor of allowing the relocation, arguing clustering affordable units (as with existing units near the Beehive on Old Route 22) integrates well into the community and does not eliminate affordable housing, just relocates it.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued strongly against a one-off exception to the code's on-site preference for AFFH units, citing risk of stigmatizing clustered affordable housing and setting a precedent that every future developer would invoke; insisted any change go through a formal code-amendment process.

Questioned whether the town's minimum-square-footage code for multifamily AFFH units was written fairly compared to single-family developments and floated (then set aside) a market-price-based trigger for allowing relocation.

Agreed the request should not be evaluated on a one-off basis and did not want to spend further public/board time revisiting it repeatedly; supported routing any policy change through a proper work session.

Stated the board should not be voting on a letter request absent a formal application, and suggested a work session to consider both the relocation-preference standard and unit-size rules together before reopening any process.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Additional Horses at 263 Bedford Banksville Road
cases.summary: The Board received supporting materials and scheduled a September 13, 2023 public hearing on a special use permit application to keep additional horses at 263 Bedford Banksville Road, after the applicant obtained favorable recommendations from the Conservation Board, Architectural Review Board, and Zoning Board of Appeals.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Increase Horses from 10 to 26 at 14 Middle Patent Road
cases.summary: The Board received the application materials, discussed SEQRA lead-agency coordination with the Planning Board, and referred the matter to town and county planning boards and scheduled a September 13, 2023 public hearing. The 42-acre parcel already had a 2008 special permit for 10 horses (since lapsed from non-use); the applicant sought to expand to 26 non-commercial, owner-occupied show/competition horses that would not all be on-site simultaneously (many spending winters in Florida), with a new barn addition and equine management plan.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Recreation Center (Pickleball) at 100 Business Park Drive
cases.summary: The Board received application materials for a special use permit to legalize an existing ~1,740 sq ft private employee gym and approve a new ~26,460 sq ft recreation area (11 indoor pickleball courts plus small retail/party space) inside a proposed mixed-use self-storage warehouse building, and referred the matter to planning boards with a September 13, 2023 hearing scheduled. A board member raised concerns about parking assumptions, whether use would be genuinely limited to town residents versus outside pickleball-league traffic, and — more broadly — the scale and setback reductions of recent warehouse development along Business Park Drive.

themes.note: Multiple new special-use-permit applications referred; Airport Campus and AFFH relocation continued.
ZBA live-televising adopted; process concerns raised about one-off code exceptions.
Two horse-boarding special use permit applications introduced.

staffInput.summary: Advised on SEQRA lead-agency mechanics for the horse-permit applications, on the procedural distinction between receiving a letter versus voting on a formal application for the AFFH relocation request, and on remote-participation/broadcast logistics.

Walked through outstanding FEIS completeness issues for Airport Campus and offered his professional opinion supporting the Byram's AFFH relocation request as comparable to the Summit Club precedent, given the small high-end multifamily building context.

meetings.attributionNote: The AFFH relocation debate involved extended, fast cross-talk among multiple board members and the applicant; attributions reflect only remarks with clear naming or role cues. The 100 Business Park Drive recreation center discussion included a skeptical board member whose identity could not be confidently determined from context, so no individual position was recorded for that case.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Board reconvened the Airport Campus (former MBIA, 113 King Street) rezoning public hearing, receiving news that the applicant had reached agreement in principle with NRDC and Riverkeeper on stormwater/phosphorus-loading and conservation-easement terms, and worked through fire department concerns, age-restricted housing marketing terms, sidewalk placement, and easement-language disputes toward deeming the FEIS complete. The Board also closed a public hearing and adopted a local law permitting accessory electric-vehicle charging stations, opened a new rezoning petition for 5 North Granite Road (to allow additional parking), and authorized a $712,000 state grant application for Sewer District 2 wastewater treatment plant improvements.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present; Supervisor Michael Schiliro presided. Board members referenced by name in discussion included Jose Berra, Barbara DiGiacinto, and Matt Milim; attribution of specific remarks to individual members is frequently uncertain due to un-diarized audio.

cases.name: Airport Campus / Former MBIA HQ (113 King Street) — Rezoning to Senior Housing & FEIS Review
cases.summary: The applicant reported an agreement in principle with NRDC and Riverkeeper covering an expanded 9+ acre conservation easement, phosphorus-loading reduction (from roughly 50% to over 80% removal) to protect the Kensico Reservoir watershed, and ongoing stormwater reporting, while preserving a disagreement over whether an existing easement is legally revocable. The board debated Armonk Fire Department concerns (lack of a ladder truck, cumulative impact of several pending town projects) and whether to hold the applicant to a specific age-targeted vs. age-restricted unit-mix percentage similar to the Eagle Ridge project, ultimately treating this site as distinguishable given its dedicated 55+ apartment building and location. The board also pressed on sidewalk connectivity to the Route 120 bus stop. The FEIS was moved toward completeness, setting up a findings statement and rezoning vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued the board should not force a specific age-restricted unit-mix percentage onto this project as it did with Eagle Ridge, citing the site's dedicated 55+ apartment building and distance from town center as distinguishing factors.

Raised concern about the Armonk Fire Department's lack of a ladder truck for a multi-story building of this scale, referencing a prior fire where North White Plains' ladder truck had to respond, and asked about a possible applicant financial contribution.
Flagged the fire chief's closing point about cumulative impact from several concurrent town development projects potentially requiring paid fire department staffing as his bigger concern.

cases.name: Local Law — Electric Vehicle Charging Stations as Accessory Use
cases.summary: After closing the public hearing, the Board adopted (via SEQRA negative declaration/neg-dec and a unanimous vote) the local law permitting level 1 and level 2 electric-vehicle charging stations as an accessory use in business, office and industrial districts, continuing the more conservative, incremental approach discussed at the prior meeting. No further amendment to allow level 3 fast chargers was made at this hearing.

cases.name: 5 North Granite Road — Petition to Rezone to Professional Business Office (PBO)
cases.summary: A new petition was introduced to rezone a 1.79-acre lot (currently split between PBO and R-1A) entirely into the Professional Business Office district to allow additional parking for an existing office use. The board received the engineering letter and planning staff report, noted informal concern from two nearby residents about existing lighting issues, and directed the applicant to consider outreach to neighbors and additional landscape screening. The matter was referred to town and county planning boards with a public hearing scheduled for September 27, 2023.
cases.publicComment: Board relayed informal concerns from two nearby residents about existing site lighting and asked the applicant to consider neighbor outreach and screening ahead of the formal hearing.

cases.name: Sewer District 2 Wastewater Treatment Plant — EFC Water Infrastructure Improvement Grant Application
cases.summary: The Board authorized submission of a $712,000 grant application to the New York State Environmental Facilities Corporation's Water Infrastructure Improvement Program to help fund Sewer District 2 wastewater treatment plant upgrades, a second attempt after an earlier unsuccessful application, and authorized the Supervisor to sign the application and related resolution.

NRDC/Riverkeeper agreement, phosphorus loading, conservation easement.
Fire department apparatus/staffing concerns raised in Airport Campus hearing.
Summit Club DEC well permit and Sewer District 2 EFC grant.

Summarized DOT, sidewalk, fire department, Riverkeeper/NRDC and floor-plan memo issues for the Airport Campus FEIS completeness determination.
Reported the near-final NRDC/Riverkeeper agreement including expanded conservation easement and phosphorus-loading reduction measures.

staffInput.role: Superintendent of Water and Sewer Operations
staffInput.summary: Presented the Summit Club DEC well permit request and the Sewer District 2 EFC grant application, noting the extended submission deadline.

meetings.attributionNote: Long stretches of the Airport Campus discussion are cross-talk between multiple unnamed board members and applicant representatives; only remarks with clear contextual or role-based cues were attributed to specific members, and several routine administrative items (grants, permits) had no controversy or individual positions worth recording.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Board promoted a police officer to sergeant, then closed the long-running Airport Campus/former MBIA (113 King Street) rezoning public hearing and adopted both the SEQRA findings statement and the rezoning resolution, after negotiating a compromise covenant requiring 50% of market-rate townhomes to have first-floor primary bedrooms. The board also received a resident letter opposing gas-powered leaf-blower restrictions and a feasibility study on a potential Quarry Heights water distribution system.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present; Supervisor Michael Schiliro presided with Jose Berra, Barbara DiGiacinto, Saleem Hussain, and Matt Milim participating. One member voted 'no' on the SEQRA findings statement roll call, though the transcript does not clearly identify which member; the rezoning resolution itself passed without a recorded dissent.

cases.name: Airport Campus / Former MBIA HQ (113 King Street) — Rezoning to Senior Housing & FEIS Review
cases.summary: After roughly eight years of the property sitting vacant and multiple years of public process, the Board closed the public hearing and adopted both the SEQRA findings statement and a resolution rezoning the former MBIA office campus for 50 age-restricted rental apartments and 125 age-targeted, fee-simple-taxed townhomes (including affordable units). The central negotiated issue was a covenant requiring that 50% of the market-rate (non-affordable) townhomes include a first-floor primary bedroom, reached after extended back-and-forth between the board and Toll Brothers over percentages ranging from 25% to 60%. The board also addressed airport-noise disclosure requirements in offering plans and rental/sale agreements, fire department sprinkler assurances, and declined to require site-wide sidewalks, leaving that to the Planning Board site plan process. Public comment included a resident (Bob Okan) and a longtime resident (Julie) expressing concern about the pace and scale of recent development in Armonk.
cases.publicComment: Two residents (Bob Okan and Julie) voiced concern about the pace and scale of recent housing development changing the character of Armonk and straining traffic, sewers, and water; one questioned whether the original 2015-era buyer's business miscalculation should be the town's problem to solve via upzoning.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed hardest for a meaningful age-targeting covenant (initially proposing 50-60% of townhomes), citing school-impact and senior-housing-shortage rationale, while explaining his broader support for the project's full fee-simple tax assessables versus condo-taxation.

Argued for a lower age-targeting percentage than Eagle Ridge's 60% given this project's distinct location and dedicated 55+ apartment building, ultimately brokering the 50%-of-market-rate-townhomes compromise.

Argued against imposing any first-floor-bedroom percentage requirement, noting the near-airport location would already make the townhomes a harder sell and that the request surfaced late; also credited with originating the project's transitional age-restricted-to-age-targeted design concept.
Pressed for stronger, more prominent airport-noise disclosure to buyers/renters beyond a buried offering-memorandum statement, given the applicant's own data showing airport-adjacent noise levels.

cases.name: Police Officer James Kehoe — Promotion to Sergeant
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle Police Department
cases.summary: The Police Chief recommended promoting Officer James Kehoe, a 7.5-year veteran of the department, to the vacant budgeted sergeant position effective August 12, 2023, following the retirement of a detective sergeant and promotion of another sergeant to lieutenant. The board approved the promotion without objection.

cases.name: Resident Letter Opposing Gas-Powered Leaf Blower Restrictions
cases.summary: The Board received a resident letter and heard extended public comment opposing any town restriction on gas-powered leaf blowers, framed around cost/practicality concerns for small landscaping businesses and broader objections to environmental regulation. The board took no policy action; the letter was simply received into the record.
cases.publicComment: A resident and part-time landscaper spoke at length against any prospective gas-powered leaf-blower restriction, citing cost and practicality for small businesses.

themes.note: Airport Campus rezoning adopted after extended negotiation.
Police sergeant promotion; fire sprinkler assurances and airport-noise disclosure in the rezoning.
Discussion of fee-simple vs. condo taxation and school tax-certiorari exposure tied to the rezoning.
Leaf-blower letter received; sustainability committee composting update.

staffInput.summary: Prepared the comprehensive SEQRA findings document for the Airport Campus rezoning and fielded board questions on noise disclosure decibel levels.
Reported on staff's site visit and assessment of the historic Weber farmhouse, concluding it had little practical use for town purposes given renovation and relocation costs.
Advised on structuring the age-targeting covenant into the rezoning resolution and on procedural requirements for the roll-call votes.

meetings.attributionNote: The lengthy, highly cross-talking negotiation over the age-targeting percentage made turn-by-turn attribution difficult; positions were assigned only where a name or clearly distinguishing context (e.g., a member referencing their own house, or being addressed by name) made attribution reasonably confident. One roll-call 'no' vote on the SEQRA findings statement could not be attributed to a specific member.

meetings.meetingSummary: A long meeting (running past midnight) covering an unusually full agenda after the board's single August meeting. The Board approved a special use permit for a horse farm at 263 Bedford Banksville Road and closed/approved the 100 Business Park Drive recreation center (pickleball courts) special use permit, but adjourned the 14 Middle Patent Road horse-boarding expansion hearing to October 11 pending a Conservation Board mitigation review. The Board heard a detailed presentation and strong advocacy from youth sports organizations for converting IBM Community Park fields 1 and 2 to artificial turf (roughly $2.7 million, chosen over a $3.7 million Lombardi Park grass renovation) and directed staff to bring back a bid specification. It also opened a new special use permit matter for building modifications at the St. Nersess Armenian Seminary (46 Bedford Road) and referred a four-lot Mittman/Gordy subdivision at 655 Bedford Road — including a roughly five-acre land donation to the town — to the Open Space Committee.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present; Supervisor Michael Schiliro presided with Jose Berra, Barbara DiGiacinto, Saleem Hussain, and Matt Milim participating. The meeting closed in memory of several long-serving residents and volunteers, including longtime ZBA member Les Berkelheimer (26 years) and Bob Caruso, son of a former four-term Supervisor and town attorney.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Additional Horses at 263 Bedford Banksville Road
cases.summary: The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the resolution approving a special use permit for a horse farm on the applicant's 21-acre property, after working through final conditions (building inspector safety inspections, delivery/manure-removal hours aligned with the noise ordinance, manure storage limits, and a requirement that future owners seek amendment for any operational changes). Neighbors and the applicant's team were highly complimentary of each other; multiple board members and residents praised the collaborative process and the low-impact, conservation-minded design preserving most of the property.
cases.publicComment: Multiple neighbors spoke in strong support, describing the applicant's outreach and the project's low impact; one commenter (Steve Brownstein) skeptically questioned how the application's 'community benefit' standard was being defined.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Increase Horses from 10 to 26 at 14 Middle Patent Road
cases.summary: The public hearing opened but was adjourned to October 11, 2023, at the applicant's request, to allow the Conservation Board (which had not met in August or September) time to weigh in on a mitigation/bonding and license-agreement issue tied to construction work extending into a conservation easement area, similar to a separate matter (the Levine project) the applicant's team was also handling.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Recreation Center (Pickleball) at 100 Business Park Drive
cases.summary: The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the SEQRA negative declaration approving the special use permit for the employee gym legalization and new 11-court indoor pickleball facility. A board member noted mixed feelings about the scale of recent warehouse development on Business Park Drive generally but supported the pickleball use itself as a good community amenity.

cases.name: IBM Community Park Fields 1 & 2 — Artificial Turf Conversion
cases.summary: Following a townwide parks survey (600+ household responses) and over a year of Parks & Recreation Advisory Board study, town youth sports organizations (baseball/softball, soccer, football, lacrosse) unanimously recommended converting IBM Community Park fields 1 and 2 to artificial turf at an estimated $2.7 million — cheaper and higher-capacity than a $3.7 million Lombardi Park grass-and-drainage alternative. Advocates cited chronic field closures from poor drainage, more than doubled practice/game capacity from cross-field layouts, and turf's greater durability under heavy, year-round youth-sports use. The Board received the memo and directed staff to bring back a construction manager/bid-specification proposal (via Kellard Sessions) for a future vote rather than acting that night.
cases.publicComment: Parks and Recreation Advisory Board member Brian Barrenakis and other youth-sports representatives spoke at length in strong support, citing capacity constraints, weather cancellations, and the field-doubling design possible with turf.

cases.name: St. Nersess Armenian Seminary, 46 Bedford Road — Special Use Permit for Building Modifications
cases.summary: Roughly a decade after its original 2012 special permit, the seminary sought approval for two small additions: a two-room addition to the married-students building for visiting guest lecturers, and a smaller residence to allow the retiring dean to remain on campus semi-retired while a new dean takes over. The Board declared itself lead agency, referred the matter to town and county planning boards, and scheduled a public hearing (targeting mid-to-late October), noting the seminary's actual activity level (currently only four enrolled students) has stayed well below what was originally anticipated or feared at approval.

cases.name: Mittman/Gordy Subdivision & Open Space Donation — 655 Bedford Road et al.
cases.summary: The applicant proposed subdividing roughly 20 acres adjacent to his estate into four lots (revised down from an original six-lot plan) — including a lot to be transferred to his daughter — while offering to donate two non-buildable lots totaling about five acres to the town, with permanent deed restrictions against building. The Board referred the donation to the Open Space Committee and referred the broader subdivision/addressing matter to the town's E-911 coordinator; the applicant noted Westchester Land Trust had declined the conservation-easement approach, leading to the direct-donation structure instead.

themes.note: Two horse-permit hearings, pickleball recreation center, and a new seminary special use permit.
IBM Park turf conversion was a major, well-attended discussion.
Two horse-boarding special use permits, one approved and one adjourned.
Land donation referred to Open Space Committee.

staffInput.summary: Presented the memo recommending pursuit of artificial turf conversion at IBM Community Park fields 1 and 2, based on the townwide parks survey and Parks & Recreation Advisory Board recommendation.
Provided input on the seminary special use permit process and general planning-referral logistics across multiple agenda items.
Advised on conditions for the horse-farm special use permit (binding future owners), lead-agency declarations, and subdivision/open-space donation structuring.

meetings.attributionNote: This was an unusually long, procedurally dense meeting (past midnight) with heavy cross-talk among unnamed board members, applicants, and residents; most substantive items were largely uncontested or procedural, so individual member positions were not confidently attributable and are omitted rather than guessed.

meetings.meetingSummary: After swearing in a new police officer, the Board's marquee item was a heavily attended public hearing on a petition to rezone a residential portion of 5 North Greenwich Road to PBO (professional business office) so the owner (who also controls several adjoining parcels) could add 12 parking spaces for a physical therapy/office tenant; roughly two dozen Byron Brook Place and North Greenwich Road neighbors spoke in organized, well-documented opposition citing traffic, noise, a recent unpermitted car-show event, drainage, property values, and fear of a larger commercial assemblage, and the Board ultimately closed the hearing and returned the petition without prejudice rather than proceed. The Board also accepted a 13-acre open-space land donation tied to the Mittman subdivision at 655 Bedford Road, discussed (and referred out for further input) a proposal to name the Wampus Park gazebo in memory of former Deputy Supervisor Becky Kitridge, approved a Stop & Shop tax certiorari consent judgment, and adjourned the IBM Community Park turf field proposal to the next meeting at Councilman Hussain's request so he could participate.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Schiliro presided in person; Councilman Hussain participated remotely for part of the meeting due to a stated public-meetings-law accommodation. DiGiacinto, Milim, and Berra were present in person.

cases.name: 5 North Greenwich Road — R-1A to PBO Rezoning for Additional Parking
cases.applicant: Reno Montforte (property owner, via Krypton Engineering)
cases.status: hearing closed; petition returned to applicant without prejudice
cases.summary: The applicant sought to rezone the residential half of a 1.79-acre lot from R-1A to PBO to add 12 parking spaces (beyond code minimums) for physical therapy and office tenants at an already fully-built-out building; the owner also controls several adjoining parcels, which numerous neighbors argued signaled a broader plan to assemble and further commercialize the block. Around two dozen Byron Brook Place and North Greenwich Road residents testified in organized opposition (a 210-plus signature petition, maps, and photos), citing an unpermitted car-show event with loud music and blocked streets, traffic safety at a nearby school bus stop, drainage/runoff concerns, property devaluation, and fear of a domino effect of further rezonings. After extended board discussion about the risk of future variances for additional structures if the parcel were rezoned, the Board closed the public hearing and effectively returned the petition to the applicant without prejudice rather than continue it, at the residents' request for finality; the applicant may reapply later.
cases.publicComment: Roughly two dozen residents of Byron Brook Place and North Greenwich Road (including Mary and Bob Sweeney, Diane Silva, Darcy DeBerry, Stephanie Samaritano and Frank Smith, Mohammed "Jose" Chase, Kristen and Byron Mathis, Jason Wong, Tom Dagostino, and Camille) testified in unified opposition, presenting a 210+ signature petition and citing traffic, noise, an unpermitted car-show event, drainage, safety at a school bus stop, and fear that the owner's control of adjacent parcels signaled a larger future commercial assemblage.

memberPositions.evidence: Opened by clarifying procedurally that without a planning board recommendation the hearing would be adjourned rather than voted on; later said the applicant would have to show the rezoning has no negative impact on the community and that resident buy-in is essential, and shared she'd felt the same fear when a similar notice affected her own property years earlier.

Pressed the applicant's engineer on whether a zoning board variance could later allow additional structures once the parcel is rezoned, articulating residents' core fear of future commercial expansion; another board member explicitly credited 'your point, Jose' on this issue.

Emphasized that communication between the applicant and neighbors is 'key' before any rezoning proceeds, drawing on his own experience living next to commercial properties and negotiating a parking accommodation; credited by the Supervisor by name for making this point earlier in the hearing.

As presiding officer, ultimately supported closing the hearing and returning the petition to the applicant without prejudice to give residents 'peace of mind,' after weighing the overwhelming opposition against giving the applicant more time to work things out.

cases.name: Mittman Subdivision — 13-Acre Open Space Donation, 655 Bedford Road
cases.summary: The Board accepted a roughly 13-acre open-space parcel donation adjacent to an existing town park, connected to the Mittman subdivision, following a favorable recommendation from the Open Space Committee; approval was conditioned on the town obtaining title insurance acceptable to the town attorney, and board members noted the donation expands contiguous town open space to nearly 24 acres and protects wetlands.

memberPositions.evidence: Walked through deed and easement-access details with the town attorney and applicant's counsel and called the donation 'a great thing to the town' that protects wetlands and connects to existing parkland.

cases.name: Naming the Wampus Park Gazebo in Memory of Becky Kitridge
cases.summary: The Board revisited a years-old, previously stalled idea to name the Wampus Park gazebo in memory of former Councilwoman and longtime Deputy Supervisor Becky Kitridge (served 1979-2011), favoring a tasteful plaque rather than prominent signage; because the Lions Club originally built and funded the gazebo and the Landmarks Preservation Committee has jurisdiction, the Board referred the matter to the LPC and the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board and asked Councilman Milim to raise it with the Lions Club before returning with a recommendation.

memberPositions.evidence: Drove the discussion, recalling his personal history with Kitridge and advocating for the gazebo specifically ('to me, this is the right one') with a tasteful plaque, while acknowledging the Lions Club and LPC need to sign off.
Agreed the gazebo idea should proceed as a collaborative effort with the relevant boards and committees.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Board opened the meeting dedicating it to the people of Israel following the October 7 attacks, with several members sharing personal reflections; this was ceremonial and not treated as a substantive case. Business included continuing two public hearings (a special use permit at 14 Middle Patent Road and a zoning text amendment to permit car washes in the P.O.B. district), authorizing a refuse/recycling collection bid, approving a tax certiorari consent judgment, and a lengthy debate over a $125,000 engineering proposal from Keller & Sessions to prepare bid documents for artificial turf at IBM Community Park fields 1 and 2. A resident also raised concerns during public comment about an unpermitted-looking debris/compost storage operation on town land near the Windmill wells.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Schiliro presided; Councilmembers DiGiacinto, Milim, Berra, and Hussain participated (no absences clearly noted in the transcript).

cases.name: Town DPW Storage/Compost Yard — Environmental Concerns
cases.address: Middle Patent Road to Banksville Road (town-owned parcel near Windmill wells)
cases.summary: A resident (Joe) told the Board during public comment that a long, narrow town-owned parcel between Middle Patent Road and Banksville Road — environmentally sensitive due to proximity to the Windmill community's wells and a headwater branch of the Mianus River — is being used to store soil, stone, brush, wood chips, and equipment beyond its originally intended small composting footprint, and urged the town to contract with a licensed outside processing facility instead. Board members recalled a prior (2022) vote to have the site cleaned up and expressed surprise it had not been fully addressed; the Supervisor directed the town administrator to research current conditions and report back rather than speculate.
cases.publicComment: Resident Joe presented photos of debris, soil, brush, and equipment stored at the site and urged the town to use a licensed outside contractor instead, citing environmental risk to nearby wells and the Mianus River headwaters.

memberPositions.evidence: As presiding officer, directed the town administrator to research the site and report back at the next meeting rather than speculate, saying he'd 'rather just have it meet fact based.'

cases.name: 14 Middle Patent Road — Special Use Permit
cases.summary: The Board reconvened the previously opened special use permit hearing, received a letter from Dan Hylis requesting an adjournment, and adjourned the hearing to the November 29, 2023 meeting without substantive discussion.

cases.name: Car Washes as Principal Permitted Use in P.O.I. District — 125 Business Park Drive (Basis Acquisitions)
cases.summary: The Board reconvened a hearing on a petition from Basis Industrial Acquisitions LLC to amend the zoning code to allow car washes as a principal permitted use in the P.O.I. (planned light industrial) district at 125 Business Park Drive, and adjourned the hearing without discussion to the October 25, 2023 meeting.

cases.name: Refuse, Recyclables Collection/Transfer/Disposal Services — Bid Authorization
cases.summary: The Board authorized the town to go out to bid for collection, transfer, and disposal of refuse and recyclables for residential and commercial properties townwide, following an executive session the prior week to finalize added/alternate bid items.

cases.summary: The Board authorized the Town Attorney to execute a consent judgment resolving a tax certiorari matter brought by J.G. Ormont, LLC against the Town, with no discussion recorded.

cases.name: IBM Community Park — Artificial Turf Fields 1 & 2 (Keller & Sessions Engineering Proposal)
cases.summary: The Board approved a roughly $125,000 proposal from Keller & Sessions Engineering (part of an estimated $2.7 million total project) to prepare bid documents, soil testing, and a stormwater pollution prevention plan for converting IBM Community Park fields 1 and 2 to artificial turf, framed as addressing overuse of existing grass fields (cited in a 600-household survey) by roughly seven-fold increasing playable capacity. A resident (Larry) questioned whether the pre-bid spend was justified and whether IBM's fields actually have drainage problems (as opposed to Lombardi Park, which does); board members disputed the drainage claim for IBM but agreed on the need for engineering work before any construction decision.
cases.publicComment: Resident Larry questioned the cost-effectiveness of a $125,000 pre-bid engineering spend and whether IBM's outfields genuinely have drainage issues versus Lombardi Park.

memberPositions.evidence: Recounted decades of personal history supporting town recreation investments (the town pool, the recreation center, coaching's effect on students as a high school teacher) and thanked Milim by name for prioritizing the fields project.

Walked through cost-offset math bringing the effective project cost from $2.7M down toward roughly $1.25M after maintenance savings and Eagle Ridge contributions; another board member directly addressed him by name disputing the math while still supporting moving forward.

Argued from personal experience (out at the fields multiple days a week for a decade, having talked to the Armonk soccer coach and the engineer) that IBM's outfields do not have a drainage problem, distinguishing them from Lombardi Park; credited elsewhere by DiGiacinto as the one who made the turf project a priority.
Guided the vote to approval as presiding officer, noting the engineering step is a necessary prerequisite to getting real bid numbers before the town commits to construction spending.

themes.note: IBM Community Park turf field engineering proposal was the meeting's most substantive debate.
Board reiterated opposition to moving town elections to even years and continued monitoring the Governor's housing compact.
Public comment on unpermitted-looking debris storage near town wells.
Two hearings continued procedurally without discussion.

staffInput.summary: Reported on 2024 budget work sessions and a home COVID test reminder; asked by the Board to research the DPW storage yard conditions and report back.
Engineering firm principal behind the IBM Community Park turf proposal; addressed drainage, soil testing, and stormwater design questions directly.
Handled correspondence, posted community resources related to Israel relief efforts, and gave a library programming update.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR; most named attribution here relies on direct-address cues (board members calling each other by first name) rather than a speaker log, so several extended exchanges (e.g., parts of the turf field debate) could not be attributed to a specific member with confidence and were left out of memberPositions.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Board's main business was an extensive, unresolved public hearing on Basis Industrial Acquisitions' petition to allow car washes as a principal permitted use in the P.O.I. district so it could build a full-service car wash at 125 Business Park Drive — a parcel with a fraught history as a former eminent-domain target and part of the original Eagle Ridge community benefits agreement; neighboring Business Park Drive tenants objected on traffic-queue and comprehensive-plan-compatibility grounds, and the Board adjourned without a decision, without setting a date, pending a fuller written response to the Planning Board's memo. The Board also opened a special use permit application for a recreational-training addition at Core Sports Physical Therapy (130 Business Park Drive), continued debate over the Lombardi Park water supply project (extend water district piping vs. rehabilitate the existing well), fielded a public-comment exchange with the Ethics Board about the process for advancing its proposed local law changes, and heard a town administrator update on the Middle Patent Road transfer/storage yard raised by a resident two weeks prior.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Schiliro presided; Councilmembers DiGiacinto, Milim, Berra, and Hussain participated (Hussain again joining part of the meeting remotely).

cases.name: Car Washes as Principal Permitted Use in P.O.I. District — 125 Business Park Drive (Basis Acquisitions)
cases.status: public hearing continued; adjourned without a set date
cases.summary: Basis Industrial Acquisitions presented a detailed proposal for a single-bay, full-service car wash with 21 parking spaces, a 39-foot front-setback variance, PFAS-free chemicals with 90%+ water recycling, and low projected volume (roughly 5-10 cars/hour); the Board spent extensive time on stacking/queue capacity, PFAS well-water testing conditions, noise, and whether a car wash counts as a 'personal service' consistent with the comprehensive plan. Neighboring Business Park Drive tenants (Arrow Hardware/Al Mayolo and Joe Gellard, a former owner of the parcel who recounted a contentious eminent-domain history tied to the town's search for a water source for the Eagle Ridge project) objected, citing queue-length spillover onto the street, incompatibility with the comprehensive plan, and unresolved neighborhood flooding they attribute to nearby development. The Board agreed it needed more information and a fuller response to the Planning and County Planning Board memos before proceeding, and adjourned the hearing without setting a return date.
cases.publicComment: Patrick McCarthy and Al Mayolo of neighboring Arrow Hardware (100/130 Business Park Drive) objected over car queue length spilling onto the street and incompatibility with the comprehensive plan; Joe Gellard, a prior owner of the 125 Business Park Drive parcel, raised a contentious history of a threatened eminent-domain taking for a town water-supply well (later found elsewhere) tied to the Eagle Ridge project's community benefits agreement, and objected to the car wash on flooding and history grounds.

memberPositions.evidence: Said that if noise and PFAS concerns are appropriately mitigated, the car wash 'would be a really great service for the town,' while pushing to keep it a higher-end, 'boutique' amenity.

Argued traffic queuing should not be treated as self-regulating, warning that a backed-up line of only 11 stacking spaces could spill into other Business Park Drive traffic, including access to the IBM Community Park fields.

Raised whether a car wash is compatible with the comprehensive plan's caution against competitive retail uses harming hamlet business districts, and flagged environmental/pollution liability risk if the business later failed, citing the comprehensive-plan committee work she, Chris McCarthy, and Jim Jensen had done.

Pushed back analytically on the comprehensive-plan-incompatibility argument, comparing the car wash favorably to a rejected big-box supermarket proposal and framing it as closer to a 'personal service' use, while agreeing more information was needed before a decision.

cases.name: Core Sports Physical Therapy — Recreational Training Center Special Use Permit, 130 Business Park Drive
cases.applicant: Core Performance of Westchester LLC (Core Sports Physical Therapy)
cases.summary: A 10-year tenant physical therapy practice sought a special use permit to formally delineate roughly 4,000 square feet of its space as a distinct youth/adult sports-development recreational training use (separate from its medical physical-therapy operation, for insurance-liability reasons), largely restoring pre-COVID group training programming. The Board received the application materials, discussed whether the use is closer to 'medical' than 'recreational' for parking-calculation purposes, and referred it to the Town and Planning Boards with a public hearing scheduled for November 29, 2023.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether the use should legally be classified closer to medical (by analogy, since it isn't reimbursable through insurance in the same way but functions similarly) and suggested the applicant's counsel speak with the Town Attorney to explore that classification.

cases.name: Lombardi Park — Public Water Supply Extension vs. Well Rehabilitation
cases.summary: The Board continued debating whether to extend Water District #4 piping to Lombardi Park (roughly $461,000 per an initial Keller & Sessions estimate) or rehabilitate the park's existing well (potentially over $300,000 once duplicate treatment infrastructure like chlorination and UV disinfection is included), given ongoing PFAS concerns and the park's heavy use by children. The town confirmed bid documents for the water-district extension had already gone out, with cost comparisons expected at the next meeting; one board member questioned whether the eventual scope (effectively a water fountain and three bathrooms) justified the six-figure cost.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued that given ongoing PFAS concerns and that Lombardi Park primarily serves children, securing municipal public water rather than a rehabbed well is an important consideration worth the added cost.

Follow-up on the Middle Patent Road transfer/storage yard raised two weeks prior.
