Addressed the eminent-domain/CBA history of the 125 Business Park Drive parcel and legal process questions raised by the Ethics Board.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR; the car wash hearing Q&A includes many rapid, overlapping board exchanges without clear speaker cues, so several individual comments (particularly mid-hearing technical questions) could not be confidently attributed to a specific member and were omitted from memberPositions.

meetings.meetingSummary: Held the night after town elections (with the Supervisor and one Council race still uncertified, including a one-vote margin), the Board covered routine business and two land-use items: a seminary campus's special use permit for building modifications (a new house and an addition to its married-student housing, requiring a setback variance) with a public hearing set for January 24, 2024, and a proposal to request renovation specifications for the deteriorating Clove Road ballfield in North White Plains after a decade of resident requests. A resident's public comment about the town's ambiguous, inconsistently-enforced political sign code prompted board discussion of tightening those rules for a future board. The meeting's longest debate was procedural: after a Board of Ethics letter requesting three code-of-ethics amendments (staggered alternate-member terms, expanded recusal triggers, and real-estate disclosure requirements), the Board argued at length over whether to hold a work session first or go straight to a public hearing, ultimately voting to schedule the hearing directly for December 13, 2023.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Schiliro presided; Councilmembers DiGiacinto, Milim, Berra, and Hussain participated.

cases.name: Board of Ethics Code of Ethics Amendments (Staggered Terms, Recusal, Disclosure)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle Board of Ethics
cases.summary: The Board of Ethics formally requested a public hearing on three code amendments: staggered terms for alternate ethics board members, expanding the recusal/abstention requirement to cover interests held within the prior six months, and revised annual real-estate-interest disclosure requirements. Town board members disagreed sharply over process — whether a joint work session with the Ethics Board should precede drafting the local law, or whether the board could proceed directly to a public hearing since the recommended language was already final and uncontroversial — with the disagreement echoing a similar process dispute from the prior meeting. The Board ultimately voted to schedule the public hearing directly for December 13, 2023, skipping a work session.
cases.publicComment: Board of Ethics representative Brett Summers pressed the Town Board on the delay in receiving/scheduling the Board of Ethics's letter and advocated skipping the work session.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he had reviewed the full proposal, found it straightforward and was in full agreement, and argued the Board should be able to move directly to and conclude the public hearing without a separate work session.

Repeatedly pressed that a work session was needed so both boards are 'on the same page' before drafting a final local law, and noted the process had been laid out and confirmed with the Town Attorney multiple times.

cases.name: St. Nersis Armenian Seminary — Special Use Permit for Building Modifications, 486 Bedford Road
cases.status: lead agency declared; public hearing scheduled (January 24, 2024)
cases.summary: St. Nersis Armenian Seminary sought a special use permit and an associated 50-foot side-yard setback variance for a new house (a future dean's residence) and a two-room guest-speaker addition to its married-student housing building, which sits roughly 30-33 feet from a residential property line (backing onto homes on Tripp Lane). The Board declared itself lead agency, asked for a clearer aerial view of the distance to adjoining residential properties before the hearing, and referred the matter to the Zoning Board of Appeals for the variance, scheduling the public hearing for January 24, 2024.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he was generally supportive given prior dealings with the applicant but pressed for a clearer picture of the setback distance to residential neighbors before the hearing, drawing a parallel to the 5 North Greenwich Road hearing's residential-protection concerns.

cases.name: Clove Road Ballfield Renovations, North White Plains
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (requested by Valhalla baseball league via Superintendent of Recreation & Parks Matt Trainor)
cases.summary: Superintendent of Recreation & Parks Matt Trainor requested authorization to have Keller & Sessions prepare a no-cost renovation proposal for the Clove Road field's outfield/infield grading and a longstanding clay 'lip' problem, following a request from Valhalla baseball league (Bob Candria) and echoing a roughly decade-old, repeatedly-deferred community request. Board members raised process concerns about moving forward without first vetting the scope through the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board and consulting other groups that use the field (as had been done for the IBM Community Park turf project), but agreed to authorize seeking a proposal while looping in the advisory board.

memberPositions.evidence: Recounted being asked by a longtime baseball-league supporter to see the field's condition firsthand and called it 'a very legitimate request' given roughly ten years of unfulfilled promises to fix it, recommending the Board move forward.

Cautioned that the request seemed premature without the same vetting process (survey, sports-organization input, Parks & Rec Advisory Board review) used for the IBM Community Park turf field project, worried about acting on one group's request alone.

themes.note: Extended procedural dispute over how to advance Board of Ethics code amendments.
Meeting held the night after town elections with two races uncertified; extensive public comment on political sign regulation.
Continued opposition to the even-year elections bill and housing compact.

staffInput.summary: Reported on a new solar speed-display sign, a road closure notice, and fall leaf collection; discussed the Clove Road field history with Matt Trainor.
Presented site-plan and setback details for the seminary special use permit application.
Explained the local-law drafting process and disputed the need for a work session before the Board of Ethics public hearing.
Requested authorization to seek a Keller & Sessions renovation proposal for the Clove Road field based on his site visit and league feedback.
Gave election-timeline and community announcement updates; handled hearing correspondence.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR; the Board of Ethics process debate and the Clove Road field discussion had several extended, rapid exchanges without clear speaker cues, so some individual remarks could not be confidently attributed to a specific member.

meetings.meetingSummary: A packed agenda featured four public hearings: the first hearing on the 2024 preliminary town budget ($39.2 million, up 5.3%, with a flat town tax rate for residents thanks to fund-balance use and strong building-department and interest revenue), a special use permit for an equestrian family's expansion to 26 horses at 14 Middle Patent Road (approved after neighbor outreach and a tightened no-horse-shows condition), the Core Sports Physical Therapy recreation-center special permit at 130 Business Park Drive (approved), and the Water District #4 extension to Lombardi Park (procedural/administrative resolutions adopted, with the Board still comparing the cost of a piped extension versus rehabilitating the existing well before a final decision in January). Public comment included recurring resident concerns about property-tax exemption policy, ZBA meeting transparency/notification, and lawn-parking and permit-enforcement code issues in North White Plains.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Schiliro presided; Councilmembers DiGiacinto, Milim, Berra, and Hussain participated. Schiliro noted this would likely be his final meeting presiding as Supervisor given the pending election transition.

cases.name: 2024 Town and Special Districts Preliminary Budget
cases.status: public hearing opened (first of two hearings)
cases.summary: Director of Finance Abbas Surah presented the $39.2 million 2024 preliminary budget (up 5.3% year over year, driven by inflation, new labor contracts, and higher pension contributions), funded 60% by property taxes and 40% by other revenue (PILOT agreements with IBM and Eagle/Berman, sales tax, interest income, and strong building-department revenue). The total tax levy is $23.3 million, roughly $2 million under the state's 2% tax cap, and the town-portion tax rate is projected flat versus 2023 for the median $1.2 million home. The Board opened the first of two required budget hearings, with the second scheduled for the sole December meeting.
cases.publicComment: A resident (self-identified as a longtime taxpayer) urged the Board to consider exemptions for late tax payments, seniors over 80, and veterans/mortgage-free homeowners.

cases.name: 14 Middle Patent Road — Special Use Permit
cases.applicant: 14 Middle Patent Road LLC (equestrian family estate)
cases.summary: The Board approved a special use permit expanding an existing private, non-commercial equestrian facility to 26 horse stalls on 41.62 acres for a family competing at the Olympic/professional level, following favorable recommendations from the ARB, Conservation Board, and Planning Board and a resident open house the applicant's team described as well received. At a board member's request, the resolution's language was tightened to flatly prohibit any horse shows (rather than only 'for-profit' shows) to close a potential future loophole, and manure/delivery truck traffic was restricted to weekday daytime hours.
cases.publicComment: A neighbor (Steve Brownstein) had raised concerns at an earlier session that were reported resolved; no opposition was voiced at this hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed for the resolution to flatly prohibit 'any horse shows' rather than only for-profit ones, reasoning that future owners might not share the current family's intentions, then confirmed support once the language was tightened.
Complimented the applicant's neighbor engagement and moved the hearing toward a vote, noting the project had cleared the ARB, Conservation Board, and Planning Board.

cases.name: Core Sports Physical Therapy — Recreational Training Center Special Use Permit, 130 Business Park Drive
cases.applicant: Core Performance of Westchester LLC (Core Sports Physical Therapy)
cases.summary: Following a favorable Planning Board recommendation and no anticipated negative impacts, the Board closed the public hearing and adopted a resolution approving the special use permit formalizing Core Sports's recreational training space as distinct from its medical physical-therapy use.

cases.name: Lombardi Park — Public Water Supply Extension vs. Well Rehabilitation
cases.status: administrative resolutions adopted; hearing opened, pending 45-day permissive referendum period
cases.summary: The Board opened a hearing and adopted the required administrative resolutions to formally propose extending Water District #4 into Lombardi Park (piped option, competitively bid after a non-competitive emergency estimate of about $461,000), triggering a mandatory 45-day permissive-referendum waiting period before a final vote in January; the Board can still choose the alternative of rehabilitating the park's existing well (about $373,000, roughly a third of which is for expanding the parks garage to house treatment equipment) or abandon the process if a cheaper option is found. Board members debated the true cost driver of the well option and future operating-cost implications of a self-run treatment system, with general agreement to keep exploring the well cost further before deciding.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether the well option's cost was really driven by needing to expand the parks garage rather than the well itself, and said he wanted to see if there was a cheaper path before committing to the pipe option.

Raised the future operating-cost implications of running a standalone well/treatment system and suggested exploring lower-cost, environmentally sound alternatives for non-potable uses like irrigation before committing.

themes.note: Public comment on ZBA meeting notification/transparency and code-enforcement consistency.

staffInput.summary: Presented the 2024 preliminary budget in detail, covering revenue sources, expense drivers, and tax-levy/tax-cap figures.
Reviewed completed and upcoming 2023-2024 capital projects (town pool purchase, Wampus Brook Park grading, paving/drainage, Wampus Brook lighting) and discussed Lombardi Park water options.
Explained the administrative/permissive-referendum steps required for the Lombardi Park water district extension and confirmed the Board retains flexibility to change course before the final vote.
Presented the equestrian facility application alongside owner's representative Steve Weiss, addressing horse-count realities, manure management, and neighbor outreach.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR; most substantive board dialogue in this meeting had reasonably clear direct-address or role cues, but some rapid procedural exchanges (especially around the Lombardi Park administrative resolutions) could not be attributed to specific members with confidence.

meetings.meetingSummary: This was Supervisor Schiliro's final meeting after 16 years on the Board (including as Supervisor), and a large portion of the meeting was devoted to tributes from board members, staff, and residents. Substantively, the Board adopted the final 2024 town budget with a 0% town tax-rate increase, approved (unanimously and with Board of Ethics representatives present) the Code of Ethics amendments first proposed in November, extended the Summit Club's temporary special use permit for its golf-course maintenance building and public golf use through the end of 2024, approved a Langan Engineering amendment for a PFOA treatment pilot study at the Windmill wells, referred a Keller & Sessions survey/consulting proposal for the Clove Road ballfields to the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board, and — after extended debate over single-stream versus dual-stream recycling economics and contamination rates — awarded the new refuse/recycling collection contract keeping the existing dual-stream, alternate-week system, with a side-letter credit for the town's new food-composting program.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Schiliro presided in his final meeting; Councilmembers DiGiacinto, Milim, Berra, and Hussain participated. The meeting ran past midnight.

cases.name: 2024 Town and Special Districts Preliminary Budget
cases.summary: The Board closed the second and final public hearing and adopted the 2024 town budget with a 0% increase in the town tax rate, which the Director of Finance described as structurally balanced; a minor adjustment was made using fund balance after department budget requests changed slightly (notably an unbudgeted increase in insurance rates) between the initial presentation and adoption.

cases.name: Board of Ethics Code of Ethics Amendments (Staggered Terms, Recusal, Disclosure)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle Board of Ethics
cases.summary: The Board held the public hearing and unanimously approved all three Board of Ethics-recommended code amendments: closing a resign-and-return loophole around recusal, staggering the terms of the two alternate ethics board members (requiring the current alternates to be reappointed to staggered five- and one-year terms), and expanding the annual real-estate disclosure statement to cover investment properties held by the officeholder/spouse and, more broadly, an enumerated list of relatives. The Board declined to fold a proposed 'advance notice of disclosure requirements at interview' practice into the formal code itself, agreeing instead it should be handled administratively (e.g., as part of the volunteer application process), and flagged a separate concern about possible campaign-contribution 'structuring' around the code's $500 recusal threshold for the incoming board to examine next year.

memberPositions.evidence: As the ethics board's council liaison, voiced full support for all three changes and moved to adopt the amendments as verbally modified.
Called the real-estate disclosure change 'really critical for public trust,' drawing an analogy to standard compliance disclosure practices from his investment-industry background.

cases.name: Summit Club Golf Course — Temporary Special Use Permit Extension (Maintenance Building / Public Golf Use)
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners (via JMC Planning and Landscape Architecture)
cases.summary: The Board granted a one-year extension (through December 31, 2024) of the temporary special use permit allowing continued public use of the golf course while the applicant finalizes the location, engineering, and pricing (now estimated near $5 million) of a proposed permanent maintenance building, correcting a resolution date reference from the 2023 to the 2024 golf season.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed a site plan cannot be approved without the maintenance building being resolved and said a one-year extension should be sufficient time for the applicant to finalize the building's location and cost.

cases.name: Windmill Wells — PFOA Treatment Pilot Study (Langan Engineering)
cases.summary: The Board approved an amendment to the Langan Engineering consulting agreement for a Health Department-mandated PFOA treatment pilot study at the Windmill wells, extending the required test run from 12 to 16 weeks per the equipment manufacturer's recommendation and covering rental of a 20,000-gallon frac tank to haul away test water (since there is no sewer connection on site and discharge to wetlands is prohibited), at an added not-to-exceed cost of $66,800; the town is separately negotiating to discharge the water at the wastewater plant instead, which could yield significant savings, and framed the pilot as a step toward a permanent treatment system that could save roughly $800,000 versus alternatives, potentially aided by grant funding.

cases.name: Clove Road Ballfield Renovations, North White Plains
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Superintendent of Recreation & Parks)
cases.status: approved; referred to Parks & Recreation Advisory Board
cases.summary: The Board approved a Keller & Sessions survey and consulting-services proposal to assess whether a capital drainage/grading project is actually needed at the Clove Road field, after the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board itself was split on whether the issue required capital spending versus maintenance, and referred the matter back to that advisory board given a decade-long resident request (via Little League volunteer Bob Candria) for improvement.

memberPositions.evidence: As a Parks & Recreation Advisory Board liaison, said it remained unclear to him and other advisory board members whether the field genuinely needs a capital project, and recommended having Keller & Sessions assess it first rather than committing to construction.

cases.name: Refuse, Recyclables Collection/Transfer/Disposal Services — Bid Award (2024-2029)
cases.summary: After a lengthy debate — including a 330-response resident survey (roughly 40% wanting the status quo, 50% wanting weekly single-stream pickup at about $80,000/year more, 10% wanting twice-weekly pickup) and Sustainability Committee testimony that single-stream recycling causes about 30% contamination and would effectively cost more than trash disposal by devaluing recovered mixed paper — the Board awarded the new multi-year refuse and recycling contract while keeping the existing dual-stream, alternate-week recycling system rather than switching to weekly single-stream, citing cost (roughly a half-percent tax-rate equivalent) and environmental contamination concerns. The Board also secured a side-letter commitment from the contractor to credit the town for its new food-scrap composting program, and directed the Sustainability Committee to spend the next year researching the tradeoffs (including surveying residents jointly with the town) before revisiting the single- vs. dual-stream decision, which the contractor confirmed can be changed annually.
cases.publicComment: Sustainability Committee co-chair Neil Singer presented data arguing against single-stream recycling (30% contamination rate, no net cost savings, and it undercuts the committee's new food-composting and 'recycle right' education initiatives).

memberPositions.evidence: Strongly favored keeping dual-stream/alternate-week pickup, citing the near-half-percent tax equivalent cost of switching, contamination concerns, and confidence that biweekly recycling and the new composting program are not a hardship for the average household.

Ran and shared a 330-response resident survey on the recycling-frequency options, found the contamination argument persuasive, but pushed to formally revisit the decision next year with a more rigorous joint survey and Sustainability Committee research process.

themes.note: Extended, data-driven debate over single- vs. dual-stream recycling in the new refuse contract.

staffInput.summary: Finalized and presented the 0%-increase 2024 budget for adoption.
Explained the Windmill wells PFOA pilot study scope, cost drivers, and water-disposal logistics.
Advised on codifying (or not codifying) the disclosure-notice practice into the ethics code and on structuring the food-composting credit as a side letter.
Presented data and recommendations opposing a shift to single-stream weekly recycling.
Answered detailed board questions on single- vs. dual-stream mechanics, contamination, and pricing, and confirmed the town can switch systems annually.
Presented the request to extend the Summit Club's temporary special use permit.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR; this was a very long, emotional final meeting for the outgoing Supervisor with extensive tributes and cross-talk. Attribution is more confident for the ethics-code and recycling debates (clearer named/role cues) than for shorter procedural exchanges, some of which were omitted from memberPositions.

meetings.meetingSummary: This was the new administration's first meeting, combining the annual organizational agenda with a regular Town Board meeting under newly elected Supervisor Joseph Rende. The board adopted 35 routine organizational items (depositories, financial policies, professional-service contracts, fire/ambulance and intermunicipal agreements, salary schedules and appointments), with a notable dispute over the Supervisor's unilateral liaison appointments. The regular agenda included a police promotion, two major development-related items (the Gateway/45 Bedford Road deed-restriction and stormwater easement, and the Airport Campus water district extension), a WIIA/EFC sewer grant, a library accessibility-ramp bid award, and various contracts and personnel actions.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present; all five members (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra) appear to have participated. Councilman Berra recused/abstained on the Long Pond Park District agreement (item 33), recorded by roll call.

cases.name: 2024 Organizational Agenda — Annual Authorizations, Policies and Contracts
cases.summary: The board reconvened from executive session and adopted the annual organizational package: designation of four depositories, ACH/facsimile payment authorization, statutory appointments (Deputy Supervisor, records/registrar officers, finance director, assessor, consultants and town counsel), legal-notice and meeting-schedule policies, the $0.67/mile mileage rate (matching the new IRS federal standard), the master fee schedule, procurement/investment/vehicle/ethics and workplace policies, salary payment dates, and numerous 2024 professional-service, legal, engineering, stormwater, fire, ambulance, hydrant and intermunicipal agreements. Nearly all passed by unanimous voice vote. The Long Pond Park District agreement (item 33) required a roll call because Councilman Berra recused, passing with the other members and the Supervisor voting aye and Berra abstaining.

memberPositions.evidence: Recused himself on the Long Pond Park District agreement and his abstention was recorded by roll call.
Voted aye on roll-call items and flagged the renaming of the Recycling & Sustainability Committee to just 'Sustainability'.

cases.name: 2024 Appointment of Departmental and Committee Liaisons
cases.summary: The Supervisor presented his slate of liaison appointments to departments, boards and committees, framing them as a supervisor's prerogative for the new administration. Councilman Milim objected to being removed as Building Department liaison, noting he had served in that role since 2014 without complaints and citing a precedent where a prior member's shared-liaison request had been honored. Councilwoman DiGiacinto similarly asked to be named a Planning Board liaison alongside others, saying she had raised it privately with the Supervisor and would mention it publicly if not addressed. The Supervisor said he had crafted the list based on his own observations, was open to future discussion, but wanted to proceed tonight; the slate was adopted by voice vote with the objections 'duly noted.'

memberPositions.evidence: 'I would like to continue being a building department liaison... I've been liaison since 2014... I don't think there's ever been any complaints,' citing a shared-liaison precedent.
Asked to be appointed Planning Board liaison with other members; said she had raised it with the Supervisor and would mention it publicly if not changed.

Defended the appointments as the Supervisor's decision made after observing town issues, said liaison roles can always change and he is open to discuss further, but wanted to get through the list tonight.

cases.name: Promotion of Detective Anthony Sabatella to Police Sergeant
cases.summary: The Police Chief requested board approval to promote Detective Anthony Sabatella, a 10-year member of the department, to the budgeted position of Sergeant effective January 13, 2024, citing his record as School Resource Officer, detective and field training officer and his top placement on the civil-service exam. Board members were enthusiastic and multiple members offered to make the motion. It passed unanimously by voice vote, followed by congratulations and a group photo.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'one of the most enjoyable opportunities that we have as members of the board' and moved the item up on the agenda.

cases.name: North Castle Library Truss Repair — Change Orders
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (library caretaker Catherine/Felix; existing contractor)
cases.summary: Councilman Hussain, the library liaison, raised the status of structural truss repairs keeping part of the library closed. The Town Administrator (Kevin) reported that outreach to eight firms produced no competing bids and that the existing contractor's four change orders totaled roughly $24,000, with the remaining work being mostly sheetrock closing-up (change orders 3 and 4 of about $9,400 and $5,800). The board debated whether to authorize a spending range now versus gathering more pricing; Councilman Milim pressed for exact figures on the remaining work while Councilman Berra urged going back to the original contractor now. No formal action was taken; the board agreed to gather information offline and bring a change order to the next meeting to reopen the library.

memberPositions.evidence: As library liaison raised the topic and pushed to 'move forward knowing that it is not a zero cost... we also just want to get the job done' so the library can reopen.
Pressed repeatedly for the exact cost of the remaining sheetrock/closing-up work and a breakdown of the change orders before agreeing to spend.
Argued the eight no-bid responses came in December when firms were busy and urged reaching out to the original contractor now for a better price rather than moving ahead.

cases.name: Gateway / former Mariani Site (45 Bedford Road) — Deed Restriction, Right-of-Way and Stormwater Easement
cases.applicant: 45 Bedford Road, LLC (attorney Tony Veneziano; developer J.D. Soma; engineer Lauren McMahon, Lane/Langan Engineering)
cases.summary: The board received three letters and heard the applicant's request, prompted by a Planning Board recommendation, to use the town right-of-way along Maple Avenue to create a shallower, better-landscaped stormwater/floodplain basin, to establish an easement (with HOA-maintained plantings), and to interpret or amend a one-acre deed restriction so rear patios and fences would be permitted. Town Planner Adam Kaufman supported the aesthetic benefit and applicant-maintenance arrangement, and attorney Roland advised the board could interpret the 'structures' language or hold a public hearing to amend it. Several residents spoke in opposition, including a St. Stephen's Church warden urging deferral to the ARB and a letter from Sharon Tombach urging the board not to schedule hearings, grant easements or weaken the deed restriction. The board declined to set a public hearing, requesting overlay renderings showing the deed-restriction line and comparative basin designs, and tabled the matter to reconvene in two weeks.
cases.publicComment: Strongly cautious to opposed: resident Fran (Nichols Road) asked about screening on the American Legion/pavilion side; John Bernson, warden of St. Stephen's Church, urged deferring all decisions to the Architectural Review Board; developer J.D. Soma disputed claims the ARB unanimously opposed the design; Ed Woodyard recounted the ARB meeting and read a letter from Sharon Tombach opposing any easement, hearing or deed-restriction relief and stressing floodplain and historic-district protection.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked detailed questions about basin depth, floodplain volume, and whether parking areas/curbs/footings within the deed-restricted area also count as 'structures'; wanted to see the deed-restriction line before acting.
Led questioning, said he did not want to 'set public hearings to myself,' asked for overlay renderings and comparative plans, and moved to table for two weeks.
Corrected the basin-depth figures 'just for accuracy,' clarifying the wider/shallower vs. narrow/deep basin dimensions.
Asked clarifying questions about the plantings and whether stormwater modeling used current post-development data, and noted much of what was requested was already provided.

cases.name: Airport Campus / former MBIA HQ (113 King Street) — Extension of Water District No. 8
cases.applicant: Airport Campus (attorney Chris Fisher, Cuddy & Feder; Jeff Ringler; Kevin Moses, Toll Brothers)
cases.summary: As required by its August SEQRA findings and rezoning, the applicant filed a petition and map/plan/report (prepared by the town's engineer D&B) to extend Water District No. 8 by running a main up King Street over I-684 to the site, with a 300,000-gallon storage tank and pump station. Attorney Roland advised adopting the order calling a public hearing while negotiating a water-contribution agreement and referring the ~$3 million cost estimate to the Kellard firm for review. Members raised questions about inflation and cost escalation (DiGiacinto), tank sizing discrepancies and coordination with a possible future combined million-gallon tank and Water District 4 extension (Milim/Rende, with Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal). The board voted by roll call to refer the map/plan to Kellard and to adopt the order calling a public hearing for February 14, 2024 (DiGiacinto, Hussain and Supervisor Rende recorded aye).

memberPositions.evidence: Voted aye but pressed on cost escalation: asked what happens if supply-chain problems or inflation drive costs above the estimate and whether the 10% contingency was adequate, and insisted on a fully negotiated contribution agreement before approval.
Questioned the 300,000 vs. 157,000-gallon tank discrepancy, economies of scale of a combined million-gallon tank, and whether pricing reflected today's private (non-prevailing-wage) costs.
Emphasized the 'huge benefit on both parties' and long-term value for Water District 8 and a future District 4 extension, invoking the Whippoorwill Hills/IBM group-effort precedent.
Recorded aye on the roll-call vote adopting the order calling the public hearing.

cases.name: Water Infrastructure Improvement Act / EFC Project Finance Agreement — Sewer District No. 2
cases.applicant: Sal Mesiti, Director of Water & Sewer Operations
cases.summary: The board received a memo from Water/Sewer Director Sal Mesiti regarding a Water Infrastructure Improvement Act award and a project finance agreement with the New York State Environmental Facilities Corporation for a Sewer District No. 2 upgrade. This is the second grant secured for the project, in addition to a $2.9 million DEC grant, with the EFC reimbursing pay applications as construction progresses. The board voted to receive the memo and to authorize Sewer District 2 to enter the finance agreement and accept the roughly $2.968 million grant, praising the Water/Sewer department's work.

memberPositions.evidence: Quipped '2.968 million reasons why we should accept that' and praised Sal Mesiti as 'a tremendous asset to the community.'

cases.name: Staying Alive Charity 11th Annual 5K Fun Run
cases.summary: The board considered a request from the Staying Alive Charity to hold its 11th annual 5K Fun Run in the Windmill community on Saturday, October 5, 2024. Members confirmed the date would not conflict with the Armonk art show (set for September 28-29). The motion passed, contingent on the charity obtaining the necessary fire, police and insurance approvals, with members praising the event and the charity.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved approval contingent on required approvals and the date not conflicting with the art show; 'I love the event... I had a lot of fun at that event.'

cases.name: Bid Award to Vinco Builders — Exterior Accessible Ramp at Community Center & Library
cases.address: North Castle Community Center and Library
cases.summary: The board considered awarding a bid to Vinco Builders for an exterior ADA-accessible ramp to the library/community-center back deck and authorizing the Supervisor to sign the agreement. Because the library fund balance was insufficient, roughly $53,000 of the cost (net of a grant) would come from the town's fund balance, drawing the library balance to near zero. Councilman Milim questioned the relatively high cost, the lack of earlier estimates and whether the existing internal ADA route was adequate, while Councilwoman DiGiacinto voiced concern about depleting the library fund balance so early in the year. Councilman Hussain, the library liaison, endorsed the long-deliberated project (including the Trex decking choice), and the board approved it.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted the building is already ADA compliant, questioned the high cost and absence of earlier estimates, and asked whether the internal-route interruptions had truly been an issue; also raised Trex slipperiness concerns citing the Wampus Brook bridge.
Concerned the library would 'end up having a zero fund balance' and that the town cannot keep drawing on its fund balance for library projects all year.
As library liaison said the project had been 'very deeply thought through' with many iterations and materials discussions, and confirmed he was comfortable with it; seconded the motion.

cases.name: 2024 Consulting Service Agreements — Weatherworks, Empire (Drug/Alcohol Testing) and KSCJ (Pool Water System)
cases.summary: The board authorized three service agreements: with Weatherworks for 2024 weather-consulting services; with Empire Consulting for 2024-2025 DOT drug- and alcohol-testing of highway personnel (subject to correcting a typo listing 2023); and with KSCJ Consulting to rehabilitate the town pool's water-supply well and disinfection system to satisfy the Westchester County Department of Health and open the pool for the season. Recreation Superintendent Matt Traynor and the Town Administrator explained the pool well defect, and members expressed confidence in the KSCJ/Kellard work. All three passed by voice vote.

cases.name: Personnel — Appointments of Egan and Carvey; Resignations
cases.summary: The board approved the appointment of Josephine Egan as Confidential Secretary to the Supervisor (effective January 1, 2024) and J. Carvey as Hourly Librarian (effective January 16, 2024), and accepted resignations from Susan Kramer (library, Jan 2), Kevin Mills (library, Dec 7, 2023) and Adam Woodruff (highway department, Dec 30, 2023). Members welcomed Egan warmly, with the Supervisor and colleagues expressing confidence she would be an asset to the whole board.

memberPositions.evidence: 'I really lucked out. I found someone who lives in town, knows the town... she's going to be a tremendous asset.'
'I'm excited. Josephine seems great. I know she's done great work with the school.'

cases.name: Consensus Agenda / Association of Towns Resolutions
cases.summary: The board approved the consensus agenda (items A through D). For item D, the Association of Towns resolutions and voting-delegate designation, Councilman Berra noted the town may have been placed in the wrong membership tier (billed as if over 50,000 population) and asked to review the resolutions more closely before the February annual meeting. The board approved the package with the understanding that the tier/category issue would be revisited and corrected in time.

memberPositions.evidence: Flagged that the Association of Towns appears to have placed North Castle in the wrong (larger-municipality) billing tier and asked to take a closer look before voting on the resolutions.

themes.note: First meeting of the new administration; organizational agenda, liaison-appointment prerogative dispute, and process for handling minutes and referrals.
Airport Campus Water District 8 extension, WIIA/EFC sewer grant, pool well rehab, and future Water District 4 coordination dominated the substantive agenda.
Gateway/45 Bedford Road deed-restriction, right-of-way and easement questions drew significant resident opposition and board caution.
Numerous 2024 professional-service and consulting agreements, plus the library ramp bid and truss change-order debate.
Statutory annual appointments, contested liaison slate, new confidential secretary, and several resignations.
Library truss repair, accessible ramp, water storage tanks and pool rehabilitation.
Enthusiastic promotion of Detective Sabatella to Sergeant plus fire/ambulance service agreements.
Concern over depleting the library fund balance and Association of Towns billing tier; annual financial policies adopted.
Conservation board tree focus, food-scrap composting rollout, and stormwater/floodplain design at the Gateway site.
Staying Alive 5K Fun Run scheduling and the Armonk Eagle restoration committee.

staffInput.summary: Delivered community announcements (school tax deadline, PEG-grant library 'vibe boards', Nixle/E-News signups), handled receipt of letters and publication of legal notices/hearing orders, and coordinated the deferral of minutes not distributed via Dropbox.

Gave the administrator update (parks groundskeeper opening, new Route 120 traffic signal), reported on library truss change orders and no-bid outreach to eight firms, explained the library fund balance shortfall requiring town fund-balance support for the ramp, and clarified the pool well defect.

Advised the board could interpret or hold a public hearing to amend the Gateway deed restriction's 'structures' language, drafted the order calling the water-district public hearing, and stressed a negotiated water-contribution agreement must precede approval of the district extension.

Water & Sewer Operations Director; explained the coordination benefits of the Airport Campus water main for a future combined storage tank and Water District 4 extension, and briefed the WIIA/EFC Sewer District 2 grant and reimbursement process.

Town Planner; supported the Gateway right-of-way basin/easement as a more aesthetically pleasing solution with applicant/HOA maintenance, and clarified the distinct roles of the Planning Board and Architectural Review Board.
Recreation & Parks Superintendent; described the pool water-well defect requiring a new disinfection system and Health Department approval to open the pool for the season.

meetings.attributionNote: The ASR transcript has no speaker labels and the presiding Supervisor voice (Joseph Rende) dominates. Roll-call votes and members addressed by name (Milim/'Matt', DiGiacinto/'Barbara', Hussain/'Saleem', Berra/'Jose') enabled confident attribution on the liaison dispute, library ramp, truss debate and water-district questions. ASR manglings normalized: Barron/Bera/Bearer/Barra/Barrack -> Jose Berra; Milam/Millam -> Matt Milim; Digacinto/Decento/De Jacinto -> Barbara DiGiacinto; Hussein -> Saleem Hussain; Rendez/Rende/'Friendly' -> Joseph Rende. The Airport Campus roll call only recorded three member ayes plus the Supervisor, so votes were not attributed to Milim or Berra on that item. No members were noted absent; Berra recused on the Long Pond Park District agreement. Sonny Vataj is correctly excluded (2026 only).

meetings.meetingSummary: In this early meeting of the new board term, a work session significantly upsized the Lombardi Park water project: rather than a narrow $461,000 emergency service line, the Board embraced Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal and engineer Joe Chamelty's recommendation to run a full 8-inch public water main up School Street, funded substantially by roughly $1.2 million in the town's remaining ARPA funds, adding fire hydrants and laying groundwork for future extensions to Cox Avenue, Anthony Court, and Byron Ridge Road. The Board also closed two public hearings — approving St. Nersis Armenian Seminary's special use permit for a guest-speaker addition and a new dean's residence (486 Bedford Road), and adopting a local law reducing the Landmarks Preservation Committee's required meetings from six to four per year — heard a first look at a Catalyze Energy battery energy storage system (BESS) proposal for New King Street with a peer-reviewed safety report from ESRG, directing the Town Planner to draft BESS-specific special-permit/local-law regulations before any site-specific approval proceeds, and approved a slate of engineering proposals for a comprehensive overhaul of the town pool and tennis club's plumbing, deck, and domestic water system.
meetings.durationNote: New Supervisor presiding (per town records, Joseph Rende, who took office in January 2024); Councilmembers DiGiacinto, Milim, Berra, and Hussain participated. A newly seated board member abstained from approving December 13, 2023 minutes, noting they were not yet on the Board at that meeting.

cases.name: Lombardi Park — Public Water Supply Extension vs. Well Rehabilitation
cases.status: in progress; engineering proposal to advance at next meeting
cases.summary: The Board held a work session and coalesced around a substantially upgraded plan: instead of a narrow, single-purpose water service line into the park, run a full 8-inch public water main up School Street to the park, roughly 1,000 feet shorter than the originally proposed route through school-easement land, extending Water District #4's boundary along the way. The upgrade is expected to be substantially funded by the town's approximately $1.2 million in remaining, use-it-or-lose-it ARPA (federal COVID relief) funds, and would add three new fire hydrants and design provisions (valves/tees) for future, resident-initiated extensions to neighboring streets (Cox Avenue, Anthony Court, Byron Ridge Road) at no cost to the town unless residents opt to connect. The Board directed staff to bring back a formal engineering proposal and district-extension paperwork (map/plan/report, EAF, notice to affected property owners, and a subsequent public hearing) for approval at the next meeting, with construction not expected to be delayed by the parallel legal process.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted as a resident/former Supervisor still engaged with the project (attending as an engineer) that the upgraded plan 'couldn't be any easier decision,' though the meeting's presiding officer and most active questioners were the new board.

cases.name: St. Nersis Armenian Seminary — Special Use Permit for Building Modifications, 486 Bedford Road
cases.summary: The Board closed the public hearing and approved St. Nersis Armenian Seminary's special use permit for a two-room addition (guest accommodations, no kitchen) to its married-students building and a new two-bedroom single-family residence for a future dean, both roughly 280 feet from the nearest Tripp Lane residence and requiring a side-yard setback variance (30 feet actual vs. 50 feet required) to be sought separately from the ZBA. The applicant committed to shielded, dimming parking-lot lighting and screening at the front of the property in response to a neighbor's written concern, and the Planning Board had already recommended approval.
cases.publicComment: A neighbor on Bedford Road submitted a written comment about tree screening and lighting brightness, which the applicant addressed by committing to shielding and dimming.

cases.name: Landmarks Preservation Committee — Reduced Required Meeting Frequency (Chapter 195)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle Landmarks Preservation Committee
cases.summary: At the LPC's request, the Board adopted a local law reducing the committee's required meeting frequency from six to four times per year (matching the state minimum), while the LPC noted it would still meet more often as needed. A related idea to expand LPC membership beyond its current 8-of-9 seats was raised but not finalized in time for this hearing and will require a separate local law and new public hearing.

cases.name: Catalyze Energy Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) — New King Street
cases.status: under review; local law/special permit framework to be drafted
cases.summary: ESRG presented its board-commissioned peer review of Catalyze Energy's proposed grid-connected battery energy storage system on New King Street (in the town's only IND-AA district), finding the initial application lacked sufficient detail against New York State fire code requirements for BESS, and offering additional recommendations given how new the technology is. The Town Planner recommended the Board decide whether to permit BESS use in that district at all and, if so, adopt a special-permit local law based on the NYSERDA model ordinance incorporating ESRG's recommendations, with fire department and NYC DEP input given the site's proximity (about 900 feet) to the Jessica (Kensico) Reservoir system; the applicant confirmed the site would be effectively exclusive on that electrical line due to grid capacity limits.

cases.name: North Castle Pool and Tennis Club — Comprehensive Infrastructure Engineering Proposals
cases.address: North Castle Pool and Tennis Club
cases.summary: The Board approved a package of engineering proposals for a comprehensive evaluation of the pool and tennis club's plumbing, deck, and domestic water treatment (required by the Health Department, separate from an already-approved item), reasoning that fixing only isolated leaks or the deck without addressing underlying infrastructure risks having to reopen or demolish the deck again later; the study will also assess whether some existing deck areas are worth retaining as the facility is reimagined, with board members acknowledging the town may need to accept losing a future season to do the work properly.

themes.note: Major upsizing of the Lombardi Park water project using ARPA funds.

staffInput.summary: Presented the upgraded Lombardi Park water-main plan, cost comparisons, and district-extension implications.
Detailed the School Street public-main routing, ARPA-fund eligibility considerations, and next design/survey steps.
Explained the legal/procedural steps (district extension order, EAF, public hearing, permissive referendum) for the Lombardi Park project and the LPC local law.
Framed the BESS policy decision for the Board and outlined next steps for a special-permit local law incorporating ESRG's recommendations.
Presented findings on the Catalyze Energy BESS application's gaps against NY fire code and general BESS siting considerations.
Presented the seminary's building modification plans and responded to neighbor and board concerns.
Coordinated the pool/tennis club engineering scoping meetings referenced in that agenda item.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR; this is the first meeting of a newly seated board and the presiding Supervisor is not named in the transcript text itself (resolved from town records to Joseph Rende, who took office in January 2024). Several individual board members' contributions to the Lombardi Park and BESS discussions could not be reliably distinguished from each other and were largely omitted from memberPositions rather than guessed.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened with a work session on bringing public water to Lombardi Park, and consensus formed around a larger public-main extension up School Street that adds fire hydrants and future connection capability, likely funded with ARPA money. Two public hearings were held and closed: a special use permit for St. Ursula's Armenian Seminary (adopted with a negative declaration and resolution) and a local law reducing the Landmarks Preservation Committee to four required meetings a year (adopted). The board received ESRG peer-review reports on a proposed Catalyze battery energy storage system at 10 New King Street and, citing fire risk to volunteer departments and the nearby Kensico Reservoir, effectively declined to advance it. Other business included approving an RFP for Water District 1 rehabilitation, scheduling a senior/disability tax-exemption public hearing, referring a gas leaf-blower ban to the Sustainability Committee, approving pool engineering studies, library truss change orders, a championship-sign panel, and several personnel appointments.
meetings.durationNote: Reconvened from executive session (opened 5:30 pm, ran long); adjourned back into executive session and did not return to public session. All five board members present (Rende, Berra, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim). Town Administrator Kevin Hay absent; his assistant sat in.

cases.name: Work Session — Public Water Main Extension to Lombardi Park
cases.address: Lombardi Park / School Street / Wampus Avenue, Armonk
cases.applicant: Water & Sewer Department (Sal) with Keller engineering (Joe Ciamelli)
cases.summary: The board weighed alternatives for supplying potable water to Lombardi Park after its private well failed to meet Health Department standards. Rather than an emergency ~$461,000 dedicated service line (or ~$375,000 in well treatment), the board favored installing a larger public water main up School Street, which shaves ~1,000 feet, adds three fire hydrants, and enables future district extension. Consensus was to fund it with ARPA money (must be designated in 2024) and place engineer approval on the next meeting agenda; a district extension and public hearing up School Street would follow. No vote taken — work session only.
cases.publicComment: No residents spoke; item was a work session, not a hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Framed the back-and-forth as a worthwhile exercise; benefits (fire hydrants, future connections, added district revenue) outweigh the additional cost.
Pressed on rock/excavation cushions and grants; called the larger-main approach effectively a 'no-brainer' and a down payment on future District 2/4 interconnection.
Explored which streets could later connect and whether the infrastructure approach qualifies for ARPA funds, favoring it over the dedicated 3-inch line.
Backed the plan but cautioned that neighbors should not be led to think they are getting town water immediately, only future provisions.
'This is great. It seems like a very easy decision... looking forward to the public hearing.'

cases.name: Special Use Permit — St. Ursula's Armenian Seminary Building Modifications
cases.applicant: St. Ursula's Armenian Seminary (architect Robert Stanzial; Dean Father Maderos)
cases.summary: Public hearing on a special use permit to modify the 5.5-acre R-2A seminary campus with a two-room/two-story guest addition to the married-students building and a new two-bedroom single-family dean's residence. Coverage remains well under limits (7% building, 15.5% land); a 30-foot side-yard setback requires a variance, and Planning Board, ARB and neighbor screening/lighting concerns were noted for follow-up. Residents (Historical Society) spoke in strong support, praising the seminary as gracious neighbors. The board closed the hearing and adopted the negative declaration and the resolution by voice vote (5-0).
cases.publicComment: Ed Woodyard and Charlene Decker (Historical Society) spoke warmly in support, citing the seminary's cooperation on artifacts and community events.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked detailed setback/variance and neighbor-notification questions and was pleased the dean would remain in the community.
'You guys are great neighbors'; noted the well-kept property and confirmed shielded, timed site lighting.
Praised the property's pristine, cared-for appearance and pride of ownership.

cases.name: Local Law — Amend Ch. 195 Landmarks Preservation, §195-4 (LPC Meeting Frequency)
cases.summary: Public hearing on a local law amending the code to require four LPC meetings per year (matching the state minimum) instead of six, while allowing additional meetings as needed. A parallel idea discussed in executive session — increasing LPC membership beyond the current 8 of 9 seats to absorb two interested applicants — was not included in the noticed law, so Roland advised adopting this amendment now and running a separate local law on membership later. The board closed the hearing and adopted the amended local law by voice vote (no roll call).
cases.publicComment: Linda Fernberg presented on behalf of the LPC; described it as a reasonable, low-burden change.

memberPositions.evidence: 'Seems like a reasonable request. I don't think it's really a big discussion.'
Raised the expected-but-missing membership increase, noting advisory bodies need not have odd numbers; agreed to handle it in a separate law.
Confirmed public-comment access at LPC meetings and supported adopting now, deferring the membership question.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes (Dec 13, 2023 and Jan 10, 2024)
cases.summary: Old business: approval of the December 13, 2023 and January 10, 2024 minutes. The December minutes were amended per Berra to clarify that the side-letter agreement with Sanipro concerns food-composting credits computed against garbage-disposal rates. December minutes adopted by roll call 4-0 (Rende abstained, having not been a board member at that meeting); January 10 minutes adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Circulated and explained the corrected side-letter wording tying food-composting credit to garbage-disposal savings.
Abstained on the December 13 minutes because he was not a board member when they were created.

cases.name: Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) — Catalyze Energy, 10 New King Street (ESRG Peer Review)
cases.applicant: Catalyze Energy (Bob Stickney); ESRG peer review (Michael Bowes)
cases.summary: The board received ESRG's code-compliance peer review and additional-considerations memo on Catalyze Energy's proposed battery energy storage system at 10 New King Street (the town's only IND-AA district, ~900 ft from Kensico Reservoir). Members voiced strong opposition, citing extensive fire-training burdens on volunteer departments, potential month-long thermal-runaway fires and noxious fumes, reservoir/pollution risk, and little local benefit for a for-profit developer. North White Plains and Armonk fire departments were reported as not supporting it. The board voted only to receive the report; Roland noted the applicant understands it will not be placed on another agenda, though members invited any 'particularly compelling' new mitigation information.
cases.publicComment: Applicant Bob Stickney (Catalyze) and consultant Michael Bowes (ESRG) presented; no residents spoke in support.

memberPositions.evidence: 'I struggle with this so immensely... I don't see a path possible where I would get my mind around this'; called it a for-profit venture where the town 'wearing all the risk' with no micro benefit.
Cited volunteer-firefighter training, month-long fires, San Diego/Warwick incidents, evacuations and Kensico Reservoir risk; went on record not to move forward at this time.
Stressed limited volunteer-fire resources and the unique drinking-water risk; benefits must far outweigh the risks, and he did not feel comfortable with the information so far.

Praised the clean-energy concept but said 'the report scared me more than gave me comfort,' flagged noxious fumes, weekly training burden and likely low tax revenue; open only to something 'particularly compelling.'

Would not support now, but noted the board only saw the risks and asked Catalyze to bring back the quantified benefits and mitigation response; sees a spreading infrastructure the town must reckon with.

cases.name: RFP — Engineering Services for Water District 1 Distribution System Rehabilitation
cases.summary: The board authorized Sal to issue an RFP for engineering services (design through construction management) to rehabilitate the nearly 100-year-old Water District 1 distribution system in North White Plains, similar to the earlier Water District 2 project. The scope emphasizes chasing grant money and heavy public-relations/coordination given construction disruption. Motion by DiGiacinto, seconded by Rende; adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Long-time champion of the project; cited fire safety, brown-water complaints and recurring winter main breaks; made the motion.
'It is absolutely key... sooner the better... grant money is out there.'
Seconded the motion and supported moving the RFP ahead.

cases.name: Local Law — Amend Ch. 288 Taxation (Senior Citizens & Disability Tax Exemptions)
cases.summary: The board received the Assessor's memo recommending a local law to update the senior-citizen and disability tax-exemption income formula: raising the qualifying threshold (roughly from the mid-$30,000s to ~$58,000, about a 40% increase) and electing not to deduct IRA distributions from income. The change is expected to roughly double eligible residents (from ~30-35 to ~60). Members favored the Assessor's recommendation; Berra also asked her to report the cost borne by other taxpayers. Item received and a public hearing set for the February 14 meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Explained the threshold jump, recommended not deducting IRA distributions ('it's real money people are receiving'), and asked the Assessor to quantify the cost to other residents.
'I'm also in favor of following Georgeanne's recommendation.'
'I am too'; moved to receive and set the public hearing.

cases.name: Resident Request — Legislation to Ban Gas-Powered Leaf Blowers / Outdoor Equipment
cases.applicant: Resident Chris Hughes; Sustainability Committee (John Edmondson)
cases.summary: The board received a resident letter urging a ban on gas-powered leaf blowers, and the Sustainability Committee (John Edmondson) reported researching a broader ban on gas outdoor equipment, noting many county municipalities and a California statewide model. The board discussed pollution data, two-stroke engines, enforcement (some laws bar charging via generators), cost impacts on residents and landscapers, and the need for a transition period. Consensus was to have the Sustainability Committee continue researching and monitoring pending state legislation and bring a formal presentation later.
cases.publicComment: John Edmondson (Sustainability Committee) spoke, framing the effort positively; will return with a formal presentation.

memberPositions.evidence: Favored limiting 'with a thumb on the scale,' cited a blower's pollution vs. driving hundreds of miles, and urged a fair transition period.
Focused on two-stroke engines being 'a disaster' and distinguishing them from four-stroke generators.
Supportive of exploring model legislation but wary of industry and resident 'government overreach' pushback and enforcement gaps like generator charging.
Urged weighing how to encourage change without laws and carefully mitigating unintended consequences and cost impacts on residents.
Flagged the 'government overreach' objection and the higher equipment costs that landscapers would pass on to residents.

cases.name: 2024 NYS Association of Towns Membership, Dues, and Voting Delegate
cases.summary: The board approved 2024 membership in the NYS Association of Towns, authorized the Comptroller to pay the (budgeted) annual dues, and designated Supervisor Rende as the town's voting delegate for the February annual meeting. DiGiacinto noted the association's dues invoice recurringly overcharges the town ($1,950 vs. the correct $1,650). Rende agreed to report back on how he votes. Adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Volunteered to attend and be the voting delegate and to report his votes; a firm believer in the value of seminars.
Might attend but found past meetings 'a big investment of time' with only 'some bits and kernels' of value.
Cannot attend this year; flagged the recurring dues overcharge that the Comptroller corrects each time.

cases.name: Shared Cost with Byram Hills School District — Additional Championship Sign Panel
cases.applicant: Town / Byram Hills Central School District (Signs Inc.)
cases.summary: The board approved splitting with the Byram Hills school district the $2,075 cost (~$1,037 each) of an additional panel for the sign recognizing Byram Hills state-championship teams, designed by Signs Inc. to match the original. DiGiacinto, tasked with the sign, pressed to proceed now; Berra supported the concept but wanted design, panel count, and cost details reviewed offline and criticized designing without circulating to colleagues. Hussain sought consistency in the rendering's curvature and spacing. Adopted by voice vote; the board opted to let Signs Inc. handle installation.

memberPositions.evidence: Championed proceeding immediately as the person tasked with the sign; made the motion, citing the need to be ready when teams win.
Supported the sign but wanted to review design/size/panel count and installation cost offline, urging colleagues to circulate designs before finalizing.
Comfortable moving forward after confirming Signs Inc. would fix rendering inconsistencies in curvature and block spacing.
Fine to proceed, reasoning that acting in an open public session substitutes for ARB review since objectors could appear.
Comfortable either way; favored staying with Signs Inc. and letting them install so they bear responsibility.

cases.name: North Castle Pool and Tennis Club — Conceptual Improvement Engineering Proposals
cases.address: North Castle Pool and Tennis Club
cases.applicant: Town (via Town Administrator Kevin Hay; Rec Superintendent Matt Traynor)
cases.summary: The board approved, as a group, engineering proposals for comprehensive conceptual improvements to the town pool facility (pool, deck, plumbing, building, tennis/basketball), separate from the already-approved domestic-water treatment needed to open this season. The goal is a full facility evaluation to avoid piecemeal work — potentially reducing unused deck area, using pervious pavers, and upgrading the building — accepting that a future season might be lost to do it properly. Members stressed opening on time this year. Adopted by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Advocated a comprehensive engineering view to build 'a gem of a town pool' once, rather than piecemeal spending.
Backed the big-picture infrastructure work but sought assurance it would not delay opening this season; floated dropping a tennis court for a playing field.

cases.name: Graham Restoration Change Orders 3 & 4 — Armonk Library Trusses
cases.address: North Castle Public Library, Armonk branch
cases.summary: The board approved change orders 3 and 4 with Graham Restoration for the structural truss repair at the Armonk library, negotiated with a $1,500 reduction. Scaffolding and coverings had kept part of the library closed, and members were eager to reopen. Rende and Berra criticized the items as things that should never have been change orders and called for tighter procurement and staff diligence, with Hussain suggesting a retrospective. Hussain made the motion; adopted by voice vote with the $1,500 reduction.

memberPositions.evidence: Approved but frustrated: covering new beams should have been obvious, 'never should have been a change order'; urged staff to be more diligent.
Backed approval but said change orders are 'the bread and butter of some contractors' and pushed for a focus on procurement.
Made the motion and suggested a retrospective to capture lessons for future projects.

cases.name: Personnel — Appointments (Board of Ethics, Librarian, GFOA Conference)
cases.summary: The board approved three personnel items by voice vote: appointing Arthur Ellis as an alternate to the Board of Ethics (5-year term to Jan 11, 2028); appointing Linda Cervich as Librarian 1 (hourly, effective Jan 29, 2024); and authorizing Finance Director Abbas to attend the 2024 NYS Government Finance Officers Association conference (April 17-19). Routine and uncontested.

cases.name: Liaison Reports and Community Updates
cases.summary: Board liaisons reported: DiGiacinto noted an overwhelming (27+) applicant response to a single middle-income housing unit, underscoring affordable-housing demand; Milim described Park & Rec momentum on turf fields, sidewalks/walking paths, and a proposed dog park at IBM Community Park; Berra reported progress on food-scrap composting bins; Hussain gave library programming and Armonk-branch construction updates. Rende reported on a planned sidewalks work session, Congressman Lawler's housing roundtable and support for home rule, and the eagle-monument restoration effort with local contractors. A student (Jack Zipper) presented a Historical Society 'Moment in North Castle History,' and the meeting closed with condolences for deceased residents.
cases.publicComment: Jack Zipper (student, Historical Society) presented a local-history segment; Ed Woodyard and Charlene Decker added historical context. Warm reception.

memberPositions.evidence: Reported an unprecedented response to the middle-income housing lottery and wished the town had more than one unit for so many deserving applicants.
Described excitement around turf fields, sidewalk extensions, and a dog park proposed at IBM Community Park (not Wampus).
Reported food-scrap recycling bins are finally arriving, crediting Neil Singer's effort.
Reported on Rep. Lawler's housing roundtable and home rule, a planned sidewalks work session, and the eagle-monument restoration with local contractors.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened with a work session on plans for the town's 2026 celebration of the 250th anniversary of American independence, hearing an enthusiastic Historical Society presentation and a request for a celebration committee and a $40,000 appropriation. It then appointed a new probationary police officer, received liaison and community updates (library smart boards, a new food-scrap composting program, parks/turf-field progress), and took extended public comment on a new credit-card surcharge law and on downtown parking policy. A developer's request to reduce affordable-housing units at the former lumberyard was heard but drew no board support to advance.

Meeting opened 5:30 PM with an executive session, then a work session that ran long; proceedings continued past 9-10 PM. No absences. (Vataj not yet on board in 2024; Berra held the seat.)

cases.name: 250th Anniversary of American Independence — Celebration Planning (Work Session)
cases.applicant: North Castle Historical Society (Ed Woodyard, Tom Rice, Connie Kehoe)
cases.summary: The Historical Society presented on North Castle's pivotal role in the 1776 Battle of White Plains and asked the board to authorize a broad-based celebration committee and appropriate roughly $40,000 (primarily for a promotional video and repair/replacement of five historic markers plus a new Mount Misery marker) ahead of a July 4, 2026 celebration. No formal vote was taken; the board was uniformly supportive and Supervisor Rende offered to convene an organizing committee meeting at his office. Members raised ideas about broadening awareness beyond town (county/state/national), engaging schools in video production, and eventually commemorating the 21 local Revolutionary patriots. Funding mechanism and a total cost estimate remain to be worked out.
cases.publicComment: Historical Society trustees and county Rev250 chair Connie Kehoe presented; former judge/HS president Sue Scheimer gave an emotional endorsement recalling the 1976 bicentennial. Tone: enthusiastic and unanimous in urging the town to act.

memberPositions.evidence: Cited his father chairing the 1975 Rye bicentennial; 'if there was ever a time we need reason to celebrate... it's now,' and offered to host and help populate the committee immediately.
'I strongly support this... a crucial time to bring our community together,' but asked to see a total cost figure when possible; said she has ideas she'll email.
Very engaged: urged broadening awareness to county/state/country, proposed a school video competition ('not one video but 500'), and emphasized lifting up historical values behind names.
'Thank you all for stepping up... I'm really excited about it and fully supported this,' and suggested making the student video effort a competition.
'It's absolutely fascinating... I strongly support this,' but as the board's numbers-focused member asked for the total cost at some point; suggested Jack Zipper produce a video.

cases.name: Probationary Appointment of Matthew Barsanti to Police Officer
cases.summary: The Police Chief presented Matthew Barsanti, a six-year transfer from the NYC Department of Environmental Protection police, recommending his appointment to a budgeted police-officer position effective February 17, 2024 after a thorough background investigation and panel interviews. The board moved the item up on the agenda so family could attend. The motion was made and approved by voice vote (all in favor), and Supervisor Rende administered the oath of office.
cases.publicComment: Barsanti's family attended; celebratory tone with photos and congratulations.

memberPositions.evidence: 'I'd like to make the motion' to appoint the officer.
'I'll second it,' and warmly congratulated the new officer.
Called it 'one that we find a lot of pleasure in,' welcomed the family, and administered the oath.

cases.name: Community Announcements & Town Board Liaison Updates
cases.applicant: Town Clerk / Town Administrator / Board liaisons
cases.summary: The Clerk and Administrator reported on new library 'vibe'/70-inch smart boards enabling hybrid meetings, new agenda software (with access-help offered), a one-day garbage-pickup delay from weather, and the President's Day closure. Saleem Hussain highlighted Black History Month library programming and the smart-board rollout. Matt Milim reported on park & rec board interest in additional sidewalks, progress at Clover Road Fields with Kensico Little League, and a call finalizing the turf-field layout at Community Park (Kellard preparing bid documents and engaging the DEC on wetland buffers). Berra promoted a police 'safe trade' program and introduced the new composting effort.

memberPositions.evidence: Promoted the new library smart boards for hybrid community meetings and detailed Black History Month and other library programming.
Reported strong park & rec interest in sidewalks, productive Clover Road Fields and turf-field project meetings; noted no ground-breaking likely this spring given DEC review.
Committed to a work session with park & rec and Kellard on sidewalk needs in Armonk Hamlet and North White Plains; clarified the Clover Road contractor arrangement with counsel.

cases.name: Food-Scrap Composting Program Launch (Sustainability Committee)
cases.summary: Councilman Berra, backed by resident committee member Stefan, presented the town's brand-new food-scrap composting program: a $25 kit (counter, mid-size, and drop bins with compostable bags, sold through the Clerk's office) with drop-off at Lombardi Park. They explained accepted materials, methane/landfill and cost-savings benefits, and stressed doing it correctly to avoid contamination. This was an informational rollout, not a vote; enthusiasm was high and Supervisor Rende noted he'd bought a kit.
cases.publicComment: Sustainability committee member Stefan demonstrated the bins and promoted the program; upbeat, promotional tone.

memberPositions.evidence: Championed the program: 'astounding what they've done,' explained the kits and the '80% is better than 100%' contamination guidance, and thanked staff who helped store the bins.
'I bought my container... I got it on Saturday,' joking about the committee's fundraising enthusiasm.

cases.name: Public Hearing — Extension of Water District 8, Airport Campus / Former MBIA HQ, 113 King Street
cases.applicant: Airport Campus (Jeff Ringler) / Toll Brothers, represented by Chris Fisher, Cuddy & Feder
cases.summary: A public hearing under Town Law was opened on a petition to extend Water District 8 to bring municipal water to the former MBIA campus (redevelopment), replacing on-site wells via a 12-inch main from New King Street over I-684 to the site, an oversized 297,000-gallon tank and pump station sized to also serve a future District 4. The applicant, building privately at 30-40% below public-bid cost, said it is not seeking action yet pending a D&B basis-of-design report (expected end of month) and a water-contribution/capital agreement. The board received the revised map, plan and report, then adjourned the hearing without a specific date, anticipating a follow-up work session.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke beyond the applicant's team.

memberPositions.evidence: Sought clarity on what was actually being asked at the hearing given the work is still being refined; moved to receive the revised map/plan and to adjourn.
Confirmed with counsel that the hearing would simply be adjourned pending the basis-of-design report due end of month.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Chapter 288 — Senior Citizen and Disability Tax Exemptions
cases.summary: A public hearing was held on the Assessor-requested amendment addressing optional state criteria for senior-citizen and persons-with-disabilities exemptions, specifically whether IRA required-minimum-distributions may be excluded from income; the Assessor recommended including them (i.e., not allowing the exclusion) to prevent abuse. No public spoke and the board was supportive. Berra flagged a drafting issue in paragraph D referencing 'federal or state income tax return.' The board closed the hearing and adopted the local law, subject to the Assessor reviewing whether to delete the 'or state income tax return' language.
cases.publicComment: No public comment.

memberPositions.evidence: 'You just take the AGI as it is without a deduction of the IRA distribution... I agree with her recommendation.'
'I totally support it... it's fair and a way to avoid abuse of this law,' crediting Assessor Gigi Richardson.
Supported the law but flagged the 'federal or state income tax return' wording and moved to adopt subject to the Assessor's review of paragraph D.

cases.name: Water District 4 — Lombardi Park Water Main Extension (School Street Route)
cases.summary: After a failed well at Lombardi Park, the board pursued a public water main up School Street (~1,000 ft) rather than a costly ~2,000 ft private service line through school property, praised as a superior, future-proof solution by counsel and Sal. The board received the engineer's cost estimate and Kellard proposal (the proposal had been missing from packets but was uploaded during the meeting; total ~$70,625), approved the Kellard proposal and the Spinelli survey proposal, and adopted the final order placing Lombardi Park into District 4 by unanimous 5-0 roll call. A separate District 4 extension proceeding for the School Street homes will follow with resident notification/work session.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed on whether including Lombardi Park in the district posed any downside if construction proved infeasible (satisfied it did not), scrutinized the Kellard cost figures, and praised Sal's 'great solution.'
Moved to approve the Kellard proposal and complimented Sal: 'nice work on this, good creative solution.'
Voted aye on the roll call and helped locate the proposal and cost figures.
Voted aye on the final-order roll call.
Voted aye and expressed comfort with the familiar cost numbers from prior work sessions.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Chapter 114 — Application Processing Restrictions (Tax Delinquency)
cases.summary: The board received a proposed amendment extending the existing 'application processing restrictions' law to bar property owners with delinquent taxes from processing development applications until cured, retaining a board waiver provision for appropriate cases. It was prompted by concern over specific delinquent development properties. Rende raised whether small residential/estate sales could be caught; counsel advised the waiver process (a simple letter, twice-monthly meetings) handles that and declined to build in a dollar-threshold exemption. The board received the law and scheduled a public hearing for February 28, 2024. Berra flagged several drafting inconsistencies to send to counsel by email.

memberPositions.evidence: Backed the law ('taxes have to be paid') but sought protection for residential/estate closings and safety-related emergency permits via the waiver's discretion.

Supported the expansion and moved to receive and to schedule the hearing, while flagging naming/wording inconsistencies (e.g., 'restrictive' vs 'restrictions,' the tax-delinquency vs building-inspector proof).
Noted the town by law ends up covering school/county taxes on liened properties, supporting stronger delinquency tools; seconded the motions.

cases.name: Request to Reduce Affordable (AFFH) Units at Former Lumberyard, 156 & 162 Bedford Road
cases.summary: Developer Mike Ferrari asked (bifurcating off a separate future request to relocate units to 470 Main Street) that the board amend the zoning code so his 20-unit condo project could immediately reduce its affordable requirement from four units (20%) to two (10%), rather than waiting for the code's existing incentive that automatically drops it to two upon obtaining COs/75% completion by June 30, 2025.
