His stated need was to finalize a condo offering plan now (his attorney said the unit-count uncertainty prevents filing). The board debated whether the uncertainty truly blocks marketing; Berra opposed advancing it (fearing it as leverage for the later relocation request), Hussain said he would hold at 20%, and Milim viewed it as only a marketing-convenience with no real delay. Ferrari, frustrated, withdrew the request after concluding the votes were not there; no action taken.
cases.publicComment: Developer Mike Ferrari presented at length and grew visibly frustrated ('this really pisses me off'), citing his 20% affordable requirement, financial hardship, and lack of county aid; an exchange with Berra turned tense before Rende called for civility.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued the matter was already resolved and worried granting the 4-to-2 reduction now would become leverage for a later off-site relocation; 'I just don't think we should go into another public hearing and waste more of the public's time.'
'If we need to put something in concrete form, I would vote for putting it at 20%.'

Said Ferrari will get the two units anyway; framed the request as purely a marketing advantage (lower common charges in the offering memo) and 'not something we should be required to do' absent a real sales delay.
Disagreed with Berra: given the project's clear progress, holding the line at four units is 'almost punitive'; she was confident he would meet the stipulation and be reduced to two.
Acted as facilitator, explained the automatic reduction mechanism, offered to have the Planner outline an amendment process, and called for civility; did not advocate a position.

cases.name: Authorization for 2024 In-Rem Tax Foreclosures
cases.summary: The board authorized the Town Attorney to commence 2024 in-rem foreclosure proceedings against roughly 30 tax-delinquent property owners who had received demand letters, with title searches to follow once the list narrows. Counsel noted one owner already made a several-hundred-thousand-dollar payment and intends full payment by March. Rende voiced concern that owners can pay 'just enough' to stay out of in-rem indefinitely, reinforcing the value of the Chapter 114 tax law. Counsel also noted a coming law change directing surplus foreclosure proceeds to the county for redistribution rather than the town. Approved by vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Framed in-rem as the town's remedy for large delinquencies and worried about owners stringing along partial payments to avoid foreclosure.
Moved to authorize and clarified the process across prior delinquent years; agreed the surplus-proceeds change was fairer to homeowners.
Seconded the authorization.

cases.name: NYSDOT Highway Work Permit — Gas Station/Convenience Market, 375 Main Street (Route 128)
cases.applicant: Shell station developer (via Town for NYSDOT permit)
cases.summary: The board approved a NYSDOT commercial access highway work permit application and checklist for frontage improvements (decorative light pole, curbing, sidewalk) at the long-delayed Shell station/convenience market at the Route 128/Kent Place corner, authorizing the Supervisor to sign. The applicant pays for the work; the town will maintain the decorative improvements as it does elsewhere. Berra flagged an indemnity provision but counsel advised the work is fully insured/bonded with minimal town exposure and that DOT permit terms cannot be changed. Approved by vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised the indemnity provision (town as deeper-pocket applicant) but accepted counsel's 'no real exposure' assessment and moved to approve.
Clarified the town applies to NYSDOT for the permit, the applicant funds the work, and the town maintains the decorative improvements going forward.

cases.name: RFP for Operation of Community Park Athletic Facilities (Tennis/Turf Bubble), 205 Business Park Drive
cases.summary: The board reviewed authorizing an RFP for a 10-year (plus 10-year option) license to operate the Community Park tennis/turf 'bubble' facilities (existing contract expires August 2024; proposed $250,000 minimum annual fee). Barbara DiGiacinto probed maintenance/parking/turf/tennis obligations (satisfied they fall on the operator) and joined Berra in pressing for an inflation hedge — 3% annual escalation 'or CPI, whichever is greater.' Hussain, Milim, and Rende preferred a clean flat 3% to attract bidders given the operator's large capital investment. Berra caught a 'three lowest bidders' typo (should be highest). DiGiacinto moved to amend to 3%-or-CPI-whichever-greater and otherwise approve; Hussain said 'nay' and declined to second, leaving the motion unresolved at the point the transcript ends.

memberPositions.evidence: 'I can't vote for this if it's just 3% in good conscience'; argued a percentage-or-CPI escalation is standard on long leases and a fiduciary duty; moved to amend accordingly.

Warned that over 20 years a flat 3% could 'leave a lot of money on the table' (citing COVID-era inflation) and said he 'wouldn't vote for it without an inflation adjustment'; also caught the 'three lowest bidders' typo.
Preferred a 'cleaner' flat 3% given the operator's high-hundreds-of-thousands capital outlay and the Fed's inflation mandate, but conceded he'd accept 3%+CPI rather than force a no vote.
Leaned to flat 3% to attract bidders and worried about too few bids; said 'nay' to DiGiacinto's amendment motion and declined to second it.
Favored a flat 3% as 'ample protection' that keeps bids attractive and the valued community facility viable, but deferred to further discussion.

cases.name: Public Comment — New Credit-Card Surcharge Law Enforcement
cases.summary: Resident Ed Loberman detailed New York's new credit-card surcharge law (Gen. Business Law Art. 29-A §518, effective Feb 11, 2024), which allows municipalities/town attorneys to enforce penalties, and urged the town to take up enforcement locally rather than defer to the county. Rende responded that the enforcement 'onus' concerned him given the town's limited staff and suggested complaints route to the county Department of Consumer Affairs, while noting the law limits vendors to passing through their actual processing fees. Loberman pushed back that local enforcement is the law's intent. No action taken; matter to be reviewed with counsel.
cases.publicComment: Ed Loberman (44-year retail business owner) urged the board to enforce the surcharge law locally to protect consumers; earnest and persistent. A separate 88-year resident gave a tangential speech on teaching the state/federal constitution.

memberPositions.evidence: Acknowledged the issue is 'on our radar' but was wary of the enforcement burden on a small town and inclined to direct complaints to county Consumer Affairs; wants to consult counsel further.

cases.name: Public Comment — Downtown Parking Pay-in-Lieu Fee and Parking District
cases.summary: Resident/developer Stefan urged the board to revive the 2018 comprehensive-plan recommendation (and Town Planner Adam Kaufman's proposed Chapter 355 amendment) allowing a $12,000-per-space 'pay-in-lieu' parking fee to fund municipal parking and incentivize shared parking districts, offering to be a 'seed investor.' He argued the town created the pay-in-lieu concept but never provided the parking facilities, and pushed for a work session. DiGiacinto agreed a work session is warranted and that the ~40-50-year-old parking legislation should be revisited. Rende and counsel (Roland) recounted the town's difficulty forming districts (contiguity, owner refusals) and endorsed signage/wayfinding to better use existing lots (e.g., Hergenhan, forthcoming Verizon lot). No action; work session to be considered.
cases.publicComment: Stefan (NYU real estate professor opening a restaurant at 12 Maple Ave) gave a detailed, constructive pitch and volunteered to fund parking improvements; apologized for 'peppering inboxes.'

memberPositions.evidence: Summarized his ask, agreed to 'definitely consider a work session,' and said the 40-50-year-old parking legislation should be revisited.
Called the plan 'well thought out' but stressed pay-in-lieu needs an actual parking location to satisfy the need; endorsed signage/wayfinding to publicize existing lots and support walkability.

cases.name: Approval of Minutes (January 24, 2024)
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of the January 24, 2024 meeting with a correction to reflect that Councilman Berra was present (he had been omitted from the attendance list). Routine; approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved to approve the minutes with the attendance correction.
Noted he was omitted as present on page 152 and confirmed he was not recused.

themes.note: Large work session on the 2026 semiquincentennial (250th) celebration dominated the meeting; broad enthusiasm.
District 8 extension (MBIA/Airport Campus) public hearing and District 4 Lombardi Park main both advanced; Lombardi order adopted 5-0.
Senior/disability exemption law, tax-delinquency application restrictions, in-rem foreclosures, and RFP escalation terms.
Kellard/Spinelli water proposals approved; Community Park RFP escalation (3% vs CPI) split the board and stalled.
Contentious developer request to cut affordable units at the former lumberyard; no board support to advance.
New probationary police officer appointed and sworn in; celebratory.
Downtown parking pay-in-lieu/district revival and Chapter 114 application restrictions discussed.
Turf-field project, sidewalks, Shell-station frontage, and parking facilities.
Launch of the town food-scrap composting program, championed by Berra and the sustainability committee.
Public comment on credit-card surcharge enforcement and downtown parking.

staffInput.summary: Provided the legal framework across most items: explained the Water District 8/District 4 process and the need for the D&B basis-of-design report before a water-contribution agreement; explained the senior/disability exemption law and the optional RMD inclusion; drafted and explained the Chapter 114 tax-delinquency amendment and its waiver process; outlined the code-amendment path for the AFFH reduction request and questioned the developer's premise that unit-count uncertainty blocks the offering plan; walked through in-rem procedure and the coming surplus-proceeds change; advised DOT permit terms cannot be altered and town indemnity exposure is minimal; recounted the town's parking-district history.

Water & Sewer Superintendent; explained the Lombardi Park well failure and why the School Street public-main route (~1,000 ft) is superior to the ~2,000 ft private service line, and reported on the District 8/District 4 basis-of-design coordination with D&B engineers. Praised by the board for the creative solution.

Reported on new library 'vibe'/smart-board systems and new agenda software (with access help offered), confirmed public sign-ups to speak, and located/uploaded the missing Kellard proposal during the meeting; also handled thermostat/logistics.

Provided community announcements (Community Center gym repairs/padding, weather-related garbage-pickup delay, President's Day closure) and was involved in the District 8 and turf-field coordination meetings.

Presented Matthew Barsanti for appointment, detailing the background investigation and interview process and recommending him as a person of high moral character; deferred oath administration to the Supervisor.

Applicant's counsel for the Water District 8 extension; gave the project overview (12-inch main, oversized 297,000-gallon tank and pump station sized for future District 4) and noted no action was being sought pending the D&B report.

meetings.attributionNote: Roll call on the Lombardi Park final order confirmed member voices: Councilman 'Millen' (Milim), 'D. Jacinto' (DiGiacinto), 'Bera' (Berra), 'Hussein' (Hussain), and 'Randy'/'Rundy' (Supervisor Rende). The presiding/supervisor voice throughout is Joseph Rende. Councilman Jose Berra was the detail-oriented member reviewing legal/financial documents (also addressed as 'councilman Bera'/'Mr. Burrard'); Saleem Hussain gave the library/250th-awareness and composting-adjacent comments; Matt Milim was the parks/finance-savvy member driving the turf-field, water-cost, and RFP discussions (his identity partly inferred by elimination among the five members and confirmed by the roll call). Barbara DiGiacinto is the board's sole woman. Berra held the seat in 2024 (Vataj not yet on the board). Non-members kept separate: Town Attorney Roland, Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal, Town Clerk Allison Simon, Town Administrator Kevin Hay, the Police Chief, and applicant counsel Chris Fisher (staffInput); residents Ed Woodyard, Tom Rice, Connie Kehoe, Sue Scheimer, Ed Loberman, Stefan, and developer Mike Ferrari (publicComment). ASR speaker labels are reused across different people, so attribution relied on role and content rather than raw diarization labels.

meetings.meetingSummary: A short Town Board meeting that opened by reconvening from executive session. The board recognized two Eagle Scouts with certificates, appointed and swore in a new police officer (Brandon Hickey), and moved through a light agenda of appointments, a special-event permit, an emergency pool water-system contract, and routine minutes/consensus items. A public hearing on a local law amending Town Code Chapter 114 (tying application processing to real-estate tax delinquency) was opened and immediately adjourned to a date uncertain given the small audience, and the meeting closed in memory of three deceased residents.
meetings.durationNote: Opened 5:30 PM, adjourned to executive session then reconvened; adjourned ~8:18 PM. Quorum present; no absences noted. Votes taken by voice ('all in favor'), not roll call.

cases.name: Recognition of Two Eagle Scouts
cases.summary: The Supervisor recognized two local Scouts who attained the rank of Eagle Scout, presenting each a certificate of recognition and inviting them to describe their service projects (fern garden with bench/signage and improved learning deck/benches, both at Westmoreland Sanctuary). The board and families took photographs. A ceremonial item with no vote, praising the young men's accomplishment.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it a great honor and 'fantastic accomplishment,' noting he attended the induction ceremony and was impressed by the example set.
Attended the induction ceremony with the Supervisor; joked 'I want them on the town board.'

cases.name: Appointment of Brandon Hickey as Police Officer
cases.summary: The Chief recommended appointing Brandon Hickey, a three-year NYC DEP police officer transferring in, to a budgeted police officer position effective March 2, 2024, after a full background investigation and panel interview. The board moved and approved the appointment by voice vote and swore him in on the spot. The Supervisor tied the hire to growing the force (now 31 officers) amid concern over local burglaries.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted the force grew from 29 to 31 officers and that reaching staffing targets matters 'because public safety is certainly important,' citing recent burglaries in the news.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Town Code Chapter 114 — Application Processing / Tax Delinquency
cases.summary: The board opened a public hearing on a local law amending Chapter 114 so that delinquency in real estate taxes becomes grounds to withhold processing of a property-improvement application. The board received the notice/affidavits and the short environmental assessment form but did not adopt the negative declaration or the law. Town Attorney Roland noted ~25 delinquent taxpayers had been sent letters under a newly authorized in-rem foreclosure and recommended adjourning the hearing to draw a larger audience. The hearing was adjourned to a date uncertain by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: No residents spoke on this item; low turnout was the stated reason for adjournment.

memberPositions.evidence: Guided the procedural receipt of documents and the adjournment, deferring to the Town Attorney on timing.

cases.name: Approval of Minutes — February 14, 2024
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of the February 14, 2024 meeting with no questions, by voice vote. Routine old business.

cases.name: Special Event Permit — Troy's Nursery / Garden Design LLC Easter Event
cases.summary: The board received a special event permit application from Troy's Nursery / Garden Design LLC for an Easter event on April 24, 2024 at 97 Bedford Banksville Road, and scheduled a public hearing for March 20, 2024 by voice vote. A council member flagged that the application stated no parking arrangements had been made, to be resolved at the hearing along with police-department requirements and insurance certificates.

cases.name: Proposal from James Turlish and Son — New Water System at North Castle Pool & Tennis Club
cases.summary: The board approved, on an emergency basis, the proposal from James Turlish and Son for a new water system at the North Castle Pool and Tennis Club, to be paid from fund balance, and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement. Approved by voice vote. The Supervisor noted the work is needed to ensure the pool opens for the season.

memberPositions.evidence: Emphasized the work was needed 'to ensure that we get the pool open for this season' and praised staff for their hard work.

cases.name: Probationary Appointment of Joseph Lee Bawardi — Groundsman
cases.summary: The board approved the probationary appointment of Joseph Lee Bawardi as groundsman, effective March 4, by voice vote. Routine personnel action.

cases.name: Terminal Leave Payment — Liz Duffy, Senior Recreation Leader
cases.summary: The board approved a terminal leave payment for Liz Duffy, senior recreation leader in the Senior Citizens Recreation Department, by voice vote. A council member noted she has been working part time remotely and will continue in a part-time in-person role starting in April, calling it a good solution for everyone.

cases.name: Probationary Promotional Appointment of Paula Landy — Full-Time Library Clerk
cases.summary: The board approved the probationary promotional appointment of Paula Landy to full-time library clerk, effective January 28, 2024, by voice vote. A council member welcomed her to the town. Routine personnel action.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda
cases.summary: The board approved the consensus agenda by voice vote with no discussion. Routine bundled procedural items.

cases.name: Communications Committee — Call for Volunteers
cases.summary: The Town Clerk announced that the technology task force spearheaded by Councilman Hussain has been elevated into a formally established Communications Committee, now seeking roughly seven volunteers with backgrounds in communications, security, or internal development. Applications go through the town's volunteer boards page and are vetted by Councilman Hussain. No vote; an outreach/announcement item.

memberPositions.evidence: Leading the effort (task force spearheaded by him, applications routed through him); encouraged anyone interested to apply even without obvious relevant skills, wanting 'lots of different perspectives... different demographics across the board.'

cases.name: Closing in Memory of Deceased Residents
cases.summary: Following tradition, the board closed the meeting in memory of three residents: Andrew Caesar (Windmill Farms, ~60-year resident and early IBM family), John Michael 'Jack' Koza Jr., and former North White Plains resident Joseph Brad Finney. Councilwoman DiGiacinto, acting as town historian, offered remembrances; the board moved and approved closing in their memory by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: As the board's 'in-house historian,' delivered personal remembrances of each deceased resident.

themes.note: Bulk of the voting agenda: police officer, groundsman, library clerk appointments and a terminal-leave payment, all approved.
Eagle Scout recognition and closing-in-memory dominated the ceremonial front and back of the meeting.
New police officer sworn in; Supervisor tied staffing growth to concern over local burglaries.
Chapter 114 amendment linking application processing to tax delinquency; hearing opened then adjourned for low turnout.
Tax-delinquency law and in-rem foreclosure of ~25 delinquent taxpayers; resident reminder to sign up for tax due-date emails.
Emergency pool water-system contract to open the pool for the season; new community center gym mats.
Communications Committee formally established from Councilman Hussain's tech task force; volunteers sought.
Minutes approval, consensus agenda, and procedural motions moved quickly.

staffInput.summary: Announced the establishment of the Communications Committee (from Councilman Hussain's tech task force) and its call for ~7 volunteers; read the public-hearing notice, affidavits, and short environmental assessment form for the Chapter 114 local law.

Explained the Chapter 114 amendment (delinquent taxes as grounds to withhold application processing), reported ~25 delinquent taxpayers were sent letters under the newly authorized in-rem foreclosure, and recommended receiving the documents but adjourning the hearing to draw a larger audience. Also advised Councilwoman DiGiacinto that state tax law allows no municipal forgiveness of late-tax penalties.

Administrator's update: new gym wall mats installed at the Community Center (thanking Matt Traynor's staff); library trust project nearing mid-March completion despite a contractor staffing delay; strong interest in a middle-income Armonk housing unit, urging residents to join the housing board mailing list.

meetings.attributionNote: The presiding/supervisor voice (Speaker A) is confidently Joseph Rende. Speaker B is confidently Barbara DiGiacinto (only woman, 'Barbara,' self-described historian, tax-reminder remarks). Speaker J, who leads and champions the Communications Committee volunteer drive, aligns with Councilman Saleem Hussain (the Town Clerk routed the effort 'through Councilman Hussein'); attributed at medium confidence. A frequent motion-maker/commenter (Speaker F — flagged the Troy's Nursery parking gap, praised staff on the pool contract, noted Liz Duffy's part-time arrangement) could not be reliably distinguished between Matt Milim and Jose Berra, so those substantive procedural comments were left unattributed rather than guessed. Staff (Allison Simon, Roland, Administrator's office) and the Police Chief were placed in staffInput; resident Tony Fu spoke in general public comment about teaching the state/federal constitutions in schools (not tied to a specific agenda item). Votes were by voice, so no roll-call vote attribution was possible.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened with a work session with the Conservation Board on proposed amendments to the town's tree-preservation code, focusing on simplifying definitions, scaling removal limits to lot size, clarifying penalties, and educating residents. After recessing to free the courtroom for an arraignment, the board handled a discussion of a reduced RPRC review fee for master-planned single-family lots, two subdivision bond releases (one approved, one tabled), several event-use requests, and a slate of personnel resignations, reappointments and board appointments. The meeting closed with liaison updates, an Armonk eagle-restoration progress report, and two closings in memoriam.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present; full board of five (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra) participated. Meeting recessed twice to give the courtroom to a judge for an arraignment. Rende recused himself from the RPRC fee item (4A) due to his IBM employment near Eagle Ridge.

cases.name: Conservation Board Proposed Tree Code Amendments
cases.summary: The Conservation Board (Jane Black, George Drapeau, Craig Benedict) presented proposed amendments to the town's tree-preservation code developed since 2022, including separating 'clearing' and 'thinning' definitions, switching from a calendar year to a rolling 12-month period, lowering the no-permit threshold from 10 trees to 3, removing the confusing landscape-buffer-zone provision, and setting a defined fine (proposed $2,000/tree) rather than an 'up to $1,000' floating amount. Town Planner Adam Kaufman said the existing law works well and the changes are reasonable but not strictly necessary. The board coalesced strongly around resident education (videos, mailers, newsletter inserts) over penalties, and agreed to refer the fine question to the town prosecutor, involve the building inspector, and bring a revised draft back for a public hearing, targeting the first April meeting. No vote taken.
cases.publicComment: Conservation Board volunteers Jane Black, George Drapeau and Craig Benedict presented at length and answered questions; tone constructive and collaborative, framing trees as central to the town's quality of life.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed hard on public education over penalties, praised Milim's short videos and suggested colorful mailers and newsletter inserts; wants to wrap it up for a public hearing by the first April meeting.
Noted he had made zero comments, then urged notices on permit applications and affirmatively notifying past permit-holders; 'I'm big on educating people instead of just penalizing them.'
Endorsed the code changes as at least as stringent as before, but pressed for clarity on whether a fine is always imposed versus remediation, wanting it clear to residents.
Championed short explainer videos and a printed diagram-style mailer to reach residents whose 'eyes just glaze over' at the website.

cases.name: Approval of Minutes — February 28, 2024
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of the February 28, 2024 meeting on a motion and second, all in favor.

cases.name: RPRC Review Fee for Master-Planned Single-Family Lots
cases.applicant: Town Planner / Town Engineer (Adam Kaufman, Keller)
cases.summary: Town Planner Adam Kaufman recommended a reduced RPRC review fee of $300 per lot (down from ~$1,800) for individual lots within approved master site plans such as Eagle Ridge and Airport Campus, since the engineering and planning is largely done and the RPRC only checks consistency. Councilman Berra argued the fee should be somewhat higher (about $400 total) so the town is not shortchanged, while other members urged deference to the department head's judgment and against micromanaging. The board adopted Kaufman's $300 recommendation and directed the master fee schedule be updated accordingly. Supervisor Rende recused himself due to his IBM employment adjacent to Eagle Ridge; the motion passed with the remaining members in favor.

memberPositions.evidence: Cautioned against setting the fee too low, suggested $200/lot ($400 total) so 'we don't get shortchanged,' but said he'd made his points and would vote in favor rather than prolong the debate.
Argued the board should trust department head Adam Kaufman's judgment on the fair fee and 'not be micromanaging.'

cases.name: Madonna Senior Housing — Water Main Extension Bond Release & 3-Year Maintenance Bond
cases.summary: On the recommendation of the town engineer (John Kellard) and special counsel, the board authorized release of the water main extension performance bond for the Madonna senior housing project and establishment of a three-year maintenance bond. Release was made conditional on the Clerk's office first receiving the maintenance bond and the Town Attorney approving and signing it, with a copy furnished to board members. Members asked that going forward a draft maintenance bond be provided when such items are on the agenda. Approved on a motion and second, all in favor.

memberPositions.evidence: Supported release but asked that the board see the draft maintenance bond and be copied once signed so 'nothing slips through the cracks,' citing public trust.
'I always like seeing things ahead of time' — agreed the board should have the draft maintenance bond in front of it when releasing the performance bond.

cases.name: Shoemaker Lane / Wampus Mill Subdivision — Roadway & Sewer Bond and Cul-de-Sac Repair
cases.applicant: Shoemaker Lane / Wampus Mill subdivision developer
cases.summary: The item concerned releasing the public roadway and sewer main performance bond and establishing a three-year maintenance bond that would also guarantee milling and repaving the cul-de-sac to the highway superintendent's satisfaction by July 1. The road dedication package was found to be dated, with open questions about who guaranteed the repairs (the father versus the son) and whether the town had been plowing the road as an emergency measure. Special counsel Roland expressed concern about accepting a bond rather than having the work completed before dedication, calling it a hybrid maintenance/performance bond. The board tabled the item pending an updated package (title report, current taxes, maintenance bond draft) from staff.

memberPositions.evidence: Said she'd feel much more comfortable seeing the maintenance bond and questioned whether the town had actually been maintaining the road over the winter; supported tabling.

cases.name: Armonk Lions Club — Annual Fall Folder Roll at Wampus Brook Park
cases.summary: The board approved the Armonk Lions Club request to hold its annual fall folder roll at Wampus Brook Park on June 6-9, 2024, subject to receiving all required documentation. Motion, second, all in favor.

cases.name: Wall Street Rides FAR — Charity Cycling Event (Oct 5, 2024)
cases.applicant: Wall Street Rides FAR (autism research charity)
cases.summary: The board approved use of town roads and the pool parking lot for the 10th annual Wall Street Rides FAR charity cycling event for autism research on October 5, 2024. Approval was conditioned on no pavement markings other than chalk that washes off with rain (responding to resident Ed Woodyard's letter about lingering spray-paint arrows), with organizers encouraged to use signs instead, plus Town Attorney approval of indemnity/releases and satisfactory insurance. Organizers were to be told the pool parking lot might not be fully available if pool construction begins. Motion, second, all in favor.
cases.publicComment: Resident Ed Woodyard submitted a letter (covering items E and F) asking that cycling groups not mark roads with indelible spray paint that has lingered for years; the board treated it as a helpful, legitimate comment and built conditions around it.

memberPositions.evidence: Suggested requiring directional signs rather than any paint to avoid the wrong can being used, citing how road races and the Armonk run use signs.
Proposed washable chalk as an allowable alternative and pushed for wording ensuring no markings are left behind when the event ends.
Flagged the remote possibility that pool construction could make the parking lot unavailable and asked that organizers be notified.

cases.name: Velocity Ride to End Cancer — Charity Ride (Oct 6, 2024)
cases.applicant: Velocity Ride to End Cancer (Columbia University Irving Cancer Center)
cases.summary: The board approved use of town roads for the Velocity Ride to End Cancer benefiting Columbia University's Irving Cancer Center on Sunday, October 6, 2024, back-to-back with the prior day's event. The same conditions as the Wall Street Rides FAR approval were applied (no paint / chalk only, signs preferred, police route review, Town Attorney sign-off, insurance). Motion, second, all in favor.
cases.publicComment: Covered by Ed Woodyard's letter regarding road paint markings (see prior item).

cases.name: Retirement Letter — Sharon Reiner (effective March 31)
cases.summary: The board received the retirement letter of Sharon Reiner, effective March 31, praising her as a devoted employee (noting Sal in Water/Sewer will miss her). A procedural gap was caught by Councilman Hussain — a motion and second had been made but the vote never formally called — so the roll/voice vote was retaken to make it official. Rende noted his practice of sending a thank-you letter from the supervisor and full board to departing employees.

memberPositions.evidence: Pointed out that a first and second had been made but no 'aye' vote was called, prompting the board to retake the vote to make it official.

cases.name: Reappointment of Mel Orlana to the Architectural Review Board
cases.summary: The board reappointed Mel Orlana to a vacated seat on the Architectural Review Board for a term expiring September 13, 2028, with Rende praising his building and construction background. Motion, second, all in favor.

cases.name: Appointment of David Affrack to the Housing Board
cases.summary: The board appointed David Affrack to the Housing Board for a five-year term expiring March 13, 2029, on the recommendation of Housing Board member Ginny McGrown, noting his volunteer work helping residents with tax returns. Motion, second, all in favor.

cases.name: Resignation of Joe Monticelli from the Zoning Board of Appeals
cases.summary: The board received Joe Monticelli's letter of resignation from the Zoning Board of Appeals, effective March 4, 2024, with Rende and DiGiacinto praising his long service (formerly on the Rec Board and years as ZBA chair). Motion, second, all in favor.

cases.name: Appointment of Edward Lashin to the Zoning Board of Appeals
cases.summary: The board appointed Edward Lashin to the Zoning Board of Appeals for a term expiring December 31, 2029; Lashin had been interviewed January 7 (originally for Les Burkhammer's seat). Councilwoman DiGiacinto objected on process grounds — Monticelli's seat had only been open since March 4, and she wanted to give other interested residents the chance to apply and interview — and cast the lone 'no.' Hussain and others stressed the standard vetting/interview process had been followed. The measure carried on a roll-call vote: Berra aye, Hussain aye, DiGiacinto no, Rende aye (recorded as a split vote, DiGiacinto opposed).

memberPositions.evidence: Voted 'no,' stressing 'it's a matter of process' — the seat had been open only since March 4 and other residents should get a chance to apply, despite holding Lashin in high regard.
Voted aye and emphasized the standard apply/vet/interview/vote process had been fully followed, and that Lashin's fit shouldn't depend on whose seat he fills.
Voted aye on the roll call.
Voted aye and confirmed for the record that Lashin had interviewed on January 7.

cases.name: Appointment of Ray Rodriguez as Chairperson of the Zoning Board of Appeals
cases.summary: The board appointed sitting ZBA member Ray Rodriguez as chairperson (at the pleasure of the board), with Rende noting Rodriguez has the full confidence and support of the ZBA. Motion, second, all in favor.

cases.name: Town Clerk Conference Request — NYS Town Clerks Association (Albany)
cases.summary: The board approved Town Clerk Allison Simon's request to attend the New York State Town Clerks Association Conference in Albany, April 21-24, 2024, which she described as a learning and networking opportunity to enhance office skills. Rende emphasized the value of continuing education for all personnel. Motion, second, all in favor.

cases.name: Consensus Agenda
cases.summary: The board adopted the consensus agenda on a motion and second, all in favor.

cases.name: Liaison Reports, Announcements & Eagle Restoration Update
cases.summary: Members gave liaison updates: Hussain announced volunteer openings for a Library board of trustees seat and the new town Technology Committee; DiGiacinto praised the police department (an arrest at a Stop & Shop break-in, and their cooperation with an FBI film shoot) and previewed an April 20 town-wide corporation cleanup day (8am-1pm) she will bring for a motion next meeting. Rende reported progress on restoring the town's eagle monument — footings poured by Oronzio Contracting, steel poles being galvanized for Verdi Electric, and the repainted eagle expected back in 3.5-4 weeks — crediting donated work by local contractors and noting an insurance claim was filed. The Town Administrator reported the trust/library section work is complete and that area should reopen next week.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public signed up to speak, and no one was present on Zoom.

memberPositions.evidence: Enthusiastically solicited volunteers for a Library trustee seat and the inaugural Technology Committee, noting existing resident interest.
Praised the police department's arrest and FBI-shoot cooperation and previewed an April 20 town-wide cleanup day, urging broad participation across North White Plains, Armonk and Banksville.
Gave an upbeat update on the eagle restoration and thanked donating contractors — 'we're all enthusiastic about' getting the eagle back up.

cases.name: Closings in Memoriam — Bill Canavan and Charity Lunder's Father
cases.summary: The board closed with two remembrances: Bill Canavan, the town's hydrogeologist and founder/president of Hydro Environmental Solutions who worked closely on the Brynwood Summit project, who died suddenly at 59; and the father of Charity Lunder, who passed away at 103. DiGiacinto and Berra offered heartfelt tributes before the board adjourned.

memberPositions.evidence: Delivered a moving tribute to hydrogeologist Bill Canavan, praising his ability to 'dumb down' complex hydrogeology and calling his sudden death at 59 a tragedy.
Remembered Charity Lunder's father, who died at 103, and reflected on perspective around loss.

themes.note: Tree-code work session dominated the first half; strong shared commitment to tree preservation paired with education-first enforcement.
Several resignations, reappointments and board appointments; only contested item was the ZBA appointment of Edward Lashin.
Recurring emphasis on process — bond drafts to the board, retaking a missed vote, and DiGiacinto's process objection on the ZBA seat.
Two charity cycling events and the Lions folder roll approved; cleanup day previewed.
RPRC fee reduction and two subdivision bond items, one approved and one tabled over incomplete documentation.
Shoemaker Lane cul-de-sac repair uncertainty and resident concern over lingering road paint from cycling events.
Eagle monument restoration progressing with donated contractor work; library/trust section work completed.
Madonna senior-housing water main bond release and reference to hydrogeologist Bill Canavan's work.
New Technology Committee launching; recurring theme of using videos and mailers to reach residents.

staffInput.summary: Town Planner: said the existing tree law works well and amendment isn't strictly necessary but the Conservation Board's changes are reasonable; explained clearing/grading limit lines and the confusing landscape-buffer provision; recommended and justified the reduced $300 RPRC review fee for master-planned lots (~$135/hr, 15-30 min per lot).

Sitting Town Attorney: advised that misdemeanor fines are capped and tiered by offense so the board can't simply pick a $2,000 figure without the prosecutor's review; raised concerns about accepting a bond rather than completed work on Shoemaker Lane and the uncertain guarantor, supporting tabling; to review event indemnity/releases.

Town Clerk: explained the Clerk's office will not release a performance bond until the maintenance bond is received and approved by the Town Attorney; confirmed the missed Sharon Reiner vote; described the value of the NYS Town Clerks conference; gave the next-meeting reminder (March 20).

Town Administrator: to carry tree-code education via the town newsletter, and to reach out to the cycling-event organizers about the possible pool parking-lot closure, paint/chalk conditions, and police route coordination.

meetings.attributionNote: Speakers were generally identifiable by role even without labels: the presiding/supervisor voice was mapped to Joseph Rende, and the roll call on the Lashin appointment named members explicitly (Berra 'Zara' aye, Hussain 'Hussein' aye, DiGiacinto 'Digesto' no, Supervisor Rende aye). ASR manglings normalized: Berra/'Zara', Hussain/'Hussein', DiGiacinto/'Digesto'/'Digacinto', Milim/'Milam'. Matt Milim spoke little and was referenced mainly via praise for his explainer videos, so few positions are attributed to him. Rende recused from the RPRC fee item (4A), which slightly reduced attribution certainty on the competing fee positions there. No absences noted; the full five-member board (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra) was present. Conservation Board presenters (Jane Black, George Drapeau, Craig Benedict) are advisory-board volunteers, treated as public comment, not board members.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Town Board opened with a work session on a draft rewrite of the town's sign law (removing content-based regulation to conform to case law), then held a brief public hearing on a special event permit, heard from the Friends of North Castle Public Library on the Armonk Outdoor Art Show, received an annual update from the Board of Ethics, authorized bidding for the Wampus Brook North Bridge replacement, granted The Bristol at Armonk a waiver to pursue amended site plan relief from the planning board over its EMS/ambulance-call burden on the volunteer fire department, formally established the North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee with $40,000 in funding, approved a parking-related easement from Bank of America in downtown Armonk, and tabled a declaration of restriction for a Bedford Banksville Road property at Councilman Berra's request.
meetings.durationNote: Supervisor Rende presided; Councilmembers Milim, Hussain, DiGiacinto and Berra participated (Berra abstained on the March 13 minutes, having been absent that meeting). No mention of Councilman Schiliro in this session.

cases.name: Town Sign Law Rewrite (Content-Neutral Update)
cases.summary: Planner Adam Kaufman presented a draft rewrite of the town's sign law stripping content-based restrictions to conform with current case law, covering prohibited sign types (e.g., pole/pylon signs, murals), residential lot signage limits, right-of-way setbacks, and grandfathering of existing signs. The board raised questions about enforcement capacity (possibly needing a part-time code enforcement officer), uniform road-setback measurements, whether temporary/A-frame signs need permits, and a proposed community sign-location alternative to signs on private property. The board agreed to submit individual comments and have the town attorney review the draft before another work session.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised concern about the town needing to hire at least a part-time code enforcement officer to handle new sign-law responsibilities, and pushed for a uniform setback measurement from the road for consistency.
Asked whether the town could distinguish sign types (e.g., gas station vs. restaurant pole signs) without regulating content, and whether repeated identical signs on one property could be limited.
Raised the question of whether one property owner repeatedly posting the same sign message could be restricted, confirming that content-based limits are off the table.

Requested a future work-session debate on a community sign-location option as a better aesthetic alternative to allowing signs on private properties, and asked staff to research how other towns handle it.

cases.name: Troy's Nursery Garden Design — Easter Event Special Event Permit
cases.summary: The board opened and closed a public hearing on a special event permit for an Easter event on April 24, 2024, with no public opposition and no applicant representative present. The board received recommendations from police, fire district, and the building inspector, adopted a negative declaration, and approved the permit resolution unanimously.

cases.name: Armonk Outdoor Art Show — Park Use, Alcohol Permit and Fee Waivers
cases.applicant: Friends of North Castle Public Library
cases.summary: The board approved the Friends of North Castle Public Library's request to use Community Park (access road and parking) for the September 28-29, 2024 Armonk Outdoor Art Show, including an alcohol permit and waivers of the alcohol and tent permit fees. Outgoing show director Nicole Blau recapped a weather-disrupted but successful 2023 show that netted $115,000 for the library and introduced incoming director Nancy Razzner.

cases.name: Board of Ethics Annual Update and Training Video
cases.summary: Board of Ethics chair David Simons and member Brett Summers presented a new annual ethics-training video (shown to 11 of 13 boards/committees so far) and gave an annual update, including a 6-month recusal look-back rule, expanded disclosure requirements covering investment real estate, 19 of 25 disclosure forms returned so far, and a proposal to create a plain-language ethics guide booklet. Board members discussed adding compliance tracking to the boards/committees spreadsheet and clarified that recusal obligations extend to executive session.

memberPositions.evidence: Said watching the video clarified that his practice of verbally recusing himself was insufficient without a written disclosure, and endorsed a culture where members openly share ethics learnings.
Noted the Board of Ethics landing page description should be corrected to reflect that conflicts will always exist and the goal is disclosure/transparency rather than eliminating conflicts.

cases.name: Wampus Brook North Bridge Replacement — Bid Authorization
cases.summary: The board authorized Parks and Recreation Superintendent Matt Trainer to go out to bid for replacement of the deteriorating wooden Wampus Brook North Bridge, after a resident/board member (Norma Hill) warned of a fall/liability risk from the worn planking. Motion to bid passed unanimously.

cases.name: The Bristol at Armonk — EMS Condition Waiver / Site Plan Amendment Referral
cases.applicationType: waiver from application processing restriction law
cases.applicant: The Bristol at Armonk (E.V. Armonk LLC)
cases.summary: The Bristol, an assisted-living facility, sought a waiver of the town's application-processing restriction law (triggered by a pending building-department summons/enforcement action) so it could go before the planning board to amend a 2012 site plan condition requiring an on-site EMT, which it says it can no longer legally staff under Department of Health rules. Board members pressed hard on why a decade-old compliance problem — non-emergency transport calls burdening the volunteer Armonk Fire Department/EMS — was only being addressed now that a summons had been issued, questioning the facility's overnight nursing coverage and the sincerity of its assurances. The board ultimately granted the waiver unanimously so the matter could proceed to the planning board, while directing that the planning board strongly urge the applicant to fund outside specialized legal counsel.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke; the applicant's COO (Amy Silvermagalese) and attorney (Nick Appadora) appeared by Zoom to answer board questions.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed the applicant on what 'teeth' would ensure compliance this time given the issue had ebbed and flowed for a decade, and proposed limiting the waiver to roughly six months to force prompt planning-board action.

Said he was 'having a hard time concluding' a February letter from the applicant's counsel about call volumes 'is not disingenuous' and stressed the impact on volunteer firefighter morale, while ultimately supporting the waiver to move the matter to the planning board.

Questioned the facility's overnight RN/LPN staffing gaps as 'very concerning' given nearly 100 residents, and proposed the condition that the planning board be urged to have the applicant fund outside specialized counsel.
Said he shared the other members' concerns but agreed the best path forward was granting the waiver so the matter could go to the planning board.

cases.name: North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee — Formation, Mission Statement and Funding
cases.summary: Following a work-session update from the 250th Anniversary Steering Committee co-chairs (including plans for a July 4, 2026 time capsule and restoration of historic markers at Miller Hill and Mount Misery, aided by a $50,000 county grant), the board formally established the North Castle Revolutionary War 250 Steering Committee, adopted its mission statement (amended to say 'understanding and appreciation'), appointed Councilmembers Milim and DiGiacinto as board liaisons, and allocated $40,000 for a commemorative video and historic marker restoration.

memberPositions.evidence: Appointed as one of two council liaisons to the steering committee and read the mission statement aloud for the public record.
Suggested a nearby historical property on Grove Road be considered by the historical society and new committee.

cases.name: Bank of America Downtown Armonk Parking Easement
cases.address: Main Street, Armonk (former Bank of America branch, adjacent to Verizon lot)
cases.summary: After roughly ten months of negotiation, Bank of America consented to a temporary construction easement and permanent easement on its former branch property to allow completion of the town's downtown Armonk parking improvement project on the former Verizon lot. The board authorized the supervisor to sign the agreement; Councilwoman DiGiacinto recused herself because relatives with an interest in a neighboring Main Street commercial property could arguably benefit.

memberPositions.evidence: Publicly disclosed and recused herself from discussion and the vote, citing her DiGiacinto relatives' potential interest in a nearby Main Street property, though board colleagues affirmed the recusal was clearly warranted under the ethics code.

cases.name: 209 Bedford Banksville Road — Declaration of Restriction (FAR Transfer)
cases.applicant: Joseph and Celeste Claimant (property owners at 191/209 Bedford Banksville Road)
cases.summary: A declaration of restriction tied to a planning board condition (de-restricting a roughly four-acre lot to permit an addition using transferred FAR from an adjoining lot) was tabled at Councilman Berra's request after he raised late concerns about missing indemnification language and an unclear condemnation-valuation clause. The supervisor asked that concerns be raised earlier in the future to give the applicant's attorney time to respond; Berra explained he had been ill and only saw the item in Friday's packet.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved to table the item, citing missing hold-harmless/indemnification language and an unexplained condemnation-valuation provision he wanted to review further.
Agreed to table but asked that future objections be raised earlier so the applicant's counsel has fair opportunity to respond before the meeting.

themes.note: Lengthy, contentious discussion of The Bristol at Armonk's ambulance-call burden on volunteer EMS.
Extended work session on a content-neutral sign law rewrite.
Formal launch of the Revolutionary War 250 steering committee with funding.

staffInput.summary: Presented the draft content-neutral sign law rewrite and fielded board questions on enforcement, setbacks, and residential signage limits.
Advised the board on the scope of the application-processing waiver for The Bristol, easement authorization procedure, and general legal points throughout the meeting.
Presented the annual ethics update and training video with member Brett Summers.

meetings.attributionNote: ASR transcript is un-diarized; most member attributions rely on direct name mentions by colleagues or self-identification (e.g., 'Jose', 'Matt', 'Barbara', 'Salim'). Some exchanges, especially rapid-fire cross-talk in the Bristol EMS discussion, could not be confidently attributed to a specific speaker and were left out of memberPositions or folded into case summaries.

meetings.meetingSummary: With Supervisor Rende participating remotely from Bermuda and Deputy Supervisor Jose Berra chairing, the Town Board handled a short agenda dominated by the Summit Club's request for a permanent special use permit (referred to the local and county planning boards, with a public hearing set for May 22) and a proposed Chapter 325 traffic local law adding no-parking zones on Byron Brook Place and a stop sign on Banksville Road (memos received, hearing set for April 24). The board approved 2023 budget transfers, two highway equipment purchases, a Netflix film permit for the Robert De Niro series 'Zero Day,' several personnel items, and the warrant/liquor-license consent items. The night's friction was over department-head salary increases: Councilwoman DiGiacinto pushed for an additional executive session citing new information, which drew objections that the matter had already been thoroughly vetted; after the session the raises were adopted 4-0 with DiGiacinto abstaining. Liaison updates covered the Armonk library reopening, a defeated state faith-based affordable-housing bill, new federal PFAS limits, a possible dog park, and town-wide cleanup day.
meetings.durationNote: Quorum present; all five members participated. Supervisor Joseph Rende appeared remotely from Bermuda (noticed on the agenda), so Deputy Supervisor Jose Berra ran the meeting. Board opened at 6:30 and went into executive session for advice of counsel, contract, and personnel matters.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes (March 20 and March 28, 2024)
cases.summary: Old-business item to approve the minutes of the March 20, 2024 regular meeting and the March 28, 2024 special (executive-session) meeting. A motion was made and seconded and passed on a voice vote. Berra noted the March 28 special meeting was an executive session, which is why an extra meeting had been held.

cases.name: Summit Club — Permanent Special Use Permit, Maintenance Building, and Golf Course Public Use
cases.address: Summit Club (former golf/country club off Route 22, near Windmill)
cases.applicant: Del Bello Donnellan Weingarten Wise & Wiederkehr (Mark Weingarten) for the Summit Club
cases.summary: The applicant seeks to convert the temporary special use permit for the golf club into a permanent one, covering operational parameters (up to 500 members, a 100-child summer camp, events, and 10 guest cottages) plus a related parking variance and the maintenance-facility site plan. After lengthy discussion, the board voted to refer the matter to the local and county planning boards (leaving the ZBA parking-variance referral to come through the planning board) and to schedule a public hearing for May 22, 2024. Town Planner Adam Kaufman framed the item and Attorney Roland advised on procedure; both referral and hearing motions carried on voice votes. Members pressed for a single consolidated submission and for tighter limits on events, cottages, social membership, and the duration of public golf access.
cases.publicComment: No residents spoke; multiple members anticipated and invited resident comment (traffic/noise near Windmill) at the scheduled public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Wants everything in one current submission rather than a 2023 letter; flagged noise/traffic impacts on Windmill, open-ended event/'season' language, guest-cottage kitchen rules, and the definition of a 'social member,' saying she intends to 'pin it down a little bit more' while still wanting the club to succeed.

As chair, raised concern that making public golf-course access permanent could 'drag on for any number of years' and proposed renewing the temporary public-use permit two years at a time as a guardrail, unpersuaded by the applicant's 'self-regulating' argument.
Said he understood and thought the self-regulation point 'makes sense' but wanted to think about it; asked practical questions about the planning-board timeline and parking.

cases.name: Local Law to Amend Chapter 325 (Vehicle & Traffic) — Byron Brook Place No-Parking Zones and Banksville Road Stop Sign
cases.address: Byron Brook Place and Banksville Road, North Castle
cases.applicant: Police Chief Peter Simonson / Police Department
cases.summary: Based on a memo from Police Chief Simonson, the proposed local law would create no-parking-anytime zones near the commercial buildings at Byron Brook Place (prompted by a since-departed telemarketing tenant's overflow parking) and add a stop sign with curb/curve reconfiguration on Banksville Road to calm traffic, similar to the School Street work in Coxsing. The board received the two memos and scheduled a public hearing for April 24, 2024. Officer Tom presented the field observations and temporary cone/signage trial. Members were broadly enthusiastic and asked mainly about unintended consequences for residents' overflow parking.
cases.publicComment: No residents spoke at this meeting; police noted affected Byron Brook Place residents were consulted, are organized, and are expected to comment at the April 24 hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it 'very clearly a great thing to do' while probing for downsides, asking whether restricting weekday parking would hurt residents' party/overflow parking and where displaced business vehicles would go.
As chair praised the work ('it's absolutely great'), cited seeing the comparable School Street/Coxsing calming firsthand, and moved the item toward a public hearing.

cases.name: Approval of 2023 Budget Transfers
cases.summary: Previously deferred so the chair could examine it further, the 2023 budget transfers were brought back for approval. Berra said he was now comfortable after digging into it and consulting Councilman Hussain. The motion was made, seconded, and carried on a voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he had held the item over to dig into it, spoke to Saleem, and was now 'fine with it,' recommending approval.

cases.name: Highway Equipment Purchases — Backhoe and 4-Ton Falcon RME Asphalt Hot Patcher
cases.summary: Two highway purchases were approved by separate voice-vote motions: a backhoe (funded in the 2024 highway operating budget with roughly $20,000 of the excess paid from the highway fund balance) and a 4-ton Falcon RME asphalt hot patcher (paid from the CHIPS balance). General Foreman Jamie Norris was present; members had reviewed the materials and had no substantive objections.

cases.name: Film Permit — Netflix Productions 'Zero Day' at Townhouse Diner and North Castle Martial Arts
cases.address: 720 N. Broadway (Townhouse Diner) and 700 N. Broadway (North Castle Martial Arts)
cases.summary: The board approved a film permit for Netflix to shoot the Robert De Niro political-thriller series 'Zero Day' on May 9, 2024, from roughly 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. Berra highlighted the excitement of a De Niro production filming in town. Attorney Roland confirmed he had resolved the earlier indemnification concern by substituting a modern indemnification agreement. The motion carried on a voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the Robert De Niro 'Zero Day' shoot 'really exciting for me' and read a description of the series to the public before moving approval.

cases.name: Salary Increases for Certain Department-Head Non-Union Employees (Effective Jan 1, 2024)
cases.summary: This item became the meeting's flashpoint. Councilwoman DiGiacinto moved to adjourn into an additional executive session, saying she had information not previously discussed; other members objected that the raises had already been vetted across three executive sessions over two months (one lasting three to four hours) and that her April 1 email hadn't identified new information. The board voted 4-0-1 (Berra abstaining) to hold the exec session at the meeting's end, met, and then reconvened. On the substantive vote to approve the raises, the motion carried 4-0 with DiGiacinto abstaining 'for the reasons I gave' (though she stated she supports the increases). A sharp exchange followed over whether the extra session was warranted and over meeting decorum/Robert's Rules.

memberPositions.evidence: Insisted she had information 'not discussed previously' and pressed for another executive session, then abstained on the final vote 'for the reasons I gave,' while stating 'I absolutely approve and support the salary increases for 2024.'
Opposed reopening the matter, calling the extra exec session 'an unfortunate use of time' with 'absolutely no new material information'; praised the raises and the thorough process and voted aye.

From Bermuda, had declined the additional session by email absent new information, said DiGiacinto's on-camera request without prior notice was 'so weird' and the behavior 'terrible,' yet voted yes on the raises and thanked staff for a thorough process.
Agreed with Milim that no further discussion was needed absent new information, but seconded the exec-session motion to accommodate, and voted aye on the raises.

As chair called the renewed exec-session push 'silly' and said the process had been very thorough, but seconded it as easier than arguing; abstained on the exec-session vote yet voted aye on the raises and helped run the roll call.

cases.name: Receipt of Resignation of Anthony J. Futia (Water & Sewer Maintenance Worker) for Retirement
cases.summary: The board received the retirement resignation of water and sewer maintenance worker Anthony J. Futia, effective April 30, 2024. Members thanked him for roughly 38 years of service, with Berra noting it would be the first time in memory that no Futia works in the water and sewer department. Motion to receive was made, seconded, and carried.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked Anthony Futia for '38 years of really very fine service' and wished him well.

cases.name: Terminal Leave Payment for Peter Chardiello (Police Department)
cases.summary: The board approved a terminal leave payment for Peter Chardiello of the Police Department on a voice vote, with members wishing him well.

cases.name: Conservation Board — Reappointment of Jane Black and Appointment of George Drapeau
cases.summary: The board reappointed Jane Black (co-chair) and appointed George Drapeau to the Conservation Board, each for two-year terms expiring April 10, 2026, on separate voice votes. Berra, the board's liaison to the Conservation Board, praised the members' dedication and noted the board could use more volunteers.

memberPositions.evidence: As Conservation Board liaison thanked Jane Black and George Drapeau, called the board 'a pretty significant lift' with a very dedicated group, and encouraged more residents to join.

cases.name: Consent Items — Warrant No. 7 Payments and Bluestone Lane Liquor License Renewal Notice
cases.applicant: Town Clerk / BL 575 Main NYLC (Bluestone Lane)
cases.summary: The board approved the audit and payment of claims on Warrant No. 7 together with receipt of the New York State liquor license renewal notice for Bluestone Lane at 575 Main Street, Armonk, on a single motion. Some members briefly noted the town clerk report was missing from their tablets but were comfortable proceeding since it was posted online. A related terminal-leave and alcohol-permit notification were part of the clerk's items.

cases.name: Town Board Liaison Updates and Community Announcements
cases.summary: Liaison and update segment: the Armonk library branch is set to reopen the week of April 15 after truss construction and cleaning; DiGiacinto reported new Hergenhan entrance/community-center signage (donor-funded), a now-defeated NYS Senate Bill 7791 faith-based affordable-housing bill she opposed as a one-size-fits-all mandate, and a solar-eclipse-glasses recycling idea; Milim flagged new federal EPA PFAS limits (4 ppt) passed to superintendent Sal, a possible dog park at IBM community park, and the push to open the town pool on time pending county Health Department sign-off. Announcements covered town-wide cleanup day (Saturday, April 20, 8 a.m.-1 p.m.), food-scrap composting kits, tax-filing reminders, autism awareness month police patches, a parks groundskeeper opening, and Wampus Park lighting replacement; the board closed in memory of several residents.

memberPositions.evidence: Said she was 'very concerned' about NYS Senate Bill 7791 (faith-based affordable housing), a streamlined version of the prior housing compact, alerted the board and residents, and was 'very grateful' when told the bill is dead — while urging the town to develop its own affordable-housing ideas rather than a state one-size-fits-all mandate.

Welcomed the stricter federal PFAS limits ('a good step') as timely given the planned Water District 2 and 4 filtration systems, and backed a proposed IBM-park dog park and getting the town pool open on time.

themes.note: Summit Club permanent special use permit dominated the meeting; referred out with a May 22 hearing amid member concerns.
Department-head raises (adopted 4-0, DiGiacinto abstaining), a retirement, terminal leave, and two Conservation Board appointments.
Contested push for an extra executive session on salaries and a decorum/Robert's Rules dispute.
Chapter 325 traffic law (Byron Brook no-parking, Banksville stop sign) plus backhoe and hot-patcher purchases; well received.
2023 budget transfers, equipment funding, warrant payments, and tax-deadline reminders.
Traffic-calming, police terminal leave, autism-awareness patches.
DiGiacinto welcomed the defeat of NYS faith-based affordable-housing bill 7791.
New federal PFAS limits noted as timely for Water District 2 and 4 filtration; long-serving worker's retirement.
Possible IBM-park dog park and pushing to open the town pool on time.
Netflix 'Zero Day' film permit, town-wide cleanup day, composting kits.

staffInput.summary: Town Planner; framed the Summit Club permit history and January 2023 parameters, explained the maintenance-facility site plan and the parking shortfall (477 required vs. 431 provided, applicant seeking a 65-space credit now needing a variance), and advised on the referral/hearing sequence.

Sitting Town Attorney (Abrams Fensterman); advised keeping the ZBA parking-variance referral coming through the planning board to avoid confusing the ZBA, resolved the film-permit indemnification issue by substituting a modern agreement, and advised on tabling/procedure for the salary-item executive session and vote.

Delivered the clerk report and tax-deadline reminder (April 30, 10% state penalty; receiver-of-taxes email sign-up), handled the warrant and liquor-license notice, and was involved in the closing decorum exchange.

Appeared for Police Chief Peter Simonson; presented field observations, resident consultations, and the temporary cone/signage trial supporting the Byron Brook Place no-parking zones and the Banksville Road stop sign.

Reported the Armonk library reopening timeline (week of April 15), a parks groundskeeper hiring, autism-awareness police patches, and the Wampus Park lighting replacement; provided the compensation data underpinning the department-head raises.
Highway general foreman present for the backhoe and asphalt hot-patcher purchases; members had reviewed the materials.

meetings.attributionNote: Speakers were identifiable with good confidence from roles and the two end-of-meeting roll calls, which named each member. ASR manglings normalized: 'Jose'/'Vera'/'Barra'/'Bearer' = Councilman Jose Berra, who chaired as Deputy Supervisor while Supervisor Joseph Rende ('Endy'/'Rendezvous') participated remotely from Bermuda; 'Digesendo'/'Te Jacindo' = Barbara DiGiacinto; 'Milam' = Matt Milim; 'Hussein'/'Seline'/'Celine' = Saleem Hussain. Care taken to separate presiding voice Berra (Jose) from Supervisor Rende (also 'Joe/Jose' in ASR) by role. Staff (Kaufman, Roland, Simon, Kevin, Jamie Norris, Officer Tom) and applicant Mark Weingarten excluded from member positions. All five members present; no absences. Vataj not on the board in 2024 and not attributed.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board reconvened after an executive session and handled a public hearing on a traffic local law (a new four-way stop at Banksville Road/Long Pond Road and no-parking restrictions on Byron Brook Place), which it adopted. It authorized Recreation Superintendent Matt Traynor to begin developing a preliminary plan and cost estimate for a proposed dog park at North Castle Community Park, over one member's push for a formal task force. The bulk of the meeting was a lengthy discussion of the Gateway (former Mariani Gardens) 34-townhouse project at 45 Bedford Road, including two town license agreements for stormwater and wetland-buffer mitigation, a community-benefit-agreement amendment, and a proposed deed-restriction amendment for patios and fences, for which the board moved toward scheduling a May 22 public hearing.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting opened 6:30 pm, immediately adjourned to executive session, then reconvened; quorum present and motions carried. Supervisor Rende and Council Members Milim, DiGiacinto, and Hussain were clearly identifiable speaking; Deputy Supervisor Jose Berra was not distinctly identified in the ASR text.

cases.name: Local Law amending Chapter 325 (Vehicles & Traffic) — Banksville Rd/Long Pond Rd stop sign and Byron Brook Place no-parking
cases.address: Banksville Road at Long Pond Road; Byron Brook Place, off Route 22
cases.applicant: Town Highway Department / Police (Lt. Tom Cormack, engineer Joe Tramelli, foreman Jamie Norris)
cases.summary: Public hearing on a local law amending Chapter 325 to formalize a new four-way stop at the Banksville Road/Long Pond Road intersection (tightening turning radii to 40 ft and 25 ft, adjusting striping) and to add no-parking zones on Byron Brook Place near two office buildings off Route 22. Lt. Cormack and engineer Joe Tramelli presented the month-long temporary trial that drew positive resident feedback. A resident (Robert Sweeney) and neighbors spoke in support. The board opened and closed the hearing and adopted the law by unanimous voice vote, with the Highway Department to complete blacktop work within a few weeks after filing with the Department of State.
cases.publicComment: Resident Robert Sweeney and neighbors on Byron Brook Place spoke in favor; residents had proactively requested both changes. Tone strongly supportive.

memberPositions.evidence: "I'm very supportive of this... residents have wanted it for a long time... I think this is a great change and you guys did a great job."

As a Banksville resident who drives the intersection, pressed on the new radius, striping, and whether the affected homeowner had been notified, but said 'it's obvious that we're all in favor of it' and praised the planning.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board meeting minutes — April 10, 2024
cases.summary: Routine old-business item to approve the minutes of the April 10, 2024 Town Board meeting. Moved, seconded, and adopted by unanimous voice vote with no discussion.

cases.name: Proposed dog park at North Castle Community Park
cases.address: North Castle (IBM) Community Park, between the platform tennis courts and the indoor sports center/new bathrooms
cases.applicant: Recreation & Parks Superintendent Matt Traynor / Park & Rec Advisory Board
cases.summary: The board considered Superintendent Matt Traynor's memo requesting permission to pursue a dog park, a project recommended by the Park & Rec Advisory Board and ranked highly in a resident survey. Residents Molly and Juliette Meyer gave a detailed presentation on siting, safety signage, separate small/large-dog areas, and maintenance. The main debate was procedural: Councilwoman DiGiacinto urged a task force (vet, dog trainer, registration/tagging, insurance review) before proceeding, while Supervisor Rende and Councilman Milim opposed a task force as needless delay and favored a later work session instead. The board unanimously passed a motion directing Traynor to develop a preliminary site plan, logistics, and cost estimate in preparation for a work session.
cases.publicComment: Molly and Juliette Meyer presented strongly in favor. Resident Peter Nawara raised a concern about lawn damage from concentrated dog urine and who would bear ongoing landscaping cost (answered: town-funded, likely wood chips rather than grass).

memberPositions.evidence: Framed the vote as merely authorizing Traynor to investigate; 'we should move forward and not delay,' explicitly 'very much against the idea of a task force' as unnecessary delay, favored a work session and getting costs first.

"Absolutely support us moving forward and looking at this," while noting risks to mitigate (impact on surroundings, signage); opposed a task force, preferring a focused work session to gather expert input.

A self-described dog lover who supports a dog park but wanted it done safely: pushed for a task force (vet, trainer), mandatory registration/tagging via Clerk and Rec, spay/neuter and vaccination checks, and an insurance review before moving ahead; 'what is the rush? I'd like to do it right.'

Voiced support at the preliminary stage but, cost-conscious, wanted to know actual costs before full commitment and flagged coordination with planned EV charging stations at the same park; attribution of the cost-focused male voice is probable but not certain in the ASR.

cases.name: The Gateway (former Mariani Gardens), 45 Bedford Road — license agreements, CBA amendment, and deed-restriction public hearing
cases.applicant: 45 Bedford Road, LLC (Tony Veneziano; Langan/Michael Tucker; architect Ron Hornet; developer JD Summa)
cases.summary: The board received a letter from Veneziano & Associates and revised plans (motion to receive carried) for the 34-townhouse Gateway project, then took up four related items flowing from Planning/Conservation/ARB review: a license to use the Maple Avenue right-of-way for expanded floodplain/stormwater storage, a license to use town land behind the annex (Cornell-Birdsall House) for 2-to-1 wetland-buffer mitigation, an amendment to the community benefit agreement adding $250,000, and a proposed amendment to the town's deed restriction to allow patios and screening fences in the deed-restricted area. Town Attorney Roland advised the deed-restriction change legally requires a public hearing (the licenses and CBA do not); the board leaned toward scheduling that hearing for May 22 and discussed whether to also let the Landmarks Preservation Committee weigh in. Extensive discussion covered future Maple Avenue widening options, density, and the historic meaning of the deed restriction; no final vote on the licenses/CBA is captured in the transcript.
cases.publicComment: Co-Town Historian Sharon Tombach opposed the framing, argued the deed restriction protects the town water supply (not just the church view), urged including the historic-district incursion in the hearing and referral to Landmarks Preservation, and raised campaign-donation/ethics concerns. Resident Ed offered historical footnotes and detailed objections to the license-agreement wording (contractor approval, workmanlike-manner clauses). Tone critical/skeptical.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed hard on preserving the option to widen Maple Avenue and on license-termination/maintenance obligations; objected to the applicant 'coming back for more and more' density via the deed-restricted area, called it a 'self-created problem,' and said he had not decided how to vote and would decide at the public hearing.
"I'm just struggling with using the deed restricted area... it just seems a little presumptuous," objecting to fences and patios (~25% of the site) intruding on the deed-restricted acre.

On record as historically against the residential rezoning ('would have loved a gateway mixed-use'), and disclosed that some in the applicant group backed his campaign, but defended the Planning/Conservation/ARB recommendations as community improvements, called the patios/fences 'reasonable,' and supported scheduling the public hearing while declining to formally refer the buffer work to Landmarks Preservation.

themes.note: Gateway/Mariani townhouse licenses, CBA amendment, and deed-restriction dispute dominated the meeting.
Proposed dog park at Community Park advanced to preliminary planning despite debate over process.
Banksville Rd four-way stop and Byron Brook Place parking law adopted after a well-received trial.
Recurring debate over process: task force vs. work session, public hearings, historic-district referral, and donation/ethics disclosure.
Wetland-buffer and floodplain mitigation on town land tied to the Gateway approvals.
Intersection safety was the core rationale for the traffic local law; blood drive announced.
Historical Society 'Moment in History,' tax-due reminder, Eagle statue repair, mock-trial team rescheduled.

staffInput.summary: Delivered community announcements (taxes due April 30, E-News/Nixle sign-ups, notary hours) and advised that the adopted traffic local law takes about two to three weeks to file with the Department of State before becoming effective; would distribute deed documents from the historian.

Advised that amending the deed restriction (which the zoning code treats fences/patios as 'structures') requires a public hearing, while the license agreements and CBA amendment do not; confirmed the deed restriction's primary intent was understood to protect the church view.
Asked to poll other town administrators on how their dog parks operate and what issues they encountered, and to help coordinate the affected Byron Brook/Banksville homeowner outreach.
Recreation & Parks Superintendent; sponsor of the dog-park memo, directed to develop a preliminary site plan, logistics, and cost estimate for a future work session.
Town Planner; summarized how the Gateway floodplain/wetland-buffer mitigation and licenses moved through the Planning and Conservation boards and addressed Maple Avenue widening feasibility.
Police lieutenant and town consulting engineer presented the Banksville Rd four-way stop design (radius tightening, striping, truck/bus turning templates) and the Byron Brook Place no-parking plan.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels; speakers inferred by role and content. Supervisor Joseph Rende (presiding voice, Banksville resident, campaign-donation disclosure), Councilman Matt Milim (traffic 'very supportive,' Gateway density/widening questions), and Councilwoman Barbara DiGiacinto (dog-park task-force advocate, deed-restriction 'presumptuous') were identified with reasonable confidence. Saleem Hussain appears (a brief Maple Avenue 'historic footnote' remark) but the cost-focused dog-park voice attributed to him is uncertain. Deputy Supervisor Jose Berra could not be distinctly identified in the text, though a quorum was present and all motions carried. Names normalized from ASR (e.g., Digacinto->DiGiacinto). Non-members kept out of member positions: staff/consultants (Allison Simon, Roland, Kevin, Matt Traynor, Adam Kaufman, Tom Cormack, Joe Tramelli, Tony Veneziano, Michael Tucker, Ron Hornet) and residents (Jack Zipper, Molly/Juliette Meyer, Peter Nawara, Robert Sweeney, Sharon Tombach, Ed).

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board reconvened from executive session and opened with two proclamations (Jewish American Heritage Month and adoption of the IHRA working definition of antisemitism) and a recognition of the Byram Hills Speech and Debate Team. The bulk of the meeting was an extended public-comment session dominated by residents alarmed at a wave of vehicle thefts in the Banksville/Windmill area, prompting board discussion of license-plate readers, cameras, patrols, and legislative remedies.
