The board also handled routine business: approval of minutes, several land/petition referrals, a veterinary-use zoning petition it declined to advance, a cycling-event permit, a tax-certiorari consent judgment, $40,000 for the Revolutionary War 250th committee, three Water & Sewer appointments, and liaison updates (including the eagle monument rededication).
meetings.durationNote: Meeting opened 5:30pm and immediately went into executive session (contract, real estate, board/committee interviews) before reconvening; quorum present, no absences noted.

cases.name: Proclamation — May 2024 Jewish American Heritage Month
cases.summary: Supervisor Rende read a proclamation declaring May 2024 Jewish American Heritage Month in the Town of North Castle, developed together with Councilman Matt Milim. The board moved to authorize the Supervisor to sign and date it effective May 8, 2024. Adopted unanimously by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Brought the proclamation forward and read it into the record; asked the board to authorize signing.
Co-developed and helped edit the proclamations with the Supervisor.

cases.name: Proclamation — Adoption of the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism
cases.summary: The board read and adopted a proclamation recognizing the growing problem of antisemitism and adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition, including its 11 contemporary examples, and directing town agencies (including the police department) to make it available as an educational resource. A council member gave an impassioned statement citing FBI hate-crime and ADL statistics and a recent neo-Nazi rally in nearby Greenwich. Adopted unanimously by voice vote effective May 8, 2024.

memberPositions.evidence: Read the proclamation; framed standing against bigotry as a leadership responsibility, invoking his first-generation Italian American immigrant father.
Helped edit the proclamation; thanked by a colleague for the editing work.

cases.name: Recognition — Byram Hills Speech and Debate Team (NYS Forensic League Championship)
cases.summary: The Supervisor recognized members of the Byram Hills Speech and Debate Team and their coach Thomas (Tom) Lustig/Andriello for their performance at the New York State Forensic League Championship, inviting the students to speak and take photos with the board. Students including Aidan Aldaya Lustig (state champion, original oratory) and Valentina Marino described their experiences. A ceremonial recognition with no formal vote.
cases.publicComment: Students spoke warmly about the program and their coach; tone celebratory and appreciative.

memberPositions.evidence: Led the recognition, praising scholastic achievement and calling the students the town's future.
Thanked the students for the courage to speak and called them an inspiration to younger kids.

cases.name: Public Safety — Vehicle Thefts and Police Response
cases.summary: Multiple residents (Jen Clark of Banksville, James Chambers, and Joe Santulo of Smith Farm, whose car was stolen the prior night) urged the board to do more about a wave of brazen vehicle thefts, criticizing 'lock your cars' messaging and lack of visible patrols near the Connecticut border. The board discussed investing in license-plate readers and cameras (with WiFi-coverage cost hurdles), adding patrol officers (two new patrolmen hired), inter-municipal cooperation with Greenwich, and possible legislative remedies. The Supervisor, also a Banksville resident and past victim, committed to bringing a funded proposal to the full board; no vote was taken.
cases.publicComment: Residents were frustrated, frightened, and felt 'forgotten'; one described his 8-year-old asking if the thieves would return. Tone urgent and emotional but respectful; several thanked the board.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it an epidemic, committed to funding plate readers/cameras and more patrols, and noted meetings with the chief and administrator.
Empathized as a past break-in victim herself and thanked residents for bringing concerns firsthand.
As a police liaison, recalled how making 1990s carjackings a federal crime stopped them and suggested a legislative solution plus community letter-writing.
Urged 'creative thinking,' mapping high-risk/repeat-offense neighborhoods and giving the board open visibility into patterns to target resources.

cases.name: Becky Kittredge Memorial Plaque (Gazebo)
cases.summary: Resident Sue Miller followed up on a long-promised plaque honoring former council member Becky Kittredge for the town gazebo, noting it had been approved months earlier but not yet made or installed. The board recalled approving the plaque (changing wording to 'in honor of'). The Supervisor asked Councilwoman DiGiacinto, a close friend of Kittredge, to coordinate getting the plaque made and installed and to plan a small dedication ceremony. No formal vote.
cases.publicComment: Resident Sue Miller was appreciative but pressed the board for follow-through after months of delay.

memberPositions.evidence: Volunteered to coordinate the plaque as Kittredge's dear friend and neighbor; agreed a dedication ceremony would be fitting.
Committed to getting the approved plaque made and installed and thanked the resident for following up.

cases.name: Approval of Minutes — April 24, 2024
cases.summary: The board approved the minutes of the April 24, 2024 meeting by motion and unanimous voice vote.

cases.name: Petition to Amend RB Zoning for a Small Animal (Veterinary) Clinic at 150 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: Petitioner (concierge small animal clinic); via Priscilla Whittington letter
cases.summary: The board received a petition to amend the Roadside Business (RB) zoning district to permit veterinary use for a small 'concierge' animal clinic, along with letters from the petitioner and Planning Director Adam Kaufman. Town Planner Kaufman recounted that the town had prohibited vet use by code amendment in the early 2000s and raised concerns about the location given newly approved adjacent multifamily housing. Councilwoman DiGiacinto strongly opposed amending RB zoning, warning it could open the door to larger 24/7 conglomerate facilities; other members agreed an industrial district might be more appropriate. The board directed Kaufman to inform the applicant the petition was not favorably received and to research how comparable municipalities treat veterinary uses, with no formal vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Very hesitant to amend Roadside Business zoning; cited adjacent multifamily development and the risk of larger conglomerate vet operations.
Noted site-specific issues (narrow driveway) and concurred that the sentiment of members was against amending RB zoning.

cases.name: Farley Request to Acquire Town-Owned Land near 101 Old Hickory Way
cases.address: near 101 Old Hickory Way, Bedford (crossroad connecting Pine Ridge Road to Old Hickory Way)
cases.summary: The board received an April 23, 2024 email from Stefana and Steve Farley regarding roughly 0.334 acres of town-owned property, with a question of whether they sought purchase or adverse possession. The board voted to receive the item and then referred it to Town Attorney Roland to review the file and neighboring property-owner letters and report back at the next meeting.

cases.name: Bonistall Request to Acquire Town-Owned In Rem Lot 101.42-28
cases.address: town-owned lot 101.42-28 (rear lot adjoining the Bonistall residence)
cases.summary: The board received a request from the Bonistalls to acquire a vacant town-owned lot the town obtained through an in rem tax foreclosure (roughly $12,000 in tax arrears accumulated over ~10 years) that the owner wishes to merge into his residence under a covenant against further subdivision. Town Attorney Roland explained the history and noted the assessor should value the parcel with and without the restriction and that any sale cannot be a gift of town funds. The board referred the matter to the town attorney, the assessor, and the Planning Board (highway foreman deemed unnecessary) by motion and vote.

cases.name: Use of Roads and Parks — Jewish Board Cycle of Support Cycling Event (Sept 15, 2024)
cases.applicant: Jewish Board of Family and Children Services
cases.summary: The board considered and approved a request from the Jewish Board of Family and Children Services to use town roads and parks for a 'Cycle of Support' cycling event on Sunday, September 15, 2024. Councilwoman DiGiacinto reiterated the standard condition of no permanent road markings, requiring temporary directional lawn signs, which is now built into the police department application. Approved by motion and unanimous voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Supported the event but insisted on no permanent road markings and use of temporary directional signs.

cases.name: Consent Judgment — ASQ LLC (Armonk Square) v. Assessor (Index 61748/2020)
cases.summary: The board authorized the town attorney to execute a consent judgment in the tax certiorari matter ASQ LLC (Armonk Square) v. Assessor of the Town of North Castle, index 61748/2020. Town Attorney Roland explained the COVID-era equalization-rate decline had pushed the property's valuation out of sync; the settlement reduces the assessment to the appraised value going forward only, with all prior years discontinued at no reduction and current-year refunds waived. Adopted by motion and unanimous voice vote.

cases.name: Authorization of $40,000 for the North Castle Revolutionary War 250th Steering Committee
cases.applicant: North Castle Revolutionary War 250th Steering Committee
cases.summary: The board acted to direct the previously committed $40,000 for the Revolutionary War 250th steering committee through the Parks and Recreation budget line, on Town Attorney Roland's advice that routing funds through a specific department eases state-auditor acceptance. The budget covers roughly $20,000 for a commemorative film/video and $20,000 for new and restored historic signage (including Mount Misery). Committee representative Ed described progress on signage restoration, the video script/filming, a logo, posters, and planned fall fundraising. The board approved instructing the town administrator to have finance make the appropriation by motion and unanimous voice vote.
cases.publicComment: Committee representative Ed reported progress and requested some flexibility in the budget line; tone collaborative and positive.

memberPositions.evidence: Championed the $40,000 appropriation and thanked the committee for its work, framing the film as a legacy for future residents.

cases.name: Probationary Appointments — Water & Sewer Department Skilled Laborers
cases.summary: The board approved, by individual motions and votes, the probationary appointments of Anthony Stevens (effective June 3, 2024), Joseph D. Santesis, and Andrew Sigenga as skilled laborers filling open positions in the Water & Sewer Department. Town Administrator Kevin said he was impressed with the candidates interviewed and glad to fill the openings under superintendent 'Sal.' All appointments adopted unanimously.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved the first appointment and supported filling the Water & Sewer positions.

cases.name: Receipt of Resignation — Allison Miller, Sustainability Committee
cases.summary: The board accepted, with regret and thanks, the resignation of Allison Miller from the Sustainability Committee effective April 27, 2024. The Supervisor noted the town clerk's office sends a formal thank-you letter to departing volunteers on behalf of the board.

memberPositions.evidence: Accepted the resignation with regret and praised the committee's members for their service.

cases.name: Town Board Liaison Updates and Announcements
cases.summary: Council members gave liaison updates: DiGiacinto announced the American Legion Memorial Day ceremony (May 27, 5pm) with poppy sales benefiting veterans and the Armonk Chamber summer concert series (first concert June 20). Berra reported for Parks & Rec that the IBM turf project is advancing with a productive NYS DEC meeting on wetland mitigation and that a draft dog-park plan and rules (with resident Molly Meyer) are ready for a board work session. Milim noted an upcoming Robert De Niro film shoot in North White Plains on May 14. The Supervisor reported major cleanup progress at the Middle Patent transfer site (tasking Berra and the sustainability/conservation boards with a future use and mitigation plan) and announced the restored North Castle eagle monument, with new poles up and a rededication ceremony planned for June 2, including recognition of the original 1976 bicentennial committee and donor companies.

memberPositions.evidence: Announced the Memorial Day poppy ceremony and Armonk Chamber concert series, urging generous support for veterans.
Reported IBM turf project progress with the DEC and a draft dog-park plan; accepted the Supervisor's task to plan future use of the Middle Patent site.
Noted the upcoming Robert De Niro film shoot in North White Plains.
Touted the Middle Patent cleanup and the eagle monument restoration/rededication, proposing markers honoring the 1976 committee and donors.

themes.note: Extended, emotional public comment on vehicle thefts drove most of the meeting; board committed to plate readers, cameras, and more patrols.
Two antisemitism/heritage proclamations, student recognition, RevWar 250th, eagle rededication, and Memorial Day events.
Vet-clinic RB rezoning petition declined; two town-land acquisition requests referred out.
Three Water & Sewer appointments approved; one committee resignation accepted.
$40,000 RevWar appropriation via Parks & Rec and a tax-certiorari consent judgment reducing an assessment.
Middle Patent transfer-site cleanup and future-use planning; DEC wetland mitigation on the turf project.
Tax certiorari settlement, in rem foreclosure land request, adverse-possession question referred to counsel.
Residents felt forgotten on safety; a resident pressed for the long-delayed Kittredge memorial plaque.

staffInput.summary: Delivered community announcements: Byram Hills and Valhalla school-district budget votes May 21, a Byram Hills community facilities event May 14, and reminders about E-News/Nixle alerts and notary services.

Town Planner; recounted the town's early-2000s prohibition of veterinary use, raised location concerns given adjacent multifamily housing, and was directed to inform the applicant the petition was unfavorable and research peer municipalities.

Advised on the in rem foreclosure lot valuation and gift-of-funds limits, the ASQ tax-certiorari consent judgment, routing the RevWar 250th funds through Parks & Rec for auditor acceptance, and agreed to review and report on the Farley land request.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels; the Supervisor (Joseph Rende) presides and speaks most, so his attributions are high-confidence. Councilwoman DiGiacinto is reliably identifiable as the board's only woman and by named references. No absences were noted; all four council members appear to have participated (2024 board: Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra).

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened after an executive session on board/committee interviews, personnel, and real-estate/contract counsel. It promoted Police Officer Stephen Vitolo to Detective, recognized officers and Good Samaritans for a motorcycle-crash water rescue, and heard an extended Police Chief presentation on vehicle thefts, staffing, license plate readers, and frustration with state bail-reform and raise-the-age laws. During public comment a resident announced the OneArmonk nonprofit and another asked for a lower speed limit on North Greenwich Road (Rt 433). The board then held two public hearings: the Summit Club (former Brynwood) request to convert its temporary special use permit to permanent, and a request to amend a town deed restriction at the Gateway (former Mariani Gardens) site to allow privacy fences and patios.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting began 5:30 PM with an immediate executive session (board/committee interviews, personnel, advice of counsel on real estate and contracts), then the public meeting was opened by motion. Quorum present; all five members (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra) appear to have participated. No absences noted.

cases.name: Probationary Promotion of Officer Stephen J. Vitolo to Detective
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Peter Simonson)
cases.summary: Chief Peter Simonson requested board approval to promote Police Officer Stephen Vitolo, employed since 2015 and recently assigned to the Detective Division, to the budgeted position of Detective effective May 25, 2024. The chief cited Vitolo's investigative work (identifying a Romanian theft group), forensic and EMT training, and prior service awards. A motion was made and seconded and the board approved it unanimously by voice vote, followed by congratulations and photographs.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided and praised swearing in/promoting officers as 'always enjoyable... a pleasure'; called for and led the approval motion.

cases.name: Recognition of Exceptional Emergency Response — May 2 Route 22 Motorcycle Crash Rescue
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Peter Simonson)
cases.summary: The chief recounted a May 2, 2024 incident in which a motorcyclist was ejected into the reservoir; Officer Bill Young, off-duty Westchester County Officer Mohammad Shandu, and two civilian Good Samaritans (Elijah Reeves and Steven Sikognagno) kept the victim's head above water and carried him up steep terrain, likely saving his life. The board recognized Officer Young and Officer Shandu (present) and thanked the Good Samaritans (who declined to attend). Every board member offered praise for the police force and the culture within the department; this was a recognition/commendation, not a vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted attending the Westchester County EMS awards with Councilmen Berra and DiGiacinto; 'we're really blessed in this town to have members of our police department that are truly dedicated... I can't thank you enough.'
'I fully agree... so grateful for the police force we have'; compared public safety to health where a good doctor matters.
'I just want to second all of these comments... it's a culture we have in the police department... thank you, Chief, for nurturing that culture.'
Praised the officers' 'moral fiber' in saving a stranger and thanked the chief for the 'incredible narrative' created for the town.

cases.name: Vehicle Thefts, Police Staffing, License Plate Readers & Bail Reform Discussion
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Peter Simonson)
cases.summary: At the supervisor's request the chief presented on a rash of larcenies from vehicles and stolen cars (50 in a decade locally, 40 with keys/fobs left inside; 216 countywide in Q1 2024), urging residents to lock cars and remove fobs. He detailed low staffing (31 officers vs. 44 in Bedford, 40 in New Castle), the department's two existing license plate readers, three more being installed (Nannyhagen/120, Rt 22/Banksville, Bedford-Banksville Rd), and a new state technology grant for additional readers and body cameras. Board members and the chief expressed strong frustration with 2020 bail-reform and raise-the-age laws, urging residents to lobby state legislators; no vote was taken. The board signaled support for funding more readers and increasing police staffing.
cases.publicComment: Resident Jim Gavigan (32-yr Windmill resident) warned the thefts are cartel-driven and worsening nationwide and asked what more can be done; tone concerned/frustrated. Board and chief agreed local tools are limited without state law changes.

memberPositions.evidence: Cited historical staffing (40 budgeted in 2009 vs. 29 at his start, now 31), compared to neighboring towns, said he is 'committed to make some changes' on staffing and met with Latimer, Lawlor, Mayer and Burdick to seek LPR funding for the Rt 22/684 intersection.

Had a 'front row seat' to Friday's high-speed chase off Maple onto Rt 22; grateful for the department's response but 'equally frustrating' that two of three suspects were released without bail hours later; spoke to Sen. Mayer and Assemblyman Burdick about bail reform.

Asked data questions about theft patterns by post to target reader placement; 'I would 100% support the investments we need to make to cover at least 80% of the thefts... that's something we just need to ensure that we support you in doing.'

'I think the bottom line is that we need bail reform... I'm just really furious at bail reform,' citing repeat offenders arrested with no consequences; opposition is to the state law, strong support for local police.
Engaged in the discussion of coordinating with other communities and pressing legislators on bail reform; asked to raise it in his group meetings. Attribution partly inferred.

cases.name: Resident Request to Lower Speed Limit on North Greenwich Road (Route 433)
cases.address: North Greenwich Road / Route 433, Armonk (Nick's Pizza to CT border)
cases.summary: Resident Dr. Salazar reported dangerous speeding on the 45 mph stretch of North Greenwich Road (Rt 433) near a special-needs center, with no sidewalks and children waiting for buses. Town Attorney Roland noted it is a state road, so the town can only request that the state lower the limit. The supervisor said he would have Town Administrator Kevin check with the chief on how a prior reduction (Rt 22/120 from 55 to 50) was achieved and advised the resident to write state representatives; treated as a referral/follow-up item, no vote.
cases.publicComment: Dr. Edgar Salazar (41 North Greenwich Row) urged the board to seek a lower limit for safety of special-needs children and pedestrians; tone earnest/concerned.

memberPositions.evidence: Committed to have the Town Administrator check with the chief on prior state speed-limit reductions and to look into whether the state could lower this limit.
Asked the resident to clarify exactly where the speeding occurs on the road. Attribution of the clarifying question is uncertain.

cases.name: Summit Club (former Brynwood) — Convert Temporary to Permanent Special Use Permit
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners, LLC (attorney Mark Weingarten, Del Bello Donnellan Weingarten Wise & Wiederkehr)
cases.summary: The applicant sought to convert the golf club's temporary special use permit (last extended Dec 2023) to a permanent one, arguing it has completed SEQRA, rezoning, subdivision and the maintenance-facility detail the board requested, and needs a permanent permit to finance the approved 72-unit golf-course community. Neighbors (Garrett Kennedy of 2 Upland Lane, a letter from Bob Green read by Ed Woodyard, Jim Gavigan, Jill O'Dell) strongly opposed, citing early-morning machinery, noise/music events, light and litter, an increase from ~300 to 500 members, and proposed rentable cottages they likened to an Airbnb hotel. The board declined to close the hearing before a holiday weekend, discussed separating the financing-critical permanent elements from the temporary public-use element, and adjourned the hearing to a date certain of June 12 by unanimous voice vote.
cases.publicComment: Heavy resident opposition: Garrett Kennedy detailed repeated ordinance violations, noise, light and litter and asked the permit be denied; a letter from Robert Green (read by Ed Woodyard) urged keeping only a temporary/revocable permit; Jim Gavigan opposed the whole project as changing the town's character; Jill O'Dell asked about noise/lighting code protections. Applicant's counsel disputed credibility and raised the possibility of litigation. Tone: contentious and strongly negative from neighbors.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided, read correspondence into the record, had Planner Kaufman clarify that project parameters were unchanged since ~12 years ago, but agreed the hearing should stay open and be continued to June 12; balanced between moving the long-running project forward and hearing residents.

'I don't think we can rush the public comment portion... I just don't think it's plausible to close the public hearing'; pushed to nail down facts (membership numbers) and to separate financing-critical permanent elements from the temporary public-use piece; cited Bob Green's concern about the interim period before units are built.

Welcomed new residents speaking 'for the first time,' stressed 'crystal clarity on the facts,' wanted to move forward fast while properly considering concerns, and 'strongly differ[ed]' with Barbara and Jose that future condo owners' concerns would match the neighbors'; defended residents' equal right to speak regardless of tenure.

Argued the future $3M condo owners will live closest and 'are going to have the same concerns... they're not going to tolerate pickleball and tennis at 11 o'clock at night,' suggesting self-regulation; noted she had not voted for the original zoning.

Shared the view that on-site residents would have the same concerns and self-regulate; emphasized noise/litter/light must be regulated 'but once it's done, it's done,' and that the applicant is entitled to what has already been approved and litigated. Attribution partly by role/context.

cases.name: Gateway (former Mariani Gardens) — Amend Town Deed Restriction for Fences, Patios & Pavement
cases.address: 45 Bedford Road, Armonk (Gateway / former Mariani Gardens)
cases.applicant: Gateway applicant (attorney Tony Veneziano; engineer Mike Tucker)
cases.summary: The applicant asked the board to amend a deed restriction (barring 'structures') on land the town conveyed, to permit seven six-foot privacy fences and eight roughly 225 sq-ft at-grade stone/paver patios on the eastern side of the 34-townhouse Gateway project — placements driven by the planning board's request to spread the units out. Town Attorney Roland explained the 1962-63 New York City deed restriction (tied to watershed/flood-control protection since rendered obsolete by the Route 22 realignment) and that the town later conveyed to Winkler intending mainly to protect the church viewshed. Residents (Julie DeFilippo of Wampus Close HOA, Ed Woodyard, and Sharon Combach by Zoom) urged denial or continuance, arguing the restriction runs with the land and can only be modified by NYC and warning against a 'camel's nose' precedent. The transcript ends mid-hearing during Combach's statement; no final vote is captured.
cases.publicComment: Julie DeFilippo (Wampus Close HOA president) asked the board not to approve, citing noise and the Armonk 'gateway' viewshed; Ed Woodyard read historical deed/landmark language and warned amending it opens the door to more density; Sharon Combach (Zoom) argued a deed restriction can only be lifted by its maker, New York City, and pressed the board to keep the hearing open. Tone: skeptical/opposed.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed no new patios were added, just a spreading-out per the planning board; said he 'never loved the density' but that decision was made long ago, and he is 'leaning toward it' since fences/at-grade patios don't offend the deed restriction's viewshed intent.

Pressed Attorney Roland on the 1963 NYC agreement ('for park, recreational, flood control... purposes only') and asked why the board should allow the deed-restricted piece to be used for patios and walls, stressing 'it's still a document that runs with the land.'

Recounted the deed history (IBM, Route 22 realignment, 1979 Winkler conveyance) supporting the view that the restriction is outdated and the intent was to protect the church viewshed; noted the more spread-out plan is more open than the former nursery.
Asked what currently sits within the deed-restricted area ('what about 22?') and engaged on the floor-area-ratio/conservation-zoning point. Attribution partly inferred.

themes.note: Detective promotion, emergency-rescue recognition, and a long vehicle-theft/staffing/LPR discussion dominated the first half; strong board support for the department.
Two contested public hearings — Summit Club special use permit and Gateway deed-restriction amendment — with heavy neighbor opposition.
Recurring theme: car-theft quality-of-life impact, speed-limit safety, and noise/light/traffic complaints against both developments.
Board strongly frustrated with state bail-reform and raise-the-age laws; deed-restriction legal interpretation debated at the Gateway hearing.
Neighbors framed Summit Club's rentable cottages as an Airbnb-style hotel and objected to the membership increase.
License plate readers and a new state grant for readers/body cameras endorsed as a key deterrent.
Debate over keeping public hearings open before a holiday weekend; Summit hearing continued to June 12.
Unanimous promotion of Officer Vitolo to Detective.
Resident request to lower the Route 433 speed limit referred to the state/administrator.

staffInput.summary: Police Chief; presented the Vitolo promotion, the emergency-rescue recognition, and the detailed briefing on vehicle thefts, staffing, license plate readers, grant funding, and the impact of bail-reform/raise-the-age laws.

Advised that Route 433 is a state road requiring a state request; explained the legal effect of temporary vs. permanent special use permits (revocation, financing) for Summit; and detailed the history and current legal weight of the NYC-origin Gateway deed restriction.

Town Planner; confirmed Summit Club's parameters were unchanged from ~12 years ago, that lighting/25-ft buffer will be code-compliant, and clarified the 350-to-500 membership figures; on Gateway, confirmed the site plan/patio details and the spreading-out recommendation.
Managed community announcements (Memorial Day ceremony, summer office hours, Lions Club folderol, E-News/Nixle) and administered public-comment sign-ups and receipt of correspondence into the record.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels; the presiding/Supervisor voice (Joseph Rende) is reliably identifiable and Matt Milim is explicitly named ('I thought Matt's statement really well said'). Saleem Hussain, Barbara DiGiacinto and Jose Berra were inferred from context, role, and cross-references (e.g., Saleem 'strongly differ[ing]' with 'Barbara and Jose'), so several member positions carry medium/low confidence. ASR mangled names (Rende as 'Rendez/Endy', DiGiacinto as 'Digacinto', Berra as 'Barra/Barron', Milim as 'Millam/Milam') were normalized to roster spellings. No absences were noted; all five members appear present. Staff/consultants (Chief Simonson, Attorney Roland, Planner Kaufman, Clerk Simon) and residents were kept out of memberPositions. The transcript ends abruptly mid-sentence during the Gateway hearing, so no final Gateway vote is recorded.

meetings.meetingSummary: A marathon Town Board meeting (running past 1:00 a.m.) dominated by a reconvened public hearing on the permanent special use permit for the Summit Golf Club (formerly Brynwood/Canyon Club), where residents pressed for construction-vs-post-construction limits on membership, noise, cottages and a landscape buffer; the board closed the hearing with a 10-day written comment period and scheduled a work session. The board also authorized a Water District 8 Airport Campus water agreement, received the 2023 audit, approved a fund-balance transfer for paving/drainage, and handled numerous land-use bonds and scheduling items. Contested split votes came on reducing AFFH units at the Armonk Close (lumberyard) project (3-2) and on a Community Benefits Agreement for a 12 Maple Avenue restaurant (3-1). Additional business included a discussion to shut down the Middle Patent Yard transfer station, a letter to the County DA on organized auto theft, personnel actions, and a memorial for a Banksville firefighter.
meetings.durationNote: Full board of five; Saleem Hussain participated remotely via Zoom from Washington D.C. and dropped off at 12:50 a.m., missing the final 12 Maple CBA vote. Meeting ran past 1:00 a.m. Town Clerk Allison Simon was away; Maria Scharf filled in.

cases.name: Summit Golf Club — Permanent Special Use Permit (Public Hearing)
cases.applicant: Del Bello, Donnellan, Weingarten, Weiss & Whitaker LLP (Summit Golf Club)
cases.summary: Reconvened public hearing on a permanent SUP to operate the golf club, allow public use during residential construction, and govern members, cottages, camps, and events. Applicant offered concessions: cottages limited to members/guests (no Airbnb), 500 members kept consistent with the old Canyon Club, outdoor music cut off at 9 p.m. until an amenities building is built, compliance with the town noise ordinance, sunset of public golf at 12/31/29, and cottages capped at 20 bedrooms (10 cottages). Residents (Garrett Kennedy, Elon Keller, Andrew Lester, Alan Blum, Jim Gavigan) argued the SUP must separate the multi-year construction phase from post-construction, enforce the 25-foot landscape buffer, and not permanently codify 500 members/public golf that were never environmentally studied (study assumed ~350 golf members). After extended debate the board voted to close the public hearing with a 10-day written comment period and to hold a work session; members will submit comment points to planner Adam Kaufman within a week.
cases.publicComment: Heavy resident participation, largely critical/concerned: neighbors demanded phasing, the 25-foot buffer, noise limits and no permanent public-golf/500-member codification; a few (Linda Fernberg) were more sympathetic and downplayed traffic fears. Tone tense at times.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided; pushed to close the hearing and resolve issues in a work session; forcefully rejected resident 'fear mongering' about safety/drugs near the school, calling the project a studied, beneficial luxury golf community the board should refine, not stop.

Pressed the 350-vs-500 membership question and noise/pickleball/buffer concerns; called the members-only cottage concession significant; urged closing the hearing and holding a structured work session with a bulleted agenda.

Raised the 25-foot buffer, outdoor social-event noise, pickleball and tennis-light impacts; proposed allowing cottages/pickleball/amplified music only after the landscape buffer is installed; flagged valet/overflow parking onto residential streets.

From Zoom, said he had ~9 follow-up points, wanted clarity on what a 'member' is and how to bar Airbnb, and favored keeping the hearing open to capture more public input on the significant changes discussed.
Questioned whether cottage/room counts (14 studied vs 20 in zoning) and on-site employee housing were consistent with the environmental record; probed the FEIS assumptions.

cases.name: Water District 8 — Airport Campus Extension Contribution & Capital Expenditure Agreement
cases.applicant: Airport Campus developer (counsel Chris Carthy team) / KSCJ Consulting
cases.summary: Second read of the water district contribution and capital expenditure agreement following the prior extension of Water District 8 to include the airport campus. The board received the KSCJ Consulting cost memo (June 5, 2024) and authorized the Supervisor to sign the agreement, which uses privately financed development to build out public water (Westchester Joint Waterworks) and lays groundwork to interconnect with Water District 4. Counsel projected closing/construction around 2025 subject to DOT and DEP approvals.

memberPositions.evidence: Called municipal water a 'blessing' and 'monumental moment,' recalling water superintendent Sal's dream of bringing WJWW water to District 4.
Thanked applicant for document revisions; noted John Kellart's numbers were 'less comfortable' but relied on good-faith-and-fair-dealing duty and voted to proceed: 'let's get it done.'
From Zoom: 'nothing bad... this is going to be a great project for the town.'
Asked about DOT crossing/entry logistics and offered congratulations, supporting the agreement.

cases.name: 2023 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report & Audit Presentation
cases.summary: The Bonadio Group (Michael Connolly, with partner Joe by video) presented the FY2023 audit, reporting an unmodified (clean) opinion consistent with prior years, no new GASB implementations, and no disagreements with management. The Town Justice Court agreed-upon-procedures report was still being finalized. Comptroller Abbas reported a strong fund balance (~$25.6M general/highway/library, ~$23M after committing ~$2.6M) and reminded the board that ARPA funds must be committed by year-end. Received as a presentation.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked the auditors and staff; no member raised concerns, board reported no questions on the financials.

cases.name: Fund-Balance Transfer for Town Paving & Drainage Projects
cases.summary: Authorization of a fund-balance transfer (~$1.2M) for three unbudgeted projects, chiefly a large Maple Avenue drainage/pipe-lining job plus additional paving (including the Windmill entrance and continuation of last year's lumberyard-area paving). Berra questioned whether much paving remained and asked for a detailed breakdown; Milim proposed authorizing now and getting the itemized breakdown at the next meeting. Approved on that basis, with staff to return with detail.

memberPositions.evidence: Wanted clarity on the paving/drainage scope, noting the town should be largely done paving and this is 'not an insignificant amount of money'; asked for a breakdown before/after voting.
Suggested authorizing the transfer now but requiring a breakdown of the $1.2M at the next meeting.

cases.name: Armonk Barber Pole — Landmark Designation (Schedule Public Hearing)
cases.summary: Received the LPC recommendation to landmark the historic Armonk barber pole and scheduled a public hearing for July 10, 2024. Members confirmed the business owner is enthusiastic and asked that owner consent/maintenance documentation be delivered to the Town Attorney before the hearing; the designation is understood to cover the pole itself.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed owners are 'very enthusiastic' and would provide written consent; supported setting the hearing.

cases.name: Orchard Roll Road Subdivision — New Town Road Naming
cases.summary: Recommendation of the Road Naming Committee for naming a new town road (with E-911 coordinator notification). Because the item arrived late and Saleem Hussain had not had time to review it with the committee, he moved to table it to a later meeting (June 26). Tabled.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the item came in late and he wanted to discuss it offline; moved to table it rather than act without review.

cases.name: Breezemont Day Camp (HZBR LLC) — Special Use Permit (Schedule Public Hearing)
cases.summary: Received the special use permit application and short-form EAF (Part 1) for operation of a summer day camp, now permitted after the town recently legalized day camps. The board scheduled the public hearing, coordinating with the Planning Board (July 8) and setting the town board hearing for July 10, 2024; not time-sensitive since operation would begin next summer.

cases.name: Base Space Armonk (100 Business Park Drive) — Wetland Mitigation Bond & Agreement
cases.applicant: WMG Armonk Warehouse Owner LLC / KSCJ Consulting
cases.summary: Received the KSCJ Consulting recommendation to establish a new wetland mitigation bond followed by a five-year monitoring/maintenance bond, and (per a June 5, 2024 letter) authorized the Supervisor to sign the wetland mitigation planting, maintenance and monitoring bond agreement with WMG Armonk Warehouse Owner LLC. Approved routinely.

cases.name: Gateway Residential Development — One-Year SUP Extension
cases.summary: Request for a one-year extension of the special use permit granted June 28, 2023; the Planning Board had just granted site plan approval two nights earlier. The board approved the extension. Milim noted he had opposed the project all along but saw no basis to deny the extension and voted in favor reluctantly.

memberPositions.evidence: 'I've opposed this project all along, but I don't think there's a basis to turn down an extension... reluctantly I'm going to vote in favor.'

cases.name: Greenwich Realty Group — Zoning Text Amendment for Light Industrial Use (Schedule Public Hearing)
cases.applicant: Greenwich Realty Group, LLC (counsel Tony Veneziano)
cases.summary: Received county and town Planning Department letters on a proposed zoning text amendment to permit light industrial use (woodworking and iron/aluminum assemblage) by special use permit in the GB General Business district; the Planning Board gave a positive recommendation. The board scheduled the public hearing for June 26. Members flagged that the drafted use language is broad and asked to tour the site before the hearing, citing an observed active/disturbing operation and environmentally sensitive wetlands to the rear. Barbara DiGiacinto recused herself (her husband owns 25% of Band Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property).

memberPositions.evidence: A self-described 'Doubting Thomas,' recounted seeing active equipment/operations on a Saturday and pushed to tour the site and pin down an operational plan before approving.
Worried the wording ('metal fabricating and wood processing') is 'so broad it could change,' wanting limits on people, storage and outside activity at this environmentally sensitive site.
Recused herself due to her husband's ownership interest in Band Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property.

cases.name: Armonk Close (Lumberyard) — Reduce AFFH Units from Four to Two
cases.applicant: Developer (Mike Ferrari / Nikki, per May 31 letter)
cases.summary: Developer sought confirmation that, having reached over 80% completion (verified by the building inspector), the affordable (AFFH) requirement drops from 20% (four units) to 10% (two units), so its offering plan can be filed with the Attorney General. Hussain and Berra objected that the justification rested on the applicant's own attorney's letter rather than a direct AG statement, and that the letter's '0?' reference was confusing; Hussain wanted a commitment this was the last AFFH request. DiGiacinto and Milim held the reduction was clearly earned and appropriate. Adopted 3-2 by roll call (Milim aye, DiGiacinto aye, Hussain no, Berra no, Rende yes), with an added recital that the developer is well beyond 80% complete.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued they merely seek to reduce 20% to 10% as agreed and that asking anything more 'is not appropriate or fair'; added the 80%-complete recital and voted aye.
Said he saw 'no downside to the town,' it helps the developer finish and sell, and it's obvious the deadline will be met; voted aye.
Framed it as a reasonable accommodation for a project well advanced toward completion; made/supported the motion and voted yes.
Voted no; found no direct AG statement that the plan couldn't be filed, the '0?' unexplained, and wanted a guarantee it was the last AFFH-related request before changing the agreement.
Voted no: 'I don't think this makes sense. I've got other concerns about it'; was 'totally convinced they did not meet the standard' as written.

cases.name: Wetland Mitigation & Construction Performance Bonds (Yip, CG East Lane/Turret, Whippoorwill Hills)
cases.address: 20 Green Valley Road; East Lane; 345 Main St / Log Cabin Way / Cider Mill, Armonk
cases.summary: Routine bond actions on KSCJ Consulting recommendations: established a wetland mitigation bond and five-year monitoring bond for the Elaine Yip residential project (20 Green Valley Road); renewed construction performance and wetland mitigation bonds for CG East Lane LLC (Turret subdivision, East Lane); and released the landscape maintenance and two-year monitoring bonds for the Whippoorwill Hills HOA (345 Main Street) after confirmed plantings. All approved without controversy.

cases.name: Salt Domes Replacement/Repair — Emergency Authorization
cases.summary: After discussion in executive session about structural issues with the salt dome(s), the board opted to proceed under an emergency authorization rather than a normal competitive bid. Approved conditionally on receiving a written letter from the Town Administrator/Highway detailing the work, cost, and the reasons the emergency justifies bypassing the bid process.

memberPositions.evidence: Moved to proceed under emergency authorization conditioned on a written justification: 'I think it's dangerous and we need to move on it.'

cases.name: Middle Patent Yard — Transfer Station Cleanup & Future Use (Discussion)
cases.address: Middle Patent Road (Water District No. 2 property, ~74 acres)
cases.summary: Discussion, requested by DiGiacinto, of the cleanup and effective shutdown of the Middle Patent Yard as an informal transfer/compost station. Records showed the town paid ~$89,300 (2023) and ~$43,062 (2024) in dumping fees to remove accumulated material, plus ~8,000 cubic yards of highway millings and other prohibited material stored there. Rende and Milim argued the expanded use was never authorized (a 1990s-era resolution allows only leaf composting), posed environmental risk to a water source, and should end; DiGiacinto agreed cleanup was overdue but pressed for cost/impact data on lost yard-waste services before closing. A sharp exchange erupted between Milim and DiGiacinto over past positions. The board agreed to refer future use to the Conservation Board and Open Space Committee for a possible restoration/passive-recreation plan.
cases.publicComment: Conservation Board member George Drapeau attended and will coordinate a site visit; no residents spoke on the item.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the millings/expanded use illegal and harmful to a water source, said you don't need a vote to stop an illegal use, and welcomed ending it; clashed with DiGiacinto over her prior record.
Pleased with cleanup but insisted the board obtain data on the cost/service impact (bagged-leaf pickup, longer hauls to Bedford/Buffamonte) before shutting the yard; objected to being 'maligned.'
Detailed the removal costs and history, favored restoring the site to a natural state with possible passive recreation, and referred it to the Conservation Board and Open Space Committee.

cases.name: Letter to Westchester County DA Miriam Rocca on Organized Auto Theft Rings
cases.applicant: Town Board (drafted by Councilman Milim, with Councilman Berra)
cases.summary: Authorization for board members to sign a letter to Westchester County DA Miriam E. Rocca expressing grave concern over organized auto theft rings from Connecticut, citing high-speed chases (120+ mph), a rammed police car, and near-misses in downtown Armonk. The letter urges tougher prosecution, enhanced penalties, and resources, treating public-safety-impacting property crimes seriously (including bail and prosecutorial discretion for youthful vs. adult offenders). Adopted with minor edits (delete 'in particular,' pluralize 'communities,' accent on Berra's name).

memberPositions.evidence: Principal author; urged targeted bail-reform advocacy and full prosecutorial use of discretion, stressing high-speed chases are more than property crimes.
Backed the letter, emphasizing the assigned ADA's plea-negotiation discretion and the value of a unified board signature; wanted the letter kept focused on North Castle.
Co-authored the letter and proposed edits broadening it to note the countywide nature of the problem; supported adoption.
From Zoom, said he was fine with the letter as drafted and with the changes.

cases.name: Community Benefits Agreement — 12 Maple Avenue Restaurant
cases.applicant: Remix / 12 Maple Owner LLC (counsel Tony Veneziano; Stefan Martinovich)
cases.summary: Authorization for the Supervisor to sign a Community Benefits Agreement providing $100,000 (over seven years) plus parking mitigations for a ~3,600 sq ft restaurant, after the ZBA waived 33 of 48 required spaces and the Planning Board conditioned site plan approval on a CBA. Berra objected that Section 2F's transfer language guts the acceleration provision and pressed to personally review the private parking leases; DiGiacinto objected to the seven-year (front-loaded gap) schedule, the $100,000 amount, and valet-parking impacts on Armonk Square, and also wanted the leases. Applicant argued total mitigation value (~$2.1M) far exceeds comparable CBAs. Adopted 3-1 by roll call (Milim aye, Berra aye, DiGiacinto no, Rende yes; Hussain had dropped off Zoom), conditioned on board members viewing the leases by June 18, moving the payment schedule up one year, and adding an anti-precedent sentence.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued Section 2F 'eviscerates' the transfer-acceleration provision and demanded to see the private parking leases as a town board member; negotiated but ultimately voted aye.
Called the seven-year payment schedule 'unprecedented' with no payment in years one-two, thought $100,000 too low, worried valet-averse diners would overflow onto other businesses; voted no.

'Begrudgingly' yes; said the Verizon lot costs the town a lot, $100,000 may not offset the impact, and wished police concerns were addressed, but valued the restaurant as an asset; made the motion and voted aye.
Facilitated the deal after multiple drafts with counsel, proposed the lease-review/payment-acceleration/anti-precedent conditions, and voted yes.

cases.name: School, Camp, License & Wetland Bond Agreements (Consent Batch)
cases.address: Byram Hills schools; 14 Tall Woods Road, Armonk
cases.applicant: Byram Hills Central School District; NYS DEC; various
cases.summary: Batch of routine authorizations for the Supervisor to sign: an MOU with Byram Hills for a School Resource Officer for 2024-25; summer camp use agreements/leases for Crittenden Middle School and Wampus Elementary (June-August 2024); an agreement with Kristen Youngers and Michelle Starr on a wetland mitigation bond at 14 Tall Woods Road; and an amendment to the NYS DEC license-issuing-agent agreement for hunting and fishing licenses. All approved without dissent.

cases.name: Personnel — Retirement, Appointment & Committee Resignation
cases.summary: Accepted the retirement resignation of Detective Sergeant Kevin Finetti (effective July 30, 2024); approved the probationary appointment of Danielle D. Thomas as Senior Office Assistant in the Building Department (effective June 13, 2024); and accepted, with regrets, the resignation of Melissa Horowitz from the Landmark Preservation Committee (effective June 23, 2024). The board noted thank-you letters are sent to departing volunteers.

cases.name: Memorial — Banksville Firefighter Preston Presley
cases.summary: The board closed in memory of Preston Presley, a Banksville firefighter since 1971 and Banksville Community House coach, remembered as a genuine, community-minded person; condolences extended to the family and a letter to be sent. Meeting adjourned.

memberPositions.evidence: Delivered the closing memorial recognition of firefighter Preston Presley and will obtain the family's address for a condolence letter.

themes.note: Dominant thread: Summit Golf Club SUP, Greenwich Realty amendment, Gateway/AFFH, day camp, and multiple bonds/scheduling items.
Noise, buffers, parking overflow, traffic and safety near schools drove much of the Summit and CBA debate.
12 Maple CBA, salt-dome emergency, water agreement, and numerous bond/lease authorizations.
Middle Patent Yard cleanup and wetland mitigation bonds, weighed against a water-source protection focus.
Water District 8 airport-campus extension hailed as a path to municipal water for District 4.
DA letter on auto theft rings, SRO MOU, and a firefighter memorial.
Clean 2023 audit, strong fund balance, and a paving/drainage fund-balance transfer.
Maple Avenue drainage and paving projects, with a member asking for a cost breakdown.
AFFH reduction split the board; Airbnb limits on Summit cottages debated.
Recurring procedural friction over public-hearing closure, comment periods, recusal, and access to private leases.
A police retirement, a Building Department appointment, and an LPC resignation.
Folderol appreciation, barber-pole landmark scheduling, and the firefighter memorial.

staffInput.summary: Town Planner; gave the overview of the Summit SUP history (positive declaration, DEIS/FEIS, findings, current 73-unit/scaled-golf plan), explained special-permit basics, membership assumptions (~300-350 studied), parking-variance math (61-space credit), and will compile the members' comment points into a work-session agenda.

Sitting Town Attorney; advised closing the Summit hearing with a 10-day comment period, framed the AFFH reduction as a self-executing confirmation the standard was met, negotiated the 12 Maple CBA transfer/lease provisions and reviewed the confidential parking leases, confirmed the salt-dome emergency requires a written justification letter, and clarified the Middle Patent leaf-only authorization.
Provided fund-balance transfer detail for paving/drainage and the salt-dome emergency work; furnished Middle Patent Yard removal invoices; coordinated site access.
Comptroller/Finance Director; reported strong fund balance (~$23M net after commitments), thanked the auditors, and flagged that ARPA funds must be committed by year-end.
External auditors presented the FY2023 audit with an unmodified (clean) opinion, no new GASB, and no management disagreements; Town Justice Court agreed-upon-procedures report still pending.
Water/Sewer superintendent; by email/conversation provided the Middle Patent Yard's purchase history (bought by the water district) and described how the composting footprint grew over the years.
Acting/filling in for Town Clerk Allison Simon; handled motions receipt, records, and correspondence for the meeting.

meetings.attributionNote: Raw ASR with no speaker labels; the Supervisor's presiding voice (Joseph Rende, mangled as 'Rendezvous/Endy/Randy') and roll-call votes anchored attribution. Two roll calls disambiguated members: AFFH 3-2 (Milim aye, DiGiacinto/'Digacinto' aye, Hussain/'Hussein' no, Berra/'Bera/Barra' no, Rende yes) and the 12 Maple CBA 3-1 (Milim aye, Berra aye, DiGiacinto no, Rende yes; Hussain dropped off Zoom at 12:50 a.m.). Saleem Hussain participated remotely and was intermittently cut off. Some Summit public-hearing remarks by residents (e.g., a lawyer citing ROWI general-counsel history) were kept in publicComment rather than risk mis-attributing them to a member. No Sonny Vataj (2026 only). Non-members Adam Kaufman, Roland, Kevin, Abbas, Sal and the Bonadio auditors were routed to staffInput.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened with a lengthy work session on the Summit Club (formerly Brynwood) permanent special use permit, working through areas of concern with the developer and town planner Adam Kaufman one at a time: guest-cottage ownership, event noise, public golf-course use during construction, membership numbers, parking, day camp, pickleball, water sampling and Audubon certification. The regular meeting then handled a recused public hearing on 23 Bedford Banksville Road, amended and approved the June 12 minutes, authorized a wetland-mitigation license/bond for the Levine property, scheduled July 24 public hearings for the Hillside Church/Little Sparrows nursery school and a local law prohibiting battery energy storage systems, named a new town road, sold a landlocked town parcel, and approved a police/highway radio system and a Westchester Joint Water Works agreement. It closed with resignations, committee appointments, liaison updates, an executive session and a memorial for community volunteer David Ashliff.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting began 5:30 PM, adjourned immediately into a Summit Club work session, then resumed the regular meeting; all five members present (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Milim, Berra). DiGiacinto recused herself from the 23 Bedford Banksville Road public hearing (family financial interest via Ban Monk Realty). Board went into executive session at the end for real-estate/advice-of-counsel matters.

cases.name: Summit Club (formerly Brynwood) — Permanent Special Use Permit Work Session
cases.address: Route 22 / Upland Avenue, Armonk (Summit Club golf course)
cases.applicant: Summit Club / developer 'Jeff' (Metropolitan Golf Group), attorney Mark Weingarten
cases.summary: Extended work session (no vote) to resolve outstanding conditions for the permanent special use permit covering the maintenance building, guest cottages and continued public golf-course use during construction of 73 residential units. The board reached near-consensus on most items: no-kitchen guest cottages limited to 20 bedrooms, a 9 PM amplified-music curfew until the amenities building is built (then the standard town noise ordinance, with events sited behind the building), public play ending October 2026 with yearly extensions, a 100-per-day day camp, deferred pickleball, water sampling per SEQRA findings, and Audubon certification applied for by April 1. The unresolved item was cottage ownership — the developer wants to pre-sell/lease units to members or passive investors placed in a management-company rental pool, while DiGiacinto and Berra worried about losing control; a no-public-posting restriction was floated as a compromise. Noise was the most contentious: Berra pushed for a stricter 'no distinctly audible noise beyond the property line' standard while the applicant and Milim argued that was legally unworkable and singled the club out. Formal action (Old Business B) was tabled for the town attorney and planner to codify the discussed terms into a resolution for a future meeting; the developer's late request to revive 88 (vs. 73) residential units was ruled out of scope.
cases.publicComment: Public hearing already closed; a few residents present but no public comment taken. Supervisor noted written comments received from Ed Woodyard, Kevin Devaney Jr., Stephen Condon, Sue Scheimer (excluded as late), Garrett Kennedy and Elon/Lon Keller. Developer disparaged neighbor Garrett Kennedy as a serial complainer, prompting a decorum reminder from Hussain.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided and steered toward resolution; thanked the applicant for removing parking-lot materials and argued 'nothing has changed in 60 years' of club use; kept the 88-unit request out of scope.

Moderated the session and played 'devil's advocate' for the applicant — argued the club-as-manager protects against bad guests regardless of who owns the cottages, and as police liaison said fears of hourly noise complaints were unrealistic.

Most resistant on noise — pressed for a stricter 'no distinctly audible noise beyond the property line' standard because the club is a for-profit venue holding frequent events, and shared DiGiacinto's unease about investor ownership of cottages.
Preferred the planner's club-owned-cottages language, worried about 'losing control' if investors buy and lease units; but found the applicant's 9 PM music limit acceptable and 'part of summer.'

Asked repeated clarifying questions on membership/guest/cottage definitions and proposed the no-public-posting compromise; publicly urged the developer to stay respectful of residents in the public forum.

cases.name: Public Hearing — 23 Bedford Banksville Road
cases.summary: A noticed public hearing on 23 Bedford Banksville Road was opened and immediately adjourned to a date uncertain because the applicant felt they were not fully ready. DiGiacinto recused herself due to a family financial interest — her husband John DiGisono owns 25% of Ban Monk Realty, which holds a mortgage on the property. The board opened and adjourned by voice votes.

memberPositions.evidence: Recused herself, citing that her husband owns 25% of Ban Monk Realty which holds a mortgage on the property.

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — June 12, 2024
cases.summary: Milim objected to minutes language stating the board 'resolved to confirm that the applicant has met the standard' to reduce the AFFH affordable-unit count from 20% to 10% (4 units to 2) on the Mock Glen project. He stated he had said clearly the applicant did NOT meet the standard but that the board was making a reasonable accommodation because the project was over 80% complete. The offending language was struck so the minutes read that the board 'agreed to allow the developer to reduce the number of AFFH units from 4 to 2.' Amended minutes approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Refused to vote until minutes were corrected — 'I don't want the record to say that we believe they met the standard. I said clearly that they did not meet the standard,' while accepting the accommodation.
Agreed with Milim's correction and framed the change as making an accommodation based on the project being over 80% complete.

cases.name: Levine Residential Project — Wetland Mitigation License Agreement & Bond, 11 Piping Brook Lane
cases.summary: The board received the town engineer's (KSCG/J) recommendation to establish a wetland mitigation bond and a five-year monitoring/maintenance bond after an encroachment of roughly 23,680 sq ft into a conservation easement abutting the Levine property. It authorized the Supervisor to sign a license agreement (already signed by Levine and the abutting owner) allowing remediation work, with the Conservation Board having approved at least 2-for-1 mitigation. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether mitigation was at least 2-for-1 and confirmed Conservation Board approval before stating he was satisfied.

cases.name: Hillside Church / Little Sparrows Nursery School — Special Use Permit Modification
cases.applicant: Hillside Church of the Christian Missionary Alliance (attorney Stephen Veneruso)
cases.summary: The board received the application to modify an existing special use permit to legalize the Little Sparrows nursery school operating six classrooms when the permit only allowed two — discovered during interior renovation permitting. The school (~60 children) also needs one likely variance for outdoor-recreation-space square footage (code requires 200 sq ft per child). The board scheduled a public hearing for July 24 and referred the application to the town and county planning boards, coordinating timing with the ZBA (meeting July 11) so the applicant can resolve everything before the September school year.

memberPositions.evidence: Worked to sequence the referral, ZBA and public hearing so the school could be legalized before September, emphasizing avoiding snags for the applicant's time constraint.

cases.name: Local Law to Prohibit Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS)
cases.applicant: Town Board / Town Planner Adam Kaufman & Town Attorney Roland
cases.summary: The board received a draft local law (with short EAF parts 1-3, a negative declaration and lead-agency intent) to strengthen the definition of 'public utility' so that battery energy storage systems cannot be claimed as public utilities and thus effectively prohibited, prompted by a dispute in neighboring Mount Kisco. The attorney flagged that a stronger version (modeled on the Town of Evans) should also define the different BESS levels. The board declared itself lead agency, referred the law to planning boards, and scheduled a July 24 public hearing. Extended discussion centered on fire risk (volunteer fire departments cannot safely fight BESS fires) versus renewable-energy benefits; the board consensus is that the risks currently outweigh the benefits.

memberPositions.evidence: Stressed the fire departments' request not to allow BESS and that a for-profit arbitrage facility offers minimal town benefit against a fire that 'can last a month or more.'

Fully backed denying BESS but asked repeatedly to see 'the other side of the argument' — examples of towns with significant installations — before the public hearing, to be sure the record covers both risks and benefits.

As a former power-utilities analyst explained BESS economics (off-peak/on-peak arbitrage, better paired with wind), concluding the reward is real but minimal and not captured by North Castle while it bears all the risk.
Recounted the prior King Street application and fire-department opposition and urged moving forward to prohibit BESS now, revisiting the code in the future.

cases.name: Road Naming — Israel Townsend Hill (Orchard Road Subdivision)
cases.summary: The board considered the Road Naming Committee's first-choice recommendation to name a new road 'Israel Townsend Hill,' honoring a Quaker patriot buried on the property whose family were town founders. Hussain objected on principle to naming roads after individuals (citing unknown historical complexities and the risk of later reappraisal) and urged instead the committee's agreed second choice 'Townsend Farm Hill,' plus a referral to the Conservation Board and board guidance/liaison for future namings. Milim, Rende and Ed Woodyard resisted micromanaging the committee. Milim moved to adopt 'Israel Townsend Hill'; it passed 4-1 on a roll call with Hussain voting no. The board agreed to appoint Hussain as liaison to the Road Naming Committee.

memberPositions.evidence: Voted NO; argued for 'Townsend Farm Hill' to honor the family rather than one man, wanted rigorous character vetting and Conservation Board input, and warned people read road signs by literal interpretation, not intent.

Made the motion for 'Israel Townsend Hill,' opposed referrals as micromanaging the committee, and argued a historically significant figure should be recognized despite the impossibility of perfect vetting.
Voted aye and cautioned against micromanaging committees, saying a knowledgeable Road Naming Committee plus a board liaison suffices without Conservation Board referral.
Voted aye ('I'm fine with the Israel Townsend Hill').
Voted aye while noting mild reservation about 'Hill' and saying Hussain's ideas could be considered in future liaison work.

cases.name: Offer to Purchase ~1 Acre Town-Owned Property Contiguous to 21 Windmill Road
cases.address: Lot 101.42-2-8, contiguous to 21 Windmill Road, Armonk
cases.summary: The board accepted an offer (over $50,000, against ~$12,000 in back taxes) from the Bonistalls to purchase a landlocked ~1-acre town parcel acquired via in-rem foreclosure that the family had always believed they owned. The buyer will merge it into their residence lot and sign a covenant against future subdivision, avoiding a 'house behind a house' scenario; the Planning Board recommended the merger 5-0. Resolution adopted subject to permissive referendum. Berra supported this unique, sympathetic case but insisted the town develop a fair, transparent process (notifying residents/neighbors) for any future sales of town property.

memberPositions.evidence: Supported this 'unique, sympathetic' sale but pressed that in future the town should notify residents/neighbors and follow a rational, fair process rather than deciding on its own.
Agreed the parcel is unique and sympathetic (buyer thought he owned it; over $50K price vs. ~$12K taxes) and supported the merger-plus-covenant while agreeing to improve the process.

cases.name: Two-Way Radio Communication System — Metrocom Wireless (Police & Highway)
cases.applicant: Metrocom Wireless Incorporated (via Town Administrator Kevin)
cases.summary: The board approved and authorized the Supervisor to sign a Metrocom Wireless proposal (off state bid, meeting procurement policy) to replace the town's 20-year-old analog police radios with an encrypted digital system, funded from general-fund balance. The system brings the Highway Department onto the same network so police and highway can communicate directly during storms and emergencies, and eliminates dead spots where cell service fails. Approved by voice vote.

memberPositions.evidence: Highlighted that highway and police currently cannot communicate directly during storms and that the system removes communication dead spots; called it overdue.
As police liaison relayed Chief Simonson's view that it is important and necessary public safety, moved/seconded approval, noting the newest current equipment is 20 years old.

cases.name: Westchester Joint Water Works Agreement — Water District No. 8 (Airport Campus Extension)
cases.applicant: Town / Westchester Joint Water Works (Town Attorney Roland, Superintendent Sal)
cases.summary: The board approved and authorized the Supervisor to sign the Westchester Joint Water Works agreement creating Water District No. 8 (Airport Campus extension), described as the final piece securing a water supply for the airport campus property. Approved by voice vote; Supervisor thanked the attorney, Sal and others.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the agreement 'the final piece of the puzzle' giving the town a water supply — 'this is big' — and thanked staff who worked on it.

cases.name: Resignations and Committee Appointments
cases.summary: The board received resignations from James Worthman (Highway Department, eff. June 25) and Alec Tobia (Police Department, eff. June 24) — with the Administrator confirming exit interviews are conducted — and made several appointments: Ed Woodyard and Nora Manueli to the Landmark Preservation Committee (three-year terms), and Elisa (surname uncertain), Doug Mancinelli and Kate Hall to the Open Space Committee. The Landmarks appointments were expedited to ensure a quorum could bless the wording of a memorial plaque for Becky (gazebo dedication targeted for an August summer concert). All approved by voice vote.

themes.note: Dominated by the Summit Club special use permit work session, plus Hillside Church, road naming and the town-parcel sale.
Special use permits for the Summit Club and the Little Sparrows nursery school.
Cottage-ownership control and event-noise impacts on Summit Club neighbors were the sharpest disputes.
Battery-storage prohibition, Levine wetland mitigation, Audubon certification and water supply.
Minutes correction, road-naming committee guidance/liaison, and calls for a fair process on town-property sales and elections/voting information.
Police/highway radio upgrade and volunteer fire-department concerns driving the BESS ban.
Water District No. 8 airport-campus extension approved; Summit Club water withdrawal permit; sewer-line jetting.
Metrocom radio system and Westchester Joint Water Works agreement.
Two resignations and five committee appointments.
Summit Club Airbnb-style guest cottages and the Mock Glen AFFH affordable-unit reduction in the minutes.
Memorial for volunteer David Ashliff, Becky memorial plaque, and Modern Barn wine award.

staffInput.summary: Town Planner; framed each Summit Club issue with a staff-recommended solution, drafted the battery-storage local law and the road-naming/land-use referrals, and coordinated the nursery-school review timeline.

Advised on the noise-ordinance limits and special-permit standards for the Summit Club, drafted and recommended strengthening the BESS 'public utility' definition (Town of Evans model), and explained the permissive-referendum mechanism and in-rem foreclosure background for the town-parcel sale.

Presented the Metrocom radio proposal (off state bid, encrypted digital, bringing highway onto the network), reported paving on Route 128 and Virginia Road, sewer-line jetting in District 2, a maintenance-mechanic opening, and confirmed exit interviews are conducted.

Gave a community announcement on primary-election logistics and voter-information resources on the town website, and assisted the nursery-school applicant with scheduling; will handle referral and document execution.
Water/Sewer superintendent acknowledged for work on the Westchester Joint Water Works Water District No. 8 agreement.

Jose Berra (Councilman, present all of 2024) was disambiguated from Supervisor 'Joe' Rende by role: Berra was the member pushing for a stricter noise standard and questioning the parcel-sale process, addressed as 'Jose.' Non-members correctly routed out of memberPositions: developer 'Jeff'/Mark Weingarten (applicant), Adam Kaufman (planner), Roland (attorney), Kevin (administrator), Allison Simon (clerk), Ed Woodyard (Road Naming Committee, not the councilman), and attorneys Hollis, Veneruso. Sonny Vataj not attributed (joined 2026). All five members present; DiGiacinto recused from the 23 Bedford Banksville Road public hearing.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Town Board swore in new police officer Matthew Giannella, heard a county update from Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins, and held public hearings on the Breezemont Day Camp special use permit and a landmark designation for the Armonk Barber Pole. The board's longest debates concerned the Summit Golf Club (formerly Brynwood) temporary and permanent special use permits, both adopted 3-1, and two legal-services retainer agreements — the assignment of Roland Barone's firm to Abrams Fensterman and special counsel to fight a Greenwich CT development — which drew sharp transparency and standing objections. The board also handled a salt-dome grant application, a highway pickup-truck purchase, several personnel appointments, and routine consensus items.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting ran 5:30 PM (executive session) to about 10:15 PM. Councilman Saleem Hussain absent (celebrating his mother's 80th birthday; attempted but could not join by Zoom). Quorum of four present.

cases.name: Appointment of Police Officer Matthew Giannella
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Peter Simon)
cases.summary: Chief of Police Peter Simon presented Matthew Giannella, a six-year NYPD transfer with EMT and field-training credentials, as a candidate for police officer effective July 13, 2024. Chief Simon detailed the background investigation and panel interview and recommended appointment in light of an upcoming retirement and a resignation. The board approved the appointment unanimously by voice vote and the Supervisor administered the oath of office.
cases.publicComment: Officer's family present; celebratory tone, no formal public comment.

memberPositions.evidence: Called swearing in new officers 'one of the most enjoyable opportunities' of being supervisor and welcomed the officer's family.

cases.name: Westchester County Update — Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins
cases.applicant: Westchester County (Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins)
cases.summary: Deputy County Executive Ken Jenkins, standing in for County Executive George Latimer, gave a mid-year update covering sales-tax stabilization, a new civil-service role easing NYPD transfers, airport flight-path concerns, free Bee-Line transit for the summer, and the Route 22 crosswalk in North White Plains. Board members asked about sales-tax impacts on town revenue and pressed for county help on the crosswalk, Health Department pool-permit delays, and roadside invasive-species trimming on county roads. No action taken; the exchange was informational and cooperative.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked Jenkins to explain the sales-tax outlook and noted it also impacts the towns that share sales-tax revenue.
Urged the county to expedite the North White Plains Route 22 crosswalk, calling it 'very, very dangerous' for residents going to the community center and ball fields.
Thanked Jenkins for coming out and updating the board and for the partnership; had no questions.
Credited county HR cooperation, asked for Health Department help expediting upcoming water projects and pool inspections, and county help trimming invasive growth on county roads.

cases.name: Community Announcements — Passport Unit, Shredder, Summer Concerts
cases.applicant: Town Clerk / Town of North Castle
cases.summary: Town Clerk Allison Simon announced a county mobile passport renewal unit at Town Hall on August 28 and a mobile shredder event on September 17, both 10 AM-1 PM. She and board members also promoted the Armonk summer music concerts at the Gazebo and Music in the Square, and reminded residents to sign up for E-News and Nixle alerts. Informational only.

memberPositions.evidence: Announced the passport unit, shredder, and concert schedule and thanked the Clerk for arranging the county events.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Breezemont Day Camp (HZBR LLC)
cases.address: Breezemont Day Camp, Armonk (Cox Avenue / Rose Hill area)
cases.summary: The board opened and held a public hearing on Breezemont Day Camp's application for a special use permit to operate a summer day camp, made permissible under a recently adopted local law allowing day camps as a special use in residential districts. Town Planner Adam Kaufman explained the planning board gave a positive recommendation, with the applicant to update plans for required 15-foot perimeter screening and parking, and to limit the PA system/bullhorn to emergencies only (no amplified music). No public spoke in opposition; board members praised the camp and its historic-building preservation. The hearing was closed with adoption of the resolution deferred until updated plans are submitted, targeting the July 24 meeting.
cases.publicComment: Camp owner Gordon Josie and director Walter Kowalczyk spoke; supportive tone. A neighbor's letter (Bonnie) found children's play sounds 'delightful' but objected to the PA system, which the applicant agreed to limit to emergencies.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the camp has never presented a traffic or noise problem for him and that residents love it; effectively made a commercial for them.
Called Breezemont a cornerstone business and 'such a good member of the community.'
Glad the applicant agreed not to use the PA/bullhorn except in emergencies, citing the neighbor's letter; praised the camp as a wonderful business.
Praised the camp's historic-building designation and work, calling it a tremendous asset, and looked forward to wrapping up the permit.

cases.name: Landmark Designation — Armonk Barber Pole
cases.address: Main Street, Armonk (in front of Manny's)
cases.summary: Following a recommendation from the Landmark Preservation Committee, the board opened and held a public hearing to landmark the roughly 100-year-old Armonk Barber Pole (a Made-in-Chicago Koch No. 909), which the property-owning family enthusiastically supported. Board members discussed only the pole (not the building) and debated adding a future designation plaque, to be placed on the building with owner permission. The hearing was closed and the board unanimously adopted the landmark designation by voice vote.
cases.publicComment: LPC representative (Ed) presented history; family (Vivian Utko, Jerry Hendricks) supportive. No opposition.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it great to landmark, praised the actively involved family, and raised adding a designation plaque so future owners know it is protected.
As LPC liaison explained landmarking only affects a building's exterior and cited Breezemont as an easy, win-win partner.
Moved to establish the landmark designation 'with gratitude' to all parties involved.

cases.name: Temporary and Permanent Special Use Permits — Summit Golf Club (formerly Brynwood)
cases.address: Summit Golf Club (formerly Brynwood), off Evergreen
cases.summary: The board considered separate resolutions for a temporary special use permit (allowing public use of the golf course during residential construction, plus a proposed maintenance building) and a permanent special use permit for the Summit Golf Club.
