Presenters Marianne Hamilton (art committee) and Father Paul (church) are non-board and treated as public/staff input; student Zelda Topolski presented the history moment.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened after an executive session, then handled a light agenda dominated by community announcements and one substantive item. Former council member Matt Milim, now a private citizen with the Armonk Lions Club, presented a $15,000 check to the North Castle Police Department. The board formally received the Armonk Parking District map plan and report and directed the town attorney to prepare an order calling for a public hearing (targeting June), after an extended debate over cost allocation and included properties. The board also approved special counsel for the Con Edison rate-settlement consortium, a filming permit, several water/sewer and parks appointments, and a librarian step increase on which Councilman Berra abstained.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Berra, Vataj); no absences noted. DiGiacinto recused herself from the parking district item (Item B).

cases.name: Armonk Lions Club $15,000 Donation to North Castle Police Department
cases.applicant: Armonk Lions Club (Matt Milim, private citizen / former council member; Mike Roseman, treasurer)
cases.summary: The Armonk Lions Club, represented by former council member Matt Milim (now a private citizen) and treasurer Mike Roseman, presented a $15,000 check to the North Castle Police Department to help fund a replacement trailer, tied to the Lions Club's 50th Fol-de-Rol. Supervisor Rende suggested he and Councilwoman DiGiacinto (both Lions members) might need to recuse, but Town Attorney Roland advised there was no conflict in merely accepting a check and that the three-member exception applied. The board voted to accept the donation by voice vote (aye).
cases.publicComment: Matt Milim, appearing as a private citizen for the Armonk Lions Club, presented the donation and recounted the club's history of gifts (rescue boats, trailers, bridge restoration); warm, celebratory tone. Police Chief accepted with gratitude.

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked the Lions Club effusively, praised Milim for saving the Fol-de-Rol, but first raised whether he and Barbara should recuse as Lions members.
Questioned why members would have to recuse ('how is that a conflict... it's a receipt'); ultimately fine after counsel's advice.

cases.name: Armonk Parking District Map, Plan and Report (dated March 18, 2026) and EAF
cases.address: West side of Main Street, Armonk
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Town Planner Adam Kaufman; Town Attorney; Town Administrator; Comptroller)
cases.summary: The board considered receipt of the Armonk Parking District map, plan and report and Environmental Assessment Form for the west side of Main Street, and whether to direct the town attorney to prepare an order calling for a public hearing. Adam Kaufman explained the district would improve and manage parking, adding a net 65 spaces (including the Verizon lot), with the town paying roughly one-third of the cost based on assessed value including the library. Councilman Berra raised substantive concerns that the town's share was really closer to 60% (counting the 49 Verizon-lot spaces) and questioned which properties were included. The board voted to receive the map plan/report (aye) and separately voted to have the attorney prepare for the public hearing (aye), with the explicit understanding the terms could still be modified; a public hearing was targeted for the first meeting in June.
cases.publicComment: Dario Amicuchi (owner near 470 Main Street, across from Casa Tequila) asked whether the district could later be expanded to include his property; staff confirmed properties can petition to join by extension once the district is formed.

memberPositions.evidence: Strongly championed moving forward after 20+ years of discussion; defended the 33% share as reasonable and necessary to get property owners to buy in, comparing to putting the town's 'best foot forward' for grants.

Concerned the town is picking up too large a share (~60% counting Verizon's 49 spaces), questioned included properties like the gas station, and noted he only saw details when it hit the agenda; still favored advancing to public hearing.
Applauded the months of work and favored moving to the public hearing, but was open to more discussion on the cost structure if the board wanted it.
Recused herself from Item B because it pertains to property owned by the children of the late John DiGiacinto Sr.

cases.name: Resolution Authorizing Hiring of Joel R. Ditchner (Ditchner Law LLC) as Special Counsel — Con Edison Rate Settlement Monitoring
cases.applicant: Ditchner Law LLC (Joel R. Ditchner) / Westchester municipal consortium
cases.summary: The board considered a resolution to hire Joel R. Ditchner of Ditchner Law LLC as special counsel to represent North Castle, alongside other Westchester municipalities, in monitoring the Con Edison rate settlement over its three-year agreement. North Castle would be municipality 38 of an expected 40 in the consortium, at the same cost as the prior engagement. After brief questions about the added cost being for ongoing monitoring ('holding their feet to the fire'), the board approved it by voice vote (aye).

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether it was the same amount paid last time and noted he hadn't realized there'd be additional costs after the rate case, but accepted it made sense for monitoring.

cases.name: Filming Permit Application — Sweet Spot (web promotional video)
cases.summary: The board considered a filming permit application from Sweet Spot for a web promotional video on April 14, 2026 at 428 Main Street in Armonk. The motion included referring the application to staff, and it was confirmed staff had already reviewed it. Approved by voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Probationary Appointments — Water & Sewer and Parks & Recreation
cases.applicant: Water & Sewer Department; Parks & Recreation Department
cases.summary: The board approved a series of probationary appointments by voice vote: Brian Kidoff as skilled laborer in Water & Sewer (effective April 13), Leroy Crawley as skilled labor in Water & Sewer (effective April 27), Nicholas Champagne as skilled labor in Water & Sewer (effective April 27), and Jorge Hodaro as groundskeeper in Parks & Recreation (effective April 13). Each passed on a motion, second, and aye vote.

cases.name: Step Increase — Employee 003949, Librarian 1 Step 3 to Step 5
cases.summary: The board considered a step increase for employee 003949 from Librarian 1 Step 3 to Librarian 1 Step 5, effective April 1, 2026. After an initial voice vote, Councilman Berra sought a roll-call vote and the board moved to rescind and re-vote so he could abstain. On the roll call it passed 4-0 with Berra abstaining (DiGiacinto aye, Vataj aye, Hussain aye, Rende aye, Berra abstain). Berra said the employee was excellent but that he opposes mid-year compensation changes absent extraordinary circumstances; Supervisor Rende argued at length that speaking against an item and then abstaining is a misuse of the abstention.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the employee great but abstained on principle against mid-year compensation changes; requested the roll call and repeatedly asserted his right to abstain.
Voted aye and argued forcefully that Berra's speaking-against-then-abstaining is a misuse of the abstention and an abdication of an elected official's duty; offered to send supporting articles.
Voted aye on the roll call.
Voted aye on the roll call.
Voted aye on the roll call (ASR 'Councilman Bataj — aye').

cases.name: Approval of Town Board Minutes — March 25, 2026
cases.summary: The board approved the town board minutes from the March 25, 2026 meeting on a motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

cases.name: Consensus Agenda
cases.summary: The board approved the consensus agenda on a motion, second, and voice vote (aye). No individual items were discussed on the record.

themes.note: Armonk Parking District map/plan/report dominated the substantive discussion.
Extended Rende-Berra dispute over the proper use of abstentions and roll-call procedure.
Debate over the town's ~33% (Berra: ~60%) share of parking district cost; tax-payment reminder.
Multiple water/sewer and parks appointments plus a contested librarian step increase.
Lions Club donation, Fol-de-Rol, 250th celebration, 'Phone Down Enjoy the Town', 914Cares.
$15,000 Lions Club gift for a police trailer; recognition of building inspector Rob Melillo.

staffInput.summary: Reminded residents town taxes are due by Thursday, April 30, and to sign up for E-News and emergency alerts; called the roll on the librarian step increase.
Town Planner explained the Armonk Parking District background, the net 65-space gain, layout efficiencies, cost allocation by assessed value, and the extension/petition process for adding properties.

Advised no conflict in accepting the Lions Club check (three-member exception); guided public-hearing and roll-call/rescind procedure; confirmed special-district properties cannot easily be removed; opined that abstentions are permitted but should reflect lack of information, not opposition.
Consulted on the parking district cost/timeline background and the Rob Melillo heroism account; no separate report ('I have nothing').

meetings.attributionNote: Speakers were identifiable largely by role and by the named roll-call vote on the librarian step increase (DiGiacinto, Vataj [ASR 'Bataj'], Hussain [ASR 'Hussein'], Rende [ASR 'Rendezv'], Berra [ASR 'Barra'] abstaining). The presiding/supervisor voice is Joseph Rende; the member polled/abstaining is Jose Berra. Matt Milim ('Millam/Milam') appears only as a private citizen for the Lions Club and is kept in publicComment, not memberPositions, per the 2026 roster. DiGiacinto recused from the parking district item (surname ASR-mangled as 'digisono'). Full board present; no absences noted.

meetings.meetingSummary: After a brief executive session on board/committee interviews and legal advice, the Town Board opened with two police ceremonies (Detective Stephen Vitello's promotion to sergeant and John Gagan's appointment as police officer), followed by youth presentations on a Parks & Rec fishing-derby internship and the town's Revolutionary War 250th history, and a reminder about the 'Phone Down, Enjoy the Town' promotion. The board then held an extended, non-binding discussion on developing dedicated pickleball courts (favoring repurposing existing tennis courts over new sites, to be revisited at a work session) before adopting an order calling a June 10 public hearing on the long-discussed Armonk Parking District, amid renewed and sharper friction over the town's cost share (Councilman Berra argued it was now closer to 49-66% rather than one-third) and which West Main Street parcels are included. The board also referred a new special-use-permit application from Live Bow Corporation for a members-only cigar lounge/social club at 911 North Broadway to the planning boards and set a May 27 public hearing, approved $9,500 in additional funding for the Revolutionary War 250th celebration (with Supervisor Rende pledging a personal $500 donation), formally created a Building Maintenance Department, and approved a slate of contracts, appointments, and a Westchester Municipal Officials Association dinner-hosting agreement that passed 3-1 over Councilman Berra's objection to the cost.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present and participating (Rende presiding, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Berra, Vataj); no absences noted. Supervisor Rende raised, then dismissed, a possible recusal question on the Lions Club Fol de Rol item as a fellow Lions Club member, concluding no conflict existed.

cases.name: Police Department Promotion and Appointment — Sergeant Stephen Vitello; Officer John Gagan
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Regan Huff-Nagle)
cases.summary: Chief Regan Huff-Nagle recommended promoting Detective Stephen Vitello to the budgeted, vacant position of police sergeant effective April 23, 2026, citing his tenure since 2015, service as a school resource officer, and promotion to detective in 2024. The Chief separately recommended appointing John Gagan, a Mount Vernon police officer and former Westchester County seasonal park ranger, to police officer effective April 25, 2026, following a full background investigation and panel interview. The board approved both by voice vote and Supervisor Rende administered oaths of office to each, with family members present for photos.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided over both swearing-in ceremonies, invited Chief Huff-Nagle to present, and administered the oaths of office personally.

cases.name: Parks & Recreation Advisory Board Memo Supporting Development of Dedicated Pickleball Courts
cases.applicant: Parks & Recreation Advisory Board (Matt Trainor, Superintendent of Recreation and Parks; resident Peter Gold)
cases.summary: Matt Trainor presented a Parks & Recreation Advisory Board memo, backed by resident Peter Gold's research on regional pickleball trends, in support of exploring dedicated pickleball courts, with Winkler Park's aging tennis/basketball courts suggested as a pilot site since they need replacement regardless. Board members broadly supported the concept but diverged on siting and trade-offs: several favored converting or sharing existing tennis courts (Winkler, Community Park's platform-tennis courts, the pool-area tennis court) over building on new/passive parkland, with concerns raised about Wampus Brook Park South's proximity to the historic district, potential loss of tennis capacity, planning/conservation board review for any new site, and possible added parking near the Winkler Park senior center. No vote was taken; the board indicated it wants Trainor's site recommendation brought back for discussion at a future work session.
cases.publicComment: Steve Ross (Overlook Road, North White Plains) and resident Peter Gold both spoke strongly in favor, citing pickleball's rapid growth, its appeal across age groups, and its role in retaining older residents and supporting home values; Gold also noted that shared tennis/pickleball lines at Lombardi Park are unsatisfactory because tennis nets sit too high for pickleball play.

memberPositions.evidence: Called pickleball a positive step for the community, cited the town's history of investing in parks (Turffield, Corey Heights, dog park) and endorsed renovating the aging, under-used Winkler Park courts to accommodate it.

Praised the idea but raised a parallel proposal to convert part of Winkler Park into additional parking near the senior center and business district given existing congestion, addressed directly by name ('sunny that you brought like an idea here').
Noted he attended the advisory board meeting as liaison, disclosed he is a pickleball player, and asked what concrete steps and work-session process would be needed to move forward.

Explicitly cued to speak next ('Jose wanted to go first'); supported exploring pickleball but said Wampus Brook Park South was not appropriate given its historic-district border, favored repurposing existing tennis courts over new sites, and flagged planning/conservation board review as necessary for any new location.

Explicitly cued to speak last ('Barbara's last'); addressed directly by a public speaker about her tennis-court comments; supported dedicated courts but cautioned against removing tennis capacity, raised safety/noise concerns about siting pickleball next to tennis, and favored studying combined use of the Community Park platform-tennis courts and the pool-area tennis court.

cases.name: Order Calling for Public Hearing on the Armonk Parking District (West Side of Main Street)
cases.address: West side of Main Street, Armonk
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Town Planner Adam Kaufman)
cases.summary: The board voted to adopt an order calling for a public hearing on June 10, 2026 regarding formation of the Armonk Parking District. Discussion revisited the town's history of funding the Verizon-lot library parking, with Supervisor Rende arguing the town's prior investment and developer-funded community benefit agreements justify moving forward. Councilman Berra raised sharpened financial and equity concerns, calculating the town's effective cost share as high as roughly 49-66% (versus the ~33% previously cited) once the existing Verizon-lot investment is counted, questioned the 'hopscotch' inclusion of some parcels (including 12 Maple Avenue) and exclusion of others (like the Citibank parcel), and warned of possible overcrowding if off-street parking requirements are relaxed for participating properties. Councilman Vataj asked about adding the Citibank parcel and the process/cost of later modifying district membership. The board ultimately voted unanimously to set the June 10 hearing, with at least one member noting she still had serious concerns but would support the hearing notice itself since the terms remain modifiable afterward.
cases.publicComment: A representative of West Main Street property interests spoke in support during a portion of the discussion not fully captured in the transcript; no one else came forward when the floor was opened to other affected West Main Street property owners.

memberPositions.evidence: Gave an extended defense of the plan, recounting the town's $1.5M Verizon-lot investment made with 'no skin in the game' at the time, and argued it would be 'foolish' not to use developer community-benefit funds earmarked for parking/infrastructure to move forward.

Recalculated the town's share as roughly 49-66% including the prior Verizon-lot spend, questioned inclusion/exclusion of specific parcels including 12 Maple Avenue and the Citibank lot, and warned that relaxing off-street parking requirements could worsen downtown crowding; said he wants the town's percentage to go down, not up.
Called the area the commercial heart of town and said he was '100% looking forward' to moving to the public hearing so specific issues could be aired there.
Asked about employee-parking signage in the rear lot and specifically about the process, timing, and cost implications of adding the Citibank parcel to the district.
Indicated the vote was 'tricky' and that she still had serious concerns on balance, but supported moving to the public hearing to gather public input since the order does not lock in final terms.

cases.name: Special Use Permit Application — Live Bow Corporation Cigar Bar/Social Club
cases.summary: The applicant's attorney presented an early-stage special use permit application for a members-only cigar lounge and social club in two vacant former retail units (previously an Oriental market) in the Sir John's shopping plaza at 911 North Broadway. The proposed low-intensity, self-contained lounge would offer lounge/table seating, cigar and accessory sales to members and guests only (not the general public), light food and beverage, a conference room, and no live entertainment, exterior alterations, or amplified sound; membership would be tiered and priced later, with occupancy capped by fire code and required parking (one space per three members plus one per seat). Board members asked about vacant-store history, projected membership size, parking calculations, alcohol/membership structures, and state tobacco licensing requirements, with no objections raised. The board voted to receive the application, refer it to the town and county planning boards, and schedule a public hearing for May 27, 2026.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked detailed questions about the prior tenants of the vacant units, projected maximum membership, and the applicable parking ratio (one space per three members plus one per seat).
Asked directly about the membership fee structure, comparing it to membership-based liquor workarounds he recalled from Utah, and whether alcohol would be served.
Asked whether any additional state or town permitting beyond this application (e.g., a tobacco license) would be required, and confirmed there was no interdependency with the town process.

cases.name: Additional Funding Request — North Castle Revolutionary War 250th Steering Committee ($9,500)
cases.applicant: North Castle Revolutionary War 250th Steering Committee
cases.summary: The 250th Steering Committee, which has worked with confidential secretary Josephine Egan and the town administrator's office, requested an additional $9,500 (roughly $1,000 above already-incurred costs) to cover July 4th celebration expenses and printing/postage for a private-fundraising outreach effort, describing the added amount as a buffer for contingencies. Supervisor Rende noted the celebration has been registered with national/state semiquincentennial programs and pledged a personal $500 donation toward it. The board approved the request unanimously.

memberPositions.evidence: Pledged a personal $500 donation toward the July 4th event and praised the committee's work, noting outside registration of the celebration may draw unpredictable attendance.
Asked whether this was the final anticipated request and expenditure, seeking clarity on the budget before supporting it.

cases.name: R&A Ice Cream — Town Pool Concession Services Agreement (2026 Season)
cases.summary: The board approved an agreement with R&A Ice Cream to operate concession services at the town pool for the 2026 season and authorized the Supervisor to sign it, with Matt Trainor confirming there were no outstanding questions.

cases.name: North Castle Historical Society — Reimbursement Request for Whippoorwill Hall Event Costs ($202)
cases.applicant: North Castle Historical Society (Sharon Tomback, co-historian)
cases.summary: The board considered a $202 reimbursement request from the Historical Society for the sound/lighting technician's fee at an April 12, 2026 event ('the Andre/Arnold conspiracy' presentation) at Whippoorwill Hall. Councilman Berra said he supported the payment but wanted advance notice in the future that the town, rather than the Historical Society, would be covering that cost; Town Clerk Allison Simon and Supervisor Rende clarified the town customarily waives its own hall-use and beverage-license fees for the Society but this technician fee is a separate, outside cost, noting a similar cost was covered for a prior Society event about two years earlier. The board approved the reimbursement.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he had no problem with the payment itself but wanted the board notified in advance that it would be picking up the technician's cost rather than the Historical Society.
Recalled the town covering a similar technician cost roughly two years earlier for a prior Historical Society presentation and praised the quality of the recent event's Q&A.

cases.name: Payment Application No. 8 — Pappa Tillo Construction, Water District No. 4 Well Project
cases.summary: The board approved payment application number eight to Pappa Tillo Construction Company for site work on the Water District No. 4 well project. Supervisor Rende asked about the remaining/final billing status; Town Administrator Kevin confirmed roughly $21,000 remained, covered by the water district, with the work not yet complete.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the final bill on the project had come in yet, confirming roughly $21,000 remained on a project not yet complete.

cases.name: Funding Approval — Laserfiche Cloud Software Upgrade
cases.summary: The board approved funding to upgrade the town's Laserfiche cloud records software, a benefit-all-departments upgrade offered at a discount outside the normal budget cycle. Councilwoman DiGiacinto initially questioned why it wasn't budgeted for 2026, but after Town Clerk Allison Simon explained the vendor's off-cycle discount rationale, DiGiacinto made the motion to approve, and Councilman Berra confirmed it should aid productivity.

memberPositions.evidence: Initially pressed whether this was budgeted for 2026, then made the motion to approve after Town Clerk Simon explained the vendor's off-cycle discount.
Asked whether the upgrade would help town productivity and expressed support once confirmed.

cases.name: Armonk Lions Club Request to Hold the Fol de Rol at Wampus Brook Park
cases.summary: The board considered the Lions Club's annual request to hold the Fol de Rol at Wampus Brook Park. Supervisor Rende, a Lions Club member, weighed whether he should recuse but concluded there was no conflict since the club receives no town funds and pays none to the town. He also flagged, as he had the prior year, that some individuals had improperly and without authorization collected parking fees at town-owned lots (Wampus South and behind the firehouse) used for the event, stating firmly that no parking charges are permitted at any town park for any festival. The board approved the request, noting town staff support the event for cleanup and liability reasons.

memberPositions.evidence: Considered and dismissed recusing himself as a Lions Club member, then firmly reiterated that unauthorized parking fees collected at town lots during past Fol de Rols must not recur.

cases.name: Creation of a Building Maintenance Department; Transfer of Anthony Ruvo
cases.summary: The board formally created a Building Maintenance Department to codify a function (a lead maintenance mechanic and two maintenance mechanics reporting directly to the Town Administrator) that had already been operating successfully outside the Parks & Recreation Department. Town Administrator Kevin confirmed the change does not alter employee duties, which remain governed by civil-service titles and job descriptions, though the crew continues to assist with snow/storm response as part of its facilities-maintenance duties. The board separately approved the retroactive transfer of Anthony Ruvo, lead maintenance mechanic, into the new department effective January 24, 2025.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked how the new department affects employee duties and benefits, and whether staff could still be pulled to assist highway or parks departments during emergencies; satisfied by Kevin's explanation that duties remain governed by civil-service job descriptions.

cases.name: Authorization to Execute Consent Judgment — Towns Center LLC v. Town of North Castle
cases.summary: The board authorized the town attorney to execute a consent judgment resolving Towns Center LLC v. Town of North Castle (index number 65584/21), approved by voice vote without discussion on the record.

cases.name: Engineering Agreements — Cider Mill Sewer Maintenance/Replacement (KSCJ Consulting; Carlin Simpson Associates)
cases.applicant: KSCJ Consulting; Carlin Simpson Associates LLC
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign agreements with KSCJ Consulting for civil engineering services and Carlin Simpson Associates LLC for geotechnical/environmental engineering and subsurface soil and foundation investigation, both tied to the proposed removal and replacement of a sanitary sewer main near Cider Mill. Supervisor Rende noted he had confirmed with Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal that the work is necessary and covered by the sewer district.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed he had spoken with the water/sewer superintendent and that the engineering work, funded by the sewer district, is necessary.

cases.name: License Agreement with Westchester County — Fisher Lane Commuter Parking
cases.summary: The board approved a license agreement with Westchester County for Fisher Lane commuter parking covering April 1, 2026 through March 31, 2027, and authorized the Supervisor to sign it. Approved by voice vote without discussion.

cases.name: Consulting Agreement — Bonadio and Company LLP (GASB 87/96 Services for 2025 Audit)
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign an agreement with Bonadio and Company LLP for 2025 GASB 87 and GASB 96 professional consulting services related to the town's annual audit, approved by voice vote without discussion.

cases.name: Agreement to Host the Westchester Municipal Officials Association Dinner at Whippoorwill Club
cases.summary: The board considered authorizing the Supervisor to sign an agreement to host the Westchester Municipal Officials Association dinner on May 14, 2026 at the Whippoorwill Club, a hosting duty that rotates among member municipalities roughly every five to six years and last fell to North Castle in 2019. Councilman Berra objected that the roughly $120-per-person cost (once gratuity and service fees are added to a $90-95 base) was extravagant for elected officials to approve amid recent tax increases, prompting Supervisor Rende to explain that comparable neighboring towns (Rye Brook, Pound Ridge, Port Chester) had hosted at similarly priced country clubs or restaurants because the town lacks an in-house venue large enough for the roughly 70-80 attendees. The item passed 3-1 on a roll call vote, with Berra dissenting.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the roughly $120-per-person cost extravagant for elected officials to approve during a period of tax increases and voted no on the roll call.
Explained the rotating hosting obligation and comparable per-person costs at peer municipalities' recent events, framing the dinner as an opportunity to showcase the town to county officials.

cases.name: Parks & Recreation Appointments, Committee Reappointment, and Conference Travel Authorization
cases.applicant: Recreation and Parks Department; Receiver of Taxes; Landmarks Preservation Committee
cases.summary: The board approved a series of personnel and committee items by voice vote: promotion/appointment of Alexander Hayder to groundskeeper in Recreation and Parks effective May 6, 2026; appointment of Casey Ennis as gym attendant in Recreation and Parks effective April 12, 2026; appointment of Natalie Broden as an intern in Recreation and Parks from April 20 to June 20, 2026; the seasonal appointment of Joshua Feldman as junior clerk in Justice Court effective April 23, 2026; reappointment of Martin Rube to the Landmarks Preservation Committee for a two-year term expiring April 22, 2028; and authorization for Receiver of Taxes Patrick Ricky to attend a NYS Association of Tax Receivers and Collectors training seminar June 7-10, 2026, including reimbursement of a roughly $200 registration fee, meals, and gas/tolls, plus use of a town-owned vehicle.

themes.note: Armonk Parking District public hearing order dominated debate; a new Live Bow cigar lounge special use permit was also referred to a May 27 hearing.
Extended pickleball courts discussion, Fol de Rol parking issues, R&A Ice Cream concession, and staff updates on the turf field and Corey Heights Park.
Police promotion/appointment ceremonies, student presentations on a fishing derby internship and Revolutionary War 250th history, Phone Down Enjoy the Town, and the 250th celebration funding.
Parking district cost-share dispute and the 3-1 WMOA dinner vote were the sharpest points of financial friction.
Formal creation of a Building Maintenance Department and a slate of Parks & Rec appointments, an intern, and a committee reappointment.
Sergeant Vitello's promotion and Officer Gagan's appointment, plus a prescription drug take-back day announcement.
Water District No. 4 well project payment and Cider Mill sewer main engineering agreements.
Consent judgment in Towns Center LLC litigation and several routine service agreements.
Fisher Lane commuter parking license with Westchester County and the contested WMOA dinner-hosting obligation.

staffInput.summary: Presented detailed recommendations for Detective Stephen Vitello's promotion to sergeant and John Gagan's appointment as police officer, and answered a question about current department staffing numbers.

Presented the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board's pickleball courts memo and fielded siting questions, answered questions on the R&A Ice Cream pool concession agreement, and gave project updates on the turf field, Corey Heights Park, and pool renovation bid documents.

Explained the Armonk Parking District's rear-lot employee-parking concept, the process and cost implications of adding parcels like the Citibank lot, and the Map, Plan and Report's path through the state comptroller's office.

Explained the rationale and civil-service basis for formally creating a Building Maintenance Department, and gave community updates including a new grapple truck, a library board volunteer call, and pool-renovation bid document timing.
Gave the town-tax payment reminder, read the Historical Society's reimbursement request email into the record, and explained the Laserfiche cloud software upgrade's off-cycle vendor discount.

meetings.attributionNote: Major discussion items (pickleball, the Armonk Parking District, and the cigar lounge) were attributable with reasonable confidence through explicit sequencing cues ('Jose wanted to go first,' 'Barbara's last'), direct address ('Sunny, that you brought...'), and content self-references (e.g., Berra's cousin Charlie/Charlene), plus a roll-call vote for the WMOA dinner (garbled by ASR but consistent with Berra's stated objection). However, most routine contract/appointment items were passed via unattributed 'motion/second/aye' exchanges with no speaker labels, and several passages (e.g., a ~20-minute gap in the parking district public comment) appear to have transcription gaps, so confidence is only medium overall.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board convened after running long in executive session (boards/committees, personnel, and real estate matters) and moved through a lengthy agenda with only one public speaker. Resident Andrew Lester and several board members debated the merits and risks of a resident-mailed survey exploring a possible special assessment or real estate transfer tax to fund future open-space purchases, with speakers favoring the town's traditional bond-financing approach over a dedicated, board-discretionary fund; the board separately approved an agreement to develop evaluation criteria for the town's broader Community Conservation Plan. The board also received a police-chief memo proposing local law amendments to Chapter 325 governing a one-way street, no-parking zones, and off-street parking in North White Plains, and scheduled a public hearing for May 27, 2026. A long slate of routine but substantive items followed by voice vote, including a Westchester County health certificate resolution for summer camp, an RFP for auditing services, three KSCJ Consulting-related capital-project actions, an animal shelter contributions resolution, a special-event fee reduction, two charity cycling road-use permits, a slate of highway materials/services contracts, renewal of an NYC DEP land-use permit tied to a discussion of adding a crosswalk near the Old Route 22 lot, and several personnel actions (a new Recreation Supervisor, a Parks groundskeeper resignation, and a Landmark Preservation Committee reappointment). Liaison updates covered a new 'Blue Envelope' program for drivers with autism/special needs, 250th-anniversary bunting going up around town, the Community Park turf field's upcoming ribbon-cutting, and continued Quarry Heights Park construction, and the meeting closed with a moment of remembrance for two recently deceased community figures.
meetings.durationNote: Meeting opened late after running long in an executive session covering boards and committees, personnel, and real estate matters; the presiding Supervisor (inferred as Joseph Rende) apologized for the delay. Councilman Jose Berra and Councilwoman Barbara DiGiacinto are each identifiable by name at least once; Saleem Hussain and Sonny Vataj are not named anywhere in the transcript, though additional voices participate in discussion and unanimous voice votes, suggesting a full or near-full board was present. No recusals or absences are explicitly stated.

cases.name: Community Preservation Survey / Open Space Funding Mechanism (Public Comment)
cases.summary: Resident Andrew Lester spoke against a mailed survey (paid for by a conservation-affiliated organization, not the town) gauging support for a special assessment or real estate transfer tax of roughly 1.25%-1.5% to fund future open-space purchases, calling the survey's wording one-sided and warning the tax would be uncapped, non-transparent, and would depress home values and complicate sales. Councilman Jose Berra questioned Lester and confirmed he supported open space in principle but preferred a bond-financed approach tied to specific projects, as used historically (e.g., the former Erika Property, now the John Fava Preserve). Supervisor Rende clarified the survey was designed and funded by the Conservation Committee and a land-trust-affiliated firm, not the town board, that the board never saw the questions in advance, and that it cost the town nothing; other unidentified board members said they personally opposed a dedicated open-space fund that could let future boards buy land without the scrutiny a bond vote requires, while noting the town's strong balance sheet gives ample borrowing capacity if a genuine opportunity arose. No vote was taken; the matter remains at the survey/discussion stage.
cases.publicComment: Andrew Lester (resident) argued the proposed open-space special assessment/transfer tax was an unnecessary, uncapped, non-transparent burden that would fall on buyers and depress property values and marketability; he said he supported open-space goals but preferred a capped, voter-approved bond instead. He noted the survey cost the town nothing but felt the questions were leading and poorly designed.

memberPositions.evidence: Directly questioned Lester on whether he supported open space generally versus only opposing the tax mechanism, and referenced the town's past use of bond financing for open-space purchases.

As presiding officer, explained the survey was designed and funded independently of the town board and that the board never reviewed the questions in advance, while acknowledging he personally found the survey's repeated 'are you sure?' follow-ups poorly executed.

cases.name: Proposed Local Law Amending Town Code Chapter 325 — One-Way, No-Parking & Off-Street Parking Changes, North White Plains
cases.address: William Street, McClure Street and Old Orchard Street, North White Plains
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief Reagan Huffnagle) and Highway Department
cases.summary: The board received a memo from Police Chief Reagan Huffnagle proposing amendments to Town Code Chapter 325 (Vehicle and Traffic): changing the direction of travel on a one-way street, adding 'no parking any time' restrictions on portions of William Street, McClure Street and Old Orchard Street, and amending an off-street parking area, all in North White Plains. The board voted to receive the memo and separately voted to schedule a public hearing on the proposals for May 27, 2026. One member cautioned that not everyone in the affected area may support the changes and urged that the hearing be well publicized; another noted some of the proposals originated from area residents themselves rather than only the police and highway departments.

cases.name: Resolution Authorizing Supervisor to Sign Westchester County DOH Certificate — 2026 Summer Camp Applications

cases.name: Approval to Issue RFP for Auditing Services

Supervisor Rende asked for a brief explanation, and it was clarified the RFP was a routine competitive check ('sharpening the pencils') to gauge market interest and confirm the town is getting the best price, not a sign of dissatisfaction with the incumbent auditor. Approved by voice vote (aye).

memberPositions.evidence: Asked for an explanation of the purpose of issuing the RFP before voting in favor.

cases.applicant: KSCJ Consulting (town engineering consultant); Aqua Works Incorporated; 111 Round Hill Realty LLC
cases.summary: On KSCJ Consulting's recommendation, the board approved three unrelated capital/land-use bond matters by separate voice votes without discussion: (1) establishing a five-year wetland mitigation monitoring and maintenance bond for the Shapiro Residence project (exact address unclear in the recording); (2) final payment (Application No. 2) to Aqua Works Incorporated for the School Street watermain extension, together with receipt of a general release and a one-year guarantee bond; and (3) a reduction of the construction performance bond for the common driveway serving the 111 Round Hill Realty LLC Rolling Hill subdivision at 10 and 20 Round Hill Road. cases.name: Fee Schedule Amendment — Special Event Application Fee Reduced from $250 to $50
cases.summary: The board approved a modification to the Master Fee Schedule reducing the special event application fee from $250 to $50. Supervisor Rende thanked Town Clerk Allison Simon for bringing the change forward, calling it 'a wise choice.' Approved on motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

memberPositions.evidence: Thanked Town Clerk Allison Simon for bringing the fee reduction to the board's attention and called it a wise choice.

cases.name: Renewal of NYC DEP Land Use Permit (Old Route 22) and Crosswalk Safety Discussion
cases.address: Old Route 22 (NYC DEP-owned parking lot across from Beehive), North Castle
cases.applicant: NYC Department of Environmental Protection (permit); North Castle Police Department
cases.summary: The board approved a five-year confirmation and renewal of NYC Department of Environmental Protection land-use permit conditions for the DEP-owned parking lot on Old Route 22. Councilman Jose Berra raised a long-standing need for a marked crosswalk near the lot (across from Beehive), noting the permit affirmatively allows the town to make safety modifications, that he had discussed it with Police Chief Reagan Huffnagle (who was supportive) and previously with former Chief Simonson, and that Town Planner Adam Kaufman had already researched the issue and had a pending grant request to the county. The board discussed the likely modest cost of a required traffic-engineering siting study plus curb/ADA-ramp and paint work, and directed staff to obtain a cost estimate so the board could decide whether to proceed immediately or wait on the grant. The DEP permit renewal itself passed on motion, second, and voice vote (aye).

memberPositions.evidence: Raised the need for a crosswalk near the DEP lot across from Beehive, reported that Police Chief Huffnagle confirmed the town has authority under the permit to make safety changes, and pushed for a cost estimate and engineering study regardless of grant timing.

cases.name: Agreement — Preparation of Evaluation Criteria for the Town Community Conservation Plan

This item followed the earlier public-comment discussion of the conservation survey and potential open-space funding mechanism, though it is a separate scope-of-work contract rather than a funding decision. meetings.meetingSummary: The Town Board opened at 5:30pm with an executive session on board/committee appointments and personnel, then reconvened for an extended work session on adding dedicated pickleball courts at Lombardi Park, drawing many residents and lengthy board debate over siting, noise, cost, and phasing. After the pledge of allegiance (delayed from the start), a student's history presentation, and public comment (including a resident raising a pending Article 78 lawsuit over a 12 Bedford Road site plan), the board accepted the town's 2025 audited financial statements (a clean opinion and a GFOA award), then held two public hearings: a special use permit for a Live Bow Corporation cigar bar and social club at 911 North Broadway (approved with a 150-member cap and a ban on hookah/marijuana after real debate, including an executive-session recess), and a local law amending one-way, no-parking, and off-street-parking rules on William and McClure Streets in the Corey (Quarry) Heights neighborhood near a recently renovated park (approved, tied to police-identified safety concerns). Residents from Quarry Heights used both the parking hearing and a later water-infrastructure item to press the board hard about a long-running PFAS-contaminated well/water crisis, the cost and process behind a new neighborhood basketball court, and the town's efforts to compel DEC/Westchester Joint Water Works action; the board approved hiring AI Engineers to prepare bid specifications for a municipal water line hookup to eight Quarry Heights homes. The board also approved an Eagle Ridge subdivision performance bond/inspection fee recommendation (with one member recusing over an IBM employment conflict), turf field project closeout items, tabled a costly crosswalk-study proposal for old Route 22 in favor of an in-house safety review, and approved several library and town clerk personnel actions.
meetings.durationNote: The full board (Rende, DiGiacinto, Hussain, Berra, Vataj) appears to have been present; the transcript's ASR provides almost no speaker labels, so individual attendance and participation could not be confirmed member-by-member. One unidentified board member recused from the Eagle Ridge subdivision bond/inspection-fee item, citing employment with IBM. No other recusals or absences were stated.

cases.name: Work Session: Dedicated Pickleball Courts at Lombardi Park
cases.address: Lombardi Park (near Anthony Court), North Castle
cases.applicant: Parks & Recreation Department / Parks and Recreation Advisory Board
cases.summary: Recreation Superintendent Matt Traynor and Town Engineer Joe Tramelli (Kellard Sessions) presented concept plans, developed from a 2023 ballfield-improvement study, to add four dedicated pickleball courts, a small maintenance building with ADA-compliant bathrooms, and additional parking at Lombardi Park, at a rough estimated cost of $300,000 for courts alone (or up to $1.4 million if ~70 new parking spaces were added) and roughly $800,000 for the maintenance building. The board and many residents debated alternative sites (Winkler Park, Wampus Park South/Mompus, IBM's paddle courts), noise impacts on Anthony Court and Winkler-area homes, whether to build in phases, and whether to fund the project from the town's recreation trust fund (roughly $582,000-$600,000, generated by developer fees, not tax dollars). No vote was taken; the board directed staff to develop firmer cost estimates and consider alternative locations for the displaced storage containers, with a future work session or meeting agenda item to follow.
cases.publicComment: Numerous residents spoke, nearly all supportive of pickleball courts generally: Steve Ross urged phased construction and use of a rubberized (not asphalt) surface and grant funding; a self-described frequent player argued Lombardi is the best site and that sound mitigation (fencing/plantings) can offset noise; Bonnie Toddman (on behalf of the Parks & Rec Advisory Board consensus) suggested pairing Lombardi with resurfacing at Winkler for two more courts; Patrice, an Anthony Court resident, asked whether sound mitigation was planned given proximity to her home; Carl Henrik, chair of the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board, confirmed the board's unanimous support for pickleball in concept.

memberPositions.evidence: As presiding officer, argued Lombardi Park is the right location, emphasized the project would be funded from the non-tax recreation trust fund, criticized the town's historical failure to maintain Winkler Park and its platform tennis courts, and framed investment in recreation amenities as important to quality of life and to winning grants, while cautioning the board should still study costs fully before committing to the maintenance building or added parking.

Opposed siting pickleball at Wampus Park South (Mompus), citing its historic-district and residential-gateway location, lack of parking, and floodplain constraints (recalling a similarly rejected dog-park proposal there); separately warned that the ~$600,000 recreation fund would be consumed quickly once courts, screening, and other pending park needs (playgrounds, Winkler resurfacing) are counted.
Raised Wampus Park South as a possible alternative site for standalone pickleball courts, which town engineering staff and Councilwoman DiGiacinto both discouraged due to site sensitivities.

cases.name: Receipt of 2025 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and Auditor's Letter (Bonadio Group)
cases.summary: Michael Connolly of the Bonadio Group presented the town's fiscal year 2025 financial statement audit, reporting an unmodified (clean) opinion consistent with the prior year and noting no significant new accounting standards this cycle. The board thanked Comptroller Abbas, Town Administrator Kevin, and department heads, and highlighted that the town again received a GFOA Certificate of Achievement for Excellence in Financial Reporting. The board voted to accept both the audit report and the required year-end communication letter.

memberPositions.evidence: Highlighted the GFOA Certificate of Achievement and credited the comptroller, town administrator, and department heads for disciplined budgeting that supports the town's bond rating.
When addressed by name, thanked staff for their hard work making the audit process efficient.

cases.name: Resident Correspondence Regarding 12 Bedford Road Litigation and Site Plan Process
cases.summary: During public comment, co-historian Sharon Tanback sought to raise concerns about the town's site-plan review process for a property at 12 Bedford Road that is now the subject of pending Article 78 litigation. Town Attorney Roland cautioned the board against engaging in any discussion or debate on the matter while litigation is pending, and the Supervisor agreed it would be prudent not to discuss it; Tanback agreed to instead submit her process concerns in a letter to the Supervisor, full board, and town attorney rather than raise them verbally.
cases.publicComment: Sharon Tanback, speaking as town co-historian, asked to read into the record concerns about the site-plan process for 12 Bedford Road but was asked to instead submit a letter given the pending Article 78 proceeding; she agreed to do so.

memberPositions.evidence: Deferred to the town attorney's advice and told the speaker he did not think it prudent to discuss the matter at the meeting given pending litigation, but welcomed a written letter on process going forward.

cases.name: Special Use Permit — Live Bow Corporation Cigar Bar and Social/Life Members Club
cases.applicant: Live Bow Corporation (represented by attorney James)
cases.summary: The board held a continued public hearing on a special use permit for a members-only cigar bar and social club in a former bakery space (18 on-site parking spaces, 50-person occupancy). Extensive debate centered on whether to cap total club membership: the applicant's attorney argued strongly against any numeric membership cap as an overreach and inconsistent with how other membership clubs (gyms, country clubs) are regulated, while board members favored a cap to preserve control over intensity of use. After a closed-door recess, the board settled on a 150-member cap (with the ability for the applicant to return and request an increase), added a condition specifically permitting cigar/cigarette smoking while excluding hookah and marijuana use (per the applicant's own proposal), and closed the hearing before adopting the special use permit resolution as amended.
cases.publicComment: Nico Marino questioned why the club should face a membership restriction when the 24-hour gym next door faces none; Pat Samma raised concerns about hours of operation and noise given proximity to Sir John's Plaza (applicant confirmed indoor-only operation, no live music, closing around midnight).

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed back on imposing a rigid membership cap as arbitrary compared to other clubs, but ultimately helped broker the compromise 150-member limit and voted to adopt the amended resolution after a closed-session recess.
When asked directly for his view, indicated he favored including a maximum membership figure (initially discussing around 100) rather than leaving it unrestricted.

cases.name: Local Law Amending Town Code Chapter 325 (Vehicle & Traffic) — One-Way Streets, No-Parking, and Off-Street Parking on William Street, McClure Street, and Old Orchard Street, North White Plains
cases.address: William Street, McClure Street, and Old Orchard Street, North White Plains (Corey/Quarry Heights)
cases.applicant: North Castle Police Department (Chief) / Highway Department
cases.summary: Following renovation of the Corey (Quarry) Heights park (including a new basketball court), the police chief and highway foreman recommended making William Street one-way southbound from James Street to Old Orchard Street and prohibiting parking on William and McClure Streets, citing dangerously narrow (13-14 foot) roadway widths that block emergency vehicle access. Several Quarry Heights residents objected strongly, tying the proposal to broader frustration over the town's handling of the park project and an unresolved multi-year PFAS well-water contamination crisis in the neighborhood; other residents supported the safety rationale, citing a documented ambulance-access delay. The board adopted the local law by voice vote, while directing police/highway staff to reconsider the proposed no-parking restriction on the single block of Old Orchard Street as potentially counterproductive.
cases.publicComment: Nico Marino and Fred Gisman (William Street residents) offered competing views — Marino objected that the town was disrupting a self-policing, close-knit street and tied the parking law to broader grievances (unresolved water crisis, cost/process of the new basketball court); Gisman supported the one-way and no-parking changes on safety grounds, citing a documented ambulance-access delay, while questioning the need for restrictions on Old Orchard Street. Martha Rosen (17 William Street) raised concern that the proposed left turn from McClure onto Old Orchard could be more dangerous than the status quo.

memberPositions.evidence: Said she would vote in favor for safety reasons given the narrow roadway, but urged the police department to gather more resident input and reconsider the no-parking restriction on the single block of Old Orchard Street as potentially counterproductive.

Defended the recommendation as driven purely by professional police/highway safety judgment rather than the park project, thanked the chief, highway foreman, and town engineer, and pushed back on a resident's suggestion that the board had ignored the neighborhood's concerns.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge Subdivision — Performance Bond and Inspection Fee (Reed/Rede North Castle Drive, Armonk)
cases.address: Reed North Castle Drive, Armonk (Eagle Ridge subdivision)
cases.applicant: Eagle Ridge (developer); recommendation from Town Engineer (KSCE/Kellard Sessions)
cases.summary: The board approved a town engineer's recommendation to establish the subdivision performance bond and subdivision inspection fee for the Eagle Ridge development. One board member recused, citing employment with IBM given the property's past association with IBM interests; the item passed by voice vote with no substantive discussion.

cases.name: North Castle Community Park Turf Field — Certificate of Final Completion and Payment Requisition No. 2 (Shaw Sports Turf)
cases.applicant: Shaw Sports Turf / Shaw Integrated Turf Solutions Inc.
cases.summary: The board authorized the Supervisor to sign a certificate of final completion for the turf field installation (completed May 1) and approved payment requisition No. 2 to the contractor, with a contractual retainage and one-year bond still held by the contractor. Board members praised the finished field and the cooperative-purchasing approach used to select the contractor, noting the same contractor and process would likely be used for the pickleball courts.
cases.publicComment: Kent Little League representatives thanked the board and Parks Department for the completed turf field renovation, urged a strong ongoing maintenance program, and offered to help coordinate field upkeep going forward.

cases.name: Proposed Crosswalk Evaluation and Design (Old Route 22, near DEC lot/Beehive)
cases.summary: The board considered a roughly $9,500 two-phase proposal (about $3,000 for a traffic study, $6,500 for design) to evaluate and design a pedestrian crosswalk across old Route 22 near a leased DEC parking lot and a restaurant, citing a handful of past traffic incidents in the vicinity. Several board members argued the expense was unnecessary for a straightforward crosswalk on a demapped town road and that town staff (highway foreman, police lieutenant, town planner) could assess and implement it directly. The board tabled the proposal so staff could evaluate it in-house first, with the understanding that an outside engineering study would still be pursued if staff determined it necessary.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the $9,000+ engineering fee for a simple crosswalk an unnecessary expense on a demapped town road and pushed to have highway/police staff evaluate and implement it directly, tabling the outside proposal pending that review.

cases.name: Water Service Connection Bid Specifications — William and James Streets (Quarry/Corey Heights)
cases.address: William Street and James Street, North White Plains (Corey/Quarry Heights)
cases.applicant: AI Engineers (proposal); Town Water & Sewer Department
cases.summary: The board approved hiring AI Engineers (fee negotiated down from roughly $200,000 to $90,000) to prepare bid specifications for extending municipal water service from an existing main to eight Quarry Heights homes affected by long-standing well contamination, with homeowners responsible for interior plumbing hookup costs. Water/Sewer Superintendent Sal detailed a multi-year fight with the state DEC and Westchester Joint Water Works over funding, describing DEC's refusal to fund hookups (unlike a prior, fully DEC-funded extension on Wampus Avenue) pending determination of a PFAS contamination source, and the town's use of subpoenas and court intervention (alongside the town attorney) to press the issue. Residents pressed for a future meeting with DEC/investigation officials to get direct answers.
cases.publicComment: A Quarry Heights resident (11 William Street, self-identified as directly affected) detailed a five-year DEC investigation into PFAS contamination potentially linked to a Harrison fire station on Park Lane, described the town and Westchester Joint Water Works' advocacy including a court appearance and subpoena of DEC, and asked the board to arrange a future meeting with DEC/state investigators to answer residents' questions directly.

memberPositions.evidence: Described personally attending a court proceeding with the town attorney to insist on a seat at the table in the Rocky Ledge landfill litigation and pushing DEC to fund hookups the way it had on Wampus Avenue; supported moving forward with the AI Engineers bid specifications for the eight affected homes.
Made the motion to approve the AI Engineers proposal (seconded by Councilwoman DiGiacinto).
Seconded the motion to approve the AI Engineers water-line bid specification proposal.

cases.name: Public Hearing and Adoption of Preliminary Resolutions Establishing Armonk Parking District No. 2
cases.address: West side of Main Street, Armonk
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Town Planner Adam Kaufman; Town Attorney; Town Administrator; Comptroller)
cases.summary: The board held the public hearing on establishing Armonk Parking District No. 2 to fund, manage, and regulate the public parking area behind the west side of Main Street, with the district members' assessed-value-based share supplemented by the town's contribution (tied to the library's parking demand). Public comment was extensive and mixed: the library board president (personal capacity) supported it but asked for traffic calming; a North White Plains resident opposed it as an inequitable taxpayer subsidy of Armonk businesses; a restaurant investor at 12 Maple Avenue criticized decades of delay and a community-benefits-agreement (CBA) obligation now in limbo after his site plan approval lapsed; an attorney for the DiGiacinto family properties and the 12 Maple Avenue owner spoke in support; and another resident said misinformation emails had caused confusion. After a lengthy, at times heated exchange between Supervisor Rende and Councilman Berra over the town's true cost share and an email Rende called "misinformation," the board closed the hearing and adopted, by 3-1 roll-call votes (Vataj, Hussain, and Rende in favor; Berra opposed; DiGiacinto recused), a SEQRA negative declaration, a resolution making certain determinations, and a preliminary resolution approving establishment of the district. The matter now proceeds to the state comptroller for final approval, expected to take several months.
cases.publicComment: Dean Rosetti (library board of trustees president, personal capacity) thanked the board and supported the district but asked for traffic-calming measures given poor road conditions behind the library. Betty Santorico (North White Plains) opposed the district as an inequitable taxpayer subsidy of Armonk businesses, contrasting it with a long-delayed North White Plains water-system replacement. Stefan (a 12 Maple Avenue-area restaurant investor who paid a $100,000 CBA impact fee) criticized decades of inaction and outdated parking regulations, and questioned why the district still isn't law; Town Planner Adam Kaufman agreed off-street parking rules are outdated for a hamlet setting. Corey Salomon (attorney for the DiGiacinto family properties) supported the district, explained that community-benefit-agreement funds (~$3.5 million) can offset the town's share, and argued the current parking district vacuum keeps storefronts vacant. Sue Miller (resident) said misinformation emails had confused otherwise-supportive neighbors and asked for the facts to be made clear. Randy, the owner of 12 Maple Avenue, confirmed he remains committed to joining the district regardless of his tenant's uncertain restaurant plans.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided over the hearing, gave an extensive history of parking studies dating to 1967, forcefully rebutted a resident email he called "misinformation" about the cost calculations, and voted yes on all three roll-call resolutions.

Gave five reasons for moving forward (the town currently lacks authority to manage the space, the issue has been studied since 1967, the town's ~$1.2M Verizon-lot investment is underused without the district, property owners gain a well-maintained space, and the spending is about management rather than adding spaces); voted aye on the roll calls and was later thanked by name ("Salim") by Rende for making these points.

Argued the town's true cost share was closer to 60-70% once the Verizon lot expense is counted, raised downtown-congestion concerns, questioned whether the CBA obligation tied to 12 Maple Avenue's now-expired site plan was still enforceable, and voted no on all three roll-call resolutions while saying he still favors a parking district done "in a more appropriate way."

Described himself as one of the youngest, newest councilmen (the matter having first come before him in early April), acknowledged past missteps and the expense involved, urged residents to trust the process and "move forward," and voted aye on the roll-call resolutions.

Read a formal recusal into the record before the hearing began, citing that the children of her late father-in-law own property on the west side of Main Street, and did not participate in discussion or voting on the item.

meetings.meetingSummary: This was a special Town Board meeting convened solely to receive the report of the volunteer Town Hall Campus Advisory Task Force, chaired by resident Alan Blum, on options for rebuilding the Town Hall/Highway Department municipal campus. Task force members (recently retired architect Rich Rosen, designer Susan Geffen, HR specialist Diana Barra, finance/construction advisor George DePue, and Town Planner Adam Kaufman) presented findings from a roughly three-month, department-by-department needs assessment, arriving at about 80,000 gross square feet of new construction and a rough order-of-magnitude cost near $85 million, to be funded eventually by a voter referendum on a municipal bond. The presentation stressed serious deficiencies on the 10-plus-acre campus — chronic flooding and a new mold problem in the Highway garage, equipment repaired outdoors in winter, no secure prisoner processing or ADA compliance in the police department and courtroom, and a failing, dry-rotted Birdsall House — and proposed keeping all existing buildings operating during construction, later demolishing Birdsall House, and preserving a historic-district-appropriate facade facing Main Street/Bedford Road. An extended public question-and-answer period followed with roughly a dozen residents; most urged the town to move forward given decades of delay (prior studies in 1980 and 2007) and documented safety and maintenance failures, while several pressed on the cost relative to the town's roughly 5,100 taxpayers, the fate of the historic Birdsall House and the former Cornell-Bezel firehouse, floodplain/wetlands and rising-water-table concerns, and whether cheaper alternative sites (333 Main Street, the American Legion Hall, an IBM-park warehouse) had been considered. Supervisor Joseph Rende closed the meeting thanking the task force, correcting the historical record on the two prior studies, citing PESH (public-sector OSHA) violations affecting highway and parks workers as further urgency, and pledging to pursue the most cost-effective path forward; no vote or resolution was taken beyond the procedural motions to open and adjourn the meeting.

cases.name: Town Hall Campus Advisory Task Force — Master Plan Presentation and Public Forum
cases.address: Town Hall municipal campus, Bedford Road, Armonk (approx. 10.5-acre site including current Town Hall/Village Hall, Highway Department, and the Birdsall House)
cases.applicant: Town Hall Campus Advisory Task Force (Alan Blum, chair; Rich Rosen, architect; Susan Geffen, designer; Diana Barra; George DePue; Adam Kaufman, Town Planner)
cases.summary: The all-volunteer Town Hall Campus Advisory Task Force presented the results of a roughly three-month needs assessment of every town department, including site visits to comparable facilities in Westchester and Rockland counties, and unveiled conceptual space-relationship diagrams (not building designs) totaling about 80,000 gross square feet — roughly 46,000 sq ft for Village Hall functions and 15,000+ sq ft for the Highway Department plus new vehicle storage. The committee estimated an approximately $85 million rough-order-of-magnitude cost driven partly by New York's Wicks Law construction-bidding requirements, corrected several inaccurate figures circulating from an earlier presentation (school contribution, town budget, and reserve fund amounts), and proposed a phased build-out that keeps existing buildings operating throughout construction before demolishing the deteriorated Birdsall House. No town board vote or resolution occurred; the board's role going forward is to decide on financing (a municipal bond subject to public referendum), phasing, and hiring a professional engineer, architect, and construction manager. Supervisor Rende closed the meeting endorsing the urgency of the project and citing PESH (public-sector OSHA) violations — lack of decontamination/shower and rest facilities for highway and parks crews — as an additional driver.
cases.publicComment: Public comment was extensive (roughly a dozen speakers) and dominated the meeting. Most speakers were supportive of urgency: a resident named Robin Rosenthal asked about timeline/cost/construction impact; a self-described real-estate-background resident praised the task force's efficiency, cited a 2007 precursor study, and described firsthand observations of a raw-sewage leak in the police locker room and a failing 1960s-era gasoline pump keeping the flooding basement (and 911 dispatch equipment) dry, calling the situation "an honest-to-goodness emergency"; Mary Ann Hamilton asked what happens if the town does nothing, prompting the task force to recount anecdotes of illegal same-room prisoner processing, a judge encountering a litigant in a shared restroom, and costly downtime on a storm-drain vacuum truck stored outdoors. Several speakers raised cost and preservation concerns: Larry Ruzzi (a Planning Board member speaking as a private citizen and former town budget/finance committee member) called the roughly $85 million estimate "significant" against about 5,100 taxpayers and urged a more cost-effective approach; Judge Schimer argued the historic, IBM-donated Cornell-Bezel building and the Birdsall House (a former firehouse) carried an obligation to consider adaptive reuse rather than demolition, which the task force rejected as not cost-effective given the buildings' condition; a following resident pressed to personally inspect the Birdsall House's rafters before accepting the "unrepairable" characterization. Other residents (Carol/Karen Hoffman, an unnamed woman, "Ed," Michael Ackerman, and a resident referred to as "Brad") asked about rising water tables/climate resilience, project oversight and accountability, bonding strategy (single bond vs. phased tranches), whether existing or alternative buildings (333 Main Street, the American Legion Hall, an IBM-park warehouse) could be retrofitted more cheaply, and future maintenance-cost tradeoffs versus the current facilities; task force members (Alan Blum, Rich Rosen, and Susan Geffen) responded that alternative sites had been ruled out as impractical or unavailable, that renewable-energy grants (NYSERDA, court-system grants) could offset costs, and that a professional design team would refine both scope and price.

memberPositions.evidence: As presiding Supervisor, thanked the task force at length, corrected the historical record (town hall studies in 1980 and 2007), cited PESH (public-sector OSHA) violations — no decontamination showers or rest facilities for highway/parks crews — as an urgent, previously under-recognized problem, and pledged to pursue the most cost-effective path to get the project done, while cautioning residents to "keep an open mind" about how it is accomplished.

Not present as a speaker; Supervisor Rende stated in his closing remarks that "Barbara over the years has been very focused on" the Highway Department's serious condition, indicating a longstanding, board-level concern attributed to her secondhand rather than in her own words.

themes.note: The entire meeting was devoted to the Town Hall Campus Advisory Task Force's master-plan findings and cost estimate (~$85 million, ~80,000 sq ft) for rebuilding the municipal campus.
Heavy resident focus on the ~$85M estimate against ~5,100 taxpayers, Wicks Law cost drivers, bonding/phasing strategy, and future operating/maintenance costs.
Highway Department flooding, mold, and outdoor vehicle/equipment storage repeatedly cited as the most urgent driver of the project.
Illegal same-room prisoner processing, courtroom security gaps, and PESH/OSHA-type violations for highway and parks staff were raised as safety failures of the current campus.
Debate over the historic district facade, the fate of the landmarked/IBM-donated Birdsall House and Cornell-Bezel building, and expedited municipal zoning review.
Wetlands/floodplain constraints behind Birdsall House, rising water table under climate change, and proposed solar/geothermal and stormwater mitigation measures.
